unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Ear, Nose and Throat
question: Mr. X, a 55-year-old man, has noticed hearing difficulty in both ears and has come for ENT consultation. (a) Define deafness. (2 marks) (b) List the aetiological factors of deafness. (4 marks) (c) Compare Weber's and Rinne's tests. (4 marks) (d) Prepare a health education plan for a patient prescribed hearing aids. (5 marks)

diagram.caption: Tuning fork tests – Rinne and Weber
labels: Rinne – vibrating 512 Hz fork on mastoid (bone conduction) then near the ear canal (air conduction); Weber – fork on the vertex/forehead with sound lateralising to the affected ear in conductive loss and to the better ear in sensorineural loss

answer_html:
(a) Definition of deafness (2 marks) Deafness (hearing loss) is the partial or complete inability to hear sounds in one or both ears. The WHO considers hearing loss present when the hearing threshold is worse than 20 dB in the better ear; hearing loss of 35 dB or more in the better ear is "disabling".

WHO grades (better ear): mild 20–34 dB, moderate 35–49 dB, moderately severe 50–64 dB, severe 65–79 dB, profound 80–94 dB, complete 95 dB or more.

Types

  • Conductive – sound cannot reach the inner ear (external or middle-ear problem).
  • Sensorineural (SNHL) – damage to the cochlea or auditory nerve.
  • Mixed – both components.
  • Central – lesion of auditory pathways in the brain.

India runs the National Programme for Prevention and Control of Deafness (NPPCD) to prevent, detect early and rehabilitate hearing loss.

(b) Aetiological factors of deafness (4 marks) 1. Causes of conductive deafness

  • External ear – impacted wax, foreign body, otitis externa, congenital atresia of the canal.
  • Middle ear – acute and chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM), otitis media with effusion (glue ear), tympanic membrane perforation, otosclerosis (fixation of stapes), ossicular disruption after head injury, Eustachian tube block, barotrauma, tumours.

2. Causes of sensorineural deafness

  • Presbycusis (age-related hearing loss) – the most likely cause in a 55-year-old with gradual bilateral loss; begins with high frequencies.
  • Noise-induced hearing loss – factories, construction, loud music, firecrackers, firearms.
  • Ototoxic drugs – aminoglycosides (streptomycin, gentamicin, amikacin), loop diuretics, cisplatin, quinine, high-dose salicylates.
  • Infections – mumps, measles, meningitis, congenital rubella and CMV, syphilis, herpes zoster oticus.
  • Ménière's disease, labyrinthitis, sudden SNHL (viral/vascular).
  • Systemic diseases – diabetes, hypertension, hypothyroidism, kidney failure, autoimmune diseases.
  • Head injury (fracture of temporal bone), acoustic neuroma.
  • Genetic/hereditary causes.

3. Causes in children (congenital/early)

  • Prenatal – rubella, CMV, ototoxic drugs in pregnancy, genetic syndromes, consanguinity.
  • Perinatal – prematurity, low birth weight, birth asphyxia, severe neonatal jaundice.
  • Postnatal – meningitis, measles, mumps, recurrent otitis media.

(c) Comparison of Weber's and Rinne's tests (4 marks) Both use a 512 Hz tuning fork. | Feature | Rinne test | Weber test | |---|---|---| | Purpose | Compares air conduction (AC) with bone conduction (BC) in the same ear | Compares bone conduction of the two ears (lateralisation) | | Procedure | Vibrating fork placed on the mastoid process; when the patient stops hearing it, the prongs are held 2–3 cm from the ear canal and the patient says whether it is still heard (or loudness is compared) | Vibrating fork placed on the vertex, forehead or upper incisors in the midline; patient says where the sound is heard | | Normal hearing | AC > BC – "Rinne positive" | Heard in the middle/equally in both ears | | Conductive deafness | BC > AC – "Rinne negative" in the affected ear | Sound lateralised to the affected (worse) ear | | Sensorineural deafness | AC > BC (positive), but both reduced | Sound lateralised to the better (normal) ear | | Caution | False negative Rinne in severe unilateral SNHL (sound heard by the other ear through bone) | Not useful when both ears are equally affected | - Absolute bone conduction (ABC) test – patient's BC compared with the examiner's; reduced in SNHL. - Results are confirmed by pure-tone audiometry, tympanometry and, when needed, BERA.

(d) Health education plan for a patient prescribed hearing aids (5 marks) Goal: Mr. X will use and care for his hearing aids correctly, adapt to them and communicate better with his family.

1. Understanding the hearing aid

  • A hearing aid amplifies sound; it does not restore normal hearing or cure the cause.
  • Types – behind-the-ear (BTE), receiver-in-canal, in-the-ear, completely-in-canal, body-worn aids; cochlear implants for severe–profound SNHL; bone-anchored aids when the ear canal cannot be used.
  • Free or subsidised aids are available under NPPCD and the ADIP scheme for eligible persons.

2. Adaptation period

  • Wear the aid for a few hours daily at first, in quiet surroundings, gradually increasing to the whole day over 2–4 weeks.
  • Initially, everyday sounds (fans, traffic, own voice) seem loud; the brain gradually adjusts.

3. Insertion, removal and use

  • Practise in front of a mirror; check correct ear (colour code – red for right, blue for left).
  • Switch on after inserting and off before removing (to prevent whistling); adjust volume gradually.
  • Whistling (feedback) means poor fit, wax or too high volume – reinsert, check for wax, see the audiologist.

4. Battery care

  • Use the correct size; remove the sticker tab and wait a minute before inserting (zinc–air cells).
  • Keep spare batteries; remove batteries at night; keep batteries away from children (swallowing is dangerous); dispose of them safely.

5. Cleaning and protection

  • Wipe the aid daily with a dry soft cloth; clean the earmould with mild soapy water after detaching it, dry fully before reattaching; change wax guards.
  • Protect from water, heat and sweat – remove before bathing, swimming, hair-dye or sprays; store overnight in a dry box with silica gel; never leave it in sunlight or near a stove.
  • Keep in its case when not in use; do not drop it.

6. Ear hygiene and follow-up

  • Do not insert cotton buds, hairpins or oil into the ears; get wax removed by the clinic.
  • Annual hearing test and servicing of the aid; report ear pain, discharge or itching from the mould.

7. Communication strategies (for patient and family)

  • Family should face the person, speak clearly and slightly slowly, not shout, reduce background noise (TV, mixer), ensure good light on the speaker's face, and rephrase if not understood.
  • Use visual alarms or vibrating alerts for doorbell and mobile phone; avoid noisy environments; use ear protection in noise.

8. Evaluation

  • Patient demonstrates insertion, battery change and cleaning; reports wearing the aid daily and improved conversation.

Prevention of deafness – role of the nurse

  1. Primary prevention – immunisation (MR, mumps where available, meningococcal and pneumococcal vaccines as indicated), good antenatal care (rubella immunity, avoiding ototoxic drugs in pregnancy), safe delivery and care of jaundiced and preterm newborns.
  2. Noise protection – educate workers in mills, mines, construction and transport to use ear plugs or ear muffs; limit headphone volume (the "60/60 rule" – not more than 60% volume for 60 minutes); avoid bursting crackers near the ear.
  3. Safe medication practice – monitor patients on aminoglycosides, high-dose loop diuretics and cisplatin for tinnitus or giddiness, and report early.
  4. Ear hygiene – no cotton buds, hairpins, matchsticks or oil; early treatment of ear discharge and colds.
  5. Early detection – support newborn hearing screening (OAE), school screening and screening of the elderly; refer anyone with a hearing complaint for audiometry.
  6. Rehabilitation – hearing aids, cochlear implants, speech therapy and sign language; inform families about disability certificates and benefits under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016.

Nursing importance

  • Untreated hearing loss in adults leads to social isolation, depression, accidents and cognitive decline; correct hearing-aid use greatly improves quality of life.
  • Nurses also prevent deafness by teaching ear hygiene, noise protection and safe use of ototoxic drugs, and by supporting newborn hearing screening.

Conclusion Deafness may be conductive, sensorineural or mixed, with causes ranging from wax and otitis media to ageing, noise and ototoxic drugs. Weber's and Rinne's tests help distinguish the type, and a structured health education plan ensures effective, comfortable and safe use of hearing aids.

question: Mrs. Y, a 70-year-old woman, came to the hospital with a burning pain on the left lingual margin of the tongue for 5 years and has been diagnosed with cancer of the oral cavity. (a) List the causes of cancer of the oral cavity. (3 marks) (b) Explain the surgical management of cancer of the oral cavity. (5 marks) (c) Discuss the palliative nursing care of Mrs. Y. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: Surgical management of tongue cancer
labels: wide excision of the lateral tongue lesion with margin (partial glossectomy)
neck dissection removing cervical lymph nodes
reconstruction with flap (pectoralis major or radial forearm free flap)

answer_html:
(a) Causes of cancer of the oral cavity (3 marks) Oral cancer (mostly squamous cell carcinoma) is one of the commonest cancers in India, especially among men, largely because of tobacco and areca nut use.

  1. Tobacco chewing – gutkha, khaini, mawa, kharra (common in Vidarbha), betel quid (paan) with tobacco, mishri.
  2. Smoking – bidi, cigarette, chutta (reverse smoking).
  3. Areca nut (supari) – even without tobacco; causes oral submucous fibrosis.
  4. Alcohol – acts synergistically with tobacco.
  5. Chronic irritation – sharp, broken or jagged teeth and ill-fitting dentures rubbing the lateral border (lingual margin) of the tongue – very relevant in this 70-year-old.
  6. Poor oral hygiene, chronic infection, candidiasis.
  7. Premalignant lesions and conditions – leukoplakia, erythroplakia (highest risk), oral submucous fibrosis, lichen planus.
  8. Human papillomavirus (HPV-16) – mainly oropharyngeal cancers.
  9. Nutritional deficiencies (iron, vitamin A), immunosuppression, old age; sun exposure (lip cancer).

(b) Surgical management of cancer of the oral cavity (5 marks) 1. Pre-operative evaluation

  • Biopsy (incisional/punch) for diagnosis; CT/MRI of the primary and neck, orthopantomogram (OPG) for jaw involvement, chest imaging; TNM staging.
  • Dental evaluation and extraction of infected teeth, nutritional build-up, anaesthesia fitness, counselling about speech, swallowing and appearance; written consent.

2. Principles of surgery

  • Wide local excision with a 1–1.5 cm margin of normal tissue (confirmed by frozen section).
  • Management of neck lymph nodes (the commonest site of spread).
  • Reconstruction to restore function and appearance.

3. Operations | Procedure | Description | |---|---| | Partial (hemi-) glossectomy | Removal of the affected part of the tongue – for lateral tongue cancers like Mrs. Y's | | Total glossectomy | Removal of the whole tongue for extensive disease (often with laryngeal protection) | | Marginal or segmental mandibulectomy | Removal of part of the jaw when the tumour is close to or invades bone | | Composite resection ("commando operation") | Combined removal of the tumour, part of the mandible and the neck nodes in one block | | Neck dissection | Selective (supra-omohyoid) for N0 neck; modified radical or radical neck dissection for node-positive disease | | Reconstruction | Primary closure or skin graft for small defects; pectoralis major myocutaneous (PMMC) flap (common in India); free flaps – radial forearm (tongue), fibula (mandible) | | Tracheostomy | Temporary, to protect the airway from swelling after major resections |

4. Adjuvant treatment

  • Post-operative radiotherapy, with concurrent chemotherapy (cisplatin) for high-risk features (positive margins, extranodal spread).
  • For an elderly patient with advanced, inoperable disease, palliative radiotherapy or chemotherapy and best supportive care are chosen.

5. Post-operative care in brief

  • Airway and tracheostomy care, flap monitoring (colour, warmth, capillary refill, Doppler), drain care, nasogastric/Ryle's tube feeding, oral hygiene, pain control, speech and swallowing therapy, and shoulder physiotherapy after neck dissection.

(c) Palliative nursing care of Mrs. Y (7 marks) Palliative care aims to give the best possible quality of life to a patient with a serious illness by relieving pain and other symptoms and supporting psychological, social and spiritual needs of the patient and family. For a 70-year-old with long-standing tongue cancer, palliative care should start alongside treatment and continue till the end of life.

1. Pain management

  • Assess pain regularly (numerical or faces scale); note burning, neuropathic and breakthrough pain.
  • Follow the WHO analgesic ladder – paracetamol → tramadol → oral morphine given "by the clock", with breakthrough doses; adjuvants such as gabapentin/pregabalin for nerve pain and steroids for swelling.
  • Topical anaesthetic mouthwash (viscous lignocaine) before meals; treat constipation caused by opioids with regular laxatives.
  • Non-drug measures – comfortable positioning, distraction, relaxation, prayer or music as she prefers.

2. Mouth care

  • Gentle oral care every 2–4 hours with a soft brush or gauze, saline or soda-bicarbonate mouthwashes; avoid alcohol-based mouthwashes.
  • Treat oral thrush (nystatin/clotrimazole), use artificial saliva and frequent sips for dry mouth after radiotherapy, lip balm for cracked lips.

3. Nutrition and swallowing

  • Soft, moist, bland, high-calorie and high-protein foods (khichdi, dal, porridge, milkshakes, eggs), small frequent meals; avoid spicy, hot, acidic and rough foods.
  • Assess for aspiration; sit upright for meals; refer for swallowing therapy.
  • Nasogastric or PEG feeding if swallowing becomes unsafe, according to her and the family's wishes.

4. Care of fungating wound and bleeding

  • Clean gently with saline; control odour with topical metronidazole and charcoal dressings; use non-adherent dressings.
  • Minor bleeding – pressure, tranexamic acid, adrenaline-soaked gauze; prepare the family for possible major bleeding – keep dark-coloured towels, sedation available, and stay with the patient.

5. Airway and breathing

  • Suction of secretions, humidified air, propped-up position; tracheostomy care if present.
  • Breathlessness – fan, positioning, low-dose oral morphine; hyoscine butylbromide/glycopyrrolate for noisy secretions near death.

6. Communication

  • Speech may be painful or unclear – provide a writing pad, picture board or mobile phone; allow time; involve family members as interpreters.

7. Psychological, social and spiritual support

  • Address fear, depression, disfigurement and loss of dignity; listen, encourage expression of feelings; involve the counsellor.
  • Respect her cultural and religious beliefs; arrange spiritual support as desired.
  • Assess family burden and finances; link to free government cancer schemes, PM-JAY and NGOs.

8. Home-based and end-of-life care

  • Teach family mouth care, feeding, medication, wound care and signs needing help; refer to the home-care palliative team under the National Programme for Palliative Care.
  • Discuss goals of care and preferred place of death; ensure comfort, dignity and family presence in the final days; provide bereavement support to the family.

Nursing diagnoses for Mrs. Y (palliative phase)

  • Chronic pain related to tumour infiltration of the tongue and nerves – goal: pain controlled at a level acceptable to her (≤3/10), allowing sleep and eating.
  • Impaired oral mucous membrane related to tumour, radiotherapy and infection – goal: clean, moist mouth without thrush.
  • Imbalanced nutrition: less than body requirements related to painful swallowing – goal: maintains weight and hydration with modified diet or tube feeding.
  • Impaired verbal communication related to tongue lesion – goal: uses alternative methods to express needs.
  • Disturbed body image and anxiety related to disfigurement and prognosis – goal: expresses feelings and accepts support.
  • Caregiver role strain in the family – goal: family members feel prepared and supported in home care.

Evaluation: comfort, sleep, intake, mouth condition, mood and the family's coping are reviewed at every visit, and the care plan is adjusted as the disease progresses.

Nursing importance

  • Head and neck cancer causes severe pain, difficulty in eating and speaking, and distressing wounds; skilled palliative nursing can make the remaining life comfortable and dignified.
  • Nurses also prevent oral cancer through tobacco-cessation counselling and oral screening (visual inspection) of adults above 30 years under the NCD programme.

Conclusion Oral cancer, strongly linked to tobacco, areca nut, alcohol and chronic irritation, is treated by wide excision, neck dissection and reconstruction with adjuvant radiotherapy. For an elderly patient like Mrs. Y, palliative nursing care – pain relief, mouth and wound care, nutrition, communication and psychosocial support – is the cornerstone of a good quality of life.

question: Mr. Sanjay, aged 32 years, is admitted to the ENT ward with mastoiditis. (a) Define mastoiditis. (2 marks) (b) List its causes. (3 marks) (c) Explain the post-operative nursing management after mastoidectomy. (10 marks)

diagram.caption: Middle ear, mastoid and complications of mastoiditis
labels: middle ear connected through aditus to mastoid antrum and air cells; complications – subperiosteal abscess behind the ear

answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks) Mastoiditis is inflammation and infection of the mucoperiosteal lining and air cells of the mastoid process of the temporal bone, usually occurring as a complication of acute or chronic otitis media. In acute coalescent mastoiditis, the bony walls between the air cells are destroyed and the mastoid fills with pus.

(b) Causes (3 marks)

  1. Untreated or inadequately treated acute otitis media – infection spreads through the aditus to the mastoid antrum.
  2. Chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM), especially the atticoantral ("unsafe") type with cholesteatoma, which erodes bone.
  3. Organisms – acute: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pyogenes; chronic: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus, Proteus and anaerobes.
  4. Predisposing factors – recurrent upper respiratory infections, poor ear hygiene, entry of dirty water, malnutrition, diabetes, immunodeficiency, poor access to early treatment.

Clinical features (for understanding)

  • Pain and tenderness behind the ear (over the mastoid antrum), post-auricular swelling and redness, pinna pushed forward and downward.
  • Fever, profuse foul-smelling ear discharge, hearing loss, headache.
  • Danger signs – facial weakness, giddiness, severe headache, vomiting, neck stiffness, drowsiness (intracranial spread).
  • Investigations – otoscopy, CT scan of the temporal bone, pus culture, audiometry, blood counts.

Medical and surgical treatment (in brief)

  • IV antibiotics (e.g. ceftriaxone, amoxicillin–clavulanate, anti-pseudomonal drugs as per culture), analgesics, aural toilet.
  • Cortical (simple) mastoidectomy in acute mastoiditis; modified radical or radical (canal-wall-down) mastoidectomy for CSOM with cholesteatoma, often with tympanoplasty to improve hearing.

(c) Post-operative nursing management after mastoidectomy (10 marks) 1. Immediate post-operative care

  • Receive the patient from OT; maintain a patent airway, give oxygen as needed, monitor vital signs every 15 minutes until stable.
  • Position: semi-Fowler's or lying on the back or on the unoperated side, with the operated ear uppermost to avoid pressure on the wound.
  • Check level of consciousness and orientation as anaesthesia wears off.

2. Assessment of facial nerve function

  • The facial nerve runs close to the operative field. Once awake, ask the patient to raise the eyebrows, close the eyes tightly, smile, show teeth and puff the cheeks; compare both sides.
  • Report any new facial weakness immediately; if eye closure is poor, protect the cornea with lubricating drops and an eye pad.

3. Care of the dressing and wound

  • A mastoid pressure bandage is applied for 24–48 hours; observe for soakage and bleeding; reinforce but do not remove without orders.
  • Do not disturb the ear pack in the canal; it is removed by the surgeon after 7–14 days.
  • Post-auricular sutures are kept clean and dry; removed in about 7 days; observe for redness, swelling or discharge.

4. Pain management

  • Give prescribed analgesics regularly; mild to moderate pain is expected; severe throbbing pain may indicate haematoma or infection.

5. Management of vertigo, nausea and vomiting

  • Surgery near the labyrinth can cause giddiness and nausea; give antiemetics/vestibular sedatives (prochlorperazine, promethazine) as ordered.
  • Prevent falls – side rails, assist with first ambulation, advise slow movements and avoid sudden turning of the head; report severe or persistent vertigo or nystagmus (labyrinthine injury).

6. Prevention and early detection of complications | Complication | What the nurse watches for | |---|---| | Haemorrhage | Soaked dressing, rising pulse, falling BP | | Facial nerve palsy | Asymmetry of face, inability to close the eye | | Infection/meningitis | Fever, discharge, severe headache, neck stiffness, vomiting, drowsiness | | Labyrinthitis | Severe vertigo, nystagmus, vomiting, sudden hearing loss | | CSF leak | Clear watery discharge from the ear or nose | | Altered taste | Metallic taste on one side of the tongue (chorda tympani injury – usually temporary) | - Give antibiotics on time and monitor temperature.

7. Care related to hearing

  • Explain that hearing will be reduced while the ear pack is in place; speak to the patient from the good side; ensure call bell is within reach.
  • After radical mastoidectomy, some permanent hearing loss may remain; plan audiometry and hearing aid if needed.

8. Nutrition, comfort and activity

  • Start fluids and soft diet when nausea settles; chewing may be painful for a few days.
  • Encourage early, gradual ambulation with support; adequate rest.

9. Psychological support

  • Reassure about expected symptoms (blocked ear, mild giddiness, numbness around the ear); involve the family; answer questions about hearing and return to work.

10. Discharge teaching

  • Keep the ear dry – during bath, plug the ear with cotton smeared with petroleum jelly; no swimming until permitted.
  • Avoid blowing the nose forcefully; sneeze and cough with the mouth open; avoid straining and heavy lifting for 2–3 weeks.
  • Do not insert anything into the ear; take medicines as prescribed; avoid air travel until the surgeon permits.
  • After canal-wall-down (radical) mastoidectomy, the open cavity needs regular cleaning (aural toilet) at the ENT clinic every few months for life; avoid water entry.
  • Report immediately: bleeding, fever, increasing pain, foul discharge, facial weakness, severe giddiness, headache or vomiting.
  • Keep follow-up appointments for pack removal and hearing assessment.

Nursing diagnoses (examples) | Nursing diagnosis | Expected outcome | Key interventions | |---|---|---| | Acute pain related to surgical incision | Pain score ≤3/10 | Regular analgesics, positioning, comfort measures | | Risk for injury (falls) related to vertigo | No falls | Side rails, assisted ambulation, antiemetics | | Risk for infection related to surgical wound | Afebrile, clean wound | Asepsis, antibiotics, wound and temperature monitoring | | Disturbed auditory perception related to ear pack/surgery | Patient communicates effectively | Speak to the good ear, written cues, reassurance | | Deficient knowledge about home care | Patient explains ear care and warning signs | Structured discharge teaching |

Pre-operative preparation (to prepare Mr. Sanjay for mastoidectomy)

  • Explain the operation, expected blocked ear, dressing and possible giddiness; obtain informed consent, which should mention possible facial weakness, taste change and hearing change.
  • Record baseline hearing (audiometry) and facial nerve function, so that post-operative changes can be compared.
  • Complete investigations – blood counts, bleeding and clotting time, blood sugar, CT scan; treat active infection with antibiotics and aural toilet.
  • Shave the hair 2–3 cm around the ear as per hospital policy; wash hair the day before; remove ornaments.
  • Keep nil by mouth as instructed; check vital signs; give premedication; ensure the patient voids before shifting.
  • Reduce anxiety by answering questions and involving his family; a young working adult like Mr. Sanjay will want to know about return to work (usually 2–3 weeks).

Nursing importance

  • Close observation for facial nerve palsy, vertigo, bleeding and intracranial infection in the first days after mastoidectomy prevents serious, sometimes permanent, harm.
  • Prevention of mastoiditis begins in the community by early treatment of ear infections and discouraging the habit of putting oil or dirty water in ears.

Conclusion Mastoiditis is infection of the mastoid air cells, usually following acute or chronic otitis media, and is treated with antibiotics and mastoidectomy. Post-operative nursing focuses on airway, facial nerve assessment, wound and pain care, vertigo and complication monitoring, and thorough discharge teaching to keep the ear dry and protected.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Ear, Nose and Throat
question: Explain Ménière's disease and its nursing management.
answer_html:
Definition Ménière's disease is a disorder of the inner ear caused by endolymphatic hydrops (excess endolymph in the membranous labyrinth), characterised by recurrent episodes of vertigo, fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus and a feeling of fullness in the ear. It usually affects adults aged 30–50 years and is mostly unilateral.

1. Pathophysiology

  • Increased production or reduced absorption of endolymph (endolymphatic sac) → distension of the cochlear duct and saccule → small ruptures allow potassium-rich endolymph to mix with perilymph → sudden attacks of vertigo and hearing loss.
  • Triggers: salt, caffeine, alcohol, smoking, stress, allergy.

2. Clinical features

  • Episodic rotatory vertigo lasting 20 minutes to several hours, with nausea, vomiting and sweating.
  • Fluctuating hearing loss (low frequencies first), becoming permanent with repeated attacks.
  • Tinnitus (roaring) and aural fullness before or during attacks.
  • Nystagmus during attacks; between attacks the patient may be normal.

3. Diagnosis

  • Clinical history; pure-tone audiometry (low-frequency SNHL), electrocochleography, glycerol test, vestibular tests; MRI to exclude acoustic neuroma.

4. Medical and surgical management

  • Acute attack: bed rest, vestibular sedatives (prochlorperazine, promethazine, dimenhydrinate, cinnarizine), antiemetics, diazepam; IV fluids if vomiting.
  • Long-term: low-salt diet (about 1.5–2 g sodium/day), betahistine 16–24 mg three times daily, diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide, acetazolamide), avoidance of caffeine, alcohol and smoking, stress management.
  • Intratympanic steroids or intratympanic gentamicin (chemical labyrinthectomy) for frequent disabling attacks.
  • Surgery – endolymphatic sac decompression, vestibular neurectomy, labyrinthectomy (destroys hearing) for resistant cases.
  • Vestibular rehabilitation exercises between attacks.

5. Nursing management

  1. Safety during attacks – help the patient lie flat and still in a quiet, dim room, fix the eyes on a stationary object, keep side rails up, keep a vomit bowl nearby; avoid sudden head movements.
  2. Prevent falls – assist with walking after attacks; remove obstacles at home; advise sitting down immediately when vertigo starts.
  3. Give medications as ordered and monitor for drowsiness (vestibular sedatives).
  4. Diet teaching – reduce salt (avoid pickles, papad, chips, processed foods, extra salt at the table), limit tea/coffee and alcohol, maintain regular meals and fluids.
  5. Advise not to drive, climb ladders, swim alone or operate machines while attacks are frequent.
  6. Stress reduction – relaxation, yoga, adequate sleep.
  7. Hearing protection – avoid noise; refer for hearing aid if loss is permanent.
  8. Emotional support – unpredictable attacks cause anxiety and depression; encourage keeping a diary of attacks and triggers.

Conclusion Ménière's disease is endolymphatic hydrops producing the classic triad of episodic vertigo, fluctuating hearing loss and tinnitus. Low-salt diet, betahistine, vestibular sedatives and safety-focused nursing care help control attacks and prevent injury.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Ear, Nose and Throat
question: Explain acute otitis media – its stages, management and nursing care.
answer_html:
Definition Acute otitis media (AOM) is acute inflammation of the middle-ear cleft (middle ear, Eustachian tube and mastoid), usually caused by bacteria entering through the Eustachian tube after an upper respiratory infection. It is very common in children under 5 years because their Eustachian tube is short, wide and horizontal.

1. Causes and predisposing factors

  • Organisms: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, and viruses.
  • Predisposing factors: colds and URTI, enlarged adenoids, bottle-feeding in lying position, passive smoking, crowding, daycare, cleft palate, Down syndrome, malnutrition.

2. Stages of acute otitis media

  1. Stage of tubal occlusion (catarrhal stage) – Eustachian tube is congested and blocked; air in the middle ear is absorbed → retracted tympanic membrane; ear fullness, mild deafness.
  2. Stage of presuppuration (hyperaemia) – inflammatory exudate forms; TM congested and red; earache, fever.
  3. Stage of suppuration – pus collects in the middle ear under pressure → red, bulging TM, severe throbbing earache, high fever, irritability in children, marked deafness.
  4. Stage of resolution – TM ruptures, pus discharges (otorrhoea), pain and fever subside; small perforations usually heal.
  5. Stage of complications – if virulent or untreated: mastoiditis, CSOM, facial palsy, labyrinthitis, meningitis, brain abscess.

3. Clinical features

  • Earache (child pulls or rubs the ear, cries at night), fever, irritability, poor feeding, vomiting, hearing loss; discharge after rupture.

4. Management

  • Antibiotics – amoxicillin (or amoxicillin–clavulanate) for 7–10 days; watchful waiting may be used in mild cases in older children.
  • Analgesics and antipyretics – paracetamol, ibuprofen.
  • Nasal decongestant drops to open the Eustachian tube.
  • Dry mopping and aural toilet when the ear is discharging; ear wicks.
  • Myringotomy for a bulging TM with severe pain or complications.
  • Treat underlying causes (adenoids, allergy).

5. Nursing care

  1. Give antibiotics and analgesics on time; complete the course.
  2. Local warmth to the ear relieves pain; keep the child propped up.
  3. Dry mop the ear with clean cotton wicks; keep the ear dry; never put oil or home remedies into the ear.
  4. Encourage fluids, rest and nutrition; monitor temperature and watch for danger signs (swelling behind the ear, facial weakness, severe headache, neck stiffness, persistent discharge).
  5. Educate parents – breastfeed in a semi-upright position, avoid bottle-feeding lying down, avoid passive smoking, treat colds early, complete immunisation including PCV, follow up to check healing of the ear drum and hearing (untreated hearing loss delays speech).

Conclusion AOM progresses through stages of tubal occlusion, presuppuration, suppuration and resolution, with complications if untreated. Timely antibiotics, pain relief, keeping the ear dry and parental education prevent complications and hearing loss.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Ear, Nose and Throat
question: (a) Define tonsillitis and list its types. (2 marks) (b) Describe the clinical manifestations and complications of tonsillitis, with the indications for tonsillectomy. (5 marks) (c) Prepare a nursing care plan for a patient undergoing tonsillectomy. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Post-tonsillectomy (tonsil) position
labels: patient lying semi-prone on the side with head turned and slightly lowered
kidney tray under the mouth to drain blood and secretions

answer_html:
(a) Definition and types (2 marks) Tonsillitis is inflammation of the palatine tonsils, usually due to viral or bacterial infection. It is most common in children aged 5–15 years. The commonest bacterial cause is group A β-haemolytic Streptococcus; viruses (adenovirus, Epstein–Barr virus) also cause it.

Types

  • Acute tonsillitis – acute catarrhal (superficial), acute follicular (pus-filled crypts – yellow spots), acute parenchymatous (whole tonsil swollen and red), acute membranous (exudate forms a membrane – differentiate from diphtheria).
  • Chronic tonsillitis – recurrent acute, chronic follicular, chronic parenchymatous (hypertrophic) with large tonsils, and chronic fibroid (small fibrosed tonsils).

(b) Clinical manifestations, complications and indications for tonsillectomy (5 marks) 1. Clinical manifestations

  • Acute tonsillitis: sore throat, painful swallowing (odynophagia), difficulty in swallowing, fever with chills, headache, body ache, malaise, referred earache, foul breath; in children – vomiting, refusal to eat, abdominal pain.
  • On examination: enlarged, red tonsils, yellow spots or exudate on the surface, congested pillars, tender enlarged jugulodigastric lymph nodes below the angle of the jaw.
  • Chronic tonsillitis: recurrent attacks of sore throat, persistent irritation, bad breath, bad taste, enlarged cryptic tonsils with cheesy material, and in children with large tonsils and adenoids – snoring, mouth breathing and obstructive sleep apnoea, poor school performance.

2. Complications

  • Local: peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) – severe unilateral pain, trismus, "hot potato" voice, drooling, uvula pushed to the other side; parapharyngeal and retropharyngeal abscess; acute otitis media; chronic tonsillitis.
  • General (post-streptococcal): rheumatic fever, acute glomerulonephritis; septicaemia.
  • Large tonsils – sleep apnoea, cor pulmonale in severe cases.

3. Indications for tonsillectomy

  • Recurrent tonsillitis – about 7 or more episodes in one year, 5 per year for 2 years, or 3 per year for 3 years (Paradise criteria), causing loss of school or work.
  • Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) – recurrent or not settling.
  • Obstructive sleep apnoea due to tonsil (and adenoid) enlargement.
  • Suspected malignancy (asymmetric enlarged tonsil).
  • Tonsillitis causing febrile seizures, or a carrier state (diphtheria/streptococcus) not responding to treatment; as part of other operations (e.g. uvulopalatopharyngoplasty).
  • Contraindications: acute infection (operate 3–4 weeks after an attack), bleeding disorders, uncontrolled systemic illness, cleft palate (relative), anaemia.

(c) Nursing care plan for a patient undergoing tonsillectomy (8 marks) A. Pre-operative care

  1. Assessment – history of recent infection, bleeding tendency, drugs (stop aspirin and NSAIDs 1–2 weeks before), allergies; check loose teeth (risk of aspiration during anaesthesia).
  2. Investigations – haemoglobin, bleeding time, clotting time/PT-INR, blood grouping, urine routine.
  3. Explanation – procedure, throat pain after surgery, soft diet, possibility of earache; preparation of the child through play and parents' presence.
  4. Nil by mouth as per anaesthesia instructions; mouth wash; remove ornaments; obtain consent (parents for children).

B. Post-operative nursing care plan | Nursing diagnosis | Goal | Nursing interventions | Rationale | |---|---|---|---| | Risk for ineffective airway clearance/aspiration related to anaesthesia, blood and secretions in the throat | Airway remains clear | Place in tonsillectomy position (semi-prone, head turned and slightly lowered) until fully awake; gentle oral suction without touching the tonsillar beds; keep suction and oxygen ready; then semi-Fowler's position | Allows blood and saliva to drain out rather than into the airway | | Risk for bleeding (haemorrhage) related to surgical wound | Bleeding detected and controlled early | Check pulse, BP and respiration every 15 minutes initially; observe for frequent swallowing (especially in a sleeping child), vomiting of fresh blood, restlessness, pallor, rising pulse; inspect the throat with a torch; apply an ice collar; inform the surgeon immediately; keep blood ready | Primary/reactionary haemorrhage occurs within 24 hours; secondary haemorrhage at 5–10 days due to infection | | Acute pain related to surgical trauma | Pain controlled; able to swallow | Give paracetamol or prescribed analgesics regularly (avoid aspirin); ice collar; cold fluids and ice cream; explain that earache is referred pain | Pain prevents swallowing and leads to dehydration | | Risk for deficient fluid volume related to painful swallowing | Adequate hydration and urine output | Start cold clear fluids when fully awake (water, cold milk, juice not citrus); encourage sips every hour; IV fluids if needed; record intake–output | Adequate fluid prevents dehydration and keeps the throat moist, reducing infection | | Imbalanced nutrition | Takes adequate diet | Progress to soft, bland, cool foods (porridge, khichdi, curd rice, custard) by day 2–3, then normal diet in about a week; avoid spicy, hot, hard, crispy and citrus foods; avoid red-coloured drinks (confused with blood) | Soft food is less painful; chewing normal food after a few days helps healing | | Risk for infection | Wound heals without infection | Mouth care, warm saline gargles after 24 hours (as advised), antibiotics if ordered; monitor temperature; explain that the white slough on the tonsillar fossae is normal for 5–10 days | Clean mouth reduces secondary haemorrhage | | Deficient knowledge regarding home care | Patient/parents describe home care and warning signs | Discharge teaching (below) | Prevents complications at home |

C. Discharge teaching

  • Plenty of fluids and soft diet; avoid heavy exercise, lifting and crowded places for about 2 weeks; school/work after 10–14 days.
  • Avoid aspirin; take prescribed analgesics; avoid vigorous gargling, coughing and throat-clearing; limit loud talking.
  • Report immediately any bleeding from the mouth, spitting or vomiting of blood, fever above 101°F, inability to drink, or severe pain.

D. Evaluation

  • Airway clear, no bleeding, pain controlled, taking adequate fluids and soft diet, afebrile; parents able to state warning signs.
  • If secondary haemorrhage occurs at home (around the fifth to tenth day), the family should bring the patient back immediately; the nurse checks vital signs, keeps the patient sitting forward, gives prescribed antibiotics and prepares for possible return to the operation theatre.

Medical management of acute tonsillitis (for completeness)

  • Bed rest, plenty of warm fluids, soft diet and warm saline gargles several times a day.
  • Analgesics and antipyretics – paracetamol or ibuprofen.
  • Antibiotics for bacterial tonsillitis – penicillin V or amoxicillin for 10 days (erythromycin/azithromycin if allergic) – the full course prevents rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis.
  • Throat swab culture or rapid antigen test where available; avoid amoxicillin when infectious mononucleosis is suspected (rash).
  • Peritonsillar abscess needs IV antibiotics and drainage.

Health education in the community

  • Early treatment of sore throat with fever, completion of antibiotic courses, oral hygiene, avoiding crowded poorly ventilated rooms, covering the mouth while coughing, and seeking help for difficulty in swallowing or breathing.
  • Parents of children with snoring and breath-holding during sleep should be advised to consult an ENT surgeon, because enlarged tonsils and adenoids can affect growth and school performance.

Nursing importance

  • Post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage is the most serious complication; frequent swallowing in a sleeping child may be the only early sign, so careful observation by the nurse is life-saving.
  • Prompt treatment of streptococcal sore throat in the community also prevents rheumatic fever and glomerulonephritis.

Conclusion Tonsillitis may be acute or chronic and can lead to quinsy, rheumatic fever and sleep apnoea; recurrent and complicated cases are treated by tonsillectomy. A structured nursing care plan focusing on airway, haemorrhage, pain, hydration, diet and teaching ensures safe recovery.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Ear, Nose and Throat
question: (a) Explain the risk factors, types and clinical manifestations of cancer of the larynx. (4 marks) (b) Describe its management. (3 marks) (c) Explain the nursing care of a patient after total laryngectomy. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Anatomy after total laryngectomy
labels: trachea brought out as a permanent stoma in the lower neck
pharynx closed and joined to the oesophagus
no connection between the mouth/nose and the lungs; tracheo-oesophageal puncture with voice prosthesis

answer_html:
(a) Risk factors, types and clinical manifestations (4 marks) Cancer of the larynx is a malignant tumour – almost always squamous cell carcinoma – of the voice box. It is common in men aged 50–70 years in India and is strongly linked to tobacco.

1. Risk factors

  • Smoking (cigarette, bidi) – the most important; risk rises with amount and duration.
  • Alcohol – multiplies the effect of smoking.
  • Tobacco chewing, occupational exposure (asbestos, nickel, wood dust, paint fumes), air pollution.
  • Laryngopharyngeal reflux, HPV infection, poor nutrition; previous radiation to the neck.

2. Types (by site)

  • Glottic (vocal cords) – presents early with hoarseness; lymph node spread is late; best prognosis.
  • Supraglottic (above the cords – epiglottis, false cords) – common in India; symptoms appear late and early spread to neck nodes occurs.
  • Subglottic (below the cords) – rare; presents with stridor.

3. Clinical manifestations

  • Persistent hoarseness of voice for more than 2–3 weeks in a smoker – an important warning sign.
  • Pain or discomfort in the throat, painful swallowing, referred earache, feeling of a lump in the throat.
  • Chronic cough, blood-stained sputum, foul breath.
  • Breathlessness and stridor in advanced disease (airway narrowing).
  • Neck swelling (enlarged lymph nodes), weight loss, anaemia.

4. Diagnosis

  • Indirect (mirror) laryngoscopy, flexible fibre-optic laryngoscopy, direct laryngoscopy with biopsy; CT/MRI of neck, chest imaging, PET-CT; staging by TNM.

(b) Management (3 marks)

  • Early cancer (T1–T2): radiotherapy or transoral laser microsurgery/partial laryngectomy – cure with voice preservation.
  • Advanced cancer (T3–T4): total laryngectomy with neck dissection and post-operative radiotherapy, or organ-preservation chemoradiotherapy (cisplatin with radiotherapy) with salvage surgery if needed.
  • Emergency tracheostomy for stridor; palliative care for incurable disease.
  • Supportive care – tobacco and alcohol cessation, nutrition, speech and swallowing rehabilitation.

(c) Nursing care after total laryngectomy (8 marks) Total laryngectomy removes the entire larynx. The trachea is brought out as a permanent tracheostoma in the lower neck and the pharynx is closed. The patient now breathes only through the stoma ("neck breather"), cannot speak normally, has reduced sense of smell and taste, and cannot blow the nose or strain against a closed glottis. Because the airway and food passage are completely separated, there is no risk of food entering the lungs through the mouth.

1. Airway management

  • Keep the stoma and laryngectomy tube patent; give humidified oxygen through a tracheostomy mask; humidification replaces the warming and moistening normally done by the nose.
  • Sterile suctioning as needed (pre-oxygenate, suction for not more than 10–15 seconds); clean the inner tube regularly; keep a spare tube and suction at the bedside.
  • Semi-Fowler's or high Fowler's position to reduce oedema and ease breathing; encourage deep breathing and coughing through the stoma; chest physiotherapy.
  • Remember that oxygen and resuscitation must be given through the stoma, not the mouth.

2. Wound, flap and drain care

  • Monitor vacuum drains for amount and colour; observe the suture line and flaps for swelling, haematoma, colour and warmth.
  • Watch for bleeding; a sudden gush of blood may indicate carotid artery rupture (especially after radiotherapy) – apply firm pressure and call for help.
  • Keep the wound clean and dry; change dressings aseptically.

3. Nutrition

  • Nil by mouth initially; nasogastric (Ryle's tube) feeding for about 7–10 days while the pharyngeal suture line heals.
  • Watch for pharyngocutaneous fistula – saliva leaking through the neck wound, swelling, redness, fever; inform the surgeon.
  • Begin oral sips and soft diet after the surgeon confirms healing (sometimes after a contrast swallow); give high-protein, high-calorie diet.

4. Communication

  • Before surgery, teach and practise alternative communication – writing pad, picture/alphabet board, gestures, mobile phone messages; keep the call bell within reach always.
  • After healing, arrange speech therapy for alaryngeal speech:
    • Oesophageal speech – swallowing air and releasing it to produce sound.
    • Electrolarynx – a battery-operated vibrating device held against the neck.
    • Tracheo-oesophageal puncture (TEP) with a voice prosthesis – air is diverted from the trachea into the oesophagus when the stoma is covered; gives the most natural voice.

5. Stoma care and patient education

  • Clean the skin around the stoma with saline and remove crusts gently; apply barrier cream if needed.
  • Cover the stoma with a stoma bib, gauze or heat–moisture exchange (HME) filter to filter dust and warm and moisten air.
  • Prevent water entry – use a stoma shield while bathing, no swimming, care during shaving; avoid powders, sprays, dust and hair clippings near the stoma.
  • Learn to clean and change the laryngectomy tube; recognise and clear blockage.
  • Increase room humidity, drink plenty of fluids to keep secretions thin.
  • Carry a medical identification card or wear a bracelet stating "neck breather", so that rescuers give mouth-to-stoma resuscitation.

6. Psychological and social support

  • Loss of voice and visible stoma cause grief, depression, body-image disturbance and social withdrawal; allow expression of feelings, involve family, and arrange meetings with rehabilitated laryngectomees/support groups.
  • Help with return to work and daily activities; involve social worker for financial support.

7. Other care

  • Shoulder exercises after neck dissection (spinal accessory nerve weakness causes shoulder drop and pain).
  • Thyroid function tests after surgery and radiotherapy (hypothyroidism is common); calcium if parathyroids were affected.
  • Care during radiotherapy – skin care, mouth care, managing dryness and taste loss.
  • Stop smoking and alcohol to prevent recurrence and second cancers; regular follow-up visits.

Nursing diagnoses (examples) | Nursing diagnosis | Key interventions | |---|---| | Ineffective airway clearance related to secretions and altered airway | Humidification, suctioning, positioning, stoma care | | Impaired verbal communication related to removal of larynx | Writing board, call bell, speech rehabilitation | | Imbalanced nutrition related to NPO and dysphagia | NG feeding, gradual oral diet, fistula watch | | Disturbed body image | Counselling, support groups, family involvement | | Deficient knowledge about stoma care | Stepwise teaching with return demonstration |

Pre-operative preparation for total laryngectomy

  • Explain clearly, with the family present, that the voice box will be removed and the patient will breathe through a permanent opening in the neck; show pictures or arrange a meeting with a person who has had laryngectomy.
  • Teach and practise the communication method to be used after surgery; agree on simple signals.
  • Improve nutrition, stop smoking and alcohol, treat dental infections, and complete investigations and consent; teach deep breathing and coughing.

Nursing importance

  • After laryngectomy, the stoma is the patient's only airway – blockage by secretions or crusts is life-threatening, so humidification, suction and teaching are vital nursing tasks.
  • Nurses play a key role in early detection by advising every smoker with hoarseness for more than 2–3 weeks to see an ENT specialist.

Conclusion Laryngeal cancer, mostly squamous cell carcinoma linked to smoking and alcohol, presents with persistent hoarseness and is treated by radiotherapy, laser or partial surgery in early stages and by total laryngectomy or chemoradiotherapy in advanced stages. After total laryngectomy, nursing care centres on stoma and airway care, nutrition, communication and voice rehabilitation, and psychosocial support.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Ear, Nose and Throat
question: Explain otosclerosis and the nursing care of a patient undergoing stapedectomy.
answer_html:
Definition Otosclerosis (otospongiosis) is a hereditary disease of the bony labyrinth (otic capsule) in which abnormal spongy bone forms, usually around the oval window, and fixes the footplate of the stapes, causing progressive conductive deafness.

1. Features and causes

  • Hereditary (autosomal dominant with variable penetrance); more common in women, onset at 20–30 years; bilateral in most; may worsen during pregnancy.
  • Symptoms: slowly progressive deafness, tinnitus, paracusis Willisii (hears better in noisy surroundings, because others speak louder), soft monotonous speech; occasional giddiness.
  • Signs: normal tympanic membrane; sometimes a reddish hue behind it (Schwartze sign – active disease).

2. Investigations

  • Rinne negative, Weber lateralised to the worse ear.
  • Pure-tone audiometry – conductive loss with a dip in bone conduction at 2000 Hz (Carhart's notch).
  • Tympanometry – type As (stiff system); absent stapedial reflex.

3. Management

  • Hearing aid – for those not fit or unwilling for surgery.
  • Surgery – stapedectomy/stapedotomy – removal of the fixed stapes (or a small hole in the footplate) and placement of a piston prosthesis (Teflon/platinum) connecting the incus to the inner ear; restores hearing in most patients.
  • Sodium fluoride is sometimes used to slow active disease.

4. Nursing care of a patient undergoing stapedectomy Pre-operative

  • Explain the procedure, that hearing may not improve immediately (ear pack), and the small risk of further hearing loss; obtain consent; baseline audiometry; treat nasal or ear infection.

Post-operative

  1. Position – lie flat or with the head slightly raised, on the unoperated side, for the first few hours as advised; avoid sudden head movements.
  2. Vertigo and nausea – common in the first 24–48 hours; give antiemetics/vestibular sedatives; side rails up, assist with ambulation to prevent falls.
  3. Observe for facial weakness, severe vertigo, sudden hearing loss, fever or ear discharge and report.
  4. Keep the ear pack and dressing dry and intact; give analgesics and antibiotics as ordered.
  5. Avoid nose blowing, sneezing with the mouth closed, straining, coughing hard and heavy lifting – these raise middle-ear pressure and can dislodge the prosthesis.

Discharge teaching

  • Keep the ear dry (cotton with petroleum jelly while bathing), no swimming for several weeks, avoid air travel until the surgeon permits (usually 2–3 weeks), avoid loud noise and contact sports; report giddiness, pain, discharge or hearing loss; attend follow-up audiometry.

Conclusion Otosclerosis is a hereditary fixation of the stapes causing progressive conductive deafness in young adults, especially women. Stapedectomy restores hearing, and careful post-operative nursing prevents vertigo-related falls and dislodgement of the prosthesis.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Ear, Nose and Throat
question: Explain the causes, first-aid and nursing management of epistaxis.
answer_html:
Definition Epistaxis is bleeding from the nose. It is common at all ages and may range from a minor bleed to a life-threatening haemorrhage.

1. Types

  • Anterior epistaxis – from Little's area (Kiesselbach's plexus) on the anterior septum; about 90% of cases; common in children and young adults; usually mild.
  • Posterior epistaxis – from the posterior nasal cavity (Woodruff's area, sphenopalatine artery); common in elderly, hypertensive and atherosclerotic patients; often severe; blood flows into the throat.

2. Causes

  • Local: nose-picking, trauma and nasal fractures, dry air, infections (rhinitis, sinusitis), foreign bodies, deviated septum, nasal surgery, tumours (juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma in adolescent boys, nasopharyngeal carcinoma).
  • Systemic: hypertension, bleeding disorders (haemophilia, ITP, leukaemia, dengue), liver disease, anticoagulants and aspirin, hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, raised venous pressure (mitral stenosis), high altitude.
  • Idiopathic in many cases.

3. First aid (Trotter's method)

  1. Keep calm; sit the patient up and lean slightly forward – blood is not swallowed and the airway stays clear.
  2. Pinch the soft part of the nose firmly (pressing the alae against the septum) for 10–15 minutes without releasing; breathe through the mouth.
  3. Apply an ice pack or cold compress to the bridge of the nose.
  4. Spit out blood; do not swallow it.
  5. Do not tilt the head back or lie flat; do not stuff cotton deep into the nose.
  6. Seek medical help if bleeding continues after 20 minutes, is heavy, follows injury, or occurs in an elderly or hypertensive person or one on blood thinners.

4. Medical management

  • Assess airway, pulse, BP, signs of shock; Hb, blood group, coagulation profile; control high BP.
  • Chemical (silver nitrate) or electric cautery of a visible bleeding point after local anaesthetic–vasoconstrictor spray.
  • Anterior nasal packing – ribbon gauze with petroleum jelly/BIPP or expandable sponge (Merocel), kept for 24–48 hours.
  • Posterior nasal packing – post-nasal pack or Foley catheter balloon; patient admitted.
  • Antibiotics while packs are in place; IV fluids and blood transfusion if needed; correction of bleeding disorders.
  • Endoscopic cautery or sphenopalatine artery ligation, or embolisation, for recurrent severe bleeding; treatment of the cause (e.g. tumour).

5. Nursing management

  1. Reassure the patient (anxiety raises BP); maintain the sitting, forward-leaning position.
  2. Monitor vital signs, amount of bleeding, swallowing movements and blood in vomitus; record intake–output.
  3. With posterior packs – monitor SpO₂ (elderly may become hypoxic), give humidified oxygen, check the pack strings are secure, watch for airway obstruction.
  4. Mouth care frequently (mouth breathing), humidified air, lip care; soft cool diet.
  5. Give analgesics, antihypertensives and antibiotics as ordered.
  6. Discharge teaching: avoid nose-picking and forceful nose blowing for 1–2 weeks; sneeze with the mouth open; avoid hot drinks, heavy lifting, bending and strenuous exercise for a few days; use saline nasal drops and humidification; avoid aspirin/NSAIDs unless prescribed; control BP; first aid for recurrence.

Conclusion Epistaxis is usually anterior and minor but may be posterior and severe in elderly hypertensive patients. Prompt first aid by pinching the nose, timely cautery or packing, treatment of the cause and careful nursing observation prevent serious blood loss.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Ear, Nose and Throat
question: Explain the management of foreign bodies in the ear and nose and of impacted wax.
answer_html:
Introduction Foreign bodies (FB) in the ear and nose are common in children, who insert beads, seeds, buttons, erasers and small toys; insects enter ears of people sleeping on the floor. Impacted wax (cerumen) is common in all ages, especially the elderly and hearing-aid users.

1. Foreign body in the ear

  • Types: animate (insects, maggots) and inanimate – vegetable (seeds, grains – swell with moisture) and non-vegetable (beads, stones, cotton, button batteries).
  • Features: discomfort, earache, deafness, buzzing noise (live insect), discharge or bleeding if injured.
  • Management:
    • Live insect – first kill or immobilise it by filling the canal with oil (mineral/olive oil) or spirit, then remove by syringing or forceps.
    • Non-vegetable smooth objects – syringing or removal with a hook or suction under direct vision.
    • Vegetable FB – do not syringe (it swells); remove with a hook or suction.
    • Button battery – emergency; remove at once (causes chemical burn and perforation); no ear drops.
    • Uncooperative children or impacted FB – removal under general anaesthesia using an operating microscope.
  • Never use forceps blindly on round objects (pushes them deeper and damages the ear drum).

2. Foreign body in the nose

  • Features: unilateral foul-smelling, blood-stained nasal discharge in a child – suspect FB until proved otherwise; obstruction, sneezing.
  • Management: remove with a blunt hook passed behind the object under good light; the "mother's kiss" technique (parent blows into the child's mouth while closing the other nostril) for anterior objects; GA if necessary.
  • Danger: pushing the object back can cause aspiration into the airway; button batteries and magnets need urgent removal.
  • Long-standing FB may become calcified (rhinolith).

3. Impacted wax

  • Features: blocked ear, deafness, tinnitus, itching, discomfort, giddiness, reflex cough.
  • Management:
    1. Wax-softening drops – soda glycerine, olive oil or liquid paraffin 3–5 drops, three times daily for 3–5 days.
    2. Syringing (irrigation) with water at body temperature (37°C) to avoid vertigo; the pinna is pulled upward and backward in adults and the stream is directed along the posterosuperior canal wall, not straight at the drum; the returning water is collected in a kidney tray.
    3. Microsuction or instrument removal (Jobson Horne probe, wax hook) by the ENT doctor.
  • Contraindications to syringing: perforated ear drum, active ear discharge/CSOM, previous ear surgery, otitis externa, only-hearing ear, vegetable foreign body.

4. Nursing responsibilities

  • Explain the procedure, keep the child calm and restrained safely, ensure good light; after syringing, dry the canal, check for pain, bleeding, dizziness or perforation.
  • Health education: never insert cotton buds, hairpins, matchsticks, pens or oil into the ears; keep small objects and batteries away from young children; sleep on cots rather than on the floor where insects are common; seek help early instead of attempting removal at home.

Conclusion Most ear and nasal foreign bodies and wax can be removed safely by trained staff using the right technique – oil for insects, no syringing for vegetable FB, urgent removal of batteries, and softening drops before syringing. Education of parents prevents many such accidents.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Ear, Nose and Throat
question: Explain deviated nasal septum and the nursing care after septoplasty.
answer_html:
Definition Deviated nasal septum (DNS) is a bending of the nasal septum away from the midline, narrowing one or both sides of the nasal cavity. A mild deviation is very common and harmless; a marked deviation causes symptoms.

1. Causes

  • Trauma – birth injury, falls, sports injuries, fights.
  • Developmental – unequal growth of the septum and facial skeleton.
  • Associated with cleft lip/palate and nasal masses.

2. Types

  • C-shaped or S-shaped deviation, septal spur (sharp projection), dislocation of the caudal (front) end, thickening of the septum.

3. Clinical features

  • Nasal obstruction (one or both sides), mouth breathing, snoring, dry mouth.
  • Headache, facial pain from a spur pressing on the lateral wall.
  • Recurrent sinusitis, recurrent nasal discharge, ear infections (Eustachian tube block).
  • Epistaxis (dry exposed mucosa), loss of smell, external nasal deformity.

4. Diagnosis

  • Anterior rhinoscopy, Cottle's test, nasal endoscopy, CT scan of nose and sinuses.

5. Treatment

  • Mild cases – no treatment; decongestants and saline for associated rhinitis.
  • Septoplasty – conservative surgery that straightens and repositions the septum, removing only the deformed parts; preferred in adults and adolescents.
  • Submucous resection (SMR) – older operation removing more cartilage and bone; risk of nasal collapse.
  • Usually combined with functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) or turbinate reduction when needed.

6. Nursing care after septoplasty

  1. Position – semi-Fowler's (head raised 30–45°) to reduce swelling and bleeding.
  2. Nasal packs/splints remain for 24–48 hours – the patient must breathe through the mouth; give frequent mouth care, lip balm, sips of water and humidified air.
  3. Observe for bleeding – changing the drip pad (moustache dressing), noting soakage, frequent swallowing, vomiting of blood, pulse and BP.
  4. Cold compresses to the nose and around the eyes reduce swelling and bruising; give analgesics (avoid aspirin).
  5. Watch for septal haematoma – increasing pain, obstruction and a swelling of the septum; it must be drained urgently to prevent infection and saddle-nose deformity.
  6. After pack removal, gentle saline nasal sprays/douching; clean crusts carefully.
  7. Discharge teaching: do not blow the nose for 1–2 weeks; sneeze with the mouth open; avoid bending, heavy lifting, strenuous exercise and contact sports for 2–3 weeks; avoid hot drinks and very hot baths in the first days; protect the nose from injury; report fever, bleeding or foul discharge; attend follow-up for splint removal and endoscopic cleaning.

Conclusion DNS causes nasal obstruction, headache and recurrent sinusitis and is corrected by septoplasty. Post-operative nursing focuses on positioning, mouth care during packing, bleeding and haematoma observation, and teaching to avoid nose blowing and strain.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Ear, Nose and Throat
question: Explain the causes and emergency management of acute laryngeal obstruction.
answer_html:
Definition Acute laryngeal obstruction is a sudden narrowing or blockage of the airway at the level of the larynx, causing difficulty in breathing. It is a life-threatening emergency because complete obstruction leads to hypoxia and death within minutes.

1. Causes

  • Infections: acute epiglottitis (Haemophilus influenzae type b – child sits forward, drools, high fever, muffled voice), croup (laryngotracheobronchitis) – barking cough, hoarseness in young children; diphtheria (membrane); Ludwig's angina, retropharyngeal abscess.
  • Foreign body – peanuts, seeds, coins, small toys in children; food bolus in elderly ("café coronary").
  • Oedema – angioedema/anaphylaxis, insect sting, burns and inhalation injury, corrosive ingestion.
  • Trauma – blunt neck injury, fracture of larynx, prolonged intubation.
  • Bilateral vocal cord paralysis (e.g. after thyroidectomy), laryngospasm (hypocalcaemia, after extubation).
  • Tumours – carcinoma of the larynx, papillomas.
  • Congenital – laryngomalacia (commonest cause of stridor in infants), laryngeal web.

2. Clinical features

  • Inspiratory stridor (harsh noisy breathing), hoarseness, difficulty in speaking or swallowing, drooling.
  • Dyspnoea, use of accessory muscles, suprasternal and intercostal recession, flaring of nostrils.
  • Restlessness, anxiety, tachycardia, sweating; later cyanosis, drowsiness, bradycardia – signs of impending arrest.
  • Choking – inability to speak, cough or breathe; clutching the throat (complete FB obstruction).

3. Emergency management

  1. Call for help; keep the patient calm and in the position of comfort (usually sitting upright); do not force a child with suspected epiglottitis to lie down or examine the throat with a spatula (may precipitate complete obstruction).
  2. Give humidified high-flow oxygen; monitor SpO₂, pulse, respiration.
  3. Treat the cause:
    • Foreign body – in a conscious choking adult/child: back blows and abdominal thrusts (Heimlich manoeuvre); infants: five back blows and five chest thrusts; then removal by laryngoscopy/bronchoscopy.
    • Anaphylaxis/angioedema – adrenaline 0.5 mg IM (1:1000), antihistamine, steroids.
    • Croup – oral/IM dexamethasone, nebulised adrenaline, humidified oxygen.
    • Epiglottitis – secure the airway in OT by an experienced anaesthetist, IV ceftriaxone.
    • Diphtheria – anti-diphtheritic serum and antibiotics.
  4. Secure the airway if obstruction is severe or worsening – endotracheal intubation; if intubation fails – emergency cricothyroidotomy (needle or surgical), followed by tracheostomy.
  5. IV access, steroids to reduce oedema, heliox where available.

4. Nursing responsibilities

  • Recognise stridor early; never leave the patient alone; keep suction, oxygen, intubation tray, cricothyroidotomy and tracheostomy sets ready at the bedside.
  • Avoid sedatives (may depress breathing); keep the child on the parent's lap to reduce crying.
  • Monitor continuously and document; after tracheostomy – humidification, suction, tube care.
  • Educate parents about keeping small objects, nuts and coins away from young children and about completing Hib, pentavalent (diphtheria) immunisation.

Conclusion Acute laryngeal obstruction has many causes – infections, foreign bodies, oedema, trauma and tumours – and presents with stridor and respiratory distress. Calm positioning, oxygen, cause-specific treatment and early airway securing by intubation, cricothyroidotomy or tracheostomy save life.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Ear, Nose and Throat
question: Explain the nursing assessment of the ear, nose and throat and the related diagnostic tests.
answer_html:
Introduction A systematic ENT assessment – history, examination and diagnostic tests – helps detect ear, nose and throat disorders early and plan care. The nurse collects the history, assists the doctor during examination and prepares patients for tests.

1. History

  • Ear: hearing loss (onset, side, progression), ear discharge (colour, smell), earache, tinnitus, vertigo, itching, ear surgery, noise exposure, ototoxic drug use, family history of deafness.
  • Nose: nasal obstruction, discharge (watery, purulent, blood-stained), sneezing, epistaxis, loss of smell, facial pain, post-nasal drip, snoring.
  • Throat: sore throat, difficulty or pain in swallowing, hoarseness, stridor, cough, lump in the neck, weight loss; tobacco, alcohol and areca-nut use.
  • General – allergies, diabetes, hypertension, bleeding disorders, occupation.

2. Physical examination (using a head mirror or headlight)

  • Ear: inspection of pinna and pre/post-auricular area; otoscopy – pull the pinna up and back in adults, down and back in children; a normal tympanic membrane is pearly grey with a cone of light antero-inferiorly; look for wax, discharge, perforation, bulging; tuning fork tests (Rinne, Weber); facial nerve function.
  • Nose: external shape; anterior rhinoscopy with a nasal speculum (septum, turbinates, discharge, polyps); cold spatula test for patency; tenderness over sinuses; posterior rhinoscopy.
  • Throat and neck: lips, teeth, gums, tongue, palate, tonsils (size, exudate), posterior pharyngeal wall; indirect laryngoscopy with a laryngeal mirror; palpation of neck lymph nodes, thyroid and salivary glands.

3. Diagnostic tests | Test | Purpose | |---|---| | Pure-tone audiometry | Measures hearing threshold (dB) at different frequencies; distinguishes conductive and sensorineural loss | | Speech audiometry | Speech discrimination; hearing-aid fitting | | Impedance audiometry (tympanometry) | Middle-ear pressure and mobility – type A normal, B flat (fluid/perforation), C negative pressure, As stiff (otosclerosis) | | Otoacoustic emissions (OAE) | Newborn hearing screening; cochlear function | | BERA (brainstem evoked response audiometry) | Hearing in infants and uncooperative patients; retrocochlear lesions | | Caloric test, videonystagmography | Vestibular function in vertigo | | Nasal endoscopy, laryngoscopy (flexible/direct) | Visualisation and biopsy of lesions | | X-ray (Water's view), CT scan of sinuses/temporal bone, MRI | Sinusitis, cholesteatoma, tumours, acoustic neuroma | | Throat swab, ear swab culture | Identify organisms | | FNAC/biopsy | Neck swellings, suspected cancers |

4. Nurse's role

  • Explain the procedure, ensure comfort and privacy, position the patient correctly (sitting upright facing the examiner), hold children safely, keep instruments and light ready, maintain asepsis, observe after procedures (e.g. gagging, bleeding after biopsy), and document findings.

Conclusion ENT assessment combines a focused history, systematic examination of ear, nose, throat and neck, and tests such as audiometry, tympanometry, OAE, BERA, endoscopy and imaging. Good nursing preparation and assistance make assessment accurate and comfortable.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Ear, Nose and Throat
question: Define Ménière's disease.
answer_html:
Ménière's disease is a disorder of the inner ear due to endolymphatic hydrops (abnormal accumulation of endolymph in the membranous labyrinth), characterised by recurrent attacks of:

  1. Rotatory vertigo lasting 20 minutes to several hours, with nausea and vomiting,
  2. Fluctuating sensorineural hearing loss (low frequency at first),
  3. Tinnitus, and
  4. A sense of fullness in the ear.

It commonly affects adults aged 30–50 years, usually in one ear. Treatment includes low-salt diet, betahistine, vestibular sedatives, diuretics and, in resistant cases, intratympanic gentamicin or surgery.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Ear, Nose and Throat
question: Define quinsy.
answer_html:
Quinsy (peritonsillar abscess) is a collection of pus in the peritonsillar space – between the capsule of the tonsil and the superior constrictor muscle – usually as a complication of acute tonsillitis in adolescents and adults.

Features: severe unilateral sore throat, painful swallowing, drooling, trismus (difficulty in opening the mouth), "hot potato" (muffled) voice, referred earache, fever; the soft palate bulges and the uvula is pushed to the opposite side.

Treatment: IV antibiotics (penicillin with metronidazole), needle aspiration or incision and drainage, analgesics, fluids; interval tonsillectomy after 4–6 weeks.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Ear, Nose and Throat
question: Differentiate between rhinorrhoea and otorrhoea.
answer_html:
Rhinorrhoea Otorrhoea
Discharge from the nose Discharge from the ear
Watery – allergic or viral rhinitis; mucopurulent – sinusitis; blood-stained – trauma, tumour Mucopurulent – CSOM (safe type); scanty, foul-smelling – CSOM with cholesteatoma; watery – otitis externa; blood-stained – trauma
CSF rhinorrhoea – clear, watery, usually one-sided, increases on bending forward; after anterior cranial fossa fracture CSF otorrhoea – clear fluid from the ear after middle cranial fossa (temporal bone) fracture
Tests – nasal endoscopy, glucose/β2-transferrin for CSF Tests – otoscopy, culture, CT temporal bone

Nursing point: if CSF leak is suspected, do not pack the nose or ear, do not suction through the nose, avoid nose blowing, keep the head elevated and report immediately (risk of meningitis).

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Ear, Nose and Throat
question: List four ototoxic drugs.
answer_html:
Ototoxic drugs damage the cochlea or vestibular system, causing tinnitus, hearing loss or giddiness.

  1. Aminoglycoside antibiotics – streptomycin (mainly vestibular), gentamicin, amikacin, kanamycin, neomycin (cochlear).
  2. Loop diuretics – furosemide (especially rapid IV injection, high doses, with aminoglycosides).
  3. Anticancer drugs – cisplatin, carboplatin.
  4. Salicylates (aspirin) in high doses (reversible tinnitus) and quinine/chloroquine. Others – vancomycin, high-dose IV erythromycin, ear drops containing aminoglycosides used with a perforated ear drum.

Nursing: baseline audiometry, monitor for tinnitus and giddiness, give IV furosemide slowly, and report early symptoms.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Ear, Nose and Throat
question: Name the types of hearing aids.
answer_html:
Types of hearing aids

  1. Body-worn (pocket) hearing aid – larger, powerful, low cost; for severe loss and elderly users.
  2. Behind-the-ear (BTE) – most commonly used, suitable for all ages and most degrees of loss.
  3. Receiver-in-canal (RIC) – small BTE with the receiver in the ear canal.
  4. In-the-ear (ITE), in-the-canal (ITC) and completely-in-canal (CIC) – custom-made, less visible; for mild to moderate loss.
  5. Spectacle hearing aids and bone-conduction aids/bone-anchored hearing aid (BAHA) – for canal atresia or chronically discharging ears.
  6. Cochlear implant – surgically implanted electronic device for severe–profound sensorineural loss (stimulates the auditory nerve directly). Modern aids are digital and programmable.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Ear, Nose and Throat
question: What is tympanoplasty?
answer_html:
Tympanoplasty is an operation to eradicate disease from the middle ear and reconstruct the hearing mechanism – the tympanic membrane (ear drum) with or without the ossicular chain.

  • Type I tympanoplasty (myringoplasty) – repair of the ear-drum perforation alone, usually with a temporalis fascia graft.
  • Higher types (II–V) also reconstruct the ossicles (ossiculoplasty).
  • Indication: chronic suppurative otitis media with a dry central perforation and conductive deafness.
  • Post-operative care: keep the ear dry, avoid nose blowing and straining, sneeze with the mouth open, avoid air travel and swimming until permitted, and report pain, discharge or giddiness.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Ear, Nose and Throat
question: What is myringotomy? Write the indications for grommet insertion.
answer_html:
Myringotomy is a surgical incision in the tympanic membrane (usually in the antero-inferior or postero-inferior quadrant) to drain fluid or pus from the middle ear and relieve pressure.

Grommet (ventilation/tympanostomy tube) – a small tube placed in the myringotomy opening to keep the middle ear ventilated for several months; it usually falls out on its own after 6–12 months.

Indications

  1. Otitis media with effusion (glue ear) persisting for 3 months or more with hearing loss, especially in children with speech delay.
  2. Recurrent acute otitis media.
  3. Acute suppurative otitis media with a bulging, painful ear drum or complications.
  4. Eustachian tube dysfunction, barotrauma.

Care: keep the ear dry (ear plugs during bathing/swimming), report ear discharge.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Eye
question: (a) Define glaucoma. (2 marks) (b) Explain the pathophysiology of glaucoma. (5 marks) (c) Discuss the collaborative management of a patient with glaucoma. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Open-angle versus angle-closure glaucoma
labels: open angle – normal-looking angle but blocked trabecular meshwork; angle closure – iris bulging forward (iris bombé) closing the angle after pupillary block; arrows showing aqueous flow from ciliary body through pupil to trabecular meshwork and Schlemm's canal

answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks) Glaucoma is a group of eye diseases characterised by a progressive optic neuropathy – damage to the optic nerve with cupping of the optic disc and characteristic visual-field loss – usually associated with raised intraocular pressure (IOP). Normal IOP is 10–21 mmHg. Glaucoma is a leading cause of irreversible blindness in India; most people with it do not know they have it, which is why it is called the "silent thief of sight".

Classification (for understanding)

  • Primary open-angle glaucoma (POAG) – angle is open; slow, painless rise in IOP.
  • Primary angle-closure glaucoma (PACG) – angle is narrow or closed; more common in Indians and other Asians; may present as an acute attack.
  • Normal-tension glaucoma – optic nerve damage with IOP within the normal range.
