  • Secondary glaucoma – due to other conditions: steroid-induced (misuse of steroid eye drops), lens-induced (swollen or hypermature cataract – common in India because of delayed cataract surgery), uveitis, neovascular (diabetes, retinal vein occlusion), trauma.
  • Congenital/developmental glaucoma – in infants (large hazy eyes, watering, photophobia – buphthalmos).

(b) Pathophysiology (5 marks) 1. Normal aqueous dynamics

  • Aqueous humour is produced by the ciliary processes at about 2–3 µL per minute.
  • It flows from the posterior chamber through the pupil into the anterior chamber, and leaves the eye mainly through the trabecular meshwork and Schlemm's canal into the episcleral veins (conventional outflow), with a smaller part through the uveoscleral route.
  • IOP depends on the balance between production and outflow. Any obstruction to outflow raises IOP.

2. Primary open-angle glaucoma

  • With age and genetic predisposition, resistance to outflow increases in the trabecular meshwork, although the angle looks open.
  • IOP rises slowly (often 22–35 mmHg) without symptoms.
  • Raised pressure compresses and distorts the optic nerve fibres at the lamina cribrosa, and reduces blood flow to the optic nerve head (mechanical and vascular theories).
  • Retinal ganglion cells die (apoptosis) and the nerve fibre layer thins, producing progressive cupping of the optic disc (cup–disc ratio above 0.6, or asymmetry between eyes).
  • Visual-field defects appear in a typical sequence – paracentral scotoma → arcuate (Bjerrum's) scotoma → nasal step → constriction of the peripheral field → tubular (tunnel) vision → finally loss of central vision.
  • Because central vision is preserved until late and there is no pain or redness, the disease is usually detected only after severe damage.

3. Primary angle-closure glaucoma

  • Occurs in eyes with a narrow anterior chamber angle – small hypermetropic eyes, a thick lens in older age, female sex, Asian ethnicity.
  • When the pupil is mid-dilated (dim light, emotional stress, dilating drops or anticholinergic drugs), the iris touches the lens and blocks the flow of aqueous through the pupil (pupillary block).
  • Pressure builds up behind the iris, which bows forward (iris bombé) and closes the angle, cutting off outflow.
  • IOP rises suddenly to 40–80 mmHg → acute angle-closure attack: severe eye pain, headache, nausea and vomiting, blurred vision, coloured haloes around lights, red eye with ciliary congestion, hazy cornea (oedema), shallow anterior chamber, fixed, mid-dilated, vertically oval pupil, and a stony-hard eye.
  • Without urgent treatment, the optic nerve and iris become ischaemic and permanent peripheral anterior synechiae form, leading to chronic angle-closure glaucoma.

4. Risk factors

  • Age above 40, family history in first-degree relatives, high myopia (POAG), hypermetropia (PACG), diabetes, hypertension, long-term steroid use, eye injury, thin cornea.

5. Diagnosis

  • Tonometry (Goldmann applanation – gold standard; non-contact air-puff), gonioscopy (angle open or closed), ophthalmoscopy (cup–disc ratio), perimetry (visual fields), optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the nerve fibre layer, pachymetry (corneal thickness).

(c) Collaborative management of glaucoma (8 marks) Collaborative management means that the ophthalmologist, nurse, optometrist, pharmacist, patient and family (and, when needed, the physician and social worker) work together to lower IOP to a "target pressure" and preserve vision for life. Lost vision cannot be restored, so the goals are early detection, adequate pressure control and lifelong adherence.

1. Medical management (ophthalmologist and pharmacist)

  • Topical drugs (first line):
    • Prostaglandin analogues – latanoprost 0.005% once at night (increase uveoscleral outflow).
    • β-blockers – timolol 0.5% twice daily (reduce aqueous production; avoid in asthma and heart block).
    • α2-agonists – brimonidine; carbonic anhydrase inhibitors – dorzolamide, brinzolamide.
    • Miotics – pilocarpine (angle closure).
    • Fixed-combination drops to reduce the number of bottles.
  • Systemic drugs – oral/IV acetazolamide; IV mannitol or oral glycerol for very high pressure.

2. Laser treatment

  • Laser peripheral iridotomy (Nd:YAG) – creates a small opening in the peripheral iris so that aqueous bypasses the pupil; treatment of choice in angle closure and prophylactically in the other eye.
  • Selective laser trabeculoplasty (SLT) – improves trabecular outflow in POAG; can be first-line or added to drops.
  • Cyclophotocoagulation – reduces aqueous production in refractory glaucoma.

3. Surgical treatment

  • Trabeculectomy – creates a guarded channel from the anterior chamber to a subconjunctival "bleb", often with mitomycin C to prevent scarring.
  • Glaucoma drainage devices (Ahmed valve, low-cost Indian aqueous drainage implants), minimally invasive glaucoma surgery; goniotomy/trabeculotomy for congenital glaucoma.

4. Emergency management of acute angle-closure (team approach)

  • Immediate IV acetazolamide 500 mg, topical timolol, brimonidine, steroid, then pilocarpine 2% once IOP begins to fall; IV mannitol if needed; analgesics and antiemetics; laser iridotomy in both eyes after the attack settles.
  • The nurse recognises the attack, starts ordered drugs promptly, keeps the patient lying supine, monitors IOP response, pain and vomiting, and avoids any dilating drugs.

5. Nursing management a) Assessment

  • Visual acuity, IOP records, pain, haloes, field loss affecting daily life; history of asthma, heart disease and kidney stones (drug choice); medication history including steroid drops and anticholinergic drugs.

b) Medication teaching and adherence

  • Teach correct instillation: wash hands, pull the lower lid, one drop, close the eye gently and press the inner corner for 1–2 minutes (reduces systemic side effects), 5-minute gap between different drops, ointment last.
  • Fix drops to daily routines (e.g. latanoprost after dinner), use reminders on the mobile phone, keep a written schedule; involve a family member for elderly patients.
  • Explain that glaucoma is lifelong – drops must be continued even when the patient feels no difference; do not stop drops without advice; bring all bottles to each visit.
  • Teach side effects – darkening of iris and longer lashes (latanoprost), slow pulse and breathlessness (timolol), tingling and frequent urination (acetazolamide); dim vision in poor light (pilocarpine).

c) Safety and daily living

  • Prevent falls – good lighting at home, remove clutter, use handrails, extra care on stairs and at night.
  • Avoid self-medication, especially steroid eye drops and cold/allergy tablets with anticholinergic effects; inform every doctor about glaucoma.
  • Moderate, regular exercise is helpful; avoid prolonged head-down postures and heavy straining; drink fluids in small amounts through the day rather than large volumes at once.

d) Care after laser and surgery

  • After iridotomy – check IOP after 1 hour, give steroid drops, report pain or blurring.
  • After trabeculectomy – eye shield (especially at night), no rubbing or pressure on the eye, avoid bending, lifting and straining, keep water and dust out of the eye, use drops as ordered; report immediately redness, pain, discharge or reduced vision (bleb infection/endophthalmitis can blind the eye).

e) Follow-up and screening

  • Regular review every 3–6 months – IOP, fundus, visual fields, OCT.
  • Screen first-degree relatives above 40 years; refer diabetics and long-term steroid users for eye checks; eye screening camps and Ayushman Arogya Mandirs help in early detection.

f) Psychosocial support and rehabilitation

  • Many patients fear blindness; give honest reassurance that treatment can preserve remaining vision.
  • Refer those with advanced loss for low-vision aids and rehabilitation; inform about free services under the National Programme for Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment (NPCBVI).

Nursing diagnoses (examples) | Nursing diagnosis | Key interventions | |---|---| | Disturbed visual sensory perception related to optic nerve damage | Safe environment, orientation, low-vision aids | | Acute pain related to raised IOP (acute attack) | Prompt drugs, supine position, analgesics, antiemetics | | Risk for ineffective self-health management related to complex lifelong regimen | Teaching, reminders, family involvement | | Anxiety related to fear of blindness | Explanation, reassurance, counselling |

Nursing importance

  • Since glaucoma damage is permanent and silent, the nurse's role in screening, teaching instillation and ensuring adherence decides whether a patient keeps or loses sight.
  • Recognising an acute angle-closure attack – a red painful eye with vomiting and haloes – and starting treatment immediately can save the eye.

Conclusion Glaucoma is a progressive optic neuropathy usually caused by raised IOP due to impaired aqueous outflow, either slowly (open angle) or suddenly (angle closure). Collaborative management – drugs, laser, surgery, careful nursing education, safety measures and lifelong follow-up – preserves the patient's remaining vision.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Eye
question: (a) Define cataract and describe its types. (3 marks) (b) Explain the clinical manifestations and diagnosis of cataract. (4 marks) (c) Describe the surgical management and the pre-operative and post-operative nursing care of a patient undergoing cataract surgery. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Types of cataract in the lens
labels: posterior subcapsular (plaque at the back of the lens)
mature (whole lens white); position of posterior chamber intraocular lens in the capsular bag after surgery

answer_html:
(a) Definition and types of cataract (3 marks) Cataract is an opacity (clouding) of the crystalline lens or its capsule that reduces the passage of light to the retina and causes gradual, painless blurring of vision. It is the commonest cause of blindness in India, responsible for about two-thirds of blindness in people aged 50 years and above, and is curable by surgery.

1. According to age of onset

  • Congenital cataract – present at birth or in the first year; causes: maternal rubella, galactosaemia, Down syndrome, hereditary; seen as a white pupil (leukocoria); needs early surgery to prevent amblyopia.
  • Developmental/juvenile cataract – in childhood and adolescence.
  • Senile (age-related) cataract – after 50 years; the commonest type.

2. According to location (morphology) – mainly senile types

  • Nuclear cataract – hardening and yellow-brown discolouration of the central nucleus; causes a myopic shift ("second sight") – elderly may read without glasses for a while.
  • Cortical cataract – spoke-like (cuneiform) opacities in the cortex, starting at the periphery; glare.
  • Posterior subcapsular cataract – plaque under the posterior capsule; early glare and poor near/reading vision; common in diabetics, steroid users and after radiation.
  • Capsular, polar, lamellar (zonular), sutural – mostly congenital types.

3. According to stage of maturity (senile cortical cataract)

  • Immature – lens partly opaque; iris shadow seen on oblique illumination.
  • Intumescent – lens swells with fluid (risk of phacomorphic glaucoma).
  • Mature – lens completely opaque and white; no iris shadow.
  • Hypermature – Morgagnian (cortex liquefies and the nucleus sinks) or shrunken; risk of phacolytic glaucoma and lens-induced uveitis.

4. According to cause (secondary/acquired)

  • Traumatic (blunt or penetrating injury), metabolic (diabetic – "snowflake", galactosaemia, hypocalcaemia), drug-induced (corticosteroids, chlorpromazine, miotics), complicated (uveitis, high myopia, retinal detachment), radiation (X-rays, infrared – glass-blower's cataract), electrical injury.
  • After-cataract – posterior capsular opacification after cataract surgery, treated by Nd:YAG laser capsulotomy.

Risk factors for senile cataract: ageing, diabetes, smoking, ultraviolet (sunlight) exposure in outdoor workers, repeated dehydrating illnesses, steroid use, malnutrition, alcohol and family history.

(b) Clinical manifestations and diagnosis (4 marks) 1. Symptoms

  • Gradual, painless, progressive blurring of vision for distance and near.
  • Glare and photophobia – difficulty driving at night due to headlights (especially posterior subcapsular).
  • Haloes and coloured fringes around lights; monocular diplopia or polyopia in early cortical cataract.
  • Frequent change of spectacles; temporary improvement of near vision ("second sight") in nuclear cataract.
  • Faded colours and poor contrast; difficulty with reading, sewing, recognising faces.
  • Eventually, only perception of light in mature cataract.

2. Signs

  • Reduced visual acuity on the Snellen chart (not fully improved by pinhole).
  • Greyish or white pupil (leukocoria in mature cataract).
  • Diminished or absent red reflex on distant direct ophthalmoscopy; dark spots against the red glow.
  • Iris shadow present in immature cataract.

3. Diagnosis

  • Visual acuity (distance and near) and torch-light examination.
  • Slit-lamp biomicroscopy – type and density of opacity.
  • Fundus examination after dilatation – to exclude retinal or optic nerve disease that would limit vision after surgery.
  • B-scan ultrasound if the fundus cannot be seen (to exclude retinal detachment).
  • IOP measurement; lacrimal sac syringing (to rule out dacryocystitis – a source of post-operative infection).
  • Keratometry and A-scan biometry to calculate the intraocular lens (IOL) power.
  • General tests – blood sugar, BP, urine, ECG in elderly patients.

(c) Surgical management and nursing care (8 marks) 1. Surgical management

  • There is no medicine that dissolves cataract; surgery is the only effective treatment. It is advised when the cataract interferes with daily activities – one need not wait for the cataract to "ripen".
  • Manual small-incision cataract surgery (SICS/MSICS) – sutureless, low-cost and fast; widely used in Indian high-volume and camp-based programmes.
  • Phacoemulsification – the lens is broken by ultrasound and aspirated through a 2–3 mm incision; a foldable IOL is inserted; quick visual recovery.
  • Extracapsular cataract extraction (ECCE) – older technique with sutures; intracapsular extraction (ICCE) is now obsolete.
  • A posterior chamber IOL is placed in the capsular bag in almost all adults; surgery is done under topical or peribulbar anaesthesia as day care.
  • Congenital cataract – early lens aspiration with IOL or contact lens, followed by amblyopia treatment.
  • Free cataract surgery with IOL is provided under NPCBVI.

2. Pre-operative nursing care

  1. Assessment – visual acuity of both eyes, general health, blood sugar control, BP, cough, urinary problems (prostate), anticoagulant use (inform surgeon).
  2. Treat infections – conjunctivitis, stye, blepharitis, dacryocystitis; sac syringing done.
  3. Explanation and consent – the patient will be awake under local anaesthesia and must keep the head still and not cough or talk during surgery; explain post-operative care; obtain informed consent; mark the operative eye.
  4. Pre-operative drops as ordered – antibiotic drops for 1–3 days, mydriatic drops (tropicamide, phenylephrine) and NSAID drops on the day of surgery to keep the pupil dilated.
  5. Face wash, clean clothes, remove ornaments and kajal; empty the bladder; continue usual antihypertensive and diabetic medicines as advised; check vital signs before shifting.

3. Post-operative nursing care (immediately and in the ward)

  1. Apply eye pad and protective shield; patient lies on the back or on the unoperated side.
  2. Monitor vital signs; provide paracetamol for mild pain; severe pain, nausea or vomiting suggest raised IOP or infection – report at once.
  3. Next-day dressing – remove the pad, clean lids gently with sterile swabs from inner to outer canthus, check vision and the eye.
  4. Start post-operative drops – antibiotic + steroid (e.g. moxifloxacin, prednisolone/dexamethasone) four to six times a day, tapered over 4–6 weeks, and NSAID drops; teach the patient and a family member the correct technique and timetable.
  5. Prevent constipation, coughing and straining (laxatives, cough treatment).

4. Discharge instructions

  • Wear the eye shield at night for 1–2 weeks (prevents rubbing during sleep) and dark glasses during the day (glare, dust).
  • Do not rub or press the eye; do not splash water into the eye; clean the face with a damp cloth; avoid head bath for about a week or as advised.
  • Avoid bending below the waist, lifting heavy weights and straining for 2–3 weeks; avoid dusty and smoky places (chulha smoke), swimming and applying kajal/surma or eye make-up for at least a month.
  • Normal walking, eating, watching TV and light reading are allowed.
  • Report immediately if there is increasing pain, redness, discharge, decreasing vision (endophthalmitis – an emergency, usually in the first week), flashes or a curtain over vision (retinal detachment), or haloes with headache (raised IOP).
  • Follow-up visits – day 1, about 1 week and 4–6 weeks (final refraction and prescription of glasses); later blurring may be due to posterior capsular opacification, which is easily treated with laser.

5. Complications to watch for

  • During surgery – posterior capsule rupture, vitreous loss.
  • Early – corneal oedema, raised IOP, endophthalmitis, iritis, wound leak, hyphaema.
  • Late – posterior capsular opacification, cystoid macular oedema, retinal detachment, IOL decentration.

Nursing importance

  • Cataract surgery is the commonest and most rewarding operation in India; good pre- and post-operative nursing – infection prevention, correct drops and clear instructions – largely decides the final visual outcome.
  • Nurses also motivate elderly people to undergo timely surgery, dispelling myths that "cataract should ripen" or that surgery is dangerous in winter or summer.

Conclusion Cataract is a clouding of the lens that may be congenital, age-related or secondary, and causes painless progressive loss of vision. Surgery with IOL implantation (SICS or phacoemulsification) restores sight, and careful pre-operative preparation, post-operative care and discharge teaching ensure a safe and lasting result.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Eye
question: (a) Define retinal detachment and describe its types. (3 marks) (b) Explain its clinical manifestations and diagnosis. (4 marks) (c) Describe the medical, surgical and nursing management of a patient with retinal detachment. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Types of retinal detachment
labels: rhegmatogenous – retinal tear allowing vitreous fluid under the retina; tractional – fibrous membranes pulling the retina (diabetic retinopathy); exudative – fluid leaking from the choroid without a tear; scleral buckle indenting the eye wall and intraocular gas bubble pressing the retina back

answer_html:
(a) Definition and types (3 marks) Retinal detachment (RD) is the separation of the neurosensory retina from the underlying retinal pigment epithelium, with accumulation of fluid in the subretinal space. The detached photoreceptors lose their nourishment from the choroid, so vision is lost in the affected area. RD is an ocular emergency, especially while the macula is still attached.

Types

  1. Rhegmatogenous RD (most common) – due to a retinal break (tear or hole) through which liquefied vitreous passes under the retina. Associated with posterior vitreous detachment in older age, high myopia, previous cataract surgery, trauma and lattice degeneration.
  2. Tractional RD – fibrovascular membranes pull the retina away without a break; seen in proliferative diabetic retinopathy, retinopathy of prematurity, sickle cell retinopathy and penetrating injuries.
  3. Exudative (serous) RD – fluid leaks from choroidal vessels without a break; seen in severe hypertension, pre-eclampsia/eclampsia, choroidal tumours, inflammation (uveitis, scleritis) and kidney failure.
  4. Combined tractional–rhegmatogenous detachment.

Risk factors: high myopia, age 50–70 years, previous RD in the other eye, cataract surgery, blunt eye injury (cricket ball, fist), diabetes, family history, connective-tissue disorders (Marfan, Stickler syndromes).

(b) Clinical manifestations and diagnosis (4 marks) 1. Symptoms (typically painless)

  • Photopsia – flashes of light, especially in the dark, caused by traction on the retina.
  • Floaters – a sudden shower of black dots, cobwebs or "flies" (from posterior vitreous detachment or bleeding).
  • A shadow, veil or curtain coming across part of the visual field, usually starting in the periphery and spreading.
  • Blurred or distorted vision (metamorphopsia) and sudden loss of central vision when the macula detaches.
  • No pain and no redness – patients often delay seeking care.

2. Signs

  • Reduced visual acuity; visual-field defect corresponding to the detached area.
  • Relative afferent pupillary defect in large detachments; low IOP in rhegmatogenous RD.
  • Fundus: the detached retina appears grey, elevated, with folds, moving with eye movements; a horseshoe tear may be seen; pigment cells in the anterior vitreous ("tobacco dust").

3. Diagnosis

  • Visual acuity and confrontation field testing.
  • Indirect ophthalmoscopy with scleral indentation after full pupil dilatation – the gold standard to find all breaks.
  • Slit-lamp examination with a 90D lens.
  • B-scan ultrasonography when the fundus is not visible (dense cataract, vitreous haemorrhage).
  • OCT of the macula; fundus photography; tests for underlying causes (blood sugar, BP).

(c) Medical, surgical and nursing management (8 marks) 1. Medical and laser management

  • A retinal tear without detachment is sealed by laser photocoagulation or cryotherapy (retinopexy), creating a scar that prevents fluid entering under the retina.
  • Exudative RD is treated by treating the cause – BP control, management of pre-eclampsia, steroids for inflammation, tumour treatment.
  • Pre-operative drugs – mydriatics/cycloplegics, antibiotics; control of diabetes and hypertension.

2. Surgical management (urgent, ideally before the macula detaches)

  • Pneumatic retinopexy – an expanding gas bubble (SF₆ or C₃F₈) is injected into the vitreous to press the retina against the wall, combined with cryo or laser; needs strict head positioning.
  • Scleral buckling – a silicone band or explant is sutured on the outer wall of the eye to indent it towards the tear, relieving traction, with cryotherapy and drainage of subretinal fluid; used mainly in younger patients.
  • Pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) – removal of the vitreous and traction membranes, flattening of the retina, endolaser, and internal tamponade with gas or silicone oil (oil is removed after 3–6 months by another operation); used for complex, pseudophakic and tractional detachments.
  • Success rates are high, but visual outcome is better when the macula was still attached at surgery.

3. Pre-operative nursing care

  1. Treat RD as an emergency – arrange early surgery; explain urgency to the patient and family.
  2. Reduce eye movement and activity as advised – bed rest or limited activity, avoid reading and sudden head movements; position the head as instructed by the surgeon so that the detachment does not spread towards the macula.
  3. Avoid straining, coughing, bending and lifting; give stool softeners if needed.
  4. Instil dilating drops as ordered; record visual acuity; complete investigations, consent and NPO instructions.
  5. Ensure safety – reduced vision increases the risk of falls; keep the call bell and personal items within reach.
  6. Relieve anxiety about loss of vision through clear explanation.

4. Post-operative nursing care

  1. Positioning – most important after gas or oil tamponade:
    • The patient may need face-down (prone) positioning or lying on a specified side for up to 1–2 weeks (for example, about 50 minutes of every hour), so that the bubble, which floats upwards, presses on the break.
    • Use special face-down pillows or a massage table; protect pressure points on the forehead, cheeks and chin; encourage short breaks as allowed; help with eating and drinking in the sitting-forward position.
    • Do not lie flat on the back while gas is in the eye (the bubble presses on the lens and angle, raising IOP and causing cataract).
  2. Pain and nausea – moderate pain is expected (more after buckling); give analgesics and antiemetics; severe pain with nausea or headache may mean raised IOP – report immediately.
  3. Eye drops – antibiotics, steroids, cycloplegics (atropine) and IOP-lowering drops as ordered; eye shield; no rubbing.
  4. Monitor vision, IOP, wound, discharge and signs of infection.
  5. Gas precautions – no air travel, no travel to high altitudes and no nitrous-oxide anaesthesia until the gas is fully absorbed (about 2 weeks for SF₆ and 6–8 weeks for C₃F₈), because the gas expands at low pressure and can cause a dangerous rise in IOP; give the patient a warning wristband or card. Vision remains blurred until the gas is absorbed (a moving "level" line is seen).
  6. Psychological support – prolonged positioning is tiring and painful; explain its purpose, involve family, provide diversion such as radio or audio books.

5. Discharge teaching

  • Continue positioning and drops exactly as advised; avoid heavy lifting, bending, straining, contact sports and driving until permitted (usually 2–6 weeks).
  • Protect the eye from injury; wear an eye shield at night.
  • Report immediately any new flashes, floaters, curtain, increasing pain, redness or decrease in vision – signs of re-detachment or infection.
  • Attend follow-up visits; silicone oil removal will be planned later.
  • People with high myopia, diabetes or RD in one eye should have regular dilated eye examinations.

Nursing diagnoses (examples) | Nursing diagnosis | Key interventions | |---|---| | Disturbed visual sensory perception related to detached retina | Orientation, safety, assistance with activities | | Risk for injury (falls) related to impaired vision and positioning | Side rails, clear pathways, assisted ambulation | | Impaired comfort related to prolonged prone positioning | Pressure-relief pillows, skin care, scheduled breaks | | Anxiety related to possible loss of vision | Explanation, reassurance, family involvement | | Deficient knowledge regarding gas precautions | Teaching, written instructions, wristband |

Nursing importance

  • Teaching the public that "flashes, floaters and a curtain" are an emergency leads to early surgery while the macula is still attached, which greatly improves the chance of good vision.
  • Correct post-operative positioning, supervised by nurses, is essential for the retina to re-attach.

Conclusion Retinal detachment – rhegmatogenous, tractional or exudative – presents with painless flashes, floaters and a curtain-like field loss and needs urgent laser, pneumatic retinopexy, scleral buckling or vitrectomy. Pre-operative rest and safety, strict post-operative positioning, gas precautions and teaching are the cornerstones of nursing care.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Eye
question: (a) Define keratitis and corneal ulcer and list their causes. (3 marks) (b) Explain the clinical manifestations and diagnosis of corneal ulcer. (4 marks) (c) Describe the management and nursing care of a patient with corneal ulcer. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Signs of infective corneal ulcer
labels: greyish-white stromal infiltrate with epithelial defect staining green with fluorescein
fungal ulcer with feathery margins and satellite lesions

answer_html:
(a) Definitions and causes (3 marks) Keratitis is inflammation of the cornea. A corneal ulcer (ulcerative keratitis) is a loss of corneal epithelium with inflammation and necrosis of the underlying stroma, usually due to infection. In India, corneal opacity is the second commonest cause of blindness after cataract, and most of it follows infective corneal ulcers.

Causes A. Infective

  • Bacterial – Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pneumoniae (hypopyon ulcer), Pseudomonas aeruginosa (rapidly progressive, especially in contact-lens wearers), Moraxella, Nocardia.
  • Fungal – Fusarium and *Aspergillus – very common in Indian farmers after injury with vegetable matter (paddy and sugarcane leaves, thorns, wooden sticks, cow's tail), especially during harvest season; Candida in debilitated patients; misuse of steroid eye drops* worsens them.
  • Viral – herpes simplex virus (dendritic ulcer), herpes zoster ophthalmicus, adenovirus.
  • Protozoal – Acanthamoeba (contact-lens wearers using tap water, swimming with lenses).
  • Chlamydial – trachoma (now eliminated as a public-health problem in India).

B. Non-infective

  • Exposure keratitis – incomplete eyelid closure (facial palsy, unconscious and ICU patients, proptosis).
  • Neurotrophic keratitis – loss of corneal sensation (trigeminal nerve damage, diabetes, herpes zoster).
  • Vitamin A deficiency – xerophthalmia and keratomalacia in malnourished children.
  • Dry eye, allergic (vernal) shield ulcers, autoimmune (Mooren's ulcer).
  • Chemical, thermal and ultraviolet injury (welder's flash), corneal foreign bodies and abrasions.

Predisposing factors: corneal trauma (most important), contact-lens misuse, chronic dacryocystitis (infected tear sac), topical steroid use, diabetes, malnutrition, immunosuppression, and harmful traditional eye medicines (putting herbal juices, breast milk or other substances into the eye).

(b) Clinical manifestations and diagnosis (4 marks) 1. Symptoms

  • Pain (often severe, worse on blinking), redness, watering, photophobia (intolerance to light), blurred vision, foreign-body sensation, discharge (purulent in bacterial ulcer), spasm of the eyelids (blepharospasm).

2. Signs

  • Circumcorneal (ciliary) congestion – deep red flush around the cornea.
  • Greyish-white infiltrate or ulcer on the cornea with surrounding stromal oedema; the epithelial defect stains bright green with fluorescein.
  • Hypopyon – a level of pus in the lower anterior chamber (bacterial and fungal ulcers).
  • Fungal ulcer – dry-looking, raised slough with feathery margins, satellite lesions and immune ring.
  • Herpes simplex – branching dendritic ulcer with reduced corneal sensation.
  • Complications – descemetocele, corneal perforation (sudden relief of pain with gush of fluid, iris prolapse), endophthalmitis, secondary glaucoma, dense corneal scar (leucoma) causing permanent visual loss.

3. Diagnosis

  • History – injury (vegetable matter), contact-lens use, steroid drops, previous episodes; visual acuity.
  • Slit-lamp examination and fluorescein staining; corneal sensation.
  • Corneal scraping under topical anaesthesia from the ulcer edge and base for:
    • Gram stain (bacteria), 10% KOH wet mount (fungal filaments – quick, cheap and very useful), Giemsa, calcofluor white.
    • Culture and sensitivity – blood agar, chocolate agar, Sabouraud's dextrose agar (fungi).
  • PCR for herpes; confocal microscopy for Acanthamoeba and fungi.
  • Sac syringing, blood sugar.

(c) Management and nursing care (8 marks) 1. Medical management

  • Bacterial ulcer – fortified antibiotic drops (e.g. cefazolin 5% + tobramycin/gentamicin) or moxifloxacin 0.5%, hourly day and night for the first 48 hours, then tapered according to response and culture.
  • Fungal ulcer – natamycin 5% suspension hourly (drug of choice for filamentous fungi), voriconazole drops; oral antifungals for deep ulcers; treatment often continues for several weeks.
  • Herpes simplex – acyclovir 3% eye ointment five times a day ± oral acyclovir; steroids are not used in epithelial herpetic ulcers.
  • Acanthamoeba – polyhexamethylene biguanide (PHMB) or chlorhexidine drops with propamidine.
  • Supportive drugs – cycloplegics (atropine 1%) to relieve ciliary spasm and pain and prevent synechiae; oral analgesics; anti-glaucoma drugs if IOP is raised; vitamin C and lubricants; no topical steroids in active infective (especially fungal) ulcers.

2. Surgical management

  • Debridement of necrotic tissue; cyanoacrylate tissue glue with bandage contact lens for small perforations.
  • Therapeutic keratoplasty (corneal transplant) for non-healing ulcers or perforation; conjunctival flap; amniotic membrane graft; tarsorrhaphy for exposure ulcers.
  • Later, optical keratoplasty with donor cornea to restore vision from a dense scar.

3. Nursing care a) Drug administration – the core of treatment

  • Prepare a written hourly drop schedule for day and night; wake the patient at night for drops in the first days; train a family member to help.
  • Strict hand hygiene before and after touching the eye; separate bottles for each patient and each eye; keep fortified drops in the refrigerator and discard as instructed.
  • Keep 5 minutes between different drops; ointment last; clean discharge gently from inner to outer canthus with sterile swabs.

b) Comfort and protection

  • Give analgesics and cycloplegic drops as ordered; nurse in a dim, quiet room; provide dark glasses for photophobia.
  • Do not apply a tight eye pad on an infected ulcer (warmth and moisture favour microbial growth), unless advised for a specific reason.
  • Prevent pressure on the eye – no rubbing, no squeezing of lids; protective shield at night; avoid straining, coughing and bending (risk of perforation in deep ulcers) – give laxatives and cough treatment.

c) Monitoring

  • Daily assessment of pain, vision, size of infiltrate, hypopyon, discharge, IOP and response to treatment; report increasing pain, spreading ulcer or perforation immediately.
  • Monitor blood sugar in diabetics; observe for drug side effects.

d) Nutrition and general care

  • Nutritious diet rich in protein and vitamin A (green leafy vegetables, yellow fruits, eggs); vitamin A supplementation in children with xerophthalmia.
  • Treat dacryocystitis and other infection sources.

e) Psychological support

  • Treatment is long and the patient fears blindness; explain progress, encourage adherence and involve family; counsel about keratoplasty when needed.

f) Health education and prevention

  • Wear protective goggles during harvesting, grass-cutting, welding and hammering; seek immediate treatment after any eye injury.
  • Never use traditional or home remedies in the eye; avoid steroid eye drops without prescription (often sold over the counter).
  • Contact-lens hygiene – wash hands, never sleep or swim in lenses, never use tap water or saliva, replace cases regularly.
  • Ensure eye care for unconscious patients (lubrication, lid closure) to prevent exposure keratitis.
  • Promote eye donation – corneal transplantation can restore sight in corneal blindness.

Nursing diagnoses (examples) | Nursing diagnosis | Key interventions | |---|---| | Acute pain related to corneal inflammation and ciliary spasm | Cycloplegics, analgesics, dim light, dark glasses | | Risk for perforation/injury related to corneal thinning | Avoid pressure, straining and rubbing; shield; close monitoring | | Disturbed visual sensory perception | Safe environment, assistance with daily activities | | Risk for ineffective therapeutic regimen related to frequent drops | Written schedule, family training, reminders |

Nursing importance

  • The outcome of a corneal ulcer depends greatly on hourly, correctly instilled drops in the first days, which nurses and trained family members deliver.
  • Preventing eye injuries in agricultural communities and stopping harmful eye remedies can prevent much of India's corneal blindness.

Conclusion Corneal ulcers are mostly infective (bacterial, fungal, viral, Acanthamoeba) and present with pain, redness, photophobia and a staining corneal infiltrate, often with hypopyon. Identification of the organism by scraping, intensive specific drops, cycloplegics, surgery when needed and meticulous nursing care save the eye and vision.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Eye
question: Briefly explain the assessment of the eye with respect to visual acuity, extraocular muscle functions and pupil function.
answer_html:
Introduction Systematic eye assessment helps detect refractive errors, neurological problems and eye diseases early. The three basic components are visual acuity, extraocular muscle (EOM) function and pupillary function.

1. Visual acuity (VA)

  • Distance VA – Snellen chart at 6 metres (20 feet) in good light; test each eye separately (cover the other eye with an occluder without pressing), first without and then with glasses.
  • Recorded as a fraction: 6/6 normal, 6/12, 6/60, etc. (numerator = testing distance; denominator = distance at which a normal eye reads that line).
  • If the top letter is not read, the patient walks closer (5/60 ... 1/60); then finger counting (CF) at 1 m, hand movements (HM), perception of light (PL) with projection of rays, or no perception of light (NPL).
  • Pinhole test – improvement indicates a refractive error.
  • Children/illiterate adults – "E" chart (illiterate E), picture charts; infants – fixation and following.
  • Near vision – Jaeger or N-notation chart at 33–35 cm (N6 normal).

2. Extraocular muscle function

  • Six EOMs – medial rectus, lateral rectus (CN VI), superior oblique (CN IV), superior rectus, inferior rectus and inferior oblique (CN III) – "LR6 SO4, rest 3".
  • Inspection – ptosis, squint (strabismus), head tilt, nystagmus.
  • Corneal light reflex (Hirschberg test) – shine a torch at the eyes from 30–40 cm; reflections should be symmetrical.
  • Cover–uncover test – movement of the uncovered eye indicates a manifest squint.
  • Six cardinal positions of gaze – patient keeps the head still and follows a pen or finger in an "H" pattern; note restriction, double vision or nystagmus.
  • Convergence – bring the target towards the nose; both eyes should converge.

3. Pupil function

  • Size (normally 2–5 mm in room light), shape (round), equality (anisocoria more than 1 mm is significant).
  • Direct light reflex – the pupil constricts when light is shone into it.
  • Consensual reflex – the other pupil constricts at the same time.
  • Swinging flashlight test – detects a relative afferent pupillary defect (Marcus Gunn pupil) in optic nerve disease.
  • Accommodation (near) reflex – pupils constrict when focusing on a near object.
  • Normal findings recorded as PERRLA – Pupils Equal, Round, Reactive to Light and Accommodation.
  • Abnormal pupils: fixed dilated (CN III palsy, raised ICP, atropine), pinpoint (opioid or organophosphate poisoning, pontine haemorrhage), mid-dilated fixed oval (acute angle-closure glaucoma).

Nursing points

  • Ensure good lighting, explain each step, record findings accurately, and report sudden loss of vision, new squint/diplopia or unequal non-reacting pupils urgently.

Conclusion Assessment of visual acuity with Snellen and near charts, EOM function by light reflex, cover test and cardinal gazes, and pupil size and reflexes gives quick, valuable information about eye and neurological health.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Eye
question: Explain the types, clinical features and nursing management of conjunctivitis.
answer_html:
Definition Conjunctivitis is inflammation of the conjunctiva – the thin transparent membrane covering the white of the eye and inner eyelids. It is the commonest cause of "red eye" and spreads easily in homes, schools and hostels, especially during the monsoon ("Madras eye" outbreaks).

1. Types and causes | Type | Cause | Key features | |---|---|---| | Bacterial | Staphylococcus, Streptococcus pneumoniae, H. influenzae | Mucopurulent discharge, eyelids stuck together in the morning | | Viral | Adenovirus (epidemic keratoconjunctivitis), enterovirus, herpes | Watery discharge, very contagious, tender pre-auricular lymph nodes, often both eyes | | Allergic | Pollen, dust, animal dander; vernal keratoconjunctivitis in boys in hot climates | Intense itching, watering, ropy discharge, cobblestone papillae (vernal) | | Chlamydial | Chlamydia trachomatis | Trachoma, inclusion conjunctivitis | | Ophthalmia neonatorum | Gonococcus (2–5 days after birth), Chlamydia (5–14 days) | Swollen lids, purulent discharge in the newborn – emergency | | Chemical/irritant | Smoke, chemicals, chlorine | Burning, watering |

2. Clinical features

  • Redness (conjunctival congestion – superficial, bright red, more towards the fornices), discharge, gritty or burning sensation, itching (allergic), lid swelling, mild photophobia.
  • Vision and pupil are normal – pain, marked photophobia or reduced vision suggest something more serious (keratitis, iritis, glaucoma) and need referral.

3. Management

  • Bacterial – antibiotic drops (chloramphenicol, moxifloxacin) and ointment at night.
  • Viral – mostly self-limiting in 1–3 weeks; cold compresses, lubricants; antibiotics only if secondary infection; no steroids without an eye specialist.
  • Allergic – avoid allergens, cold compresses, antihistamine/mast-cell stabiliser drops (olopatadine), short course of steroid drops by the specialist.
  • Ophthalmia neonatorum – urgent systemic and topical antibiotics (e.g. ceftriaxone for gonococcal), cleaning of discharge; treat parents.

4. Nursing management

  1. Hand hygiene – the most important measure to prevent spread; avoid touching or rubbing the eyes.
  2. Clean discharge with boiled and cooled water and clean cotton, wiping from the inner to the outer corner, using a separate swab for each eye.
  3. Instil drops correctly; do not share drops, towels, handkerchiefs, pillows or eye cosmetics.
  4. Do not bandage or patch an infected eye.
  5. Dark glasses for comfort; cold compresses for viral and allergic types.
  6. Children should stay home from school while the eyes are discharging; patients should avoid swimming pools and crowded places.
  7. Avoid self-medication with steroid drops and harmful home remedies.
  8. Clean frequently touched surfaces; isolate patients in wards during outbreaks.

Conclusion Conjunctivitis may be bacterial, viral, allergic, chlamydial or neonatal; it causes red, discharging eyes with normal vision. Specific treatment, strict hand hygiene and good nursing care cure it and prevent outbreaks.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Eye
question: Explain eye donation and eye banking, with the role of the nurse.
tags: Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act
answer_html:
Introduction Eye donation is the voluntary gift of eyes after death so that the cornea can be transplanted to restore sight to people with corneal blindness. India has a large number of people waiting for donor corneas, and the shortage of donated eyes is a major barrier to curing corneal blindness. Eye donation and transplantation are regulated by the Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act (THOTA), 1994, amended 2011.

1. Facts about eye donation

  • Anyone can donate – of any age, sex, religion or blood group; people who wear spectacles, have had cataract surgery, or have diabetes or hypertension can donate.
  • A person may pledge eyes during life, but consent of the next of kin after death is essential.
  • Eyes must be removed within 6 hours of death; removal takes about 15–20 minutes and does not disfigure the face; it is free of cost and does not delay funeral rites.
  • The identity of donor and recipient is kept confidential.

2. Contraindications to eye donation

  • Death due to unknown cause; rabies, tetanus, HIV/AIDS, hepatitis B and C, syphilis, septicaemia, active encephalitis or meningitis, leukaemia and lymphoma, retinoblastoma and other eye cancers, Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease.

3. What to do after death (until the eye bank team arrives)

  1. Close the eyelids and cover them with moist cotton.
  2. Switch off overhead fans; keep the room cool (air-conditioner on if available).
  3. Raise the head with a pillow (about 6 inches) to reduce bleeding during removal.
  4. If possible, put ice packs over the closed eyes.
  5. Inform the nearest eye bank at once (national toll-free number 1919); keep the death certificate and consent ready.

4. Eye banking An eye bank is a non-profit organisation that collects, evaluates, preserves and distributes donated eyes.

  • Collection – whole eye (enucleation) or in-situ corneoscleral rim excision.
  • Evaluation – slit-lamp and specular microscopy (endothelial cell count); donor blood tested for HIV, hepatitis B and C, syphilis.
  • Preservation – McCarey–Kaufman (MK) medium at 4°C (about 4 days), Optisol (up to about 2 weeks), organ culture (weeks), glycerine (for emergency tectonic grafts).
  • Distribution to corneal surgeons for keratoplasty – penetrating (full thickness), lamellar (DALK) or endothelial (DSEK/DMEK).
  • Hospital Cornea Retrieval Programme – trained grief counsellors approach families of persons dying in hospitals; this is the most productive source of donor eyes.

5. Role of the nurse

  • Motivate and educate the public and patients' families; correct myths (religious objections, disfigurement, rebirth beliefs).
  • Identify potential donors in wards and ICUs, inform the eye bank promptly and support the family's decision with empathy.
  • Carry out care of the eyes after death as above; assist the eye-bank team; maintain records.
  • Care for keratoplasty patients – long-term drops, IOP checks and teaching the warning signs of graft rejection ("RSVP" – Redness, Sensitivity to light, Vision loss, Pain).
  • Participate in the National Eye Donation Fortnight (25 August–8 September).

Conclusion Eye donation is a simple, painless and free gift that restores sight to people with corneal blindness. Prompt preservation of the donor eyes, efficient eye banking and the nurse's motivation and support of families are essential to meet India's need for corneas.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Eye
question: Define blindness. Explain its causes in India and the National Programme for Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment.
answer_html:
Definition Blindness is defined (WHO; adopted in India in 2017) as presenting visual acuity of less than 3/60 in the better eye, or a visual field of less than 10 degrees around the centre of fixation. Visual impairment includes moderate (worse than 6/18 to 6/60) and severe (worse than 6/60 to 3/60) categories. India earlier used less than 6/60 as the cut-off for blindness.

1. Causes of blindness in India In adults (50 years and above)

  • Cataract – the leading cause (about two-thirds of blindness).
  • Corneal opacity – after infections, injuries and vitamin A deficiency.
  • Complications of cataract surgery (poor outcomes, uncorrected aphakia).
  • Glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy and other posterior-segment diseases (age-related macular degeneration).
  • Uncorrected refractive errors – the commonest cause of visual impairment.

In children

  • Refractive errors, amblyopia, congenital cataract and glaucoma, vitamin A deficiency (xerophthalmia), retinopathy of prematurity (ROP), congenital anomalies, injuries, cortical visual impairment.

2. National Programme for Control of Blindness and Visual Impairment (NPCBVI)

  • Launched in 1976 as the National Programme for Control of Blindness – India was among the first countries to start such a programme; renamed NPCBVI in 2017.
  • Goal: reduce the prevalence of blindness and visual impairment.
  • Main activities:
    1. Free cataract surgery with IOL at government and NGO hospitals and through outreach camps.
    2. School eye screening and free spectacles for children with refractive errors; free reading glasses for elderly persons.
    3. Collection of donated eyes and support to eye banks and keratoplasty.
    4. Screening and treatment of diabetic retinopathy, glaucoma and ROP.
    5. Eye care at primary level – vision centres and eye care as a service package at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs.
    6. Training of ophthalmic manpower, IEC activities, mobile ophthalmic units.

3. Rehabilitation of the blind

  • Low-vision aids (magnifiers, telescopes, large-print materials), Braille, white cane, orientation and mobility training, screen-reader software and mobile accessibility.
  • Vocational training, disability certificate and UDID card, benefits under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016 (blindness and low vision are recognised disabilities).

4. Role of the nurse

  • Prevention – vitamin A supplementation, measles immunisation, eye hygiene, protective eyewear, control of diabetes and hypertension, avoiding harmful eye remedies.
  • Early detection – vision screening in schools, antenatal and NCD clinics, ROP screening in neonatal units.
  • Motivation for timely cataract surgery and eye donation.
  • Caring for blind patients – introduce yourself, explain surroundings, use the clock method for describing food on the plate, use the sighted-guide technique (patient holds the nurse's arm above the elbow), keep furniture in place.

Conclusion Blindness, defined as presenting vision below 3/60 in the better eye, is mainly due to cataract, corneal opacity, glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy and refractive errors in India. NPCBVI, preventive measures and rehabilitation, with active nursing participation, can greatly reduce avoidable blindness.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Eye
question: Explain refractive errors and their correction.
answer_html:
Definition A refractive error (ametropia) is a condition in which parallel rays of light are not brought to a focus exactly on the retina when the eye is at rest, resulting in blurred vision. A normal eye is emmetropic. Uncorrected refractive error is the commonest cause of visual impairment in India and a major cause of poor school performance.

1. Types a) Myopia (short-sightedness)

  • Light focuses in front of the retina – distant objects are blurred; near vision is good.
  • Causes – longer eyeball (axial) or increased curvature of cornea/lens; hereditary; increased near work and screen time with less outdoor activity in children.
  • Correction – concave (minus) lenses; high myopia increases the risk of retinal detachment and glaucoma.
  • Myopia control – at least 1–2 hours of outdoor play daily, low-dose atropine drops (specialist), regular check-ups.

b) Hypermetropia (long-sightedness)

  • Light focuses behind the retina – near vision blurred, eye strain and headache on reading; children may develop a convergent squint.
  • Short eyeball; correction – convex (plus) lenses; adults with hypermetropia have a higher risk of angle-closure glaucoma.

c) Astigmatism

  • Unequal curvature of the cornea in different meridians – blurred or distorted vision at all distances; correction – cylindrical (toric) lenses.

d) Presbyopia

  • Age-related loss of accommodation after about 40 years – difficulty in reading small print and doing near work; corrected by convex reading glasses (strength increases with age).

e) Anisometropia

  • Different refractive power in the two eyes; may cause amblyopia (lazy eye) in children if not corrected early.

2. Symptoms

  • Blurred vision, squinting of eyes, headache and eye strain, watering; children sit close to the TV, hold books near, or lose interest in studies.

3. Diagnosis

  • Visual acuity with pinhole, retinoscopy (objective refraction, under cycloplegia in children), autorefractometer and subjective refraction.

4. Correction

  • Spectacles – safest, cheapest and most common.
  • Contact lenses – need strict hygiene.
  • Refractive surgery – LASIK, PRK, SMILE (after 18–21 years when the power is stable); implantable lenses for high myopia.

5. Nursing responsibilities

  • Participate in school eye-screening programmes (free spectacles under NPCBVI/RBSK); refer children with poor vision.
  • Teach care of spectacles (clean with soft cloth and water, store in a case) and regular wearing.
  • Advise good lighting, correct reading distance, the 20-20-20 rule for screen users (every 20 minutes, look 20 feet away for 20 seconds) and outdoor play.
  • Encourage yearly eye check-ups, especially for children and people above 40.

Conclusion Myopia, hypermetropia, astigmatism and presbyopia are common, easily diagnosed and easily corrected with spectacles, contact lenses or surgery. Screening and timely correction prevent visual impairment and amblyopia.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Eye
question: Explain the common disorders of the eyelids and their management.
answer_html:
Introduction The eyelids protect the eye, spread tears and keep the cornea moist. Disorders of the lids are common and, if neglected, can damage the cornea.

1. Stye (external hordeolum)

  • Acute staphylococcal infection of an eyelash follicle and its glands (Zeis/Moll).
  • Painful red swelling at the lid margin with a yellow pus point.
  • Management: warm compresses 3–4 times a day, antibiotic ointment, removal of the affected lash; do not squeeze; recurrent styes – check for diabetes, refractive error and poor hygiene.

2. Chalazion (meibomian cyst)

  • Chronic, painless granulomatous inflammation of a meibomian gland – a firm, painless swelling away from the lid margin.
  • Management: warm compresses; incision and curettage under local anaesthesia; steroid injection; recurrent chalazion in elderly – biopsy to exclude cancer.

3. Blepharitis

  • Chronic inflammation of the lid margins – itching, burning, red margins, scales or crusts on lashes (dandruff-like), meibomian gland dysfunction.
  • Management: lid hygiene – warm compresses and lid scrubs with diluted baby shampoo, antibiotic ointment, treatment of scalp dandruff, lubricants; long-term care.

4. Entropion and trichiasis

  • Entropion – inward turning of the lid margin; trichiasis – misdirected lashes rubbing the cornea.
  • Causes – ageing (senile), scarring (trachoma, chemical burns).
  • Effects – irritation, watering, corneal abrasion and ulcer.
  • Management: epilation or electrolysis of lashes; surgical correction of the lid.

5. Ectropion

  • Outward turning of the lid margin (usually lower lid) – watering (epiphora), dryness, exposure keratitis.
  • Causes – ageing, facial nerve palsy, scarring.
  • Management: lubricants, surgical tightening.

6. Ptosis

  • Drooping of the upper eyelid – congenital (risk of amblyopia in children) or acquired (ageing, third nerve palsy, myasthenia gravis, Horner's syndrome, trauma).
  • Management: treat cause; surgery (levator resection, frontalis sling); urgent evaluation of sudden ptosis with a dilated pupil (aneurysm).

7. Lagophthalmos

  • Inability to close the eyelids completely (facial palsy, proptosis, unconscious patients) – risk of exposure keratitis.
  • Management: lubricating drops by day, ointment and taping/moisture chambers at night, tarsorrhaphy if severe.

Nursing management

  • Teach warm-compress technique (clean cloth dipped in warm water, 10 minutes) and lid hygiene; discourage squeezing styes and sharing towels and cosmetics.
  • Protect the cornea in patients with entropion, ectropion and lagophthalmos; give eye care to unconscious and ICU patients every 2–4 hours.
  • Prepare patients for minor lid surgery and give post-operative care (pressure pad, ointment, cold compresses).

Conclusion Styes, chalazia, blepharitis and lid malpositions are common lid disorders. Warm compresses, lid hygiene, protection of the cornea and timely surgery prevent complications.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Eye
question: Explain the types of eye injuries and the first-aid and nursing management of chemical injuries of the eye.
answer_html:
Introduction Eye injuries (ocular trauma) are a major cause of monocular blindness, especially in young men, agricultural and industrial workers, children playing with sticks and during festivals (firecracker injuries during Diwali). Many are preventable.

1. Types of eye injuries

  • Mechanical – blunt (closed-globe) injuries: black eye, subconjunctival haemorrhage, hyphaema (blood in the anterior chamber), traumatic cataract, lens dislocation, retinal tear or detachment, blow-out fracture of the orbit (double vision, numbness of cheek).
  • Mechanical – sharp/penetrating (open-globe) injuries: corneal or scleral lacerations, perforating injuries, intraocular foreign bodies (metal chips during hammering).
  • Superficial injuries: corneal foreign body, corneal abrasion.
  • Chemical injuries: alkalis (lime – chuna, cement, ammonia, caustic soda) and acids (toilet cleaners, battery acid).
  • Thermal injuries: burns from firecrackers, hot liquids.
  • Radiation injuries: ultraviolet keratitis (welding, snow blindness), solar retinopathy (viewing an eclipse without protection).

2. General first aid

  • Blunt injury – cold compress, rest with head raised 30–45° (hyphaema), eye shield, avoid aspirin; urgent referral if vision is reduced.
  • Penetrating injury – do not press on the eye, do not remove an embedded object, do not apply ointment; cover with a rigid shield (or a paper cup); keep NPO; give tetanus prophylaxis and IV antibiotics as ordered; arrange urgent surgery.
  • Corneal foreign body – removed by trained staff under topical anaesthesia using a sterile needle; antibiotic ointment.

3. Chemical injuries – why alkalis are more dangerous

  • Alkalis penetrate deeply and cause liquefactive necrosis of the cornea, limbus and inner structures; acids coagulate surface proteins, which limits penetration.
  • Severe burns lead to limbal ischaemia, corneal opacity, symblepharon (lid adhering to the eyeball), glaucoma and blindness.

4. First aid and management of chemical injuries – an emergency

  1. Immediate, copious irrigation with clean tap water, normal saline or Ringer's lactate for at least 15–30 minutes, keeping the eyelids open – start at the place of injury; do not wait for transport or for an eye specialist.
  2. Evert the eyelids (including double eversion of the upper lid) and remove particles such as lime with a moist cotton bud.
  3. Do not try to neutralise with acid or alkali.
  4. Check the pH with litmus paper and continue irrigation until it is near neutral (about 7).
  5. Then: topical antibiotics, cycloplegics for pain, steroid drops in the first week (by specialist), vitamin C (oral and topical) and doxycycline in alkali burns, lubricants, IOP-lowering drugs; glass-rod sweeping of fornices to prevent symblepharon; amniotic membrane grafting and later limbal stem-cell transplant or keratoplasty in severe cases.

5. Nursing responsibilities and prevention

  • Triage eye injuries as emergencies; record visual acuity (if possible after irrigation); relieve pain and anxiety.
  • Educate about protective goggles for welders, grinders, farmers and construction workers; safe handling of lime and chemicals (keep out of reach of children); supervised use of firecrackers at a safe distance; protective sports eyewear; never view a solar eclipse directly.

Conclusion Eye injuries may be blunt, penetrating, chemical, thermal or radiational. Immediate prolonged irrigation in chemical burns, shielding without pressure in penetrating injuries, early specialist care and preventive education save vision.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Eye
question: Explain diabetic retinopathy – stages, screening, management and the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Definition Diabetic retinopathy (DR) is a microvascular complication of diabetes mellitus in which damage to the small retinal blood vessels causes leakage, closure and abnormal new vessel growth, leading to visual loss. With India's large diabetic population, DR is an important and growing cause of preventable blindness.

1. Risk factors

  • Duration of diabetes (most important), poor glycaemic control (high HbA1c), hypertension, high lipids, diabetic kidney disease, pregnancy, smoking, anaemia.

2. Pathogenesis and stages

  • High blood sugar damages capillary walls (loss of pericytes, thickened basement membrane) → microaneurysms and increased permeability → haemorrhages, hard exudates and retinal oedema; capillary closure → ischaemia → release of VEGF → growth of fragile new vessels (neovascularisation).
  • Non-proliferative DR (NPDR) – mild (microaneurysms), moderate (dot-blot haemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton-wool spots), severe (extensive haemorrhages, venous beading, intraretinal microvascular abnormalities).
  • Proliferative DR (PDR) – new vessels on the disc or elsewhere → vitreous haemorrhage, tractional retinal detachment, neovascular glaucoma.
  • Diabetic macular oedema (DMO) – swelling of the macula at any stage; the commonest cause of visual loss in diabetes.

3. Symptoms

  • Often no symptoms until advanced disease – hence the need for screening.
  • Later – blurred or fluctuating vision, difficulty reading, floaters, sudden loss of vision (vitreous haemorrhage).

4. Screening

  • Dilated fundus examination – type 2 diabetes at diagnosis and then every year; type 1 – from 5 years after diagnosis; more often in pregnancy and in established DR.
  • Fundus photography with tele-ophthalmology and artificial-intelligence-based grading is increasingly used at NCD clinics and primary centres.

5. Management

  • Control of blood sugar, BP and lipids; stop smoking; treat kidney disease and anaemia.
  • Laser photocoagulation – pan-retinal photocoagulation (PRP) for PDR; focal/grid laser for some macular oedema.
  • Intravitreal anti-VEGF injections (ranibizumab, bevacizumab, aflibercept) – first-line for macular oedema and useful in PDR; intravitreal steroid implants.
  • Vitrectomy – for non-clearing vitreous haemorrhage and tractional RD.

6. Role of the nurse

  • Educate every diabetic that yearly eye examination is needed even when vision is normal; arrange referral and track attendance.
  • Reinforce diet, exercise, medication adherence and BP control.
  • Prepare patients for laser and intravitreal injections (povidone-iodine antisepsis, explanation); after injection teach warning signs of infection (pain, redness, reduced vision); explain that PRP may reduce night and side vision.
  • Refer patients with low vision for rehabilitation; screen for other diabetic complications (feet, kidneys).

Conclusion Diabetic retinopathy progresses silently from non-proliferative to proliferative disease and macular oedema. Regular screening, good control of diabetes and BP, timely laser, anti-VEGF injections or surgery, and nursing education prevent most diabetic blindness.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Eye
question: Write a note on refractive errors.
answer_html:
Refractive errors are conditions in which light rays are not focused exactly on the retina, causing blurred vision.

  1. Myopia (short-sightedness) – distant objects blurred; image forms in front of the retina; corrected with concave lenses.
  2. Hypermetropia (long-sightedness) – near objects blurred, eye strain; image forms behind the retina; corrected with convex lenses.
  3. Astigmatism – unequal curvature of the cornea; blurred/distorted vision; cylindrical lenses.
  4. Presbyopia – age-related loss of accommodation after 40 years; difficulty in near work; reading glasses (convex). Diagnosis by visual acuity with pinhole and refraction; correction by spectacles, contact lenses or refractive surgery. School eye screening helps early detection in children.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Eye
question: Give reason: Artificial tears and moisturisers are advised for patients who cannot close their eyelids fully.
answer_html:
Patients who cannot close their eyelids completely (lagophthalmos) – e.g. in facial (Bell's) palsy, unconsciousness, sedation and ventilation in ICU, stroke, or proptosis of thyroid eye disease – have an exposed cornea.

  • Without blinking and lid closure, the tear film evaporates and the cornea dries.
  • Drying causes epithelial erosions (exposure keratopathy), which can progress to corneal ulcer, infection, perforation and loss of vision.
  • Artificial tears (carboxymethylcellulose, hypromellose) during the day and lubricating ointment or moisture chambers at night replace the tear film, keep the cornea moist, reduce friction and protect the epithelium.
  • Taping the lids closed and regular eye care every 2–4 hours are also part of care.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Eye
question: What is a Snellen chart? How is it used?
answer_html:
A Snellen chart is a chart with rows of letters (optotypes) of decreasing size, used to test distant visual acuity (central vision).

Use

  • The patient sits or stands 6 metres (20 feet) from the well-lit chart.
  • Each eye is tested separately while the other is covered, with and without glasses.
  • The smallest line read correctly is recorded as a fraction – e.g. 6/6 (normal), 6/9, 6/60 – where the numerator is the test distance and the denominator is the distance at which a normal eye reads that line.
  • A pinhole is used to check whether reduced vision is due to a refractive error.
  • For illiterate persons and children, the "E" chart or picture charts are used; near vision is tested with a Jaeger or N-chart.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Eye
question: What is trachoma?
answer_html:
Trachoma is a chronic keratoconjunctivitis caused by Chlamydia trachomatis (serotypes A–C), spread by eye-seeking flies, fingers, shared towels and clothes, in areas with poor hygiene and water shortage.

  • Features: follicles and papillae on the upper tarsal conjunctiva → scarring → entropion and trichiasis (lashes rubbing the cornea) → corneal opacity and blindness.
  • Control – WHO "SAFE" strategy: Surgery for trichiasis, Antibiotics (single-dose azithromycin, tetracycline ointment), Facial cleanliness, Environmental improvement (water, sanitation).
  • India – once a major cause of blindness; the WHO validated India's elimination of trachoma as a public-health problem in 2024; surveillance and face-washing education continue.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Disorders of Eye
question: Differentiate between enucleation and evisceration of the eye.
answer_html:
Enucleation Evisceration
Removal of the entire eyeball (with a segment of optic nerve), leaving the eye muscles and conjunctiva Removal of the contents of the eyeball (uvea, retina, vitreous, lens ± cornea), leaving the sclera with muscles attached
Indications: intraocular malignancy (retinoblastoma, choroidal melanoma), severe trauma with risk of sympathetic ophthalmia, painful blind eye Indications: endophthalmitis/panophthalmitis (avoids spreading infection along the optic nerve sheath to the brain), painful blind eye
Not preferred in severe infection Not done for tumours
In both, an orbital implant is placed and an artificial eye (prosthesis) is fitted after 4–6 weeks; the patient is taught socket and prosthesis care.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Kidney and Urinary Problems
question: Mr. Y, aged 43 years, has left flank pain radiating to the thigh and burning micturition for 2 days. He is diagnosed with renal calculi. (a) Define renal calculi. (2 marks) (b) Mention the types of renal calculi. (3 marks) (c) Discuss the surgical and nursing management of Mr. Y. (10 marks)

diagram.caption: Treatment options for urinary stones
labels: ESWL – external shock waves focused on a kidney stone; ureteroscopy with laser for a ureteric stone; PCNL – nephroscope through the flank into the kidney for a large stone; DJ stent from the renal pelvis to the bladder

answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks) Renal calculi (kidney stones, urolithiasis) are hard crystalline masses formed in the urinary tract – kidney, ureter, bladder or urethra – from salts and minerals normally dissolved in urine, which precipitate when urine becomes supersaturated. Stones cause pain, bleeding, infection and obstruction. Mr. Y's pain from the flank radiating to the thigh/groin is typical renal (ureteric) colic, caused by a stone moving down the ureter.

(b) Types of renal calculi (3 marks) 1. According to chemical composition

  • Calcium stones (calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate) – most common (about 75–80%); hard, radio-opaque; associated with dehydration, high-salt and high-protein diets, hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, low urinary citrate and hyperparathyroidism.
  • Struvite (magnesium ammonium phosphate, "infection stones") – 10–15%; form in alkaline urine with urease-producing bacteria (Proteus, Klebsiella); may grow into staghorn calculi filling the renal pelvis and calyces; more common in women and catheterised patients.
  • Uric acid stones – 5–10%; in acidic urine, gout, high-purine diet, cancer chemotherapy; radiolucent on X-ray.
  • Cystine stones – 1–2%; due to inherited cystinuria; begin in childhood.
  • Rare – xanthine stones, drug stones (indinavir, sulfonamides).

2. According to location

  • Renal (calyceal, pelvic, staghorn), ureteric (commonly lodge at the pelvi-ureteric junction, pelvic brim and vesico-ureteric junction), vesical (bladder) and urethral stones.

(c) Surgical and nursing management of Mr. Y (10 marks) A. Initial assessment and medical (conservative) management

  • Assessment: pain score and pattern, nausea and vomiting, fever with chills (infected obstructed kidney – an emergency), urine colour (haematuria), previous stones, diet and fluid intake, occupation (outdoor work in heat).
  • Investigations: urine routine (RBCs, pus cells, crystals, pH) and culture, serum creatinine, electrolytes, calcium, uric acid, CBC; non-contrast CT KUB (most accurate), ultrasound KUB, X-ray KUB.
  • Pain relief: NSAIDs (e.g. diclofenac injection) are the first choice for colic; opioids if needed; antiemetics; local warmth.
  • Medical expulsive therapy (MET) for small ureteric stones (less than 5–6 mm): tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily (relaxes the ureter), 2.5–3 litres of fluids, walking, and straining urine to catch the stone; review with imaging.
  • Emergency decompression if there is infection with obstruction, a single kidney, or kidney failure – double-J (DJ) ureteric stent or percutaneous nephrostomy (PCN) with IV antibiotics; definitive stone treatment later.

B. Surgical/interventional management | Procedure | Description | Used for | |---|---|---| | ESWL (extracorporeal shock-wave lithotripsy) | Shock waves from outside the body break the stone into fragments that pass in urine; out-patient procedure | Renal stones up to about 2 cm, upper ureteric stones up to 1 cm | | Ureteroscopy (URS) with laser lithotripsy | Endoscope passed through urethra and bladder into the ureter; holmium laser breaks the stone; basket removal | Ureteric stones – likely for Mr. Y | | RIRS (retrograde intrarenal surgery) | Flexible ureteroscope into the kidney with laser | Renal stones less than 2 cm | | PCNL (percutaneous nephrolithotomy) | Track made through the flank into the kidney; nephroscope used to fragment and remove stone | Large renal stones (more than 2 cm) and staghorn calculi | | Open or laparoscopic surgery (pyelolithotomy, nephrolithotomy, ureterolithotomy) | Surgical removal | Rarely now – very large or complex stones | | Cystolitholapaxy | Endoscopic crushing of bladder stones | Bladder stones | - A DJ stent is often left after URS/RIRS for 2–6 weeks to prevent obstruction from oedema and fragments.

C. Pre-operative nursing care

  1. Explain the procedure and expected after-effects (stent discomfort, haematuria); obtain informed consent.
  2. Ensure urine is sterile (treat UTI first), check coagulation profile, haemoglobin, creatinine, blood group; stop antiplatelets/anticoagulants as advised.
  3. Keep NPO as ordered; give prescribed prophylactic antibiotic; manage pain.
  4. For PCNL – teach deep breathing; mark the side; prepare for possible nephrostomy tube.

D. Post-operative nursing care

  1. Vital signs every 15–30 minutes initially; watch for fever and chills (urosepsis – a serious complication), hypotension.
  2. Pain management – analgesics; renal colic may recur with passage of fragments; antispasmodics as ordered.
  3. Urine monitoring – measure output; light pink urine is expected for 24–48 hours; bright red urine, clots or decreasing output must be reported.
  4. Fluids – encourage 2.5–3 litres per day (unless restricted) to flush fragments and prevent infection; IV fluids until oral intake is adequate.
  5. Catheter care – keep the drainage closed and below bladder level, secure the catheter, perineal care.
  6. Nephrostomy tube care (after PCNL) – keep the tube secured and free of kinks, never clamp or irrigate without an order, measure output separately, aseptic dressing of the site, watch for leakage, bleeding and dislodgement.
  7. After PCNL – observe breath sounds and breathing (risk of pneumothorax/hydrothorax with upper-pole access), Hb (bleeding), abdominal signs (colon injury).
  8. After ESWL – expect mild haematuria, bruising on the flank and passage of gravel; strain all urine and send fragments for stone analysis; watch for "steinstrasse" (a column of fragments blocking the ureter) – severe colic, fever.
  9. DJ stent teaching – stents may cause frequency, urgency, burning and flank pain during voiding and mild haematuria; give the patient a stent card with the removal date – a forgotten stent becomes encrusted and damages the kidney.
  10. Early ambulation – walking helps the passage of fragments and prevents DVT.

E. Discharge teaching and prevention of recurrence (stones recur in about half of patients within 5–10 years)

  • Drink enough water to pass at least 2–2.5 litres of pale urine daily – more in hot weather and during outdoor work; spread fluids throughout the day and drink a glass at bedtime.
  • Reduce salt (less than 5 g/day – avoid pickles, papad, chips) and limit animal protein.
  • Do not restrict dietary calcium – normal milk and curd intake actually reduces oxalate absorption; avoid calcium supplements unless prescribed.
  • For calcium oxalate stones – limit oxalate-rich foods (spinach, beetroot, nuts, chocolate, strong tea), avoid excess vitamin C supplements; lemon water/citrus fruits add citrate, an inhibitor of stones.
  • For uric acid stones – limit red meat, organ meats and seafood; alkalinise urine (potassium citrate); allopurinol if prescribed.
  • For struvite stones – complete treatment of UTI; follow-up cultures.
  • Maintain healthy weight, control diabetes; avoid long periods without drinking water.
  • Report fever, severe pain, blood in urine or reduced urine output; attend follow-up imaging and stent removal.

Nursing diagnoses (examples) | Nursing diagnosis | Key interventions | |---|---| | Acute pain related to ureteric spasm and stone movement | NSAIDs/analgesics, warmth, positioning, fluids | | Impaired urinary elimination related to obstruction | Measure output, strain urine, catheter/stent care | | Risk for infection related to stasis and instrumentation | Asepsis, antibiotics, temperature monitoring, fluids | | Deficient knowledge regarding prevention of recurrence | Diet and fluid teaching, follow-up plan |

Nursing importance

  • Severe colic, risk of urosepsis and post-procedure complications make careful monitoring essential; nurses' teaching about fluids, diet and stent removal prevents recurrence and long-term kidney damage.

Conclusion Renal calculi are mostly calcium oxalate stones formed in concentrated urine, presenting with colic, haematuria and infection. Small stones pass with medical expulsive therapy, while larger ones need ESWL, ureteroscopy, RIRS or PCNL. Good post-procedure nursing and lifelong preventive teaching are key to recovery and prevention of recurrence.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Kidney and Urinary Problems
question: (a) Define chronic kidney disease and list its stages. (3 marks) (b) Explain the causes and clinical manifestations of chronic kidney disease. (4 marks) (c) Describe the medical and nursing management of a patient with chronic kidney disease. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Systemic effects of chronic kidney disease (uraemic syndrome)

answer_html:
(a) Definition and stages (3 marks) Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is defined as abnormalities of kidney structure or function present for more than 3 months with implications for health – that is, a GFR below 60 mL/min/1.73 m² and/or markers of kidney damage such as albuminuria, abnormal urine sediment, structural abnormalities on imaging or a history of kidney transplantation. CKD is common in India and is often detected late, when dialysis is already needed.

Stages (by GFR – KDIGO) | Stage | GFR (mL/min/1.73 m²) | Description | |---|---|---| | G1 | 90 or more | Kidney damage with normal GFR | | G2 | 60–89 | Mildly decreased | | G3a | 45–59 | Mild to moderately decreased | | G3b | 30–44 | Moderately to severely decreased | | G4 | 15–29 | Severely decreased | | G5 | Below 15 | Kidney failure (end-stage kidney disease) – dialysis or transplant needed | CKD is also staged by albuminuria – A1 (normal to mild), A2 (moderate), A3 (severe).

(b) Causes and clinical manifestations (4 marks) 1. Causes

  • Diabetic nephropathy – the commonest cause.
