  • Hypertension (hypertensive nephrosclerosis).
  • Chronic glomerulonephritis.
  • Chronic interstitial nephritis – long-term painkiller (NSAID) use, herbal/heavy-metal medicines, recurrent pyelonephritis, reflux.
  • Obstructive uropathy – stones, BPH, strictures.
  • Polycystic kidney disease and other hereditary diseases.
  • CKD of unknown aetiology in some farming communities (heat stress, dehydration, agrochemicals).
  • SLE, vasculitis, nephrotoxic drugs, repeated AKI.

2. Clinical manifestations (uraemic syndrome)

  • Early stages – often no symptoms; nocturia, mild oedema, hypertension found on screening.
  • General – fatigue, weakness, loss of appetite, weight loss.
  • Fluid and electrolytes – oedema (puffy face, swollen feet), hypertension, fluid overload, breathlessness, hyperkalaemia (muscle weakness, arrhythmias), metabolic acidosis (deep sighing respiration).
  • Cardiovascular – left ventricular hypertrophy, heart failure, uraemic pericarditis (chest pain, friction rub), accelerated atherosclerosis.
  • Blood – anaemia (low erythropoietin) causing pallor and tiredness; bleeding tendency (platelet dysfunction).
  • Gastrointestinal – nausea and vomiting (especially in the morning), metallic taste, uraemic (ammonia-like) breath, mouth ulcers, gastric bleeding.
  • Nervous system – poor concentration, sleep disturbance, restless legs, burning feet (peripheral neuropathy), flapping tremor, confusion, seizures, coma.
  • Bones and minerals (CKD–mineral bone disorder) – bone pain, fractures, muscle cramps (high phosphate, low calcium, low active vitamin D, high PTH).
  • Skin – pallor with sallow (yellow-brown) colour, dryness and severe itching, bruising; uraemic frost in very late disease.
  • Reproductive and immune – amenorrhoea, infertility, erectile dysfunction; frequent infections.
  • Urine – polyuria and nocturia early, oliguria late; proteinuria, haematuria.

3. Investigations (for understanding)

  • Serum creatinine and eGFR, urea, electrolytes, bicarbonate, haemoglobin, calcium, phosphate, PTH, urine albumin–creatinine ratio, urine routine; ultrasound – small, shrunken, echogenic kidneys (normal or large in diabetes and polycystic disease); kidney biopsy when indicated.

(c) Medical and nursing management (8 marks) 1. Medical management a) Slowing progression

  • BP control (target usually below 130/80 mmHg) with ACE inhibitors or ARBs, especially when albuminuria is present.
  • Glycaemic control in diabetes; SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) now protect the kidneys in many CKD patients.
  • Avoid nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast), treat infections and obstruction early; statins for cardiovascular risk; stop smoking.

b) Treating complications

  • Anaemia – erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (erythropoietin SC) with iron (often IV iron); target Hb about 10–11.5 g/dL.
  • Mineral bone disorder – phosphate binders taken with meals (calcium carbonate/acetate, sevelamer), active vitamin D (calcitriol), cinacalcet for high PTH.
  • Hyperkalaemia – diet, potassium binders, correction of acidosis; emergency treatment if severe.
  • Metabolic acidosis – sodium bicarbonate tablets.
  • Fluid overload and hypertension – loop diuretics (furosemide), salt and fluid restriction, antihypertensives.
  • Vaccination – hepatitis B (higher dose schedule), influenza, pneumococcal.

c) Renal replacement therapy (stage 5)

  • Haemodialysis – usually 3 times a week for 4 hours through an arteriovenous fistula, which is created a few months in advance.
  • Peritoneal dialysis – CAPD at home.
  • Kidney transplantation – the best long-term treatment.
  • Conservative kidney management for very elderly or frail patients who choose not to have dialysis.
  • Pradhan Mantri National Dialysis Programme provides free dialysis for poor patients in district hospitals; PM-JAY covers dialysis and transplantation.

2. Nursing management a) Assessment and monitoring

  • Daily weight (same time, same scale), intake–output, BP, pulse, respiration, oedema, lung crepitations, JVP, mental status, skin.
  • Laboratory values – urea, creatinine, potassium, Hb, calcium, phosphate; ECG changes of hyperkalaemia (tall peaked T waves).

b) Fluid management

  • Fluid allowance in oliguric patients = previous day's urine output + about 500 mL (insensible loss); include all liquids (tea, dal, curd, fruits).
  • Help the patient manage thirst – small cups, ice chips, sucking sour candy, chewing gum, mouth rinses, spreading fluids across the day, avoiding salty foods.

c) Diet (with dietitian)

  • Protein – about 0.6–0.8 g/kg/day in non-dialysis CKD stages 3–5 (mostly high-quality protein), 1.0–1.2 g/kg/day once on dialysis; adequate calories (30–35 kcal/kg) so that protein is not burnt for energy.
  • Salt – less than 5 g salt/day; no added salt, avoid pickles, papad, namkeen, processed foods.
  • Potassium (if high) – limit bananas, coconut water, oranges, tomatoes, potatoes and dry fruits; leach vegetables (cut, soak in warm water for 2 hours, discard the water and boil in plenty of water).
  • Phosphorus – limit colas, processed foods, excess milk products; take binders with meals.

d) Medication safety

  • Give ESA injections, iron, binders, bicarbonate and antihypertensives correctly; monitor BP (ESA can raise BP).
  • Avoid over-the-counter painkillers, magnesium/aluminium antacids and herbal remedies; ensure doses are adjusted for kidney function.

e) Protect the veins and dialysis access

  • "Save the veins" – avoid venepuncture and IV lines in the non-dominant arm of CKD patients (future fistula).
  • Teach fistula care – check the thrill and bruit daily, no BP measurement, injections or tight bangles on the fistula arm.

f) Skin, mouth and comfort

  • Relieve itching – emollients, cool baths, short nails, prescribed antihistamines; mouth care for metallic taste and stomatitis; manage nausea.
  • Safety for patients with neuropathy, confusion or bone disease; prevent infection.

g) Psychological and social support

  • CKD and dialysis bring depression, anxiety, loss of work, financial strain and dependence; listen, counsel, involve family and social workers; link to government schemes and patient support groups.

h) Education

  • Self-monitoring of BP, weight and sugar; diet and fluid plan; medication timing.
  • Warning signs – breathlessness, chest pain, very low urine, marked weakness or palpitations (hyperkalaemia), fever, confusion.
  • Help the patient and family choose a dialysis modality and prepare for transplant evaluation; discuss advance care planning.

Nursing diagnoses (examples) | Nursing diagnosis | Key interventions | |---|---| | Excess fluid volume related to reduced urine output | Fluid and salt restriction, daily weight, diuretics | | Imbalanced nutrition: less than requirements related to anorexia and diet restrictions | Dietitian plan, small frequent meals, mouth care | | Risk for injury related to hyperkalaemia, bone disease and bleeding | Monitor K⁺, safe environment, avoid trauma | | Impaired skin integrity related to pruritus and oedema | Emollients, positioning, nail care | | Ineffective coping related to chronic illness and dialysis | Counselling, support groups, family involvement |

Nursing importance

  • CKD is largely preventable through control of diabetes and hypertension; nurses at NCD clinics screen with BP, blood sugar, urine albumin and creatinine.
  • Good nursing teaching on diet, fluid and medicines delays dialysis and improves quality of life.

Conclusion CKD is a progressive, irreversible loss of kidney function, staged by GFR and albuminuria and caused mainly by diabetes and hypertension. Management aims to slow progression, treat complications and prepare for dialysis or transplantation, with nurses playing a vital role in monitoring, diet and fluid control, access care, education and emotional support.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Kidney and Urinary Problems
question: (a) Define acute kidney injury and classify its causes. (3 marks) (b) Explain the phases and clinical manifestations of acute renal failure. (4 marks) (c) Describe the management and nursing care of a patient with acute kidney injury. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Prerenal, intrinsic and postrenal causes of acute kidney injury
labels: reduced blood flow to the kidney (dehydration
damage within the kidney (acute tubular necrosis

answer_html:
(a) Definition and causes (3 marks) Acute kidney injury (AKI), earlier called acute renal failure, is an abrupt decrease in kidney function over hours to days, leading to retention of urea and creatinine and disturbance of fluid, electrolyte and acid–base balance. According to KDIGO, AKI is present if any of the following occurs:

  • Rise in serum creatinine by 0.3 mg/dL or more within 48 hours, or
  • Rise to 1.5 times baseline or more within 7 days, or
  • Urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hour for 6 hours. AKI is staged 1–3 according to the rise in creatinine and fall in urine output; stage 3 includes patients needing dialysis.

Classification of causes 1. Pre-renal (reduced blood flow to the kidneys – most common)

  • Hypovolaemia – haemorrhage, severe diarrhoea and vomiting (gastroenteritis, cholera), burns, excessive diuretics.
  • Low cardiac output – heart failure, cardiogenic shock, MI.
  • Systemic vasodilation – sepsis, anaphylaxis.
  • Renal vasoconstriction – NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors in renal artery stenosis, hepatorenal syndrome.

2. Intrinsic renal (damage to kidney tissue)

  • Acute tubular necrosis (ATN) – ischaemic (prolonged pre-renal state) or nephrotoxic – aminoglycosides, contrast media, amphotericin, cisplatin, myoglobin (rhabdomyolysis after crush injury), haemoglobin (haemolysis in falciparum malaria, G6PD deficiency), snake venom (Russell's viper), multiple wasp stings, poisons (copper sulphate, paraquat).
  • Acute glomerulonephritis, acute interstitial nephritis (drugs), vasculitis, haemolytic uraemic syndrome, malignant hypertension.
  • Obstetric causes – septic abortion, postpartum haemorrhage, pre-eclampsia/HELLP, puerperal sepsis.
  • Tropical infections – leptospirosis, malaria, dengue, scrub typhus.

3. Post-renal (obstruction to urine outflow)

  • BPH, bilateral ureteric stones or a stone in a single kidney, carcinoma of cervix or prostate, urethral stricture, blocked urinary catheter, retroperitoneal fibrosis.

(b) Phases and clinical manifestations (4 marks) 1. Initiation phase – from the insult until injury is established (hours to days); urine output begins to fall; this is the best time to reverse the cause.

2. Oliguric (maintenance) phase – usually lasts 1–2 weeks:

  • Urine output less than 400 mL/day (some patients are non-oliguric).
  • Rising urea and creatinine → nausea, vomiting, anorexia, drowsiness, confusion, flapping tremor, seizures (uraemia).
  • Fluid overload – oedema, hypertension, raised JVP, pulmonary oedema (breathlessness, crepitations).
  • Hyperkalaemia – muscle weakness, arrhythmias, tall peaked T waves; may cause cardiac arrest.
  • Metabolic acidosis – deep rapid breathing (Kussmaul).
  • Hyponatraemia, high phosphate, low calcium; bleeding tendency; pericarditis; infections (a leading cause of death).

3. Diuretic phase – urine output rises (often 1–3 litres or more per day) as tubules recover but cannot yet concentrate urine:

  • Risk of dehydration, hypokalaemia and hyponatraemia; urea may still be high in the early days.

4. Recovery phase – kidney function gradually returns over weeks to months; some patients are left with CKD.

Investigations (for understanding)

  • Serum creatinine, urea, potassium, sodium, bicarbonate (ABG), calcium, phosphate, CBC.
  • Urine – routine (muddy-brown granular casts in ATN, RBC casts in GN), urine sodium and fractional excretion of sodium (low in pre-renal, high in ATN).
  • Ultrasound KUB – obstruction; kidney size (normal or large in AKI, small in CKD).
  • ECG (hyperkalaemia); tests for the cause – CK (rhabdomyolysis), malaria, dengue and leptospira tests, 20WBCT in snakebite.

(c) Management and nursing care (8 marks) 1. Medical management a) Treat the cause

  • Pre-renal – restore volume with IV normal saline/Ringer's lactate, blood for haemorrhage, treat shock and sepsis (antibiotics within the first hour).
  • Intrinsic – stop nephrotoxic drugs, treat infections (malaria, leptospirosis), give ASV in snakebite, forced alkaline diuresis in rhabdomyolysis as ordered, treat GN.
  • Post-renal – relieve obstruction – urinary catheter, ureteric stents or nephrostomy.

b) Fluid balance

  • In the oliguric phase, fluid intake = previous day's urine output + about 500 mL (more with fever or losses); avoid overload.
  • Diuretics (furosemide) may be tried in overloaded patients but do not "cure" AKI.

c) Emergency treatment of hyperkalaemia (K⁺ above 6.5 mEq/L or ECG changes)

  1. Calcium gluconate 10%, 10 mL IV over 5–10 minutes – protects the heart (repeat if ECG changes persist).
  2. Regular insulin 10 units IV with 50 mL of 50% dextrose – shifts potassium into cells; monitor blood sugar.
  3. Salbutamol nebulisation – shifts potassium into cells.
  4. Sodium bicarbonate if acidotic.
  5. Potassium binders (calcium/sodium polystyrene sulphonate) to remove potassium from the gut.
  6. Dialysis for refractory hyperkalaemia.

d) Other measures

  • Correct acidosis (bicarbonate), control BP, adjust all drug doses for kidney function.
  • Nutrition – adequate calories mainly from carbohydrates and fats; moderate protein (more if on dialysis or catabolic); restrict potassium, sodium and phosphate.

e) Renal replacement therapy – indications ("AEIOU")

  • Acidosis (severe, pH below about 7.1), Electrolytes (refractory hyperkalaemia), Intoxication (methanol, lithium, salicylates), Overload (pulmonary oedema not responding to diuretics), Uraemia (pericarditis, encephalopathy, bleeding).
  • Modalities – intermittent haemodialysis, continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) for unstable ICU patients, peritoneal dialysis (children, resource-limited settings), SLED.

2. Nursing care

  1. Monitor urine output hourly (catheter with urometer in ICU) and record a strict intake–output chart; daily weight.
  2. Vital signs, JVP, breath sounds and oedema – detect fluid overload early; propped-up position and oxygen for breathlessness.
  3. Cardiac monitoring for arrhythmias; know the signs of hyperkalaemia; keep calcium gluconate, insulin and dextrose ready.
  4. Laboratory monitoring – creatinine, urea, electrolytes, ABG, Hb; report trends.
  5. Neurological observation – drowsiness, confusion, twitching, seizures; seizure precautions.
  6. Infection prevention – strict asepsis with catheters, IV lines and dialysis catheters, hand hygiene, early removal of the urinary catheter, oral and skin care; monitor temperature.
  7. Diet and fluids – plan with dietitian; avoid high-potassium foods (banana, coconut water, oranges, tomatoes, potatoes, dry fruits) in hyperkalaemia; help with thirst (ice chips, mouth care).
  8. Medication safety – avoid NSAIDs and other nephrotoxins; double-check doses; monitor drug levels.
  9. Dialysis care – care of the temporary dialysis catheter (dressing, no use for other purposes), monitor for hypotension, bleeding and disequilibrium during and after sessions.
  10. Diuretic phase – replace fluids and electrolytes as ordered; watch for dehydration and low potassium.
  11. Psychological support – explain that AKI is often reversible; involve family.
  12. Follow-up and prevention – AKI survivors need kidney-function check-ups (risk of CKD); in hospitals, prevent AKI by hydration before contrast, avoiding nephrotoxic combinations, early treatment of sepsis and close monitoring of high-risk patients.

Nursing diagnoses (examples) | Nursing diagnosis | Key interventions | |---|---| | Excess fluid volume related to oliguria | Fluid restriction, I/O, daily weight, diuretics, dialysis | | Risk for decreased cardiac output related to hyperkalaemia | ECG monitoring, potassium-lowering treatment | | Risk for infection related to uraemia and invasive lines | Asepsis, early catheter removal, monitoring | | Imbalanced nutrition related to nausea and restrictions | Dietitian plan, antiemetics, small frequent meals |

Nursing importance

  • Many cases of AKI are preventable and many are reversible if the cause is corrected early; the nurse's hourly urine output and fluid chart are often the first warning of kidney injury.
  • In rural India, prompt treatment of diarrhoea, malaria, leptospirosis, snakebite and obstetric emergencies prevents a large share of AKI.

Conclusion AKI is a sudden loss of kidney function due to pre-renal, intrinsic or post-renal causes, passing through oliguric, diuretic and recovery phases. Treatment of the cause, careful fluid and electrolyte management, emergency treatment of hyperkalaemia, timely dialysis and meticulous nursing care give the best chance of full recovery.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Kidney and Urinary Problems
question: (a) Define benign prostatic hyperplasia and list its risk factors. (3 marks) (b) Explain the clinical manifestations and diagnostic evaluation of BPH. (4 marks) (c) Describe the management of BPH and the nursing care of a patient after transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP). (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Continuous bladder irrigation after TURP
labels: three-way Foley catheter in the bladder with balloon in the prostatic fossa
inflow port connected to normal saline bag
catheter taped to the thigh under traction
drainage colour changing from light pink to clear

answer_html:
(a) Definition and risk factors (3 marks) Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is a non-cancerous enlargement of the prostate gland due to an increase in the number of stromal and glandular (epithelial) cells, mainly in the transition (periurethral) zone. The enlarged gland compresses the prostatic urethra and obstructs the outflow of urine from the bladder. It is the commonest cause of urinary symptoms in older men – about half of men above 50 years and most men above 80 years have BPH on microscopy, though not all have symptoms.

Risk factors

  • Increasing age – the most important factor; rare before 40 years.
  • Hormonal factors – dihydrotestosterone (DHT), formed from testosterone by the enzyme 5-alpha reductase, stimulates prostatic growth; relative increase of oestrogen with ageing also contributes; functioning testes are necessary (BPH does not develop in men castrated before puberty).
  • Family history of BPH.
  • Metabolic syndrome – obesity, diabetes, hypertension and raised lipids.
  • Physical inactivity; possibly a diet high in red meat and fat.
  • BPH is not a precancerous condition, although BPH and prostate cancer may coexist in the same patient.

(b) Clinical manifestations and diagnostic evaluation (4 marks) 1. Lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS)

  • Obstructive (voiding) symptoms – hesitancy (delay in starting), weak or poor stream, intermittency (stream stops and starts), straining, terminal dribbling and a feeling of incomplete emptying.
  • Irritative (storage) symptoms – frequency, urgency, nocturia (often the first complaint – waking two or more times at night) and urge incontinence.

2. Complications

  • Acute urinary retention – sudden, painful inability to pass urine with a tender, distended bladder; often precipitated by cold weather, alcohol, constipation, delaying micturition, immobility after surgery, or drugs (anticholinergics, antihistamines and decongestants in cold remedies).
  • Chronic retention with overflow incontinence (constant dribbling from a painless distended bladder).
  • Urinary tract infection, bladder stones, bladder diverticula and haematuria.
  • Hydronephrosis and obstructive kidney failure from back pressure – anorexia, nausea, oedema, raised creatinine.
  • Inguinal hernia and haemorrhoids from chronic straining.

3. Diagnostic evaluation

  • History with the International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS) – 0–7 mild, 8–19 moderate, 20–35 severe; a 3-day frequency–volume chart (bladder diary).
  • Digital rectal examination (DRE) – smooth, firm, rubbery, symmetrically enlarged prostate with a preserved median groove; a hard, irregular, nodular gland suggests cancer.
  • Urine routine and culture; serum creatinine and electrolytes.
  • Serum PSA (prostate-specific antigen) – to help exclude cancer (usually below 4 ng/mL; may be mildly raised in BPH).
  • Ultrasound KUB – prostate volume, post-void residual (PVR) urine, bladder wall thickness, stones and upper-tract dilatation; transrectal ultrasound in selected cases.
  • Uroflowmetry – reduced maximum flow rate (Qmax below 10 mL/second suggests obstruction).
  • Cystoscopy and pressure–flow urodynamic studies when the diagnosis is uncertain or before surgery.

(c) Management and nursing care after TURP (8 marks) A. Watchful waiting with lifestyle advice (mild symptoms)

  • Reduce fluids in the evening, avoid tea, coffee and alcohol at night, practise double voiding and bladder training, treat constipation, avoid cold medicines containing decongestants or antihistamines, and review every 6–12 months.

B. Medical management

  • Alpha-1 adrenergic blockers – tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily, silodosin, alfuzosin, terazosin, doxazosin – relax the smooth muscle of the prostate and bladder neck and give rapid relief of symptoms; side effects are postural hypotension and dizziness (give at bedtime and teach to rise slowly), retrograde ejaculation and "floppy iris" during cataract surgery (inform the eye surgeon).
  • 5-alpha reductase inhibitors – finasteride 5 mg daily, dutasteride – shrink the gland over 6–12 months and reduce the risk of retention and surgery; they lower PSA by about half (important when interpreting PSA), and may reduce libido.
  • Combination therapy for large glands with moderate to severe symptoms; antimuscarinics or tadalafil for selected patients.

C. Management of acute retention

  • Aseptic urethral catheterisation with a Foley catheter (or suprapubic catheterisation if urethral catheterisation fails); drain the bladder and record the volume; start an alpha blocker and plan a trial without catheter (TWOC) after a few days.

D. Surgical management Indications – refractory or recurrent retention, recurrent UTI, bladder stones, recurrent haematuria, hydronephrosis or kidney impairment, and failure of drug therapy.

  • TURP (transurethral resection of the prostate) – the standard operation; obstructing prostatic tissue is removed in small pieces with a resectoscope passed through the urethra under spinal anaesthesia; there is no skin incision.
  • Laser procedures – HoLEP (holmium laser enucleation of the prostate) and photoselective vaporisation – less bleeding, suitable for large glands and patients on anticoagulants.
  • Bipolar TURP, transurethral incision of the prostate (TUIP) for small glands, and newer minimally invasive procedures.
  • Open, laparoscopic or robotic simple prostatectomy for very large glands.

E. Pre-operative nursing care

  • Explain the operation, the catheter, bladder irrigation and the possible sexual effect (retrograde ejaculation); obtain informed consent.
  • Treat UTI so that urine is sterile before surgery; check renal function, haemoglobin, coagulation profile, blood group and cross-match; stop antiplatelet and anticoagulant drugs as advised.
  • Prevent constipation, complete the pre-anaesthetic check-up and keep the patient NPO as ordered.

F. Post-operative nursing care after TURP

  1. Vital signs frequently – detect haemorrhage (tachycardia, hypotension, pallor) and urosepsis (fever with chills, hypotension, confusion).
  2. Continuous bladder irrigation (CBI) through a three-way Foley catheter using sterile normal saline (never plain water, which causes haemolysis and hyponatraemia):
    • Adjust the flow to keep the outflow light pink to clear and free of clots; bright red, thick drainage with clots suggests arterial bleeding – increase the flow and inform the surgeon immediately.
    • True urine output = total drainage − volume of irrigant instilled; record accurately on the intake–output chart.
    • The catheter may be taped to the thigh under traction for a few hours so that the balloon compresses the prostatic bed – maintain it as ordered and release it at the specified time.
  3. Maintain catheter patency – if drainage stops and the patient has lower abdominal pain or a distended bladder, check for kinks and clots and perform manual bladder washout with a bladder syringe under aseptic technique as ordered.
  4. Bladder spasms – painful urge to void with leakage around the catheter; give antispasmodics (oxybutynin) and analgesics, remove clots, reassure the patient and avoid unnecessary handling of the catheter.
  5. Observe for TURP syndrome (dilutional hyponatraemia from absorption of irrigating fluid during surgery) – confusion, restlessness, nausea and vomiting, bradycardia, hypertension, visual disturbances and seizures; check serum sodium, restrict fluids and give diuretics or hypertonic saline as ordered.
  6. Fluids and bowel care – once oral intake is allowed, encourage 2.5–3 litres of fluid daily; give stool softeners; avoid straining, enemas, rectal thermometers and rectal tubes, which can cause bleeding from the prostatic bed.
  7. Early ambulation, leg exercises, deep breathing and DVT prophylaxis.
  8. Catheter removal and voiding – the catheter is usually removed after 2–3 days when the urine is clear; observe the first few voids for volume, stream, haematuria and retention; explain that mild frequency, burning and temporary dribbling are common and improve over weeks.

G. Discharge teaching

  • Avoid heavy lifting, straining, long bicycle or motorcycle rides, vigorous exercise and sexual intercourse for about 4–6 weeks.
  • Drink plenty of fluids, prevent constipation, and limit alcohol and caffeine.
  • Mild haematuria may recur around 10–14 days after surgery when the scab in the prostatic bed separates; report heavy bleeding, clots, inability to pass urine, fever or severe burning at once.
  • Pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises to regain control of dribbling.
  • Explain retrograde ejaculation (semen enters the bladder – "dry orgasm"), which is harmless but reduces fertility; erections are usually not affected.
  • Avoid over-the-counter cold remedies with decongestants; attend yearly follow-up, as regrowth may occur after several years.

Nursing diagnoses (examples) | Nursing diagnosis | Key interventions | |---|---| | Urinary retention related to bladder outlet obstruction | Catheterisation, alpha blockers, monitoring of PVR | | Acute pain related to bladder spasms after TURP | Antispasmodics, analgesics, maintaining catheter patency | | Risk for deficient fluid volume related to haemorrhage | CBI, monitoring drainage colour, vital signs and Hb | | Risk for infection related to the indwelling catheter | Aseptic catheter care, fluids, early removal | | Sexual dysfunction related to retrograde ejaculation | Explanation, counselling, privacy |

Nursing importance

  • Elderly men often hide urinary symptoms out of embarrassment or accept them as part of ageing; sensitive enquiry, early referral and teaching about the precipitants of acute retention prevent serious complications such as kidney damage.
  • Skilled management of bladder irrigation and early recognition of bleeding and TURP syndrome are key post-operative nursing responsibilities.

Conclusion BPH is an age-related benign enlargement of the prostate that causes LUTS, retention and back-pressure damage to the kidneys. Lifestyle measures, alpha blockers and 5-alpha reductase inhibitors control mild to moderate disease, while TURP or laser surgery relieves significant obstruction. Careful post-TURP nursing – irrigation, monitoring for bleeding and hyponatraemia, catheter care and discharge teaching – ensures a safe recovery.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Kidney and Urinary Problems
question: Explain the clinical features and nursing management of a patient with nephrotic syndrome.
answer_html:
Definition Nephrotic syndrome is a clinical syndrome caused by increased permeability of the glomerular filtration barrier to protein. It is characterised by:

  1. Heavy proteinuria – more than 3.5 g/day in adults (urine protein–creatinine ratio above about 3 g/g).
  2. Hypoalbuminaemia – serum albumin below 3 g/dL.
  3. Generalised oedema.
  4. Hyperlipidaemia and lipiduria.

Causes

  • Primary glomerular diseases – minimal change disease (commonest in children, also seen in adults), membranous nephropathy (common in adults), focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), membranoproliferative GN.
  • Secondary causes – diabetes mellitus (the commonest secondary cause in adults), SLE, amyloidosis, infections (hepatitis B and C, HIV, malaria, syphilis), drugs (NSAIDs, gold, penicillamine), malignancy (lymphoma, solid tumours) and snakebite.

Clinical features

  • Oedema – begins as periorbital puffiness in the morning, then swelling of the feet, ankles, genitalia and abdominal wall; ascites and pleural effusion, and anasarca in severe cases; weight gain.
  • Frothy urine due to protein; urine output may be reduced.
  • Fatigue, anorexia, breathlessness (effusions) and abdominal discomfort; BP may be normal or raised.
  • Complications – infections (loss of immunoglobulins – peritonitis, cellulitis, pneumonia), thromboembolism (renal vein thrombosis, DVT, pulmonary embolism – due to loss of antithrombin III), hyperlipidaemia and atherosclerosis, AKI, protein malnutrition, hypovolaemia with excessive diuresis, and side effects of steroids.

Investigations (for understanding) – urine dipstick (3+ to 4+ protein), 24-hour urine protein or protein–creatinine ratio, serum albumin, lipid profile, creatinine and blood sugar, tests for secondary causes, and renal biopsy in adults.

Medical management

  • Corticosteroids (prednisolone) – first-line for minimal change disease; immunosuppressants (cyclophosphamide, tacrolimus, cyclosporine, mycophenolate, rituximab) for steroid-resistant, frequently relapsing or membranous disease.
  • ACE inhibitors or ARBs to reduce proteinuria; diuretics (furosemide ± spironolactone) for oedema; albumin infusion with a diuretic for severe refractory oedema.
  • Statins for hyperlipidaemia, anticoagulants in high-risk patients, prompt treatment of infection, and treatment of the underlying cause (e.g. control of diabetes).

Nursing management

  1. Assessment and monitoring – daily weight, strict intake–output, abdominal girth, site and degree of oedema, BP, breath sounds; daily urine dipstick for albumin; serum albumin, creatinine and electrolytes.
  2. Diet and fluids
    • Salt restriction – no added salt, avoid pickles, papad and processed foods; fluid restriction only for severe oedema or hyponatraemia.
    • Normal protein intake (about 0.8–1 g/kg/day) of good quality – high-protein diets are not advised because they increase proteinuria; adequate calories.
    • Low-fat diet, fresh vegetables and fruits; sugar control in diabetics.
  3. Skin care – oedematous skin breaks down easily: change position every 2 hours, elevate oedematous limbs, give scrotal support in men, keep skin folds clean and dry, use soft linen, and avoid IM injections into oedematous tissue.
  4. Prevention of infection – hand hygiene, avoid contact with infected people, monitor temperature, pneumococcal and influenza vaccination (avoid live vaccines during high-dose steroids), early treatment of infections.
  5. Prevention of thrombosis – early mobilisation, leg exercises, adequate hydration and avoidance of over-diuresis; watch for calf pain and swelling, flank pain, haematuria or sudden breathlessness.
  6. Drug therapy – give steroids in the morning after food; monitor blood sugar, BP, weight, mood, sleep and gastric symptoms; never stop steroids suddenly; monitor potassium with diuretics and ACE inhibitors.
  7. Rest – bed rest during severe oedema, with gradual return to activity.
  8. Psychological support – body-image changes (moon face, swelling) and the relapsing course cause anxiety; reassure and involve the family.
  9. Health education – home dipstick testing of urine protein with a record; recognise relapse (puffiness, frothy urine, weight gain) and report early; drug adherence, diet and regular follow-up.

Conclusion Nephrotic syndrome is characterised by heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hyperlipidaemia. Steroids and other immunosuppressants, diuretics and ACE inhibitors control the disease, while nursing care focuses on careful monitoring, salt restriction, skin care, prevention of infection and thrombosis, and teaching the patient to detect relapse.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Kidney and Urinary Problems
question: Explain peritoneal dialysis and the nursing management of a patient on peritoneal dialysis.

diagram.caption: Peritoneal dialysis exchange (CAPD)
labels: Tenckhoff catheter passing through the abdominal wall into the peritoneal cavity
dialysate bag hung above the patient for inflow
drainage bag kept below for outflow
peritoneum acting as a semi-permeable membrane

answer_html:
Definition Peritoneal dialysis (PD) is a form of renal replacement therapy in which the peritoneum acts as a natural semi-permeable membrane. Dialysis fluid (dialysate) is run into the peritoneal cavity through a catheter; waste products and excess electrolytes pass from the blood in the peritoneal capillaries into the fluid by diffusion, and excess water is removed by osmosis (ultrafiltration) because of the dextrose (glucose) or icodextrin in the dialysate. The used fluid is then drained out and replaced with fresh fluid.

Types

  • Acute (intermittent) PD – through a temporary catheter in AKI, especially in children and in hospitals without haemodialysis facilities.
  • CAPD (continuous ambulatory peritoneal dialysis) – done by the patient at home, usually 4 exchanges a day of about 2 litres each, with a dwell time of 4–6 hours (longer overnight).
  • APD (automated peritoneal dialysis) – a cycler machine performs the exchanges at night while the patient sleeps.

Procedure – one exchange

  • A soft silicone Tenckhoff catheter is placed surgically through the abdominal wall with its tip in the pelvis; ideally it is allowed to heal for about 2 weeks before regular use.
  • Each exchange has three phases: inflow (fill) – warmed dialysate runs in by gravity over about 10 minutes; dwell – the fluid stays in the abdomen while exchange occurs; outflow (drain) – the fluid drains by gravity into an empty bag over about 20 minutes.

Advantages – done at home, no needles, fewer hospital visits, gentle and steady (suitable for cardiac patients, elderly people and children), helps preserve residual kidney function, fewer diet restrictions and no vascular access needed. The Pradhan Mantri National Dialysis Programme has been extended to include peritoneal dialysis.

Complications

  • Peritonitis – the most important complication: cloudy effluent, abdominal pain and fever.
  • Exit-site and tunnel infection – redness, swelling and discharge around the catheter.
  • Catheter problems – poor outflow (constipation, kinking, fibrin plugs, catheter migration) and fluid leaks.
  • Hernias, back pain, hyperglycaemia and weight gain (glucose absorption), hypoalbuminaemia (protein loss into dialysate) and fluid overload when ultrafiltration fails.

Nursing management

  1. Before starting – explain the procedure; record weight, vital signs, blood sugar and electrolytes; ask the patient to empty the bladder and prevent constipation, which hampers drainage.
  2. Strict asepsis – mask, thorough hand washing and a clean surface; check the dialysate bag for strength, expiry date, clarity and leaks; warm the bag to body temperature with dry heat (never in hot water or a microwave).
  3. Perform the exchange as prescribed with the patient in a comfortable semi-Fowler's position; observe for pain or breathlessness during inflow.
  4. Record every exchange on a PD chart – inflow volume, outflow volume, net ultrafiltration (outflow minus inflow), colour and clarity of effluent, and daily weight.
  5. Inspect the effluent – it should be clear and pale yellow; cloudy fluid suggests peritonitis – send a sample for cell count and culture and inform the doctor (intraperitoneal antibiotics are usually given); report blood-stained fluid.
  6. Exit-site care – clean daily with antiseptic, keep dry, secure the catheter to prevent pulling, and observe for infection.
  7. Poor drainage – change the patient's position, check for kinks and closed clamps, treat constipation with laxatives, and add heparin to the dialysate for fibrin as ordered.
  8. Monitor fluid balance, BP, blood sugar, electrolytes and serum albumin; provide a high-protein diet (about 1.2–1.3 g/kg/day) because protein is lost into the dialysate, and a fibre-rich diet to prevent constipation.
  9. Patient and family training for CAPD – hand hygiene, exchange technique in a clean, closed room, storage of bags, recognising peritonitis (cloudy fluid, pain, fever) and reporting immediately, protecting the catheter while bathing (no swimming in ponds or tubs), keeping records and attending follow-up.

Conclusion Peritoneal dialysis uses the patient's peritoneum to remove waste products and excess water, and can be done at home as CAPD or APD. Strict asepsis, accurate exchange records, close observation of the effluent, exit-site care and thorough patient training are the key nursing responsibilities that prevent peritonitis and ensure adequate dialysis.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Kidney and Urinary Problems
question: Explain haemodialysis and the nursing care of a patient before, during and after haemodialysis.

diagram.caption: Haemodialysis circuit with AV fistula
labels: radial artery–cephalic vein fistula at the wrist
arterial needle leading to the blood pump
dialyser with dialysate flowing opposite to blood
air detector and venous line returning cleaned blood to the patient

answer_html:
Definition Haemodialysis (HD) is a procedure in which the patient's blood is pumped through an artificial kidney (dialyser) outside the body, where waste products, excess electrolytes and fluid are removed across a semi-permeable membrane into the dialysis fluid, and the cleaned blood is returned to the patient.

Principles

  • Diffusion – solutes such as urea, creatinine and potassium move from the blood (higher concentration) into the dialysate (lower concentration).
  • Ultrafiltration – excess water is removed by a pressure gradient across the membrane; convection carries some solutes along with the water.
  • Countercurrent flow of blood and dialysate maintains the concentration gradient, and heparin prevents clotting in the circuit.

Indications – end-stage kidney disease (CKD stage 5), AKI with life-threatening complications (severe acidosis, refractory hyperkalaemia, fluid overload, uraemic pericarditis or encephalopathy), and poisoning with dialysable substances (methanol, lithium, salicylates). For ESKD the usual schedule is 3 sessions a week, each of about 4 hours.

Vascular access

  • Arteriovenous (AV) fistula – surgical joining of an artery and a vein, usually the radial artery to the cephalic vein at the wrist; it is the best access with the fewest infections and lasts for years, but needs 6–8 weeks or more to mature.
  • AV graft – a synthetic tube joining an artery and a vein when veins are unsuitable.
  • Temporary or tunnelled double-lumen dialysis catheter in the internal jugular or femoral vein for emergency or short-term dialysis.

Nursing care before dialysis

  1. Record weight and compare it with the patient's dry weight (weight without excess fluid) to plan the ultrafiltration; check vital signs, temperature, breath sounds and oedema.
  2. Review laboratory values – urea, creatinine, potassium and haemoglobin; check viral markers (HBsAg, anti-HCV, HIV) – HBsAg-positive patients are dialysed on separate, dedicated machines (and HCV-positive patients as per unit policy).
  3. Assess the access – feel the thrill and listen for the bruit of the fistula and look for signs of infection; inspect the catheter dressing.
  4. Explain the procedure; withhold antihypertensives on the morning of dialysis if advised, to prevent hypotension.

Nursing care during dialysis

  1. Cannulate the fistula under strict asepsis (or connect the catheter with sterile technique); secure needles and lines so that they cannot dislodge.
  2. Monitor BP and pulse at least every 30 minutes, machine pressures, blood flow rate and alarms.
  3. Watch for and manage complications:
    • Hypotension (most common) – lie the patient flat with legs raised, reduce ultrafiltration and give a saline bolus as ordered.
    • Muscle cramps – reduce ultrafiltration, give saline, stretch the muscle.
    • Dialysis disequilibrium syndrome – headache, nausea, restlessness and seizures due to rapid removal of urea (cerebral oedema), mainly in the first sessions; prevented by short, slow initial sessions.
    • Air embolism, bleeding from needle sites, clotting of the circuit, fever and chills (infection or pyrogen reaction), chest pain and arrhythmias.
  4. Give heparin and other drugs (erythropoietin, iron) as prescribed.

Nursing care after dialysis

  1. Remove the needles and apply gentle pressure until bleeding stops without occluding the fistula; check for bleeding later.
  2. Record post-dialysis weight and vital signs; watch for postural hypotension when the patient stands up.
  3. Avoid invasive procedures and IM injections for a few hours because of heparin.

Health education

  • Limit interdialytic weight gain (ideally not more than about 2 kg between sessions) by controlling salt and fluid intake.
  • Diet – restrict potassium, phosphorus and salt; take adequate protein (about 1.2 g/kg/day); take phosphate binders with meals.
  • Fistula care – check the thrill daily, keep the arm clean, and avoid BP measurement, injections, blood sampling, tight sleeves, watches, bangles and sleeping on that arm.
  • Hepatitis B vaccination, regular attendance for every session, and early reporting of breathlessness, chest pain or weakness.

Conclusion Haemodialysis removes waste and excess fluid by passing blood through an artificial kidney using diffusion and ultrafiltration. Careful assessment before, close monitoring during and observation after each session, along with protection of the vascular access and education about fluid and diet, keep the patient safe on long-term dialysis.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Kidney and Urinary Problems
question: Explain the nursing management of a patient with urinary tract infection, including prevention of catheter-associated urinary tract infection.
answer_html:
Definition Urinary tract infection (UTI) is the invasion and multiplication of microorganisms in the urinary tract, usually confirmed by significant bacteriuria (10⁵ or more colony-forming units/mL) on urine culture. It is classified as lower UTI (urethritis, cystitis, prostatitis) or upper UTI (pyelonephritis), and as uncomplicated (healthy non-pregnant women) or complicated (men, pregnancy, catheters, stones, obstruction, diabetes, immunosuppression).

Causes and risk factors

  • Escherichia coli causes most UTIs; others are Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterococcus, Staphylococcus saprophyticus and, in hospitals, Pseudomonas.
  • Female sex (short urethra close to the anus), sexual activity, pregnancy and menopause (low oestrogen).
  • Indwelling urinary catheters – the commonest cause of hospital-acquired UTI.
  • Obstruction and stasis – stones, BPH, strictures, neurogenic bladder.
  • Diabetes, immunosuppression, poor perineal hygiene, low fluid intake and holding urine for long periods (lack of clean toilets at schools and workplaces).

Clinical features

  • Cystitis – burning micturition (dysuria), frequency and urgency, suprapubic pain, cloudy or foul-smelling urine and sometimes haematuria; usually no high fever.
  • Pyelonephritis – high fever with chills, flank (loin) pain and renal-angle tenderness, nausea and vomiting, often with lower urinary symptoms.
  • Elderly patients may present only with confusion, falls, new incontinence or loss of appetite.

Diagnosis – urine routine (pus cells, nitrites, leucocyte esterase), midstream clean-catch urine culture and sensitivity, blood culture in pyelonephritis, and ultrasound KUB for complicated or recurrent infection.

Medical management

  • Uncomplicated cystitis – e.g. nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for 5 days or a single dose of fosfomycin, as per the local antibiogram.
  • Pyelonephritis – oral or IV antibiotics (e.g. ceftriaxone) for 7–14 days according to culture; admission if severe.
  • Analgesics and urinary alkalinisers for symptom relief; treatment of underlying obstruction or stones.

Nursing management

  1. Collect a midstream clean-catch specimen before starting antibiotics – teach the patient to clean the area, pass the first stream into the toilet and collect the midstream urine in a sterile container; send within 1–2 hours or refrigerate. In catheterised patients, aspirate from the sampling port with aseptic technique – never from the drainage bag.
  2. Give antibiotics on time and stress completion of the full course.
  3. Encourage fluids (2–3 litres/day) unless restricted, to flush out bacteria.
  4. Relieve discomfort – warm sitz baths or a hot-water bag over the suprapubic area, analgesics and frequent voiding.
  5. Monitor temperature, pain, urine output and character; watch for urosepsis (rigors, hypotension, tachycardia, confusion), especially in the elderly and in diabetics.
  6. Perineal hygiene – wipe from front to back, wear cotton undergarments, and avoid harsh soaps and douches.
  7. Prevention of catheter-associated UTI (CAUTI) – bundle approach
    • Avoid unnecessary catheterisation; use alternatives such as a condom catheter or intermittent catheterisation where possible.
    • Aseptic insertion by trained staff with sterile equipment and the smallest suitable catheter.
    • Maintain a closed drainage system – never disconnect the catheter from the tubing.
    • Keep the drainage bag below bladder level and off the floor; keep the tubing free of kinks.
    • Empty the bag regularly into a separate clean container for each patient.
    • Clean the meatus daily with soap and water and secure the catheter to the thigh.
    • Review the need for the catheter every day and remove it as early as possible.
    • Hand hygiene before and after any handling of the catheter.
  8. Health education for prevention of recurrence – drink enough water, void every 3–4 hours and do not hold urine, void after sexual intercourse, wipe front to back, prevent constipation, control blood sugar, use vaginal oestrogen in post-menopausal women if advised, and never self-medicate with antibiotics.

Conclusion UTI, most often due to E. coli, ranges from simple cystitis to pyelonephritis and urosepsis. Correct specimen collection, appropriate antibiotics, fluids and comfort measures, strict CAUTI-prevention bundles and education about hygiene and voiding habits form the core of nursing management.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Kidney and Urinary Problems
question: Describe the clinical features and nursing management of a patient with acute glomerulonephritis.
answer_html:
Definition Acute glomerulonephritis (AGN) is an acute, usually immune-mediated inflammation of the glomeruli that presents as the nephritic syndrome – haematuria, mild to moderate proteinuria, oedema, hypertension and oliguria, with a rise in blood urea and creatinine.

Causes

  • Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (PSGN) – the classic form; follows a throat infection after 1–3 weeks or a skin infection (impetigo, infected scabies) after 3–6 weeks with group A beta-haemolytic Streptococcus; common in children of 5–12 years, but also seen in adults in crowded, unhygienic living conditions.
  • Other infections – staphylococcal infection, infective endocarditis, hepatitis B and C, HIV and malaria.
  • IgA nephropathy, lupus nephritis (SLE), vasculitis and anti-GBM (Goodpasture) disease.

Pathophysiology (brief) – antigen–antibody complexes deposit in the glomeruli and activate complement, causing inflammation; the reduced GFR leads to retention of salt and water (oedema and hypertension), and the damaged glomeruli leak red cells and protein into the urine.

Clinical features

  • Haematuria – smoky, cola-coloured or tea-coloured urine.
  • Oedema – periorbital puffiness, especially in the morning, with facial and ankle swelling.
  • Hypertension – headache; may lead to hypertensive encephalopathy (severe headache, vomiting, blurred vision, convulsions).
  • Oliguria and mild proteinuria; fatigue, anorexia, nausea, loin discomfort and low-grade fever.
  • Complications – acute pulmonary oedema and heart failure (fluid overload), hypertensive encephalopathy, AKI, and rarely rapidly progressive GN or CKD.

Investigations – urine: RBCs and RBC casts, protein; serum urea, creatinine and electrolytes; raised ASO titre (after throat infection) or anti-DNase B (after skin infection); low C3 complement, which returns to normal in 6–8 weeks; throat or skin swab; chest X-ray; renal biopsy if the course is atypical.

Medical management

  • Penicillin (erythromycin if allergic) to eradicate any remaining streptococci and prevent spread to contacts – it does not change the course of the kidney disease.
  • Loop diuretics (furosemide) for oedema and hypertension; antihypertensives such as calcium-channel blockers.
  • Dialysis for severe AKI or uncontrolled fluid overload; steroids and immunosuppressants for other types of GN.
  • Most patients with PSGN recover completely within a few weeks.

Nursing management

  1. Rest – bed rest during the acute phase until oedema subsides, BP is controlled and gross haematuria clears, followed by gradual ambulation.
  2. Monitoring – BP every 4 hours (more often when high), daily weight, strict intake–output, urine colour and volume, oedema, breath sounds and neurological status (headache, vomiting, convulsions).
  3. Fluid restriction – intake equal to the previous day's urine output plus about 500 mL for insensible loss.
  4. Diet – salt restriction (no added salt); protein restriction only if urea is high and urine output is low; potassium restriction during oliguria; enough carbohydrates for calories.
  5. Medications – give antibiotics, diuretics and antihypertensives as prescribed; monitor potassium and BP response.
  6. Seizure precautions in severe hypertension – padded side rails, suction and oxygen at the bedside, antihypertensive and anticonvulsant drugs ready.
  7. Skin care of oedematous areas and prevention of infection.
  8. Urine testing – daily urine examination for blood and protein.
  9. Health education – early and complete treatment of sore throat, impetigo and infected scabies; personal hygiene; follow-up of BP and urine for several months until haematuria and proteinuria clear; report reduced urine, swelling or headache promptly.

Conclusion AGN, commonly post-streptococcal, presents with haematuria, oedema, hypertension and oliguria. Rest, salt and fluid restriction, BP control, diuretics and careful monitoring for pulmonary oedema and hypertensive encephalopathy, together with prevention of streptococcal infections, are the key elements of nursing management.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Kidney and Urinary Problems
question: Explain the nursing care of a patient undergoing kidney transplantation.

diagram.caption: Placement of a transplanted kidney
labels: donor kidney placed in the right iliac fossa outside the peritoneum
donor renal artery joined to the external iliac artery
renal vein to the external iliac vein
donor ureter implanted into the bladder with a DJ stent
patient's own kidneys left in place

answer_html:
Introduction Kidney transplantation is the surgical placement of a healthy kidney from a living or deceased donor into a patient with end-stage kidney disease (ESKD). It is the best form of renal replacement therapy, giving longer survival, better quality of life and lower long-term cost than dialysis. In India it is regulated by the Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act (THOTA), 1994, amended 2011, and NOTTO (National Organ and Tissue Transplant Organisation) runs the national network and registry. Most kidney transplants in India are from living related donors.

1. Types of donors

  • Living donors – near relatives (parents, siblings, children, spouse, grandparents); unrelated donors need approval of the authorisation committee, which guards against organ trade.
  • Deceased (brain-dead) donors – after certification of brain-stem death by a panel of doctors and consent of the family.

2. Pre-transplant evaluation and preparation

  • Recipient – cardiac evaluation, screening for infection (HIV, hepatitis B and C, TB, dental and urinary sources) and cancer; blood group compatibility, HLA typing and crossmatch (a positive crossmatch indicates preformed antibodies and a risk of hyperacute rejection); vaccination (hepatitis B, pneumococcal) before surgery.
  • Donor – detailed medical and psychological assessment, kidney function and imaging of the renal vessels.
  • Dialysis within 24 hours before surgery to correct potassium and fluid status; induction immunosuppression as ordered; informed consent and psychological preparation.

3. Surgery (brief)

  • The new kidney is placed outside the peritoneum in the iliac fossa; the renal artery and vein are joined to the iliac vessels and the ureter is implanted into the bladder, often with a DJ stent. The patient's own kidneys are usually left in place.

4. Post-operative nursing care

  1. Monitor urine output hourly – a well-functioning graft may produce large volumes immediately (post-transplant diuresis); replace fluids as ordered (often hourly urine output plus insensible loss). A sudden fall in output may mean rejection, acute tubular necrosis, renal artery or vein thrombosis, obstruction or urine leak – report at once.
  2. Vital signs, CVP and daily weight; daily serum creatinine and electrolytes, especially potassium and sodium.
  3. Catheter care – keep it patent (clots can block it); it is usually removed after about 5 days; observe for haematuria.
  4. Wound and drain care – observe for bleeding, lymphocele and urine leak.
  5. Immunosuppression – give triple therapy (e.g. tacrolimus + mycophenolate mofetil + prednisolone) exactly on time; ensure tacrolimus trough levels are checked; observe side effects – nephrotoxicity, tremors, high blood sugar (new-onset diabetes), hypertension, GI upset, bone-marrow suppression and infections.
  6. Infection prevention – strict hand hygiene, single room, restriction of visitors with infections, aseptic care of lines, oral care and temperature monitoring; prophylaxis against CMV, Pneumocystis (co-trimoxazole) and fungal infections as ordered.
  7. Observation for rejection
    • Hyperacute – within minutes to hours, due to preformed antibodies; the graft fails immediately (prevented by crossmatching).
    • Acute – commonest in the first months: fever, reduced urine output, weight gain, oedema, rising creatinine and BP, and tenderness over the graft; treated with high-dose steroids or antibody therapy.
    • Chronic – gradual decline of graft function over months to years.
  8. Psychological support – fear of rejection, feelings of guilt or obligation towards the donor, and body-image changes due to steroids.
  9. Donor care – post-nephrectomy pain relief, early ambulation and long-term follow-up of BP and kidney function.

5. Discharge teaching

  • Take immunosuppressive drugs for life – never miss, stop or change doses; avoid herbal remedies and drugs that interact (several antibiotics and antifungals alter tacrolimus levels); keep a written medicine schedule.
  • Recognise and immediately report signs of rejection and infection.
  • In the early months avoid crowded places, wear a mask, avoid live vaccines, drink boiled or filtered water, eat freshly cooked food and avoid street food.
  • Keep daily records of weight, BP and urine output; attend regular blood tests; use sunscreen (higher risk of skin cancer); follow a healthy, low-salt diet and exercise regularly.

Conclusion Kidney transplantation offers the best outcome for ESKD. Careful donor and recipient preparation, meticulous post-operative fluid management, punctual immunosuppression, infection prevention, early recognition of rejection and lifelong patient education are the pillars of nursing care.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Kidney and Urinary Problems
question: Explain the assessment of a patient with genitourinary disorders and the nurse's role in common diagnostic tests.
answer_html:
Introduction A systematic genitourinary (GU) assessment helps detect kidney, bladder and prostate disorders early and plan care. It includes a focused history, physical examination and diagnostic tests, in which the nurse prepares the patient, collects specimens correctly and monitors for complications.

1. History

  • Urinary symptoms – dysuria, frequency, urgency, nocturia, hesitancy, poor stream, dribbling, retention, incontinence, haematuria, frothy urine, and change in volume – oliguria (less than 400 mL/day), anuria (less than 100 mL/day) or polyuria (more than 3 litres/day).
  • Pain – dull flank (loin) pain from the kidney, colicky pain radiating to the groin from the ureter, suprapubic pain from the bladder and perineal pain from the prostate.
  • Systemic symptoms – puffiness of the face, swelling of feet, breathlessness, fatigue, nausea, itching and fever.
  • Past history – diabetes, hypertension, stones, UTIs, recent sore throat or skin infection (GN), urological surgery and catheterisation.
  • Drug history – painkillers (NSAIDs), nephrotoxic antibiotics, herbal or traditional medicines, anticholinergics and diuretics.
  • Family history – polycystic kidney disease, stones and kidney failure.
  • Personal history – daily fluid intake, salt and protein intake, occupation (heat exposure, dyes and chemicals), smoking (bladder cancer), sexual and reproductive history.

2. Physical examination

  • General – BP, weight, oedema (periorbital, pedal, sacral), pallor, hydration, skin (dryness, scratch marks, uraemic colour) and breath odour.
  • Abdomen – inspection for a distended bladder or mass; bimanual palpation of the kidneys; suprapubic palpation and percussion of the bladder (dullness in retention); renal-angle tenderness by gentle fist percussion at the costovertebral angle (pyelonephritis); auscultation for renal artery bruit.
  • Genitalia – meatal discharge, phimosis, scrotal swellings; digital rectal examination of the prostate by the doctor.
  • Bladder scan for post-void residual urine.

3. Common diagnostic tests and nursing role | Test | Purpose | Nursing role | |---|---|---| | Urine routine and microscopy | Protein, sugar, pus cells, RBCs, casts, crystals | Fresh early-morning sample; send within 1–2 hours | | Urine culture | Identify organism and sensitivity | Midstream clean-catch in a sterile container before antibiotics | | 24-hour urine collection | Protein, creatinine clearance | Discard first morning urine, collect all urine for 24 h including next morning's first sample; keep cool | | Blood tests | Urea, creatinine, eGFR, electrolytes, PSA | Explain; avoid PSA soon after DRE or catheterisation | | X-ray and ultrasound KUB | Stones, kidney size, hydronephrosis, residual urine | Full bladder for pelvic ultrasound; bowel preparation if advised | | CT urography (contrast) | Stones, tumours, obstruction | Check creatinine, allergy and metformin; hydrate before and after | | Renal scan (DTPA/DMSA) | Function of each kidney, scarring | Hydration; explain the tracer dose is small | | Cystoscopy | View urethra and bladder, biopsy | Consent, sterile urine; observe urine and pain afterwards | | Uroflowmetry and urodynamics | Flow rate, bladder pressures | Comfortably full bladder; privacy |

4. Renal biopsy – nursing care

  • Before – informed consent; check coagulation profile, platelet count, haemoglobin and BP; stop antiplatelets and anticoagulants as advised; blood grouping and cross-matching; NPO for 4–6 hours; teach the patient to hold the breath during needle insertion; position prone with a pillow under the abdomen.
  • After – apply pressure to the site and keep the patient on bed rest, lying supine, for 6–24 hours as per protocol; check vital signs every 15 minutes at first and then less often; inspect the dressing; observe serial urine samples for haematuria; encourage fluids; report flank pain, falling BP or rising pulse (bleeding); avoid heavy lifting and strenuous activity for about 2 weeks.

5. General nursing responsibilities

  • Explain each test in simple language and obtain consent where needed; maintain privacy and dignity during genital and rectal examination; label and dispatch specimens correctly; keep accurate intake–output records; hydrate patients before contrast studies and observe for allergic reactions; monitor after invasive procedures and report abnormal results promptly.

Conclusion GU assessment combines a careful history of urinary symptoms and risk factors, a focused physical examination and appropriate investigations. The nurse's preparation of the patient, correct specimen collection and post-procedure monitoring ensure accurate results and patient safety.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Kidney and Urinary Problems
question: Explain the causes, clinical features, management and nursing care of urethral stricture.
answer_html:
Definition Urethral stricture is a narrowing of the urethral lumen due to scar tissue (fibrosis) in the lining of the urethra and the surrounding spongy tissue, which obstructs the flow of urine. It occurs mainly in men because the male urethra is long and more exposed to injury.

Causes

  • Trauma – straddle injury (falling astride a bar, bicycle frame or wall) damaging the bulbar urethra; pelvic fracture in road traffic accidents injuring the posterior urethra.
  • Iatrogenic – traumatic or prolonged catheterisation, use of large catheters, cystoscopy, TURP and other transurethral instruments.
  • Inflammation and infection – gonococcal and other urethritis, lichen sclerosus (balanitis xerotica obliterans), tuberculosis.
  • Congenital (rare) and idiopathic.

Clinical features

  • Thin, weak urinary stream, straining, spraying or splitting of the stream, prolonged voiding, post-void dribbling, a feeling of incomplete emptying and frequency.
  • Recurrent UTI, prostatitis, epididymitis, urethral discharge and haematuria.
  • Complications – acute or chronic retention of urine, bladder stones and diverticula, hydronephrosis and kidney failure, periurethral abscess and multiple urethral fistulae ("watering-can perineum").

Diagnosis – uroflowmetry (low, flat, plateau-shaped flow curve), retrograde urethrogram (RGU) with micturating cystourethrogram (MCU) to show the site and length of the stricture, urethroscopy, ultrasound for residual urine and urine culture.

Management

  • Urethral dilatation – gradual stretching with graduated dilators; gives temporary relief and may need repetition or clean intermittent self-dilatation.
  • Optical internal urethrotomy (OIU) – endoscopic incision of a short stricture with a cold knife or laser, followed by a catheter for a few days.
  • Urethroplasty – open surgical reconstruction; excision and primary anastomosis for short bulbar strictures and buccal mucosa graft (taken from the inner cheek) for longer strictures; gives the best long-term results.
  • Suprapubic cystostomy (SPC) – diverts urine through the lower abdomen when a urethral catheter cannot be passed in acute retention or after a pelvic-fracture urethral injury.

Nursing care

  1. Never force a urethral catheter when a stricture or urethral injury is suspected (e.g. blood at the meatus after trauma); inform the urologist, as suprapubic drainage may be needed.
  2. Pre-operative – ensure sterile urine (treat UTI), explain the procedure and obtain consent; for buccal grafts, oral hygiene and chlorhexidine mouthwash.
  3. Post-operative
    • Catheter care – secure the catheter, keep a closed drainage system and maintain patency; after urethroplasty the catheter usually stays for 2–3 weeks.
    • Monitor urine output and haematuria; care for the perineal wound; give analgesics and antibiotics as ordered.
    • After buccal graft harvest – oral care, cold soft diet and pain relief.
    • Prevent constipation and straining.
  4. SPC care – aseptic dressing around the tube, secure the tube, ensure patency, encourage fluids and change the catheter as scheduled.
  5. Follow-up for recurrence – teach the patient to watch for thinning of the stream; arrange uroflowmetry; teach clean intermittent self-dilatation if prescribed.
  6. Health education – safe catheterisation practices in hospitals (correct size, adequate lubrication, early removal), early treatment of urethritis and sexually transmitted infections, safe sexual practices, and prevention of road and straddle injuries.

Conclusion Urethral stricture is a scar-induced narrowing of the urethra, commonly due to trauma, instrumentation or infection, causing a poor stream and retention. Dilatation, internal urethrotomy, urethroplasty or suprapubic drainage relieve the obstruction, while nursing care focuses on catheter and wound care, avoidance of iatrogenic injury and follow-up for recurrence.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Kidney and Urinary Problems
question: Explain the types of urinary incontinence and the nursing management of a patient with urinary incontinence, including neurogenic bladder.
answer_html:
Definition Urinary incontinence is the involuntary leakage of urine. It is common in older women, after childbirth and menopause, after prostate surgery and in people with neurological diseases. Because of embarrassment it is often hidden, yet it causes skin breakdown, falls, infections, social isolation and depression.

Types

  1. Stress incontinence – leakage on coughing, sneezing, laughing, lifting or exercise due to weak pelvic floor muscles and urethral sphincter; common in multiparous women, after menopause, in obesity and chronic cough, and in men after prostatectomy.
  2. Urge incontinence (overactive bladder) – a sudden, strong desire to void followed by leakage before reaching the toilet, with frequency and nocturia; due to detrusor overactivity (idiopathic, UTI, stroke, Parkinson's disease, bladder stones).
  3. Mixed incontinence – features of both stress and urge incontinence.
  4. Overflow incontinence – frequent dribbling from an overdistended bladder with chronic retention – BPH, urethral stricture, diabetic neuropathy, anticholinergic drugs, spinal cord lesions.
  5. Functional incontinence – the urinary tract is normal, but the person cannot reach the toilet in time because of dementia, immobility, arthritis or barriers in the environment.
  6. Continuous (total) incontinence – constant leakage, e.g. from a vesicovaginal fistula after obstructed labour or pelvic surgery, or an ectopic ureter.
  7. Transient incontinence – due to delirium, infection, drugs (diuretics, sedatives), constipation or restricted mobility; it resolves when the cause is treated.

Neurogenic bladder

  • Bladder dysfunction due to damage to the nerves controlling the bladder – spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis, stroke, diabetic neuropathy, spina bifida.
  • Spastic (reflex, upper motor neuron) bladder – lesion above the sacral micturition centre (S2–S4); a small bladder empties reflexly and without control; lesions above T6 carry a risk of autonomic dysreflexia.
  • Flaccid (atonic, lower motor neuron) bladder – lesion at or below the sacral centre; a large bladder fails to contract, causing retention with overflow.

Management

  • Stress – pelvic floor muscle training, weight reduction, treatment of cough and constipation, vaginal pessary, and surgery (mid-urethral sling, colposuspension).
  • Urge – bladder training, reduction of caffeine, antimuscarinic drugs (oxybutynin, solifenacin, tolterodine) or mirabegron, and botulinum toxin injection into the bladder.
  • Overflow – relief of obstruction (BPH, stricture) and clean intermittent catheterisation (CIC).
  • Neurogenic bladder – CIC every 4–6 hours (preferred to long-term indwelling catheters), antimuscarinics for spastic bladder, and regular kidney and urodynamic follow-up.

Nursing management

  1. Assessment – type, frequency and amount of leakage, triggers, a 3-day bladder diary, fluid intake, medicines, mobility and cognition; post-void residual volume; urine test for infection.
  2. Pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises – identify the muscles by imagining stopping the flow of urine or holding back wind; contract for 5–10 seconds and relax for 10 seconds, 10–15 times, three times a day; improvement takes 6–12 weeks.
  3. Bladder training – void by the clock and gradually lengthen the interval (from every hour to every 3–4 hours); teach urge-suppression (stand still, squeeze the pelvic floor, breathe slowly, then walk calmly to the toilet).
  4. Timed and prompted voiding for the elderly and patients with dementia; a bedside commode or urinal, clear pathways, a night light and easy-to-remove clothing.
  5. Fluid advice – drink about 1.5–2 litres a day (restricting fluids concentrates urine and irritates the bladder); reduce tea, coffee, colas and alcohol, especially in the evening; prevent constipation.
  6. CIC teaching – hand washing, clean technique, lubricated catheter, regular timing, recording volumes (ideally below 400–500 mL each time) and recognising UTI.
  7. Skin care – prevent incontinence-associated dermatitis by gentle cleansing after each episode, patting dry and applying barrier cream; use absorbent pads or a condom catheter in men; change wet linen promptly; avoid long-term indwelling catheters where possible.
  8. Psychological support – maintain privacy and dignity, reassure the patient that incontinence is treatable, and encourage them to seek help rather than hide the problem.

Conclusion Urinary incontinence may be stress, urge, mixed, overflow, functional or continuous, and neurogenic bladder results from nerve damage. Careful assessment, pelvic floor exercises, bladder training, appropriate drugs or surgery, intermittent catheterisation, skin care and emotional support help restore continence and dignity.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Kidney and Urinary Problems
question: Explain carcinoma of the urinary bladder and the nursing care of a patient with urinary diversion (ileal conduit).

diagram.caption: Ileal conduit urinary diversion
labels: isolated segment of ileum with both ureters implanted into it
stoma brought out on the right lower abdomen
urostomy pouch with anti-reflux valve and drainage tap
continuity of the bowel restored by anastomosis

answer_html:
Introduction Carcinoma of the urinary bladder is the commonest malignancy of the urinary tract. Most are urothelial (transitional cell) carcinomas arising from the lining of the bladder; squamous cell carcinoma is associated with chronic irritation from long-term catheters, stones and schistosomiasis. It is more common in men above 60 years.

Risk factors

  • Cigarette and bidi smoking – the most important risk factor, responsible for about half of cases.
  • Occupational exposure to aromatic amines – dye, rubber, leather, paint, textile and printing industries.
  • Chronic irritation – long-term catheters, bladder stones and recurrent infection; schistosomiasis in endemic countries.
  • Previous pelvic radiotherapy, cyclophosphamide therapy and arsenic in drinking water.

Clinical features

  • Painless, intermittent, gross haematuria – the classic and commonest symptom; every adult with painless haematuria must be investigated.
  • Irritative symptoms – frequency, urgency and dysuria (especially in carcinoma in situ).
  • Advanced disease – pelvic pain, clot retention, hydronephrosis, bone pain and weight loss.

Diagnosis – urine cytology, ultrasound and CT urography, cystoscopy with biopsy (the key investigation) and TURBT for diagnosis and staging; CT/MRI for spread.

Management

  • Non-muscle-invasive tumours – TURBT (transurethral resection of bladder tumour) followed by intravesical therapy – a single instillation of mitomycin C after surgery and/or intravesical BCG weekly for 6 weeks with maintenance doses; regular check cystoscopies are needed because recurrence is common.
  • Muscle-invasive tumours – radical cystectomy (removal of the bladder with the prostate and seminal vesicles in men, or with the uterus, ovaries and part of the vagina in women) with urinary diversion; cisplatin-based chemotherapy before surgery; bladder-preserving chemoradiation in selected patients; immunotherapy in advanced disease.
  • Types of urinary diversion – ileal conduit (the commonest: both ureters are joined to an isolated segment of ileum brought out as a stoma on the right lower abdomen, and urine drains continuously into a pouch), continent cutaneous reservoir (emptied by catheter through a stoma), orthotopic neobladder (joined to the urethra) and cutaneous ureterostomy.

Nursing care of a patient with an ileal conduit

  1. Pre-operative
    • Counselling about the diagnosis, surgery, stoma and body image, involving the family.
    • Stoma-site marking by a stoma nurse – a site the patient can see, away from skin folds, scars, bony prominences and the belt line.
    • Bowel preparation as ordered, informed consent and pre-anaesthetic preparation.
  2. Post-operative
    • Monitor urine output hourly – urine drains continuously from the stoma, initially through ureteric stents; output below 30 mL/hour or none may mean obstruction or anastomotic leak – report immediately.
    • Observe the stoma – it should be moist and red or pink; dark red, purple or black colour indicates poor blood supply; also watch for retraction, bleeding and oedema (mild swelling is normal in the first weeks).
    • Mucus in the urine is normal (from the ileal segment); encourage fluids to keep it thin.
    • Monitor for paralytic ileus (nasogastric tube care, bowel sounds), electrolyte imbalance (hyperchloraemic acidosis), wound infection and DVT.
  3. Stoma care and appliance management
    • Use a urostomy pouch with an anti-reflux valve and drainage tap; cut the base plate about 2–3 mm larger than the stoma; change it every 3–5 days or whenever it leaks, preferably early in the morning before drinking (less urine flow).
    • Clean the peristomal skin with warm water only, pat dry and protect with a barrier film; hold a rolled gauze on the stoma to absorb urine while changing.
    • Empty the pouch when one-third to half full, and connect it to a night drainage bag at bedtime.
    • Watch for peristomal skin irritation, crystal encrustation (alkaline urine) and UTI (cloudy, foul-smelling urine, fever).
  4. Education and rehabilitation – self-care of the stoma, fluid intake of 2–3 litres a day, warning signs, obtaining supplies, clothing, bathing and travel, sexual counselling, referral to stoma (ostomy) support groups, stopping smoking and long-term follow-up of kidney function and vitamin B12.

Conclusion Bladder cancer, strongly linked to smoking and occupational chemicals, typically presents with painless haematuria. Treatment ranges from TURBT with intravesical BCG to radical cystectomy with urinary diversion. Skilled stoma assessment, appliance management, monitoring of urine output and patient education help the patient adapt to life with an ileal conduit.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Kidney and Urinary Problems
question: Define benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) and list four clinical features.
answer_html:
Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is a non-cancerous enlargement of the prostate gland due to an increase in the number of glandular and stromal cells, mainly in the periurethral (transition) zone, which obstructs the outflow of urine in elderly men.

Clinical features

  1. Frequency and nocturia (waking at night to pass urine).
  2. Hesitancy and a weak or poor stream.
  3. Straining, intermittency and terminal dribbling.
  4. Feeling of incomplete emptying and urgency.
  5. Complications – acute urinary retention, UTI, bladder stones, haematuria and hydronephrosis.

It is diagnosed by DRE, ultrasound with post-void residual urine, uroflowmetry and PSA, and treated with alpha blockers, 5-alpha reductase inhibitors or TURP.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Kidney and Urinary Problems
question: What is ESWL? Mention the nursing care after ESWL.
answer_html:
ESWL (extracorporeal shock-wave lithotripsy) is a non-invasive procedure in which shock waves generated outside the body are focused on a kidney or upper ureteric stone (located by X-ray or ultrasound) to break it into small fragments, which then pass out in the urine. It is used for renal stones up to about 2 cm and is usually done as a day-care procedure under analgesia. It is avoided in pregnancy, bleeding disorders, untreated UTI and obstruction below the stone.

Nursing care after ESWL

  • Encourage 2.5–3 litres of fluid a day and walking to help pass the fragments.
  • Strain all urine and send fragments for stone analysis.
  • Explain that mild haematuria and bruising over the flank are expected for a day or two; give analgesics for colic.
