  • Teach the patient to report fever, severe colic or reduced urine output (infection or steinstrasse – blockage of the ureter by a column of fragments).

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Kidney and Urinary Problems
question: Define hydronephrosis and list its causes.
answer_html:
Hydronephrosis is dilatation of the renal pelvis and calyces due to obstruction to the outflow of urine (or reflux), causing back pressure that, if not relieved, leads to atrophy of kidney tissue and loss of function. When the ureter is also dilated, it is called hydroureteronephrosis.

Causes

  • In the lumen – renal or ureteric stones, blood clots, sloughed papilla.
  • In the wall – congenital pelviureteric junction (PUJ) obstruction, ureteric or urethral stricture, tumours of the ureter or bladder, neurogenic bladder.
  • Pressure from outside – BPH, carcinoma of the prostate, carcinoma of the cervix, pregnancy (more on the right side), retroperitoneal fibrosis and pelvic masses.
  • Vesicoureteric reflux and posterior urethral valves (in children). It is detected by ultrasound and treated by relieving the obstruction (DJ stent, nephrostomy or pyeloplasty).

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Kidney and Urinary Problems
question: What is TURP syndrome?
answer_html:
TURP syndrome is a complication of transurethral resection of the prostate caused by the absorption of large volumes of hypotonic irrigating fluid (glycine 1.5% or sterile water used in monopolar TURP) through opened prostatic venous sinuses, resulting in fluid overload and dilutional hyponatraemia (serum sodium often below 125 mEq/L).

Features – confusion, restlessness, headache, nausea and vomiting, visual disturbances (temporary blindness with glycine), hypertension followed by hypotension, bradycardia, breathlessness from pulmonary oedema, seizures and coma.

Management – stop the surgery quickly, check serum sodium, restrict fluids, give loop diuretics (furosemide) and hypertonic (3%) saline for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia, with oxygen and supportive care. The risk is reduced by bipolar TURP or laser surgery using normal saline irrigation and by keeping resection time under about one hour.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Kidney and Urinary Problems
question: Write the nursing care of a patient undergoing cystoscopy.
answer_html:
Cystoscopy is the direct visual examination of the urethra and bladder with a cystoscope passed through the urethra, for diagnosis (haematuria, tumours, stones, strictures), biopsy, stent insertion or removal of small stones.

Before – explain the procedure and obtain consent; ensure the urine is sterile (treat UTI first); check coagulation if biopsy is planned; local anaesthetic gel for flexible cystoscopy or spinal/general anaesthesia for rigid cystoscopy (keep NPO accordingly); ask the patient to void.

After

  • Monitor vital signs and urine output, colour and clots; mild pink urine, burning and frequency are common for 24–48 hours.
  • Encourage fluids of 2–3 litres a day; give warm sitz baths and analgesics for discomfort.
  • Watch for and report urinary retention, bright red bleeding and fever with chills (infection).
  • After anaesthesia, check for postural hypotension and help with the first ambulation.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Kidney and Urinary Problems
question: Define haematuria and list its causes.
answer_html:
Haematuria is the presence of red blood cells in the urine. It is gross (macroscopic) when the urine is visibly red, pink or cola-coloured, and microscopic when detected only under the microscope (3 or more RBCs per high-power field).

Causes

  • Kidney – glomerulonephritis (cola-coloured urine), pyelonephritis, renal stones, polycystic kidney disease, renal cell carcinoma, renal tuberculosis and trauma.
  • Ureter – stones and tumours.
  • Bladder – cystitis, bladder cancer (painless haematuria), stones, radiation cystitis and cyclophosphamide.
  • Prostate and urethra – BPH, prostate cancer, urethritis, catheter trauma and after TURP.
  • Systemic – excess anticoagulants, bleeding disorders (haemophilia, thrombocytopenia), sickle cell disease, dengue and leptospirosis. Red or dark urine without RBCs – haemoglobinuria (falciparum malaria, haemolysis), myoglobinuria (crush injury), beetroot and rifampicin – must be differentiated. Painless haematuria in an adult must always be investigated to exclude cancer.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Disorders of Male Reproductive System
question: Define male infertility. Explain its causes, investigations, management and the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Definition Infertility is the failure of a couple to achieve pregnancy after 12 months or more of regular, unprotected sexual intercourse. Male infertility is infertility due to a problem in the male partner. Male factors are responsible, alone or together with female factors, in about half of infertile couples. In Indian society the woman is often wrongly blamed, so both partners must be evaluated from the beginning.

Causes

  1. Pre-testicular (hormonal) – hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (pituitary or hypothalamic disease, Kallmann syndrome), hyperprolactinaemia, thyroid disorders, use of anabolic steroids or testosterone, and obesity.
  2. Testicular – varicocele (the commonest correctable cause), undescended testes (cryptorchidism), mumps orchitis after puberty, torsion or trauma, genetic causes (Klinefelter syndrome 47,XXY, Y-chromosome microdeletions), chemotherapy, radiotherapy and heat exposure.
  3. Post-testicular (obstructive and ejaculatory) – blockage of the epididymis or vas deferens (infections such as tuberculosis and gonorrhoea, congenital absence of the vas, previous hernia surgery or vasectomy), retrograde ejaculation (diabetes, after TURP), erectile dysfunction, premature ejaculation and anti-sperm antibodies.
  4. Lifestyle and environmental factors – smoking, alcohol and tobacco chewing, drug abuse, obesity, stress, heat to the testes (tight clothing, hot baths, long hours of driving, laptops on the lap, work near furnaces and boilers), pesticides, heavy metals and certain drugs (sulfasalazine, cimetidine, anticancer drugs).
  5. Idiopathic – no cause is found in a significant proportion of men.

Investigations

  • History – duration of infertility, frequency and timing of intercourse, sexual problems, mumps, STIs, surgery, medicines, occupation and habits.
  • Physical examination – secondary sexual characteristics, size and consistency of testes, presence of the vas deferens, and varicocele (feels like a "bag of worms" on standing).
  • Semen analysis – the most important test; collected by masturbation into a sterile wide-mouthed container after 2–7 days of abstinence and delivered to the laboratory within 1 hour at body temperature; at least two samples are examined. WHO lower reference limits are about 1.4–1.5 mL volume, 15–16 million sperm/mL, 40–42% total motility and 4% normal forms. Reports use the terms oligozoospermia (low count), azoospermia (no sperm), asthenozoospermia (poor motility) and teratozoospermia (abnormal forms).
  • Hormone tests – FSH, LH, testosterone, prolactin and TSH.
  • Scrotal ultrasound with Doppler, transrectal ultrasound; karyotype and Y-microdeletion tests in severe oligozoospermia or azoospermia; testicular biopsy when needed.

Management

  • Lifestyle measures – stop smoking, alcohol and tobacco; reduce weight; avoid heat to the testes (loose cotton underwear, no hot baths); balanced diet rich in fruits and vegetables; stress management; timing intercourse around ovulation.
  • Medical treatment – treatment of infections; hormone therapy (hCG, FSH) for hypogonadotropic hypogonadism; treatment of hyperprolactinaemia; drugs for erectile dysfunction and retrograde ejaculation.
  • Surgical treatment – varicocelectomy, microsurgical vasovasostomy or vasoepididymostomy for obstruction; orchidopexy in childhood for undescended testis (prevention).
  • Assisted reproductive techniques (ART) – intrauterine insemination (IUI), in-vitro fertilisation (IVF), intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) (a single sperm injected into the egg), surgical sperm retrieval (PESA, TESA, micro-TESE) for azoospermia, and donor sperm. ART clinics and sperm banks in India are regulated under the ART (Regulation) Act, 2021.

Role of the nurse

  1. Counsel the couple together – reduce blame, guilt and stigma; explain that infertility can be due to either partner or both.
  2. Teach the correct method of semen collection and provide privacy.
  3. Health education on lifestyle and occupational risk factors; promote MMR vaccination (prevents mumps orchitis), early treatment of STIs, and early surgery for undescended testes in childhood.
  4. Support during treatment – explain procedures, give medicines, prepare for surgery and ART, and give emotional support, since repeated failures cause stress, depression and marital strain.
  5. Maintain confidentiality; refer to infertility clinics and counselling services; discuss alternatives such as adoption.

Conclusion Male infertility contributes to about half of all infertility and may be hormonal, testicular, obstructive, sexual or lifestyle-related. Semen analysis is the key investigation, and treatment ranges from lifestyle changes and surgery to assisted reproduction. Sensitive counselling, education and emotional support by the nurse are essential at every stage.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Disorders of Male Reproductive System
question: Explain the inflammatory disorders of the male reproductive system – prostatitis, epididymitis and orchitis – with their nursing management.
answer_html:
Introduction Infection or inflammation may affect the prostate, epididymis or testes. These conditions cause pain and fever and, if not treated properly, may lead to abscess, chronic pain or infertility.

1. Prostatitis

  • Inflammation of the prostate gland.
  • Types – acute bacterial (E. coli and other urinary organisms, often after catheterisation or instrumentation), chronic bacterial (recurrent UTI), chronic prostatitis/chronic pelvic pain syndrome (the commonest type, with no infection found) and asymptomatic inflammatory prostatitis.
  • Features of acute prostatitis – high fever with chills, pain in the perineum, low back and rectum, dysuria, frequency, urgency, poor stream or retention; the prostate is swollen and very tender on rectal examination (vigorous examination or massage is avoided because it can cause septicaemia).
  • Management – antibiotics (e.g. a fluoroquinolone or co-trimoxazole) for 2–4 weeks in acute and 4–6 weeks in chronic bacterial prostatitis; analgesics and alpha blockers; suprapubic catheter if retention occurs (urethral catheterisation is avoided); drainage of a prostatic abscess.

2. Epididymitis

  • Inflammation of the epididymis, often spreading to the testis (epididymo-orchitis).
  • Causes – in sexually active men below 35 years – Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae; in older men – E. coli and other urinary pathogens (associated with BPH, catheters and instrumentation); also tuberculosis, filariasis (in endemic districts, including much of Vidarbha), brucellosis and some drugs (amiodarone).
  • Features – gradual onset of pain and swelling of one side of the scrotum, tenderness, redness, fever, dysuria and urethral discharge; pain is often relieved by lifting the scrotum (Prehn's sign).

3. Orchitis

  • Inflammation of the testis.
  • Causes – mumps virus (the commonest viral cause, affecting about 20–30% of post-pubertal males with mumps, about 4–8 days after parotitis), bacterial spread from epididymitis and other viruses.
  • Features – sudden testicular pain and swelling, high fever, malaise and nausea; testicular atrophy and reduced fertility may follow, especially if both testes are affected.

Differentiation from testicular torsion – torsion causes sudden severe pain in boys and young men with a high-riding testis and an absent cremasteric reflex; it is a surgical emergency (the testis can usually be saved if operated within 6 hours). Every acute scrotal pain must therefore be evaluated urgently, usually with Doppler ultrasound, which shows increased blood flow in epididymo-orchitis and absent flow in torsion.

Diagnosis – urine routine and culture, urethral swab or nucleic acid test for Chlamydia and gonococcus, blood counts, scrotal Doppler ultrasound and mumps serology.

Medical management

  • STI-related epididymitis – ceftriaxone as a single IM dose plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 10 days; for urinary organisms, a fluoroquinolone; anti-TB treatment for tuberculous epididymitis.
  • Mumps orchitis – supportive care only (rest, analgesics, cold application).
  • Surgical drainage of an abscess; orchidectomy rarely.

Nursing management

  1. Bed rest in the acute stage with scrotal elevation – a rolled towel between the thighs or a scrotal support (suspensory bandage).
  2. Cold compresses or ice packs wrapped in cloth, for 15–20 minutes at a time, in the first 24–48 hours to reduce swelling; warm sitz baths later.
  3. Give analgesics, antipyretics and antibiotics as prescribed and stress completion of the course.
  4. Encourage plenty of fluids; monitor temperature, urinary symptoms, pain and swelling; watch for abscess formation and urinary retention.
  5. Avoid sexual intercourse until treatment is complete and the partner has also been treated (STI-related cases); teach condom use; help with partner notification.
  6. Prevention – MMR vaccination, safe sexual practices, aseptic catheterisation, early treatment of UTI, and participation in mass drug administration against filariasis.
  7. Counselling – address fears about fertility and sexual function; arrange follow-up semen analysis when indicated.

Conclusion Prostatitis, epididymitis and orchitis are common inflammatory disorders caused by urinary pathogens, sexually transmitted organisms and the mumps virus. Prompt antibiotics, scrotal support, cold application, rest and analgesia, together with urgent exclusion of testicular torsion and preventive education, form the basis of care.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Disorders of Male Reproductive System
question: Explain erectile dysfunction and other male sexual dysfunctions, with their management and the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction Male sexual dysfunction is a persistent problem with sexual desire, erection, ejaculation or orgasm that causes distress to the man or the couple. It becomes more common with ageing, diabetes and hypertension, but men rarely report it because of embarrassment. Nurses can identify it during routine care and help patients get treatment.

Types

  1. Erectile dysfunction (ED) – persistent inability to achieve or maintain an erection sufficient for satisfactory sexual intercourse.
  2. Premature (early) ejaculation – ejaculation within about 1 minute of penetration with little control and distress; the commonest sexual complaint of younger men.
  3. Delayed ejaculation or anorgasmia, and retrograde ejaculation (after TURP, in diabetes, with alpha blockers).
  4. Low sexual desire (hypoactive libido) – due to low testosterone, depression, stress, relationship problems or drugs.
  5. Peyronie's disease (curvature of the erect penis due to a fibrous plaque) and priapism (a painful erection lasting more than 4 hours – an emergency; seen in sickle cell disease and with drugs injected into the penis).

Causes of erectile dysfunction

  • Vascular – the commonest; atherosclerosis, hypertension, diabetes, smoking and high cholesterol – ED can be an early warning sign of heart disease.
  • Neurological – diabetic neuropathy, spinal cord injury, multiple sclerosis, stroke and pelvic surgery (radical prostatectomy).
  • Hormonal – low testosterone, hyperprolactinaemia and thyroid disease.
  • Drugs and substances – beta blockers, thiazides, antidepressants (SSRIs), antipsychotics, anti-androgens and finasteride; alcohol, tobacco and drug abuse.
  • Psychological – performance anxiety, stress, depression, relationship conflict, guilt and myths, such as anxiety about "loss of semen" (Dhat syndrome, seen in South Asia).
  • Others – chronic kidney and liver disease, obesity and ageing.

Assessment – a private, non-judgemental sexual history (e.g. the IIEF-5 questionnaire), medical and drug history, examination (BP, genitals, peripheral pulses, secondary sexual characteristics), blood sugar, lipid profile, testosterone, prolactin and TSH; penile Doppler in selected patients.

Management

  • Treat causes and risk factors – control diabetes, BP and lipids; stop smoking and alcohol; exercise and lose weight; review and change causative drugs.
  • Oral PDE-5 inhibitors – sildenafil, tadalafil and vardenafil, taken before sexual activity; they work only with sexual stimulation.
    • Absolutely contraindicated with nitrates (glyceryl trinitrate, isosorbide mononitrate/dinitrate) because of severe hypotension; used with caution after recent MI or stroke and in severe heart disease.
    • Side effects – headache, flushing, nasal congestion, indigestion, visual disturbance and rarely priapism (seek emergency care if an erection lasts more than 4 hours).
  • Vacuum erection devices, intracavernosal injections (alprostadil) and intra-urethral therapy.
  • Penile prosthesis (implant) when other treatments fail.
  • Testosterone replacement only for proven hypogonadism.
  • Psychosexual therapy and couple counselling, including sensate-focus exercises.
  • Premature ejaculation – behavioural methods (stop–start and squeeze techniques), topical anaesthetic sprays and SSRIs such as dapoxetine on demand.

Role of the nurse

  1. Create a safe environment for discussion – privacy, a non-judgemental attitude, simple language and respect for cultural and religious values.
  2. Use the PLISSIT model – Permission (allow the patient to talk about sexual concerns), Limited Information (correct myths and explain effects of illness and drugs), Specific Suggestions (positions, timing, lubricants, correct use of medicines) and Intensive Therapy (referral to a specialist or sex therapist).
  3. Educate about safe use of PDE-5 inhibitors and the danger of combining them with nitrates; discourage unregulated "sex tonics" and quack remedies.
  4. Counsel patients after MI, stroke, prostate surgery, stoma surgery and spinal cord injury about resuming sexual activity.
  5. Screen diabetic, hypertensive and cardiac patients for ED, involve the partner when appropriate and maintain confidentiality.

Conclusion Erectile dysfunction, premature ejaculation and low desire are common male sexual problems with physical and psychological causes. Risk-factor control, PDE-5 inhibitors, devices, surgery and counselling are effective, and the nurse's sensitive, well-informed approach using the PLISSIT model helps men seek and benefit from treatment.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Disorders of Male Reproductive System
question: Explain the common scrotal disorders – hydrocele, varicocele, testicular torsion and testicular tumour – and their nursing management.

diagram.caption: Common scrotal disorders
labels: hydrocele – fluid around the testis in the tunica vaginalis
transilluminating; varicocele – dilated pampiniform veins above the testis ("bag of worms"); torsion – twisted spermatic cord with high-riding testis; testicular tumour – hard mass within the testis

answer_html:
Introduction Scrotal swellings are common at all ages. Some are harmless, but testicular torsion and testicular tumours need urgent attention, so every scrotal swelling should be examined and, if needed, evaluated by ultrasound.

1. Hydrocele

  • Collection of serous fluid in the tunica vaginalis around the testis.
  • Types – congenital (patent processus vaginalis in infants; usually resolves by 1–2 years), primary (idiopathic) in adults, secondary to epididymo-orchitis, trauma or tumour, and filarial hydrocele (common in lymphatic filariasis-endemic districts, including much of Vidarbha).
  • Features – painless, gradually enlarging, smooth, cystic swelling; the examiner can get above the swelling; it is transillumination positive (glows when a torch is shone through it); the testis may not be felt separately.
  • Management – observation in infants; surgery (Jaboulay's eversion of the sac or Lord's plication) in adults; aspiration is not preferred because of recurrence and infection. Hydrocele surgery is offered under the national filariasis elimination programme, along with mass drug administration (MDA) for prevention.

2. Varicocele

  • Dilated, tortuous veins of the pampiniform plexus in the spermatic cord; left-sided in about 90% of cases (the left testicular vein drains at a right angle into the left renal vein).
  • Features – dull, dragging ache that is worse on standing and in the evening; a soft swelling like a "bag of worms" that decreases on lying down; may cause subfertility and testicular atrophy. A sudden right-sided or non-reducing varicocele in an older man needs evaluation for a kidney tumour.
  • Management – scrotal support and analgesics for mild cases; microsurgical varicocelectomy or embolisation for pain, infertility or testicular atrophy.

3. Testicular torsion

  • Twisting of the spermatic cord, cutting off the blood supply to the testis – a surgical emergency; commonest in adolescents (12–18 years) and newborns; often associated with a "bell-clapper" deformity.
  • Features – sudden, severe scrotal pain (often at night or after exercise) radiating to the groin and lower abdomen, nausea and vomiting, a tender, high-riding testis lying horizontally and an absent cremasteric reflex.
  • Management – urgent surgical exploration, untwisting and fixation of both testes (bilateral orchidopexy) to prevent torsion of the other side; a dead testis is removed. The testis can usually be saved if surgery is done within 6 hours, so surgery should not be delayed for investigations when the diagnosis is clinically clear.

4. Testicular tumour

  • The commonest solid cancer in young men (15–35 years); about 95% are germ cell tumours – seminoma and non-seminomatous tumours (teratoma, embryonal carcinoma, yolk-sac tumour, choriocarcinoma).
  • Risk factors – undescended testis (cryptorchidism), previous testicular cancer, family history, Klinefelter syndrome and HIV.
  • Features – a painless, hard, heavy lump or enlargement of one testis, dull ache or dragging sensation, gynaecomastia (hCG-secreting tumours), and back pain or cough when metastases are present.
  • Diagnosis – scrotal ultrasound, tumour markers (AFP, beta-hCG and LDH) and CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis for staging; biopsy through the scrotal skin is avoided because of tumour seeding.
  • Management – radical (high) inguinal orchidectomy, followed by surveillance, chemotherapy (cisplatin-based BEP regimen) or radiotherapy according to type and stage; cure rates are above 90% even in many advanced cases. Sperm banking should be offered before treatment.

Nursing management

  1. Pre-operative – explain the procedure and obtain consent, prepare the skin, relieve anxiety (especially fears about masculinity and fertility); urgent preparation and NPO for suspected torsion.
  2. Post-operative – scrotal support or elevation, ice packs for 24–48 hours, analgesics, observation for scrotal haematoma, bleeding and infection, wound care, early ambulation and avoidance of heavy lifting for 2–4 weeks.
  3. Psychological support – reassure that one healthy testis is enough for normal sexual function and fertility; discuss a testicular prosthesis after orchidectomy and sperm banking before chemotherapy.
  4. Health education – monthly testicular self-examination, especially in men with a history of undescended testis; seek help immediately for sudden scrotal pain; take part in filariasis MDA; regular follow-up with tumour markers after cancer treatment.

Conclusion Hydrocele and varicocele are common, usually benign scrotal conditions treated surgically when troublesome, while testicular torsion and testicular tumour need prompt surgery. Careful assessment, timely referral, post-operative scrotal care, psychological support and teaching testicular self-examination are important nursing roles.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Disorders of Male Reproductive System
question: Explain phimosis, paraphimosis and balanitis, and the nursing care of a patient undergoing circumcision.
answer_html:
Introduction The prepuce (foreskin) covers and protects the glans penis. Disorders of the foreskin are common in boys, elderly men and diabetics, and poor genital hygiene is an important contributing factor.

1. Phimosis

  • Inability to retract the foreskin over the glans because of a narrow preputial opening.
  • Physiological phimosis – normal in infants and young boys; the foreskin gradually becomes retractable, usually by 5–7 years and sometimes only by adolescence; forcible retraction must be avoided.
  • Pathological phimosis – due to scarring from recurrent balanitis, lichen sclerosus (balanitis xerotica obliterans), poor hygiene or uncontrolled diabetes (common in elderly men).
  • Features – ballooning of the foreskin during micturition, thin stream, pain during erection or intercourse and recurrent infection; long-standing phimosis is a risk factor for carcinoma of the penis.
  • Management – topical steroid cream (e.g. betamethasone) with gentle retraction exercises for 4–8 weeks; circumcision or preputioplasty for pathological phimosis.

2. Paraphimosis

  • The retracted foreskin is trapped behind the corona of the glans and cannot be returned to its normal position – an emergency.
  • Causes – failure to replace the foreskin after catheterisation, cleaning, examination or intercourse.
  • Features – painful swelling of the glans with a tight constricting ring of foreskin; untreated, it may lead to ischaemia and gangrene of the glans.
  • Management – manual reduction after reducing the oedema (ice pack, firm compression with a gauze bandage, granulated sugar or multiple punctures under local anaesthesia); dorsal slit if reduction fails; circumcision later to prevent recurrence.
  • Prevention – nurses must always replace the foreskin after catheterisation and perineal care.

3. Balanitis and balanoposthitis

  • Inflammation of the glans (balanitis), or of both the glans and foreskin (balanoposthitis).
  • Causes – poor hygiene with collection of smegma, Candida infection (especially in diabetics), bacteria, STIs, irritants such as strong soaps, and fixed drug eruptions.
  • Features – redness, soreness, itching, discharge, foul smell and pain on micturition.
  • Management – daily washing with plain warm water and gentle drying, avoiding soap irritants, topical antifungal (clotrimazole) or antibiotic cream, control of blood sugar, treatment of the partner when needed, and circumcision for recurrent cases.

4. Circumcision – nursing care Circumcision is the surgical removal of the foreskin. Indications include pathological phimosis, recurrent paraphimosis or balanitis, and religious or cultural reasons.

  • Pre-operative – explain the procedure and expected appearance, obtain consent (from parents for children), check blood sugar and bleeding tendency, keep NPO if general anaesthesia is planned, and ensure perineal cleanliness.
  • Post-operative
    1. Observe for bleeding – check the dressing frequently in the first few hours, apply gentle pressure and report active bleeding.
    2. Make sure the patient passes urine within 6–8 hours.
    3. Relieve pain – analgesics, topical anaesthetic gel and loose clothing; a bed cradle can keep linen off the penis.
    4. Wound care – keep the area clean and dry; apply antibiotic ointment or petroleum jelly to prevent sticking to clothes; warm sitz baths from the next day; dissolvable sutures fall off in 7–14 days.
    5. Watch for infection – increasing swelling, pus or fever.
    6. In adults – avoid sexual activity for 4–6 weeks; ice packs help reduce swelling and discomfort from erections.

Health education – daily genital hygiene, gentle retraction and cleaning under the foreskin after puberty, control of diabetes and safe sexual practices.

Conclusion Phimosis, paraphimosis and balanitis are common disorders of the foreskin; paraphimosis is an emergency that nurses can prevent by always replacing the foreskin after procedures. Good hygiene, diabetic control, appropriate medical treatment and circumcision with careful post-operative care resolve most problems.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Disorders of Male Reproductive System
question: Explain no-scalpel vasectomy and other methods of male contraception, with the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction Male participation is important for sharing the responsibility of family planning. In India, female sterilisation still makes up the great majority of sterilisations and vasectomy only a very small share, mainly because of myths and fears. No-scalpel vasectomy (NSV) is a simple, safe and highly effective method promoted under the National Family Planning Programme, especially during the annual Vasectomy Fortnight (held around late November to early December).

1. Methods of male contraception

  • Temporary methods
    • Condoms – a barrier method that also protects against STIs including HIV; supplied free through government health facilities ("Nirodh") and through social marketing; failures are mainly due to incorrect or inconsistent use.
    • Coitus interruptus (withdrawal) – unreliable.
    • Periodic abstinence during the fertile period (natural family planning).
    • Under research – hormonal male contraceptives and RISUG (reversible inhibition of sperm under guidance), an injectable polymer placed in the vas, developed in India.
  • Permanent method – vasectomy (conventional or no-scalpel).

2. No-scalpel vasectomy

  • A permanent method of male sterilisation in which both vasa deferentia are blocked, so that sperm cannot enter the semen.
  • Done under local anaesthesia through a single tiny puncture in the front of the scrotum using special instruments (a ring clamp and sharp dissecting forceps); each vas is lifted out, divided and occluded; no stitches are needed, and the procedure takes about 10–15 minutes.
  • Advantages over conventional vasectomy – no incision or sutures, less pain, bleeding and infection, and quicker recovery (light work in 1–2 days).
  • Eligibility – a married man, usually aged 22–60 years, with at least one child, who has chosen the method voluntarily with informed consent (as per national standards).
  • Vasectomy is not effective immediately – sperm already stored beyond the blocked portion remain for some time, so another method must be used for 3 months, until semen analysis shows no sperm (azoospermia).
  • Vasectomy does not affect sexual desire, erection, ejaculation (semen volume remains almost the same), masculinity, strength or the ability to do heavy physical work.
  • The government provides compensation for loss of wages to the acceptor and coverage under the Family Planning Indemnity Scheme.

3. Complications – pain, scrotal haematoma, infection, sperm granuloma, rarely chronic scrotal pain, and very rarely recanalisation (failure).

4. Role of the nurse

  1. Counselling – explain all available methods; make clear that vasectomy is permanent (reversal is difficult and not guaranteed); involve the wife; ensure voluntary informed consent and that the couple has completed their family.
  2. Correct myths – vasectomy does not cause weakness, impotence or weight gain and is safe for manual labourers.
  3. Pre-procedure care – history of bleeding disorders, scrotal infection, hernia or hydrocele; bath and clean undergarments; consent forms.
  4. Post-procedure instructions
    • Rest for a few hours; keep the puncture site dry for 24–48 hours; wear scrotal support or close-fitting underwear for a few days; ice packs for swelling; analgesics.
    • Avoid heavy lifting and cycling for about a week; intercourse can be resumed after 2–3 days when comfortable.
    • Use condoms (or the wife's contraceptive) for 3 months and get a semen examination at 3 months to confirm azoospermia.
    • Report fever, increasing swelling, pus or severe pain.
  5. Promotion – involve community leaders and ASHAs, use satisfied NSV acceptors as motivators and mobilise men during the Vasectomy Fortnight.

Conclusion Male contraception includes condoms as a temporary method and vasectomy as a permanent one. No-scalpel vasectomy is safe, quick and highly effective, but backup contraception is needed for 3 months until azoospermia is confirmed. The nurse's counselling, correction of myths and follow-up are essential to increase male participation in family planning.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Disorders of Male Reproductive System
question: Explain gynaecomastia and carcinoma of the male breast, with their nursing management.
answer_html:
Introduction Although the male breast has only rudimentary tissue, it can be affected by enlargement (gynaecomastia) and, rarely, by cancer. Both cause embarrassment and anxiety, so a sensitive nursing approach is necessary.

1. Gynaecomastia

  • Benign enlargement of glandular breast tissue in males due to an imbalance between oestrogen and androgen activity; it may be one-sided or on both sides.
  • Pseudogynaecomastia – enlargement due to fat only (obesity), without glandular tissue.
  • Causes
    • Physiological – in newborns (maternal oestrogen), during puberty (in many boys; usually resolves within 6 months to 2 years) and in old age.
    • Drugs – spironolactone, cimetidine, ketoconazole, digoxin, anti-androgens used for prostate cancer, anabolic steroids, some antipsychotics and antiretrovirals, alcohol and marijuana.
    • Diseases – liver cirrhosis, chronic kidney disease, hyperthyroidism, hypogonadism (Klinefelter syndrome), oestrogen- or hCG-secreting testicular and adrenal tumours, and refeeding after malnutrition.
    • Idiopathic.
  • Features – a rubbery or firm disc of tissue directly beneath the nipple and areola, sometimes tender; anxiety and embarrassment, especially in adolescents.
  • Assessment – history (drugs, alcohol, liver or kidney disease), examination of the breasts and testes, liver and thyroid function tests, hormones (testosterone, LH, oestradiol, hCG), and ultrasound or mammography for a suspicious lump.
  • Management – reassurance in pubertal gynaecomastia; stopping or changing causative drugs; treating the underlying disease; tamoxifen for painful or persistent cases; surgery (subcutaneous mastectomy, liposuction) for long-standing gynaecomastia or cosmetic distress.

2. Carcinoma of the male breast

  • Rare (about 1% of all breast cancers), usually in men aged 60–70 years; mostly invasive ductal carcinoma, usually hormone-receptor positive.
  • Risk factors – increasing age, BRCA2 (and BRCA1) mutations, family history of breast cancer, Klinefelter syndrome, radiation exposure, liver cirrhosis, obesity and other high-oestrogen states, and testicular disorders.
  • Features – a painless, hard lump beneath or near the nipple, nipple retraction, discharge (sometimes bloody), ulceration and axillary lymph nodes; often diagnosed late because men are unaware of the risk or embarrassed.
  • Diagnosis – mammography, ultrasound, core needle biopsy, hormone-receptor status and staging investigations.
  • Treatment – mastectomy (modified radical or simple mastectomy with sentinel node biopsy), radiotherapy, chemotherapy and hormone therapy (tamoxifen) for receptor-positive cancer; genetic counselling for the patient and family.

Nursing management

  1. Psychological support – address embarrassment, body-image concerns and the stigma of having a "woman's disease"; provide privacy and reassurance.
  2. Education – men should report any breast lump or nipple change promptly; men with BRCA mutations or Klinefelter syndrome need regular examination and should be taught breast self-examination.
  3. Drug review – identify drugs that cause gynaecomastia; reassure adolescents that pubertal gynaecomastia is common and usually temporary; discourage anabolic steroids and alcohol.
  4. Post-mastectomy care – as for women: drain and wound care, pain relief, arm exercises to prevent stiffness and lymphoedema, protection of the affected arm and regular follow-up.
  5. Medication counselling – side effects of tamoxifen (hot flushes, reduced libido, risk of DVT).
  6. Family counselling – genetic testing of relatives for BRCA mutations, because female relatives have an increased risk of breast and ovarian cancer.

Conclusion Gynaecomastia is a common, usually benign breast enlargement due to hormonal imbalance, drugs or disease, whereas male breast cancer is rare but often diagnosed late. Careful evaluation, treatment of causes, timely surgery and cancer care, combined with sensitive psychological support and education, are the essentials of nursing management.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Disorders of Male Reproductive System
question: Define orchitis and list four symptoms.
answer_html:
Orchitis is inflammation of one or both testes, usually due to infection – most commonly the mumps virus in post-pubertal males (a few days after parotid swelling), or bacterial spread from the epididymis (epididymo-orchitis) caused by sexually transmitted organisms (Chlamydia, gonococcus) or urinary pathogens (E. coli).

Symptoms

  1. Sudden pain in the testis, which may radiate to the groin.
  2. Swelling, redness and warmth of the scrotum with tenderness.
  3. Fever with chills, malaise, nausea and vomiting.
  4. Pain on urination or urethral discharge (bacterial), and pain during ejaculation; preceding parotid swelling in mumps.

It may lead to testicular atrophy and reduced fertility. Treatment includes rest, scrotal support, ice packs, analgesics and antibiotics for bacterial infection; MMR vaccination prevents mumps orchitis.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Disorders of Male Reproductive System
question: Differentiate between hypospadias and epispadias.
answer_html:
Both are congenital anomalies of the male urethra in which the external urethral opening (meatus) is abnormally placed because of incomplete development of the urethra during fetal life. Hypospadias is common, whereas epispadias is rare and usually part of the bladder exstrophy–epispadias complex.

Hypospadias Epispadias
Meatus on the ventral (under) surface of the penis – glanular, coronal, penile, scrotal or perineal Meatus on the dorsal (upper) surface of the penis
Common – about 1 in 250–300 male births Rare
Often with chordee (downward curvature), hooded foreskin and sometimes undescended testis Often with bladder exstrophy, upward curvature and urinary incontinence
Repair (urethroplasty with chordee correction) usually at 6–18 months Complex reconstruction of urethra and bladder neck in infancy

Nursing points – circumcision must not be done in a baby with hypospadias, because the foreskin is used for the repair; after surgery, care of the urethral stent or catheter and dressing, pain relief, adequate fluids, preventing the child from pulling at tubes, and counselling parents about follow-up of the urinary stream and cosmetic result.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Disorders of Male Reproductive System
question: Write the steps of testicular self-examination (TSE).
answer_html:
Testicular self-examination (TSE) is a simple monthly self-check that helps young men (15–40 years, especially those with a history of undescended testis) detect testicular cancer early.

Steps

  1. Do it once a month after a warm bath, when the scrotal skin is relaxed.
  2. Stand in front of a mirror and look for swelling or changes in the scrotal skin.
  3. Examine each testis separately with both hands – place the index and middle fingers under the testis and the thumb on top, and gently roll the testis between the fingers and thumb.
  4. Feel for lumps, hard areas, or changes in size, shape or consistency, heaviness or tenderness (it is normal for one testis to be slightly larger or to hang lower).
  5. Identify the epididymis – a soft, comma-shaped tube at the back of the testis – so that it is not mistaken for a lump.
  6. Report any lump, swelling or persistent ache promptly to a doctor.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Disorders of Male Reproductive System
question: What is male climacteric (andropause)?
answer_html:
Male climacteric (andropause, or late-onset hypogonadism) refers to the gradual decline of testosterone with ageing (roughly 1% per year after about 40 years) accompanied by symptoms. Unlike menopause in women, it is slow and incomplete, and fertility is often maintained.

Features – reduced libido and erectile problems, fatigue, loss of muscle mass and strength, increased abdominal fat, mood changes (irritability, depression), poor concentration, sleep disturbance, occasional hot flushes and osteoporosis.

Management – confirm a low morning testosterone level; healthy lifestyle (exercise, weight control, avoiding alcohol and smoking); treatment of diabetes and depression; testosterone replacement only in selected men with proven deficiency (monitor haematocrit and PSA). The nurse provides counselling, reassurance and health education.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Disorders of Male Reproductive System
question: (a) Explain the history collection and physical examination of a patient with a disorder of the male reproductive system. (7 marks) (b) Describe the diagnostic tests used in male reproductive disorders and the nurse's responsibilities in each. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Examination of the scrotum and prostate
labels: palpation of testis between thumb and fingers
transillumination of a scrotal swelling with a torch
digital rectal examination in left lateral position showing the prostate with median sulcus

answer_html:
Introduction Disorders of the male reproductive system – infections, scrotal swellings, prostate disease, sexual dysfunction, infertility and cancers – are often hidden because of embarrassment, stigma and cultural taboos. A sensitive, systematic assessment and correctly performed investigations help in early diagnosis, especially of emergencies such as testicular torsion and of cancers.

(a) History collection and physical examination (7 marks) A. Preparation

  • A private room, a calm, non-judgemental approach and simple language; explanation of each step and verbal consent.
  • A chaperone during intimate examination; examination by a male nurse or doctor where the patient prefers.
  • Warm room (cold causes the scrotum to contract), gloves, good light, torch, lubricant.

B. History

  1. Biographic data – age (torsion in adolescents, BPH and prostate cancer in older men, testicular cancer at 15–35 years), occupation (heat, chemicals, pesticides, radiation, long driving), marital status.
  2. Presenting complaints – scrotal pain or swelling, penile discharge, ulcers, warts or rashes, lower urinary tract symptoms (frequency, urgency, nocturia, hesitancy, poor stream, dribbling, retention, haematuria), blood in semen, erectile or ejaculatory problems, reduced libido, infertility, breast enlargement.
  3. History of present illness – onset (sudden severe scrotal pain suggests torsion), duration, progression, relation to trauma, fever, urinary symptoms.
  4. Past history – mumps orchitis, undescended testis, hernia repair, scrotal or pelvic surgery, vasectomy, diabetes, hypertension, spinal injury, tuberculosis, kidney disease, radiotherapy or chemotherapy, sexually transmitted infections.
  5. Drug history – antihypertensives, antidepressants, anti-androgens, anabolic steroids, opioids, medicines for prostate disease; alcohol, tobacco and drug use.
  6. Sexual history – asked respectfully and confidentially: number of partners, condom use, symptoms in partner, erectile function, premature or painful ejaculation, libido.
  7. Reproductive history – children, duration of trying to conceive, contraception used, partner's evaluation.
  8. Family history – prostate or testicular cancer, infertility, diabetes.
  9. Psychosocial history – stress, relationship problems, anxiety, depression, body-image concerns, beliefs and myths about sexuality.
  10. Lifestyle – smoking, alcohol, obesity, physical activity, tight underwear, hot baths, long hours of cycling or sitting.

C. Physical examination

  1. General – vital signs, BMI, secondary sexual characteristics (facial and body hair, voice, muscle mass), signs of hormonal disorders.
  2. Breasts – gynaecomastia, lumps, nipple discharge.
  3. Abdomen and groin – bladder distension, masses, inguinal lymph nodes (enlarged in infections and penile cancer), hernia (inspection and palpation for a cough impulse with the patient standing).
  4. Penis
    • Inspection – skin lesions, ulcers, warts, discharge; position of the urethral meatus (hypospadias, epispadias); foreskin – whether it retracts (phimosis) or is stuck behind the glans (paraphimosis); hygiene and balanitis.
    • Palpation – tenderness, plaques or curvature (Peyronie's disease); gentle milking of the urethra for discharge.
  5. Scrotum and contents
    • Inspection – size, symmetry, skin changes, redness, swelling; a high-riding, horizontally lying testis suggests torsion.
    • Palpation – each testis between thumb and fingers for size, consistency, tenderness and any hard lump (testicular tumour is a painless, hard mass); epididymis behind the testis (tender and swollen in epididymitis); spermatic cord and vas deferens (a varicocele feels like a "bag of worms" and increases on standing or straining).
    • Transillumination – a swelling that glows with a torch is fluid-filled (hydrocele); solid masses do not transilluminate.
    • Cremasteric reflex (stroking the inner thigh raises the testis) – usually absent in torsion; Prehn's sign – lifting the scrotum relieves pain in epididymitis but not in torsion.
  6. Digital rectal examination (DRE) – in the left lateral or knee-chest position, with lubricant and explanation; assesses the prostate for size, consistency, tenderness and nodules (smooth and enlarged in BPH, hard and nodular in cancer, tender and boggy in prostatitis), the median sulcus and anal tone.
  7. Neurological examination – perineal sensation and lower-limb reflexes in erectile dysfunction of neurological origin.
  8. Teach testicular self-examination at the end of the assessment.

(b) Diagnostic tests and the nurse's responsibilities (8 marks)

  1. Urine tests – routine and microscopic examination, culture and sensitivity (clean-catch midstream sample), and first-void urine for nucleic-acid tests for chlamydia and gonorrhoea.
    • Nurse – teach clean-catch collection, label and send samples promptly.
  2. Tests for sexually transmitted infections – urethral swab for Gram stain and culture (gonorrhoea), tests for syphilis (VDRL/RPR, TPHA), HIV testing with pre- and post-test counselling, hepatitis B and C.
    • Nurse – counselling, consent, strict confidentiality, partner notification and treatment.
  3. Semen analysis – the basic test for male infertility and for confirming success of vasectomy.
    • Nurse – advise 2–7 days of sexual abstinence; sample collected by masturbation into a clean, sterile, wide-mouthed container (no condom or lubricant); deliver it to the laboratory within about one hour, kept near body temperature; an abnormal result is repeated after a few weeks; after vasectomy the test is done about 12 weeks later.
  4. Hormone assays – serum testosterone (early-morning sample), FSH, LH, prolactin, oestradiol and thyroid tests – in infertility, low libido, erectile dysfunction and gynaecomastia.
    • Nurse – correct timing of the sample.
  5. Tumour markers
    • Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) – for prostate cancer screening and follow-up; nurse advises avoiding ejaculation and vigorous cycling for about 48 hours before, and records any recent catheterisation or urinary infection, which can raise the level.
    • Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), beta-hCG and LDH – for diagnosis, staging and follow-up of testicular tumours.
  6. Imaging
    • Scrotal ultrasound with colour Doppler – differentiates torsion (absent blood flow), epididymo-orchitis (increased flow), hydrocele, varicocele and tumour. In suspected torsion, surgery must not be delayed for imaging.
    • Transrectal ultrasound (TRUS) and multiparametric MRI of the prostate; CT scan and bone scan for staging of cancers.
    • Penile Doppler ultrasound after injection of a vasoactive drug – for vascular causes of erectile dysfunction.
    • Nurse – explain the procedure; ensure privacy; full bladder where required.
  7. Biopsies
    • Prostate biopsy (transrectal or transperineal) – nurse ensures consent, checks that anticoagulants were stopped as advised, gives prophylactic antibiotics and bowel preparation as ordered; afterwards watches for bleeding (blood in urine, semen or stool), fever and chills (infection) and urinary retention.
    • Testicular biopsy and sperm retrieval – in azoospermia; nurse advises scrotal support, ice packs and analgesics after the procedure. A testis suspected to contain cancer is not biopsied through the scrotum; it is removed through an inguinal incision (radical orchidectomy).
  8. Urodynamic and endoscopic tests – uroflowmetry and post-void residual urine (bladder scan) in BPH; cystourethroscopy for strictures and bladder involvement.
    • Nurse – ask the patient to come with a comfortably full bladder for uroflowmetry; after cystoscopy, encourage fluids and observe for burning, haematuria and retention.
  9. Tests for erectile dysfunction – blood sugar, lipid profile and testosterone; questionnaires such as the International Index of Erectile Function (IIEF-5); nocturnal penile tumescence testing; psychological assessment.
  10. Genetic tests in infertility – karyotype (e.g. Klinefelter syndrome, 47,XXY), Y-chromosome microdeletion, and CFTR gene testing when the vas deferens is absent.

General responsibilities of the nurse

  • Reduce embarrassment and anxiety through privacy, explanation and a professional attitude.
  • Obtain informed consent and prepare the patient (fasting, bowel preparation, bladder filling) as each test requires.
  • Collect, label and transport specimens correctly; record and report results.
  • Provide aftercare and teach warning signs after invasive procedures.
  • Maintain confidentiality, especially for STIs, HIV and infertility; give emotional support and counselling, and involve the partner when the patient agrees.

Conclusion Assessment of the male reproductive system requires a sensitive history – urinary, sexual, reproductive, drug and lifestyle – and a careful examination of the breasts, groin, penis, scrotum and prostate, including transillumination, cremasteric reflex and DRE. Investigations such as urine and STI tests, semen analysis, hormone assays, PSA and testicular tumour markers, scrotal Doppler, TRUS, biopsies, urodynamic and genetic tests confirm the diagnosis, and the nurse ensures privacy, preparation, correct specimen handling, aftercare and confidentiality.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Burns, Reconstructive and Cosmetic Surgery
question: Mrs. Sonia, aged 30 years, is admitted to the burns unit with 50% burns. (a) Define burns. (2 marks) (b) Explain the types and classification of burns. (5 marks) (c) Prepare a nursing care plan for Mrs. Sonia. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Depth of burn injury in relation to skin layers
labels: superficial partial-thickness reaching papillary dermis with blisters
full-thickness through the whole dermis into fat
fourth-degree burn reaching muscle and bone

answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks) A burn is an injury to the skin and deeper tissues caused by heat (thermal energy), chemicals, electricity, radiation or friction, which leads to destruction of cells, loss of the protective skin barrier, fluid loss and, in large burns, a severe body-wide (systemic) response. A scald is a burn caused by moist heat such as hot water, steam or hot oil. Burns are a major cause of injury and death in India, and young women are especially affected by kitchen and household fires.

(b) Types and classification of burns (5 marks) 1. According to cause

  • Thermal burns – the commonest; flame (kerosene stoves, LPG leaks, loose clothes catching fire while cooking, firecrackers), scalds (hot water, tea, milk, oil – common in children), contact with hot objects and flash burns from explosions.
  • Chemical burns – acids (sulphuric, hydrochloric, nitric acid, toilet cleaners, acid attacks) and alkalis (lime, cement, caustic soda, drain cleaners); alkalis penetrate deeper.
  • Electrical burns – low-voltage domestic current, high-voltage power lines (linemen, farmers handling pumps, children on rooftops) and lightning; small skin wounds may hide severe deep damage.
  • Radiation burns – ultraviolet rays (sunburn), radiotherapy and ionising radiation accidents.
  • Friction burns – road traffic accidents ("road rash"), treadmill injuries.
  • Cold injury (frostbite) is sometimes grouped with burns because the tissue damage and care are similar.

2. According to depth

  • Superficial (first-degree) burn – epidermis only; red, dry, painful, no blisters, blanches on pressure; heals in 3–7 days without a scar (e.g. sunburn).
  • Superficial partial-thickness (second-degree) burn – epidermis and upper (papillary) dermis; blisters, moist, pink, very painful, blanches on pressure; heals in 10–21 days with minimal scarring.
  • Deep partial-thickness burn – extends into the deep (reticular) dermis; mottled red and white, less moist, reduced sensation, slow blanching; heals in more than 3 weeks with hypertrophic scarring, so grafting is often needed.
  • Full-thickness (third-degree) burn – destroys the whole epidermis and dermis; white, brown or black, dry and leathery (eschar), painless because nerve endings are destroyed, does not blanch; cannot heal on its own except from the edges and needs skin grafting.
  • Fourth-degree burn – extends into fat, muscle, tendon or bone (high-voltage electrical and prolonged flame burns); may require amputation or flap surgery.

3. According to extent – percentage of total body surface area (TBSA)

  • Rule of nines (adults) – head and neck 9%, each upper limb 9%, front of trunk 18%, back of trunk 18%, each lower limb 18% and perineum 1%.
  • Lund and Browder chart – more accurate, and preferred in children, whose head is relatively larger and legs smaller.
  • Palm method – the patient's palm with fingers is about 1% of TBSA, useful for scattered burns.
  • Superficial (first-degree) burns are not included when calculating TBSA for fluid resuscitation.

4. According to severity

  • Minor burns – partial thickness less than 15% TBSA in adults (less than 10% in children and the elderly) and full thickness less than 2%, without involvement of special areas.
  • Moderate burns – partial thickness 15–25% in adults (10–20% in children) or full thickness 2–10%, without special-area involvement.
  • Major burns – partial thickness more than 25% in adults (more than 20% in children) or full thickness more than 10%; any burn of the face, eyes, ears, hands, feet, genitalia, perineum or major joints; inhalation injury; high-voltage electrical and major chemical burns; burns with fractures or other trauma; and burns in patients with serious illness. Mrs. Sonia's 50% burns are a major burn needing burns-unit care.

5. According to phase of care – emergent (resuscitative) phase (first 24–72 hours, until capillary leak stops), acute phase (until wounds are closed) and rehabilitative phase (until return to the best possible function).

(c) Nursing care plan for Mrs. Sonia (8 marks) Assessment data (assumed for planning): 30-year-old woman, about 50 kg, with 50% TBSA flame burns of the face, neck, chest and both upper limbs (partial and full thickness), sustained 2 hours before admission; restless, in severe pain, pulse 124/min, BP 100/70 mmHg, singed nasal hair and hoarse voice.

Nursing diagnosis 1: Risk for ineffective airway clearance and impaired gas exchange related to inhalation injury and oedema of the face and neck

  • Goal: patent airway and SpO₂ above 94% throughout.
  • Interventions: assess hourly for hoarseness, stridor, soot in sputum, wheeze and breathlessness; give 100% humidified oxygen through a non-rebreather mask; check carboxyhaemoglobin (pulse oximetry may read falsely normal in carbon monoxide poisoning); keep the head of the bed elevated 30°; keep intubation equipment ready and assist with early intubation before swelling closes the airway; suction and chest physiotherapy; observe chest movement and report the need for chest escharotomy if circumferential chest burns restrict breathing.
  • Evaluation: airway remains patent; ABG and SpO₂ within normal limits.

Nursing diagnosis 2: Deficient fluid volume related to increased capillary permeability and fluid shift (burn shock)

  • Goal: urine output 0.5 mL/kg/hour (about 25–50 mL/hour), stable pulse and BP.
  • Interventions: secure two large-bore IV cannulas; calculate fluids by the Parkland formula – 4 mL × 50 kg × 50% = 10,000 mL of Ringer's lactate in 24 hours, with 5,000 mL in the first 8 hours from the time of burn (because 2 hours have already passed, this is given over the next 6 hours, about 830 mL/hour) and 5,000 mL over the following 16 hours (about 310 mL/hour); use infusion pumps; insert a Foley catheter and record hourly urine output; adjust the rate as ordered according to urine output, pulse, BP and sensorium; monitor electrolytes, haematocrit and creatinine; watch for overload (crepitations, breathlessness) once capillary leak settles.
  • Evaluation: adequate urine output, improving pulse and BP, clear sensorium.

Nursing diagnosis 3: Acute pain related to burn injury, exposed nerve endings and dressing procedures

  • Goal: pain score kept at 3/10 or below.
  • Interventions: assess pain with a pain scale regularly; give IV opioids (morphine) in small titrated doses (IM injections are avoided because absorption is unpredictable in burns); give analgesia or sedation 30 minutes before dressings; handle gently; keep a bed cradle to keep linen off wounds; use distraction, music and relaxation; maintain a calm environment.
  • Evaluation: patient reports tolerable pain and cooperates with dressings.

Nursing diagnosis 4: Risk for infection related to loss of skin barrier, invasive lines and reduced immunity

  • Goal: no wound or systemic infection.
  • Interventions: strict hand hygiene and aseptic technique; nurse in a clean burns room with protective isolation; restrict visitors and do not allow flowers or plants; sterile dressings with topical antimicrobials (e.g. silver sulfadiazine 1%) as ordered; regular wound inspection for discolouration, odour, discharge or sudden eschar separation; wound swabs for culture; care of IV lines and catheter; give tetanus prophylaxis; monitor temperature, WBC and signs of sepsis.
  • Evaluation: wounds remain free of infection; temperature and WBC normal.

Nursing diagnosis 5: Risk for hypothermia related to loss of skin and exposure during care

  • Interventions: keep the room warm, cover unburnt areas, use warmed IV fluids, minimise exposure time during dressings and monitor temperature.

Nursing diagnosis 6: Imbalanced nutrition, less than body requirements, related to hypermetabolism and protein loss

  • Goal: weight maintained within 10% of pre-burn weight; wounds healing.
  • Interventions: start early enteral feeding through a nasogastric tube within 24 hours; provide a high-calorie, high-protein diet (protein 1.5–2 g/kg/day) with vitamins C and A and zinc; small frequent meals and supplements when oral intake starts (milk, eggs, dal, paneer, soya); monitor weight, intake, blood sugar and albumin; give stress-ulcer prophylaxis (PPI) as ordered to prevent Curling's ulcer.

Nursing diagnosis 7: Risk for impaired physical mobility and contractures related to burns over the neck and joints

  • Interventions: maintain anti-contracture positions – neck slightly extended without a pillow, shoulders abducted to about 90°, elbows extended and hands in the position of function with splints; active and passive range-of-motion exercises several times a day with the physiotherapist; early ambulation when stable; later, pressure garments and silicone sheets to control scarring.

Nursing diagnosis 8: Disturbed body image and anxiety related to facial burns, pain and uncertainty about the future

  • Interventions: explain each procedure, listen to her fears, allow expression of grief and involve the family; provide counselling and referral to a psychologist; introduce rehabilitation and recovered survivors; respect privacy and dignity.
  • Medico-legal and psychosocial aspects: burns in a young married woman may be accidental, suicidal or homicidal, so register the case as a medico-legal case (MLC), inform the police as per hospital policy, document the history in her own words, preserve burnt clothing for the police, arrange a dying declaration by a magistrate if her condition becomes critical, and screen sensitively for domestic violence or dowry harassment while ensuring her safety and confidentiality.

Nursing importance

  • The first 24–48 hours decide survival; accurate fluid calculation from the time of burn, hourly urine output monitoring and early airway protection are life-saving nursing responsibilities.
  • Infection control, nutrition, positioning and psychological care determine how well the survivor heals and returns to family and work.

Conclusion Burns are classified by cause, depth, extent and severity, and Mrs. Sonia's 50% burns are a major injury. A systematic nursing care plan addressing airway, fluid resuscitation, pain, infection, temperature, nutrition, mobility, body image and medico-legal needs, delivered by a skilled multidisciplinary team, gives her the best chance of survival and good recovery.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Burns, Reconstructive and Cosmetic Surgery
question: (a) Define reconstructive surgery and list its indications. (3 marks) (b) Explain the types of skin grafts and flaps. (4 marks) (c) Describe the nursing care of a patient with a skin graft, including care of the donor site and flap monitoring. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Split-thickness and full-thickness skin grafts
labels: split-thickness graft containing epidermis and part of the dermis taken with a dermatome from the thigh
meshed graft expanded over a wound
full-thickness graft containing epidermis and whole dermis taken from behind the ear
donor site healing from remaining skin appendages

answer_html:
(a) Definition and indications (3 marks) Reconstructive (plastic) surgery is the branch of surgery that restores the form and function of body parts damaged or deformed by burns, injury, congenital defects, infection, tumours or disease, using techniques such as skin grafts, flaps, tissue expansion and microsurgery. It differs from cosmetic (aesthetic) surgery, which reshapes normal structures to improve appearance. Surgeons follow the "reconstructive ladder" – direct closure, healing by secondary intention, skin graft, local flap, distant flap and free flap – choosing the simplest method that will give a good result.

Indications

  • Burns – covering raw areas after excision of burnt tissue, and releasing post-burn contractures of the neck, axilla, elbow, hand and knee.
  • Trauma – lacerations, degloving injuries, facial fractures, hand, nerve and tendon injuries, and replantation of amputated fingers or limbs.
  • Congenital anomalies – cleft lip and palate, hypospadias, syndactyly (fused fingers), microtia (small ear) and vascular birthmarks.
  • Cancer surgery – breast reconstruction after mastectomy and reconstruction after head and neck cancer surgery.
  • Chronic wounds – pressure ulcers, diabetic foot ulcers and non-healing ulcers.
  • Others – facial palsy, lymphoedema, post-bariatric skin excess, acid-attack injuries and gender-affirming surgery.

(b) Types of skin grafts and flaps (4 marks) A skin graft is a piece of skin completely separated from its blood supply and transferred to a new site, where it survives by gaining a new blood supply from the wound bed. A flap is tissue moved with its own blood supply intact.

1. Skin grafts according to source

  • Autograft – the patient's own skin (permanent cover).
  • Isograft – from an identical twin.
  • Allograft (homograft) – from another person, usually a cadaver donor through a skin bank; temporary cover because it is eventually rejected.
  • Xenograft (heterograft) – from another species, usually pig skin; temporary cover.
  • Skin substitutes – synthetic or biosynthetic dressings, dermal substitutes and cultured epidermal autografts.

2. Skin grafts according to thickness

  • Split-thickness skin graft (STSG, Thiersch graft) – contains the epidermis and part of the dermis; taken with a dermatome or Humby's knife from the thigh, buttock or upper arm. It "takes" easily, can be meshed (cut into a net) to cover large burns, and the donor site heals by itself in about 10–14 days; however, it contracts more and looks less natural.
  • Full-thickness skin graft (FTSG, Wolfe graft) – contains the epidermis and whole dermis; taken from behind the ear, above the clavicle, the upper eyelid or the groin. It gives better colour match and less contraction, so it is used for the face, eyelids and hands; the donor site is closed with stitches.

3. How a graft "takes"

  • Plasmatic imbibition (first 48 hours) – the graft absorbs nutrients from wound fluid.
  • Inosculation (48–72 hours) – graft and wound-bed capillaries connect.
  • Revascularisation (about day 4–7) – new vessels grow into the graft, which becomes pink and adherent.
  • Causes of graft failure – haematoma or seroma under the graft (the commonest), shearing or movement, infection (especially beta-haemolytic Streptococcus and Pseudomonas), and a poorly vascular bed (bare bone, tendon or cartilage).

4. Flaps

  • By blood supply – random-pattern flaps (supplied by small unnamed vessels) and axial-pattern flaps (based on a named artery).
  • By location – local flaps moved from adjacent skin (advancement, rotation, transposition, Z-plasty for releasing contracture bands); regional or distant pedicle flaps (e.g. pectoralis major flap for head and neck defects, groin flap and cross-finger flap for hand injuries); and free flaps, in which tissue is detached and its vessels are joined to vessels at the new site by microvascular surgery (e.g. radial forearm or anterolateral thigh flap).
  • By composition – skin only, fasciocutaneous, myocutaneous (with muscle) and osteocutaneous (with bone).
  • Tissue expansion – a silicone balloon placed under normal skin is gradually filled with saline over weeks to grow extra skin for reconstruction.

(c) Nursing care (8 marks) A. Pre-operative care

  1. Prepare the recipient bed – regular dressings until healthy red granulation tissue forms; wound swab to ensure there is no beta-haemolytic Streptococcus; control oedema.
  2. Optimise healing – correct anaemia (haemoglobin ideally above 10 g/dL) and low albumin with a high-protein diet; control blood sugar; stop smoking, as nicotine constricts vessels and causes graft and flap failure.
  3. Explain the procedure, the need for immobilisation of the grafted part, the appearance of the graft and the donor site, and expected pain; obtain informed consent; mark or prepare the donor site; give pre-medication as ordered.

B. Care of the grafted (recipient) site

  1. Immobilise the graft with splints, a bulky tie-over (bolster) dressing or negative-pressure dressing for 3–5 days; avoid any movement or shearing; position so that there is no pressure on the graft.
  2. Elevate the grafted limb to reduce oedema; for leg grafts, keep the leg raised and allow standing only when permitted, with crepe bandage support.
  3. The first dressing is usually done on the 3rd to 5th day as advised by the surgeon; soak and remove dressings gently, inspect the graft – a successful graft is pink, adherent and blanches on pressure; small collections of blood or serum may be gently rolled out or drained as directed.
  4. Watch for failure – dark, pale, floating or non-adherent graft, foul smell, discharge or fever; report early.
  5. Remove staples or sutures at 7–10 days as ordered; continue non-adherent dressings until fully healed.
  6. Give analgesics, antibiotics if prescribed, and DVT prophylaxis during immobility.

C. Care of the donor site

  1. The donor site of a split-thickness graft is often more painful than the grafted area because many nerve endings are exposed; give adequate analgesia.
  2. Cover with a non-adherent or moisture-retaining dressing (paraffin gauze, hydrocolloid, alginate or transparent film) as per unit policy; keep it clean, dry and undisturbed for about 10–14 days unless there is infection or excess exudate; reinforce rather than remove soaked outer layers.
  3. Observe for bleeding, infection (redness, pus, increased pain, odour) and conversion to a deeper wound.
  4. After healing – apply moisturiser to prevent dryness and itching, protect from sunlight to prevent pigmentation, and avoid scratching.

D. Flap monitoring (especially free flaps)

  1. Check flap viability every hour for the first 24–48 hours, then less often: colour, temperature, capillary refill (normally 2–3 seconds), tissue turgor and Doppler signal.
  2. Arterial insufficiency – pale, cool flap with slow or absent capillary refill and no Doppler signal.
  3. Venous congestion – dusky, bluish, swollen flap with very brisk refill and dark bleeding on pin-prick; report immediately, as a failing flap can often be saved only within a few hours by re-exploration; medicinal leech therapy may be used for venous congestion.
  4. Avoid pressure on the pedicle – no tight dressings, tapes or straps; position carefully; keep the patient and room warm (cold causes vasospasm); maintain hydration and blood pressure; no smoking; avoid caffeine and vasoconstrictor drugs.

E. Rehabilitation and education

  • Begin physiotherapy when permitted; use splints and pressure garments to prevent contracture and hypertrophic scarring of grafted areas; massage healed grafts with moisturiser.
  • Protect grafts from sun, injury and extreme temperatures – grafted skin has poor sensation and sweating; wear sunscreen and protective clothing.
  • Explain that colour and texture improve over 12–18 months; give psychological support for body-image changes and arrange follow-up.

Nursing importance

  • Most graft failures are due to preventable causes – haematoma, movement and infection – so careful immobilisation, gentle dressings and observation by the nurse decide whether the graft takes.
  • Hourly flap observation and immediate reporting of colour change are critical nursing skills in reconstructive units.

Conclusion Reconstructive surgery restores form and function after burns, injuries, congenital defects and cancer. Skin grafts (split-thickness or full-thickness) and flaps (local, pedicle or free) are the main techniques. Good preparation of the patient and wound bed, immobilisation and protection of the graft, donor-site care, close flap monitoring and rehabilitation are the keys to successful outcomes.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Burns, Reconstructive and Cosmetic Surgery
question: Describe the emergency management of a patient with 30% burns in the casualty (emergency) department.
answer_html:
Introduction A burn of 30% TBSA in an adult is a major burn. Such a patient is at risk of airway obstruction, burn shock, hypothermia and kidney failure in the first hours, and needs systematic emergency care, IV fluid resuscitation and transfer to a burns unit. First aid at the scene (stopping the burning and cooling with running water) should be continued only until the patient reaches hospital.

1. Primary survey (ABCDE) – treat life-threatening problems first

  • A – Airway with cervical-spine protection
    • Look for signs of inhalation injury – burns in a closed room, facial burns, singed nasal hair and eyebrows, soot in the mouth or sputum, hoarseness, stridor, cough and wheeze.
    • Airway oedema increases over the first 24 hours, so the patient may need early endotracheal intubation before swelling makes it impossible; keep intubation equipment ready.
    • Protect the cervical spine if there was a fall, explosion or electrical injury.
  • B – Breathing
    • Give 100% oxygen through a non-rebreather mask to all major burns (treats carbon monoxide poisoning; pulse oximetry can be falsely normal).
    • Observe chest expansion; circumferential full-thickness chest burns may need escharotomy.
  • C – Circulation
    • Insert two large-bore IV cannulas, preferably through unburnt skin; take blood for CBC, urea, creatinine, electrolytes, blood sugar, ABG, carboxyhaemoglobin and blood grouping.
    • Start Ringer's lactate using the Parkland formula (4 mL × kg × % TBSA in 24 hours, half in the first 8 hours from the time of burn).
    • Monitor pulse, BP and peripheral circulation of burnt limbs.
  • D – Disability – assess level of consciousness (AVPU/GCS); confusion may indicate hypoxia, carbon monoxide poisoning or head injury.
  • E – Exposure with environmental control – remove all clothing, jewellery, rings and bangles; estimate the TBSA and depth with a burn chart; prevent hypothermia by covering the patient with clean, dry sheets and warm blankets and keeping the room warm.

2. Secondary survey

  • Head-to-toe examination for associated injuries; history of time, place and mechanism of burn, closed space, chemicals or electricity, and AMPLE history (allergies, medications, past illness, last meal, events).

3. Other emergency measures

  1. Foley catheter – measure hourly urine output (target 0.5 mL/kg/hour in adults); it is the best guide to adequacy of fluids.
  2. Nasogastric tube – burns above 20–25% commonly cause paralytic ileus and vomiting; it also allows early enteral feeding.
  3. Pain relief – IV morphine in small, titrated doses; avoid IM injections.
  4. Tetanus prophylaxis – tetanus toxoid (Td) and immunoglobulin if immunisation is incomplete.
  5. Wound care – cover burns with clean, dry sheets or cling film; do not apply creams or home remedies before assessment by the burns team; elevate burnt limbs.
  6. Escharotomy for circumferential full-thickness burns of limbs that compromise circulation (cold, pale limb, absent pulses).
  7. Stress-ulcer prophylaxis (PPI) as ordered.
  8. Specific care – copious irrigation for chemical burns; ECG monitoring for electrical burns.

4. Documentation, medico-legal aspects and transfer

  • Record the time of burn and arrival, TBSA chart, fluids given, urine output and drugs.
  • Register the case as a medico-legal case (MLC) and inform the police as per policy; preserve clothing; arrange a dying declaration by a magistrate if the patient's condition is critical.
  • Transfer to a burns unit with a nurse escort, continuing oxygen, IV fluids and monitoring.

5. Nursing responsibilities

  • Hourly vital signs, SpO₂, urine output and intake–output chart; maintain IV lines and fluid rates; observe for airway compromise; give psychological support to the patient and family.

Conclusion Emergency care of a patient with 30% burns follows the ABCDE approach – securing the airway, giving 100% oxygen, establishing IV access and fluid resuscitation, monitoring hourly urine output, relieving pain, preventing hypothermia and infection, documenting the medico-legal details and transferring promptly to a burns unit.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Burns, Reconstructive and Cosmetic Surgery
question: Explain fluid resuscitation in a patient with major burns and the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction In major burns, the injured tissues release inflammatory mediators that greatly increase capillary permeability. Water, electrolytes and plasma proteins leak from the blood vessels into the tissues, causing massive oedema, hypovolaemia and haemoconcentration – a condition called burn shock. The leak is greatest in the first 8–12 hours and usually settles by 24–48 hours. Correct fluid resuscitation prevents shock, kidney failure and deepening of burn wounds.

1. Indications for IV fluids

  • Burns of more than 15% TBSA in adults and more than 10% in children and the elderly; also electrical burns and patients with inhalation injury.
  • Smaller burns can usually be managed with oral fluids (ORS) if the patient can drink.

2. Formulas for the first 24 hours (calculated from the time of burn, not from the time of admission)

  • Parkland (Baxter) formula – 4 mL × body weight (kg) × % TBSA of Ringer's lactate in 24 hours; half in the first 8 hours and the remaining half in the next 16 hours.
  • Modified Brooke formula – 2 mL × kg × % TBSA of Ringer's lactate.
