  • Current ATLS guidance starts adults with thermal burns at 2 mL/kg/% TBSA, children at 3 mL, and electrical burns at 4 mL, then titrates to urine output.
  • Children – in addition to the resuscitation fluid, give maintenance fluid containing dextrose, because small children have low glycogen stores and develop hypoglycaemia.
  • Example – a 60 kg patient with 30% burns: 4 × 60 × 30 = 7,200 mL; 3,600 mL in the first 8 hours (450 mL/hour) and 3,600 mL in the next 16 hours (225 mL/hour). If the patient arrives 2 hours after the burn, the first 3,600 mL must be given in the remaining 6 hours (600 mL/hour).

3. Fluids in the second 24 hours

  • Capillary leak decreases, so colloids (e.g. 5% albumin) may be given to restore plasma volume, along with maintenance fluid (5% dextrose) to replace evaporative water loss from the burns; the total volume is usually less than in the first day.
  • Blood transfusion is given later for anaemia caused by red cell destruction and repeated surgery.

4. Choice of fluid

  • Ringer's lactate is the crystalloid of choice; large volumes of normal saline cause hyperchloraemic acidosis; colloids are generally avoided in the first 8–12 hours because they leak into the tissues.

5. Monitoring the adequacy of resuscitation

  • Hourly urine output – the most important guide: 0.5 mL/kg/hour (30–50 mL/hour) in adults and 1 mL/kg/hour in children below 30 kg; in electrical burns with dark urine (myoglobinuria), 1–1.5 mL/kg/hour until the urine is clear.
  • Pulse (ideally below 120/min), BP (mean arterial pressure above 65 mmHg), sensorium, capillary refill, haematocrit, serum lactate and base deficit, and central venous pressure in critically ill patients.
  • The infusion rate is increased or decreased by about 10–20% each hour according to the urine output; boluses are given only for hypotension.

6. Complications of incorrect resuscitation

  • Under-resuscitation – shock, acute kidney injury and conversion of partial-thickness burns to full thickness.
  • Over-resuscitation ("fluid creep") – pulmonary oedema, increased oedema of the airway and wounds, abdominal compartment syndrome, limb compartment syndrome and raised eye pressure.
  • Electrolyte imbalance – hyperkalaemia early (cell destruction), hyponatraemia, and later hypokalaemia and hypophosphataemia.

7. Role of the nurse

  1. Note the exact time of burn and calculate fluids correctly; double-check calculations and infusion rates.
  2. Maintain two patent IV lines and use infusion pumps; label fluids and record volumes hourly.
  3. Insert and maintain a Foley catheter; record hourly urine output, colour and specific gravity on the intake–output chart; report output below target for two consecutive hours.
  4. Monitor vital signs, sensorium, peripheral circulation, breath sounds, daily weight and abdominal girth.
  5. Monitor electrolytes, blood sugar, haematocrit and renal function as ordered.
  6. Watch for fluid overload during the mobilisation (diuretic) phase after 48–72 hours.
  7. Begin oral or nasogastric feeds when bowel sounds return, and include them in the fluid record.

Conclusion Fluid resuscitation in major burns replaces the massive fluid lost through leaking capillaries. Ringer's lactate calculated by the Parkland formula from the time of burn, adjusted hourly to urine output, colloids in the second day and careful monitoring by the nurse prevent both burn shock and the dangers of fluid overload.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Burns, Reconstructive and Cosmetic Surgery
question: Explain the complications of burns and the nursing measures to prevent them.
answer_html:
Introduction Burns affect almost every system of the body. Complications vary with the phase of burn care – early complications are related to shock and the airway, later ones to infection and metabolism, and long-term complications to scarring and psychological trauma. Most of them can be prevented or reduced by good nursing care.

1. Early complications (emergent phase – first 48–72 hours)

  • Burn (hypovolaemic) shock – due to massive capillary leak.
  • Acute kidney injury – due to hypovolaemia, and to myoglobin and haemoglobin released from damaged muscle and red cells (electrical and deep burns).
  • Airway obstruction and inhalation injury – oedema of the upper airway, chemical injury of the lungs, carbon monoxide and cyanide poisoning.
  • Hypothermia – loss of skin and exposure.
  • Electrolyte and acid–base disturbances – hyperkalaemia, hyponatraemia, metabolic acidosis.
  • Compartment syndrome of limbs and chest restriction from circumferential burns.
  • Cardiac arrhythmias – especially after electrical injury.

2. Complications of the acute phase

  • Infection and sepsis – the commonest cause of death after the first few days; burn wound infection (Staphylococcus aureus including MRSA, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter, Klebsiella, Candida), pneumonia, line-related bloodstream infection and urinary infection.
  • Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) and pneumonia.
  • Curling's ulcer – acute stress ulcer of the stomach or duodenum causing bleeding.
  • Paralytic ileus in large burns.
  • Hypermetabolism and malnutrition – metabolic rate may nearly double, with muscle wasting, poor healing and weight loss.
  • Anaemia, hyperglycaemia, deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism, pressure injuries, and graft loss.
  • Conversion of burn depth – partial-thickness wounds become full thickness because of infection, poor perfusion or pressure.

3. Late complications (rehabilitative phase)

  • Hypertrophic scars and keloids – thick, raised, itchy scars.
  • Contractures – shortening of scar across the neck, axilla, elbow, hand and knee, causing deformity and disability.
  • Marjolin's ulcer – squamous cell carcinoma arising in a chronic, unstable burn scar after many years.
  • Itching, pigment changes, dryness, heat intolerance (loss of sweat glands) and loss of hair.
  • Psychological effects – post-traumatic stress disorder, depression, anxiety, sleep disturbance, altered body image, social isolation and loss of employment.
  • Others – cataract (electrical burns), amputation and heterotopic ossification around joints.

4. Nursing measures for prevention

  1. Accurate fluid resuscitation with hourly urine output monitoring to prevent shock and kidney injury; maintain higher urine output in electrical burns.
  2. Airway care – early oxygen, observation for stridor, readiness for intubation and chest physiotherapy.
  3. Strict infection control – hand hygiene, aseptic dressings, topical antimicrobials, protective isolation, early removal of lines and catheters, and early excision and grafting of deep burns.
  4. Prevent hypothermia – warm room, warmed fluids and short dressing times.
  5. Early enteral feeding and stress-ulcer prophylaxis to prevent Curling's ulcer, ileus and malnutrition.
  6. Neurovascular checks of burnt limbs and elevation; report signs of compartment syndrome early for escharotomy.
  7. DVT prophylaxis, frequent change of position and pressure-relieving mattresses.
  8. Anti-contracture positioning, splints and exercises from the first day; pressure garments and silicone sheets once wounds heal.
  9. Long-term follow-up of chronic scar ulcers; biopsy of any non-healing scar ulcer.
  10. Psychological support – counselling, family involvement and referral to mental-health services.

Conclusion Burns can lead to shock, kidney injury, airway problems and electrolyte disturbances early; infection, Curling's ulcer and hypermetabolism in the acute phase; and contractures, abnormal scars and psychological problems later. Timely fluid therapy, airway care, infection control, nutrition, positioning and psychological support prevent most of these complications.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Burns, Reconstructive and Cosmetic Surgery
question: Explain the hospital management of inhalation injury, electrical burns and chemical burns.
answer_html:
Introduction Inhalation, electrical and chemical burns are special burns – the visible skin damage often does not show the true severity, and each needs specific treatment in addition to routine burn care. All three are criteria for referral to a burns unit.

1. Inhalation injury

  • Types – (i) thermal injury of the upper airway above the vocal cords, causing oedema and obstruction within 24–48 hours; (ii) chemical injury of the lower airways from toxic smoke, causing bronchospasm, loss of cilia, pneumonia and ARDS; (iii) systemic poisoning by carbon monoxide (CO) and cyanide from burning plastics and furniture.
  • Suspect when – fire in a closed space, facial burns, singed nasal hair, soot in the mouth or sputum, hoarseness, stridor, wheeze, cough and altered consciousness.
  • CO poisoning – headache, confusion, nausea, cherry-red colour (late); pulse oximetry shows falsely normal SpO₂, so measure carboxyhaemoglobin (COHb); 100% oxygen reduces the half-life of COHb from about 4–5 hours to about 1 hour; hyperbaric oxygen in selected cases.
  • Cyanide poisoning – persistent lactic acidosis and unconsciousness; antidote hydroxocobalamin.
  • Management – humidified 100% oxygen, early intubation if airway oedema is developing, bronchoscopy, suction, chest physiotherapy, bronchodilators, lung-protective ventilation and treatment of pneumonia.
  • Nursing – monitor respiratory rate, voice, stridor, SpO₂ and ABG; head elevation; frequent suction and oral care; ensure ventilator and tube security.

2. Electrical burns

  • Low-voltage (household, below 1,000 volts) and high-voltage (power lines – linemen, farmers handling pumps and wires, children flying kites near lines) injuries, and lightning.
  • "Iceberg effect" – small entry and exit wounds on the skin, but extensive deep damage to muscles, nerves and vessels along the path of the current.
  • Complications – cardiac arrhythmias (ventricular fibrillation, asystole), rhabdomyolysis with myoglobinuria (dark, tea-coloured urine) leading to acute kidney injury, compartment syndrome, fractures and spinal injury (falls, violent muscle contraction), neurological damage, and late cataracts.
  • Management – CPR if needed; ECG and cardiac monitoring for at least 24 hours in high-voltage injury, loss of consciousness or abnormal ECG; cervical-spine protection; IV fluids exceeding the formula, to maintain urine output of 1–1.5 mL/kg/hour until the urine is clear; sodium bicarbonate or mannitol in selected cases; early fasciotomy and debridement; amputation if limbs are non-viable.
  • Nursing – hourly urine output and colour, neurovascular checks of limbs, cardiac monitoring and serum potassium and CK; eye check-ups on follow-up.

3. Chemical burns

  • Alkalis (lime – chuna, cement, caustic soda, drain cleaners) cause liquefaction necrosis and penetrate deeply, so they are more dangerous than acids (sulphuric, nitric, hydrochloric acids, toilet cleaners), which cause coagulation necrosis.
  • Management – staff wear gloves, gown and eye protection; remove contaminated clothing; brush off dry powder before wetting; copious irrigation with running water for at least 30 minutes (alkalis need longer – often 1–2 hours) until the skin or eye pH is near neutral; never try to neutralise (heat is produced); identify the chemical from the label or safety data sheet.
  • Specific chemicals – hydrofluoric acid: apply 2.5% calcium gluconate gel and monitor serum calcium and ECG (risk of severe hypocalcaemia); phenol: wipe with polyethylene glycol; phosphorus: keep wet and remove particles.
  • Eye burns – continuous irrigation with eyelids held open and urgent ophthalmology referral.
  • Acid attacks – medico-legal case; all hospitals must give free immediate treatment and inform the police.

Conclusion Inhalation injury threatens the airway and causes CO and cyanide poisoning; electrical burns hide deep muscle damage, arrhythmias and kidney failure; and chemical burns continue to damage tissue until the chemical is washed away. Early airway control, cardiac and urine monitoring, prolonged irrigation and specific antidotes, with vigilant nursing, are essential.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Burns, Reconstructive and Cosmetic Surgery
question: Explain the methods of burn wound care and the nursing responsibilities during burn dressing.
answer_html:
Introduction The goals of burn wound care are to prevent infection, remove dead tissue, promote healing or prepare the wound for grafting, reduce pain and heat loss, and minimise scarring. Wound care continues from admission until all wounds are closed.

1. Cleansing

  • Wash wounds gently with lukewarm water or saline and a mild antiseptic such as chlorhexidine, on a shower trolley (hydrotherapy) or at the bedside; remove loose dead skin and old cream.
  • Blisters – small, intact blisters are usually left alone; large, tense blisters or those over joints are deroofed as per unit protocol.
  • Clip hair around the wound (not the eyebrows); clean the face and perineum frequently.

2. Methods of dressing

  • Open (exposure) method – the wound is left uncovered after applying a topical agent; used for the face, neck and perineum; allows easy observation but needs a warm, clean environment.
  • Closed (occlusive) method – layers of non-adherent dressing, absorbent gauze and bandage; protects the wound, reduces pain and heat loss and allows movement; bandage from distal to proximal, with fingers and toes dressed separately.
  • Semi-open method – thin covering over the topical agent.

3. Topical antimicrobial agents

  • Silver sulfadiazine 1% cream – the most widely used; broad-spectrum, soothing; may cause transient leucopenia; avoided in sulfa allergy, late pregnancy and newborns under 2 months.
  • Mafenide acetate – penetrates eschar (useful for ears and cartilage), but is painful and can cause metabolic acidosis.
  • Silver nitrate 0.5% solution – stains skin and linen black; can cause hyponatraemia.
  • Nanocrystalline silver dressings – release silver for several days, so fewer painful changes are needed.
  • Others – povidone-iodine, mupirocin (MRSA), antibiotic ointments for the face, and medical-grade honey.

4. Biological and synthetic dressings (temporary skin cover)

  • Allograft (cadaver skin from skin banks), xenograft (pig skin), amniotic membrane (cheap and widely available in India), collagen sheets and biosynthetic dressings; they reduce pain, fluid loss and infection until healing or grafting.

5. Debridement

  • Autolytic (by the body's own enzymes under moist dressings), mechanical (during cleansing and dressing changes), enzymatic (collagenase or papain-based ointments), and surgical – early tangential excision of deep burns within the first few days followed by skin grafting, which reduces infection and hospital stay.

6. Nursing responsibilities during dressing

  1. Give analgesia (and sedation if needed) 20–30 minutes before the dressing; explain the procedure.
  2. Keep the room warm and expose only the part being dressed to prevent hypothermia; work quickly.
  3. Follow strict asepsis – sterile gown, mask, gloves and instruments; separate trolley and equipment for each patient.
  4. Soak dressings before removal; assess and document the wound – size, depth, colour, exudate, odour, eschar, granulation and epithelialisation.
  5. Apply the topical agent in a thin, even layer (about 2–4 mm) with sterile gloves; apply non-adherent dressings and bandages without tightness.
  6. Position and splint joints in anti-contracture positions after dressing.
  7. Take wound swabs or tissue samples for culture when infection is suspected.
  8. Recognise signs of wound infection – change from red to dark brown, black or violet colour, green discharge (Pseudomonas), foul smell, sudden separation of eschar, conversion of partial-thickness to full-thickness wounds, and fever, confusion or falling urine output (sepsis).
  9. Infection control – hand hygiene, protective isolation, limited visitors, no flowers or plants, and careful environmental cleaning.
  10. Provide emotional support – dressing changes are frightening and painful; involve the patient in care when possible.

Conclusion Burn wound care includes gentle cleansing, appropriate dressing methods, topical antimicrobials, temporary biological cover and timely debridement or excision. Pain control, warmth, strict asepsis, careful wound assessment and early recognition of infection are the key nursing responsibilities.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Burns, Reconstructive and Cosmetic Surgery
question: Explain the nutritional needs and nutritional management of a patient with major burns.
answer_html:
Introduction Major burns cause the most severe hypermetabolic and catabolic response seen in any illness. Stress hormones (catecholamines, cortisol and glucagon) rise, the metabolic rate may nearly double in burns over 40% TBSA, and this state can last for months. Muscle protein is broken down for energy, causing weight loss, weakness, poor wound healing, reduced immunity and graft failure. Nutritional support is therefore an essential part of treatment.

1. Assessment

  • Pre-burn weight and height, dietary history, daily or weekly weight, calorie count, serum albumin and prealbumin, blood sugar, electrolytes, nitrogen balance and, where available, indirect calorimetry.

2. Requirements

  • Calories – Curreri formula for adults: 25 kcal × body weight (kg) + 40 kcal × % TBSA per day. For a 60 kg patient with 40% burns: 1,500 + 1,600 = 3,100 kcal/day.
  • Protein – 1.5–2 g/kg/day (about 20–25% of calories) to replace losses from wounds and muscle breakdown.
  • Carbohydrates – the main energy source and protein-sparing; avoid excess glucose, which causes hyperglycaemia and fatty liver.
  • Fats – moderate amounts, including omega-3 fatty acids.
  • Micronutrients – vitamin C (collagen formation), vitamin A (epithelial repair), vitamin E, zinc and selenium (healing and immunity), and iron once the acute phase is over.
  • Fluids – to replace evaporative losses from wounds.

3. Route of feeding

  • Early enteral feeding within 24 hours (often within 6–12 hours) through a nasogastric or nasojejunal tube in burns above 20%, facial burns or ventilated patients; it maintains gut integrity, reduces bacterial translocation, prevents Curling's ulcer and reduces hypermetabolism.
  • Oral diet – high-calorie, high-protein, small frequent meals with supplements when the patient can eat.
  • Parenteral nutrition – only when enteral feeding is not possible, because of higher infection risk.

4. Suitable Indian foods

  • Milk, curd, paneer, eggs, dal and pulses, soya chunks, sprouts, chicken and fish; groundnut and chikki, dry fruits; vitamin-C-rich fruits such as amla, guava and oranges; high-protein milkshakes and commercial protein supplements.

5. Drugs that modify metabolism (as prescribed)

  • Insulin for hyperglycaemia, oxandrolone (anabolic steroid) to improve lean body mass, propranolol to reduce the hypermetabolic response, and glutamine supplementation in some units.

6. Nursing responsibilities

  1. Start tube feeds early as ordered; check tube position; keep the head of the bed raised 30–45°; monitor tolerance (vomiting, distension, diarrhoea).
  2. Avoid long interruptions of feeding for dressings and surgery – plan procedures and restart feeds promptly.
  3. Maintain a daily calorie count and intake–output chart; weigh regularly.
  4. Monitor blood sugar, electrolytes, albumin and wound healing.
  5. Give analgesia before meals, provide mouth care, make meals attractive and allow family to bring preferred home-cooked food that meets the diet plan.
  6. Encourage self-feeding with adaptive aids when hands are burnt; help with feeding when needed.
  7. Educate the patient and family about continuing a high-protein diet after discharge until wounds and grafts heal.

Conclusion Major burns greatly increase energy and protein needs. Early enteral feeding, a high-calorie, high-protein diet calculated by formulas such as Curreri's, adequate vitamins and minerals, glucose control and careful nursing monitoring prevent malnutrition and promote healing and graft survival.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Burns, Reconstructive and Cosmetic Surgery
question: Explain the rehabilitation of a burns patient, with emphasis on prevention of contractures and hypertrophic scars.
tags: position of comfort position of contracture
answer_html:
Introduction Rehabilitation of a burns patient aims to restore the best possible physical function, appearance and psychological and social well-being. It begins on the day of admission, not after wounds heal, and continues for months or years. Contractures and hypertrophic scars are the main causes of long-term disability.

1. Positioning – "the position of comfort is the position of contracture" Patients naturally keep burnt joints flexed, so the nurse maintains anti-contracture positions:

  • Neck – slight extension; no pillow under the head (a small roll under the shoulders) for front-of-neck burns.
  • Shoulder (axilla) – abducted to about 90° with slight forward flexion.
  • Elbow – extended; wrist – slightly extended (20–30°).
  • Hand – position of function (metacarpophalangeal joints flexed 70–90°, finger joints straight, thumb abducted).
  • Hip – extended with slight abduction; knee – extended.
  • Ankle – at 90° (neutral) to prevent foot drop.

2. Splinting

  • Thermoplastic splints to maintain positions, especially at night; dynamic splints to stretch tightening tissues.

3. Exercises and mobility

  • Active and passive range-of-motion exercises several times a day, including during dressings when possible; early ambulation once the patient is stable; strengthening exercises; activities of daily living training (eating, dressing, writing).

4. Scar management

  • Pressure garments – custom-made elastic garments giving about 20–30 mmHg pressure, worn about 23 hours a day for 12–18 months until the scar matures; they flatten and soften scars.
  • Silicone gel sheets – hydrate and soften scars.
  • Scar massage with non-perfumed moisturisers several times a day, to keep the skin supple and reduce itching.
  • Sun protection – sunscreen and protective clothing for at least a year to prevent darkening of scars.
  • Intralesional steroid (triamcinolone) injections, laser therapy and, later, surgical release of contractures (Z-plasty, release and grafting, flaps).
  • Control of itching with moisturisers, antihistamines or gabapentin.

5. Psychological rehabilitation

  • Burns survivors may suffer from post-traumatic stress disorder, depression, anxiety and altered body image; provide counselling, encourage expression of feelings, involve family, connect with survivor support groups and teach camouflage techniques.

6. Social and vocational rehabilitation

  • Plan return to school or work; occupational therapy and job retraining; help in obtaining a disability certificate – acid attack victims are a recognised disability category under the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016; link survivors to compensation and welfare schemes.

7. Education and follow-up

  • Teach the home exercise programme, use and care of pressure garments and splints, skin care, sun protection and signs of skin breakdown.
  • Burn prevention education for the community – cook on a raised platform, avoid loose synthetic clothing while cooking, check LPG cylinders and pipes, keep children away from the kitchen, kerosene lamps and hot liquids, test bath water before bathing children, store chemicals safely, practise electrical safety and supervise children with firecrackers; teach "Stop, Drop and Roll".

Conclusion Burn rehabilitation starts from the first day and includes anti-contracture positioning, splints, exercises, pressure garments and scar care, psychological support and social reintegration. Consistent nursing care and teaching prevent contractures and disfiguring scars and help survivors return to a productive life.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Burns, Reconstructive and Cosmetic Surgery
question: Explain the special therapies used in burns, reconstructive and cosmetic care – vacuum dressing, laser therapy, liposuction, skin rejuvenation and dermal fillers – with nursing care.
answer_html:
Introduction Modern plastic and cosmetic care uses several special therapies to speed wound healing, improve scars and enhance appearance. Nurses prepare patients, assist with procedures, ensure safety and give after-care.

1. Vacuum dressing – negative pressure wound therapy (NPWT, VAC)

  • An open-cell foam dressing sealed with an adhesive film is connected to a vacuum pump, which applies continuous or intermittent negative pressure (commonly about −125 mmHg).
  • Actions – removes exudate, reduces oedema, improves blood flow, promotes granulation tissue and wound contraction, and holds skin grafts firmly in place.
  • Uses – chronic wounds, diabetic foot, pressure ulcers, wound dehiscence, open fractures, burns and fixation of skin grafts.
  • Contraindications – malignancy in the wound, untreated osteomyelitis, exposed blood vessels or organs, thick necrotic eschar and active bleeding.
  • Nursing – maintain an airtight seal (foam should look collapsed; listen for hissing leaks); respond to alarms; change the canister when full; dressings are usually changed every 48–72 hours with analgesia given beforehand; if bleeding occurs, stop the pump, apply pressure and inform the surgeon; record exudate amount and colour; if the pump stays off for more than about 2 hours, the dressing should be removed and replaced.

2. Laser therapy

  • Ablative lasers (CO₂, erbium) for skin resurfacing; fractional lasers for remodelling hypertrophic burn scars and acne scars; pulsed dye laser for redness of scars and vascular lesions; Q-switched lasers for pigmentation and tattoo removal; laser hair removal.
  • Nursing – consent; eye protection (goggles) for the patient and staff, fire safety and warning signs on the door; cooling of the skin; after-care with moisturisers, strict sun protection, no picking of crusts, and watching for infection; antiviral prophylaxis before facial resurfacing if advised.

3. Liposuction (suction-assisted lipectomy)

  • Removal of localised subcutaneous fat through small incisions with suction cannulas after injecting tumescent fluid (saline with lignocaine and adrenaline); it is body contouring, not a weight-loss treatment.
  • Complications – bleeding, fluid shifts, lignocaine toxicity, fat embolism, DVT and pulmonary embolism, seroma, infection and uneven contour.
  • Nursing – monitor vital signs, SpO₂ and fluid balance; compression garments for 4–6 weeks; early ambulation and DVT prophylaxis; pain relief; watch for breathlessness, chest pain or confusion.

4. Skin rejuvenation

  • Chemical peels (glycolic, salicylic, trichloroacetic acid), microdermabrasion, microneedling, platelet-rich plasma (PRP), topical retinoids and botulinum toxin injections for wrinkles.
  • Nursing – patch test, explanation of temporary redness and peeling, gentle cleansing, moisturising and sun protection.

5. Dermal fillers

  • Injectable substances, most commonly hyaluronic acid, used to restore lost volume, smooth wrinkles, enhance lips and fill depressed scars.
  • Complications – bruising, swelling, lumps and infection; rarely vascular occlusion causing skin necrosis or blindness – an emergency treated with hyaluronidase.
  • Nursing – aseptic technique; ice packs; instruct the patient not to press or massage unless advised and to avoid make-up for 24 hours; report immediately any blanching, severe pain or visual disturbance.

6. General nursing responsibilities

  • Ensure procedures are done by qualified practitioners in approved settings; obtain informed consent with realistic expectations; check allergies, bleeding tendency and medications; take photographs with consent; maintain records and follow-up.

Conclusion NPWT, lasers, liposuction, skin rejuvenation and fillers are useful special therapies in wound healing, scar improvement and cosmetic enhancement. Safe use requires careful patient selection, informed consent, procedural safety and attentive after-care by the nurse.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Burns, Reconstructive and Cosmetic Surgery
question: Explain the common cosmetic (aesthetic) surgical procedures and the nursing care of patients undergoing cosmetic surgery.
answer_html:
Introduction Cosmetic (aesthetic) surgery reshapes normal structures of the body to improve appearance and self-esteem. Although done on healthy people, it carries the same risks as other surgery, so careful selection, preparation and post-operative nursing are needed.

1. Common cosmetic procedures

  • Face – rhinoplasty (reshaping the nose), blepharoplasty (removing excess eyelid skin and fat), rhytidectomy (facelift), otoplasty (correcting prominent ears), chin and cheek augmentation.
  • Breast – augmentation with implants, reduction mammoplasty (also relieves back and neck pain), mastopexy (breast lift) and correction of gynaecomastia in men.
  • Body – abdominoplasty (tummy tuck), liposuction and body contouring after massive weight loss.
  • Others – hair transplantation (follicular unit methods), scar revision and minimally invasive procedures such as fillers and botulinum toxin.

2. Patient selection and pre-operative care

  1. Assess the patient's motives and expectations; screen for body dysmorphic disorder (excessive preoccupation with a minor or imagined defect) and refer for psychological evaluation when needed.
  2. Obtain informed written consent, explaining realistic results, scars, possible need for revision, complications and costs.
  3. Take a medical history and investigations; stop smoking at least 4 weeks before surgery (smoking causes skin necrosis and poor healing); stop aspirin, NSAIDs and herbal supplements (garlic, ginkgo, vitamin E) that increase bleeding, as advised.
  4. Take standard pre-operative photographs with consent; the surgeon marks the operative site.
  5. Teach post-operative care and arrange for a responsible adult to accompany the patient.

3. General post-operative nursing care

  • Airway and breathing – facial swelling can affect the airway after facial surgery; keep the head elevated 30–45°.
  • Swelling and bruising – cold compresses for the first 48 hours; elevation.
  • Bleeding and haematoma – the commonest early complication (especially after facelift); report sudden pain, swelling or tightness immediately.
  • Pain relief, antiemetics, drain care, wound care and observation for infection.
  • Compression garments or supportive bras after liposuction, abdominoplasty and breast surgery.
  • Early ambulation and DVT prophylaxis, especially after long body-contouring procedures.

4. Procedure-specific care

  • Rhinoplasty – nasal packs and splint; mouth breathing (keep lips moist); do not blow the nose; sneeze with the mouth open; avoid spectacles resting on the nose for about 6 weeks; protect from injury.
  • Blepharoplasty – cold compresses and lubricating eye drops; head elevation; report sudden eye pain, bulging or loss of vision immediately (retrobulbar haematoma – an emergency).
  • Facelift – head elevation, avoid turning the neck sharply, watch for haematoma and facial nerve weakness.
  • Breast augmentation or reduction – supportive bra, avoid lifting the arms above the head and heavy lifting for a few weeks; watch for asymmetry, haematoma and infection.
  • Abdominoplasty – nurse in semi-Fowler's position with knees flexed to reduce tension on the suture line; walk bent forward at first; abdominal binder.
  • Hair transplant – sleep semi-upright, avoid touching or rubbing grafts and avoid head-washing until advised.

5. Psychological support and follow-up

  • Reassure that swelling and bruising settle over weeks and that scars take 12–18 months to mature; support patients who are dissatisfied; ensure regular follow-up visits.

Conclusion Cosmetic surgery includes facial, breast and body procedures done to improve appearance. Careful psychological and medical selection, informed consent, cessation of smoking, and attentive post-operative care with early detection of haematoma and infection ensure safe results and patient satisfaction.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Burns, Reconstructive and Cosmetic Surgery
question: Discuss the legal and ethical aspects of caring for patients with burns and those undergoing reconstructive and cosmetic surgery.
answer_html:
Introduction Burns are frequently medico-legal – they may be accidental, suicidal or homicidal – and reconstructive and cosmetic procedures raise issues of consent, expectations and professional conduct. Nurses must understand the legal duties and ethical principles involved.

1. Burns as medico-legal cases

  • Register all burns other than clearly accidental minor ones as a medico-legal case (MLC) and inform the police as per hospital policy.
  • Treatment comes first, but the nurse must document accurately – date and time of the burn and of arrival, who brought the patient, the history in the patient's own words, level of consciousness, the burn chart (TBSA and depth) and photographs with consent.
  • Preserve evidence such as burnt clothing (sealed, labelled and handed over to the police) and note any smell of kerosene.

2. Dying declaration

  • A statement by a person about the cause or circumstances of their death, admissible in court under Section 26(a) of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023 (earlier Section 32(1), Indian Evidence Act).
  • Preferably recorded by a magistrate; if there is no time, by a doctor or any other person. The doctor certifies that the patient is conscious, oriented and fit to give a statement before and after recording.
  • It is recorded in the patient's own words, preferably in question–answer form, with signature or thumb impression (an unburnt finger or toe may be used); the nurse may act as a witness and should not influence the patient.

3. Dowry death and domestic violence

  • Dowry death (Section 80, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023) – death of a woman by burns or bodily injury, or otherwise than under normal circumstances, within 7 years of marriage, when she was subjected to cruelty or harassment for dowry soon before death; cruelty by husband or relatives is an offence under Section 85, BNS. A magistrate's inquiry into such deaths is required under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS).
  • Nurses should screen sensitively for domestic violence, ensure privacy and safety, and inform patients about the women's helpline (181) and One Stop Centres.

4. Acid attacks

  • Acid attack is an offence under Section 124, BNS. Under Section 397, BNSS, all hospitals, public or private, must immediately provide free first aid and medical treatment to acid-attack victims and inform the police; refusal is punishable.
  • The Supreme Court (Laxmi v. Union of India) directed regulation of acid sales, compensation and free treatment including reconstructive surgery; acid-attack victims are recognised as persons with disability under the RPwD Act, 2016.

5. Consent and confidentiality

  • Informed consent for surgery, grafting, blood transfusion, photographs and research; in emergencies, life-saving treatment is given under the doctrine of implied consent; parents or guardians consent for minors.
  • Maintain confidentiality and privacy – burns patients are often targets of media and community curiosity.

6. Ethical issues in burns care

  • Adequate pain relief is a patient's right.
  • In massive burns with very poor prognosis, decisions about aggressive treatment versus comfort (palliative) care are made with the family, respecting the patient's wishes and advance directives, as per Supreme Court guidelines on withholding or withdrawing life-sustaining treatment.
  • Fair allocation of scarce burn beds, blood and skin; promotion of skin donation to skin banks, which is regulated as tissue donation under the Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act.

7. Ethical issues in reconstructive and cosmetic surgery

  • Respect autonomy while ensuring realistic expectations – no guarantee of results; disclose risks, costs and the possibility of revision.
  • Screen for body dysmorphic disorder; take extra care with minors.
  • Procedures only by qualified, registered practitioners; avoid misleading advertisements; maintain records and before-and-after photographs; patients may seek redress for negligence under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.
  • Gender-affirming surgery – the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 provides for access to medical care including such surgery; nurses must give respectful, non-discriminatory and confidential care.

Conclusion Burn care involves important legal duties – MLC registration, careful documentation, dying declarations, and awareness of laws on dowry deaths and acid attacks – while reconstructive and cosmetic surgery demands valid informed consent, realistic expectations and ethical professional conduct. The nurse protects both the patient's rights and the integrity of the legal process.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Burns, Reconstructive and Cosmetic Surgery
question: State the Parkland formula and calculate the 24-hour fluid requirement for a 70 kg man with 40% burns.
answer_html:
Parkland (Baxter) formula – fluid needed in the first 24 hours = 4 mL × body weight (kg) × % TBSA burnt, given as Ringer's lactate. Half is given in the first 8 hours from the time of burn and the remaining half over the next 16 hours. Only partial- and full-thickness burns are counted.

Calculation – 4 × 70 × 40 = 11,200 mL in 24 hours.

  • First 8 hours: 5,600 mL, i.e. 700 mL/hour.
  • Next 16 hours: 5,600 mL, i.e. 350 mL/hour.

The rate is then adjusted to keep the urine output at about 0.5 mL/kg/hour (about 35 mL/hour) for this patient. Colloids (albumin) may be added in the second 24 hours.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Burns, Reconstructive and Cosmetic Surgery
question: What is Curling's ulcer?
answer_html:
Curling's ulcer is an acute stress ulcer of the stomach or duodenum that develops in patients with extensive burns, usually within days of the injury.

  • Cause – reduced blood flow to the gut (hypovolaemia), mucosal ischaemia, increased gastric acid, decreased protective mucus and release of stress hormones.
  • Features – often painless; presents with upper GI bleeding (haematemesis, coffee-ground nasogastric aspirate, melaena), a sudden fall in haemoglobin, or perforation.
  • Prevention – adequate fluid resuscitation, early enteral feeding, proton pump inhibitors or H2 blockers and monitoring of nasogastric aspirate and stools for blood. (A similar stress ulcer after head injury is called Cushing's ulcer.)

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Burns, Reconstructive and Cosmetic Surgery
question: What is escharotomy? Mention its indications.
answer_html:
Escharotomy is a surgical incision through the burn eschar – the hard, leathery, inelastic dead tissue of a full-thickness burn – down to the fat, to release constriction caused by circumferential burns. As oedema develops under the rigid eschar, the pressure rises and cuts off circulation or restricts breathing.

Indications

  • Circumferential full-thickness burns of limbs with signs of poor circulation – cold, pale limb, weak or absent pulses, delayed capillary refill, numbness and increasing pain.
  • Circumferential burns of the chest or abdomen restricting chest expansion and ventilation.

It is done at the bedside along the sides of the limbs or chest with a scalpel or cautery, with analgesia. Nursing care includes hourly neurovascular checks, limb elevation and control of bleeding. Deeper muscle swelling (electrical burns) needs fasciotomy.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Burns, Reconstructive and Cosmetic Surgery
question: Explain Jackson's zones of burn injury.

diagram.caption: Jackson's three zones of burn injury
labels: central zone of coagulation with dead tissue
middle zone of stasis with reduced blood flow that can be saved
outer zone of hyperaemia with increased blood flow that recovers

answer_html:
Jackson described three concentric zones in a burn wound:

  1. Zone of coagulation – the central area of maximum damage; tissue is dead (coagulation necrosis) and cannot recover.
  2. Zone of stasis (ischaemia) – the surrounding area with reduced blood flow; tissue is potentially salvageable but can die within 24–48 hours if there is hypoperfusion, oedema, infection or hypothermia. Good fluid resuscitation and wound care aim to save this zone.
  3. Zone of hyperaemia – the outermost area with increased blood flow due to inflammation; it usually recovers within 7–10 days. In large burns (above about 25% TBSA), the inflammatory response spreads to the whole body.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Burns, Reconstructive and Cosmetic Surgery
question: Differentiate between hypertrophic scar and keloid.
answer_html:
Both are abnormal, raised scars caused by excessive collagen deposition during healing; they are common after deep burns, especially in people with darker skin.

Hypertrophic scar Keloid
Stays within the boundary of the original wound Extends beyond the wound margins into normal skin
Appears within weeks of injury May appear months later, even after minor injury (ear piercing, acne)
Often improves and flattens over 12–18 months Rarely regresses; may keep growing
Common across joints and flexures; may cause contractures Common on earlobes, chest, shoulders and back; contractures rare
Recurrence after excision is less common High recurrence after excision

Management – pressure garments, silicone gel sheets, scar massage, intralesional triamcinolone injections, laser therapy and cryotherapy; surgical excision of a keloid is combined with steroid injection or radiotherapy because recurrence is high. The nurse teaches correct, continuous use of pressure garments, massage with non-perfumed moisturiser and sun protection, and reassures that hypertrophic scars soften as they mature.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurological Disorders
question: Mr. Raju, aged 45 years, is admitted with sudden right-sided weakness and slurred speech and is diagnosed with cerebrovascular accident (CVA). (a) Define CVA. (2 marks) (b) Explain the types and causes of CVA. (5 marks) (c) Describe the nursing management of Mr. Raju. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Types of stroke
labels: ischaemic stroke – thrombus or embolus blocking a cerebral artery with an area of infarction beyond the block; haemorrhagic stroke – rupture of a small artery deep in the brain with blood collecting in the brain tissue; subarachnoid haemorrhage – ruptured berry aneurysm bleeding around the brain

answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks) A cerebrovascular accident (stroke) is defined by WHO as rapidly developing clinical signs of focal (or global) disturbance of brain function, lasting more than 24 hours or leading to death, with no apparent cause other than a vascular origin. It results from interruption of blood supply to part of the brain (ischaemia) or rupture of a blood vessel (haemorrhage). A transient ischaemic attack (TIA) is a brief episode of neurological deficit, usually lasting minutes and resolving completely within 24 hours, without permanent infarction – it is a warning sign of an impending stroke. Stroke is a leading cause of death and adult disability in India, and since millions of brain cells die every minute of ischaemia, "time is brain".

(b) Types and causes of CVA (5 marks) 1. Ischaemic stroke (about 80% of strokes)

  • Thrombotic stroke – a clot forms on an atherosclerotic plaque in a large artery (carotid, middle cerebral artery) or blocks a small penetrating artery (lacunar stroke) due to long-standing hypertension and diabetes; onset is often during sleep or early morning, sometimes in a stepwise manner.
  • Embolic stroke – a clot travels from elsewhere, mostly from the heart – atrial fibrillation, rheumatic heart disease (mitral stenosis), recent myocardial infarction, prosthetic valves and infective endocarditis – or from carotid plaques; onset is sudden, often during activity.
  • Other causes – low cerebral perfusion in shock or cardiac arrest (watershed infarcts), arterial dissection, vasculitis (including tuberculous meningitis), blood disorders (sickle cell disease, polycythaemia, hypercoagulable states) and cerebral venous thrombosis, which is relatively common in young Indian women in the postpartum period and with dehydration.

2. Haemorrhagic stroke (about 15–20%; a higher proportion in India)

  • Intracerebral haemorrhage – bleeding into brain tissue, commonly due to uncontrolled hypertension (basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, cerebellum); other causes are anticoagulant and antiplatelet drugs, amyloid angiopathy in the elderly, arteriovenous malformations (AVM), tumours and bleeding disorders.
  • Subarachnoid haemorrhage – bleeding into the subarachnoid space, mostly from a ruptured berry aneurysm or AVM; presents with a sudden, severe ("worst ever") headache.

3. Risk factors

  • Modifiable – hypertension (the most important), diabetes, smoking and tobacco chewing, alcohol, high cholesterol, obesity, physical inactivity, unhealthy diet high in salt, atrial fibrillation and other heart disease, oral contraceptives with smoking, and stress.
  • Non-modifiable – increasing age, male sex, family history and previous stroke or TIA.

4. Clinical picture in Mr. Raju

  • Sudden right hemiparesis and slurred speech (dysarthria) or aphasia suggest a lesion of the left cerebral hemisphere (middle cerebral artery territory), because motor pathways cross to the opposite side. Other stroke signs include facial deviation, numbness, loss of half the visual field (hemianopia), dysphagia, neglect (right-hemisphere lesions), vertigo and ataxia (posterior circulation). The public is taught BE FAST – Balance, Eyes, Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call 108.

(c) Nursing management of Mr. Raju (8 marks) A. Emergency and acute care

  1. Note the time of onset (last seen normal) – it decides eligibility for clot-dissolving treatment; activate the stroke team.
  2. Airway, breathing and circulation – position on the side if consciousness is reduced; suction secretions; give oxygen only if SpO₂ is below 94%; check blood sugar immediately (hypoglycaemia can mimic stroke).
  3. Urgent non-contrast CT (or MRI) brain to differentiate ischaemic from haemorrhagic stroke – the nurse ensures rapid transfer.
  4. Ischaemic stroke – IV thrombolysis with alteplase or tenecteplase within 4.5 hours of onset in eligible patients, and mechanical thrombectomy for large-artery blockage (up to 24 hours in selected patients); BP must be below 185/110 mmHg before and below 180/105 mmHg for 24 hours after thrombolysis; aspirin is started after excluding haemorrhage (24 hours after thrombolysis).
  5. Care during and after thrombolysis – neuro checks and vital signs every 15 minutes for 2 hours, every 30 minutes for the next 6 hours and then hourly up to 24 hours; watch for bleeding, worsening neurological status, severe headache, vomiting and tongue/lip swelling; stop the infusion and inform the doctor if these occur; avoid IM injections, arterial punctures, nasogastric tubes and catheters for the first 24 hours where possible.
  6. Haemorrhagic stroke – careful BP lowering as ordered (often to a systolic of about 140 mmHg), reversal of anticoagulants, measures to reduce raised intracranial pressure and neurosurgical evacuation when indicated.

B. Ongoing nursing care by nursing diagnoses 1. Ineffective cerebral tissue perfusion

  • Monitor GCS, pupils, limb power, speech, BP, pulse, respiration and temperature; report deterioration (falling GCS, new weakness, unequal pupils, headache, vomiting).
  • Keep blood sugar between about 140 and 180 mg/dL, avoid hypoglycaemia, and treat fever promptly; elevate the head of the bed to 30° if there is raised ICP or aspiration risk.

2. Risk for aspiration and impaired swallowing

  • Keep nil by mouth until a bedside swallow screen is done; feed through a nasogastric tube if unsafe; when oral feeding starts, sit the patient upright, give soft or thickened foods in small amounts on the unaffected side, check for food pocketing in the cheek, and keep upright for 30 minutes after meals; give good mouth care.

3. Impaired physical mobility related to right hemiplegia

  • Positioning – change position every 2 hours; support the affected arm on a pillow to prevent shoulder subluxation; never pull the patient by the weak arm; keep the hand in a functional position and the feet supported to prevent foot drop.
  • Range-of-motion exercises from the first day; early mobilisation (sitting, standing, walking with support) once stable, with the physiotherapist.
  • DVT prevention – leg exercises, intermittent pneumatic compression or prophylactic heparin as ordered.

4. Impaired verbal communication (aphasia/dysarthria)

  • Speak slowly and clearly in short sentences; ask yes/no questions; allow enough time to respond; use gestures, pictures and communication boards; do not shout or finish sentences for him; refer to a speech therapist.

5. Self-care deficit

  • Assist with bathing, dressing, feeding and toileting; encourage use of the unaffected left hand; teach to dress the affected side first and undress it last; provide adaptive aids.

6. Impaired urinary and bowel elimination

  • Avoid long-term indwelling catheters; use timed voiding and bladder training; high-fibre diet, adequate fluids and stool softeners to prevent constipation.

7. Risk for impaired skin integrity and injury

  • Pressure-relieving mattress, skin inspection, padded side rails, call bell within reach on the unaffected side, and fall-prevention measures; protect anaesthetic skin from hot water bags.

8. Ineffective coping and risk of depression

  • Post-stroke depression and emotional lability are common; encourage expression of feelings, involve family, praise small achievements and arrange counselling.

C. Discharge teaching and secondary prevention

  • Regular antiplatelet drugs (or anticoagulants if he has atrial fibrillation), statins and antihypertensives without interruption.
  • BP control (usually below 130/80 mmHg), diabetes control, stopping smoking, tobacco and alcohol, low-salt diet, regular exercise and weight control.
  • Continue physiotherapy and speech therapy at home; home safety modifications; regular follow-up.
  • Teach the family the BE FAST warning signs and to call 108 immediately for any new symptoms.

Nursing importance

  • Rapid recognition, timing and transfer for CT and thrombolysis save brain tissue; nurses' swallow screening, positioning and early mobilisation prevent aspiration pneumonia, contractures and shoulder pain, which are common causes of poor recovery.

Conclusion CVA results from ischaemia or haemorrhage in the brain, with hypertension as the leading risk factor. Mr. Raju's recovery depends on emergency reperfusion where eligible, close neurological monitoring, prevention of complications, early rehabilitation, communication support and lifelong risk-factor control, all of which rely heavily on skilled nursing care.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurological Disorders
question: Mr. X, aged 40 years, is brought to the emergency department with spinal cord injury following a fall. (a) Explain the pre-hospital management of a patient with spinal cord injury. (4 marks) (b) Explain the clinical manifestations of spinal cord injury. (4 marks) (c) Describe the nursing management of Mr. X. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: Level of spinal cord injury and resulting function
labels: C1–C4 injury – quadriplegia with breathing affected (phrenic nerve C3–C5)
C5–C8 – quadriplegia with partial arm function
below L1 – cauda equina injury with flaccid legs

answer_html:
(a) Pre-hospital management (4 marks) Spinal cord injury (SCI) should be suspected in every patient with major trauma – falls from height (trees, roofs, wells), road traffic accidents, diving injuries, assault, unconscious trauma victims and anyone with neck or back pain, numbness or weakness after injury. The aim is to prevent secondary injury to the cord from movement, hypoxia and hypotension.

  1. Ensure scene safety and call 108; do not allow bystanders to lift the patient by the arms and legs or carry him sitting up in a private vehicle – a common cause of further cord damage.
  2. Spinal motion restriction
    • Manual in-line stabilisation of the head and neck by one rescuer until immobilised.
    • Apply a correctly sized rigid cervical collar.
    • Log-roll the patient with at least 4 trained persons, keeping the head, neck and trunk in one line, onto a spine board or scoop stretcher; secure with straps and head blocks.
  3. Airway – open with the jaw-thrust manoeuvre (no head-tilt, chin-lift); clear the mouth; if vomiting, log-roll the whole body to the side as one unit.
  4. Breathing – give high-flow oxygen; watch for diaphragmatic (abdominal) breathing and weak cough in cervical injuries (C3–C5 supply the diaphragm); support ventilation with a bag-valve-mask if needed.
  5. Circulation – control bleeding; start IV access; distinguish neurogenic shock (low BP with slow pulse and warm, dry skin) from haemorrhagic shock (low BP with fast pulse, cold, clammy skin); give IV fluids cautiously as directed.
  6. Disability and exposure – check GCS and quickly assess movement and sensation in all limbs; prevent hypothermia, as patients with SCI cannot regulate body temperature.
  7. Transport gently to a trauma centre with spinal care facilities; give nothing by mouth; monitor vital signs and record the time of injury and neurological findings.

(b) Clinical manifestations of spinal cord injury (4 marks) 1. According to completeness

  • Complete injury – total loss of motor and sensory function below the level of injury, including the lowest sacral segments (ASIA grade A).
  • Incomplete injury – some function preserved below the level:
    • Central cord syndrome – weakness of arms more than legs; common in elderly people after neck hyperextension.
    • Anterior cord syndrome – loss of motor power, pain and temperature sensation, with preserved position and vibration sense.
    • Brown-Séquard syndrome (hemisection) – loss of motor power and position sense on the same side and loss of pain and temperature on the opposite side.
    • Conus medullaris and cauda equina syndromes – flaccid weakness of legs, saddle anaesthesia and loss of bladder and bowel control.
  • Severity is graded by the ASIA impairment scale (A to E).

2. According to level

  • C1–C4 – quadriplegia (tetraplegia) with paralysis of breathing muscles – ventilator support is often needed.
  • C5–C8 – quadriplegia with partial arm and hand function; weak cough and breathing.
  • T1–L1 – paraplegia (both legs) with variable trunk control.
  • Below L1 – cauda equina injury with flaccid paralysis of the legs, bladder and bowel.

3. Spinal shock

  • Temporary loss of all reflex activity below the level of injury – flaccid paralysis, absent reflexes, loss of sensation, urinary retention and paralytic ileus; it lasts days to weeks, and the return of reflexes marks its end.

4. Neurogenic shock

  • In injuries above T6, loss of sympathetic tone causes hypotension, bradycardia, warm dry skin and poikilothermia (body temperature varies with the environment).

5. Other features

  • Pain and tenderness at the injury site; respiratory problems (hypoventilation, atelectasis, pneumonia); loss of sweating below the lesion; priapism; and later spasticity in upper motor neuron lesions and autonomic dysreflexia in lesions at or above T6.

(c) Nursing management of Mr. X (7 marks) 1. Maintaining spinal alignment and immobilisation

  • Keep the spine straight; log-roll every 2 hours with adequate staff; maintain the cervical collar.
  • Skeletal traction (Gardner-Wells tongs) – weights must hang freely, never be removed or lifted; give pin-site care as per protocol; halo vest care when applied.
  • After surgical decompression and fixation – wound care, drain care and mobilisation as ordered.

2. Respiratory care

  • Monitor respiratory rate, depth, SpO₂, ABG and vital capacity; report a falling vital capacity (impending respiratory failure).
  • Deep breathing, incentive spirometry and chest physiotherapy; assisted ("quad") cough by giving an upward abdominal thrust during expiration; suction secretions; ventilator care for high cervical injuries.

3. Cardiovascular care

  • Maintain the mean arterial pressure at about 85–90 mmHg in the first days as ordered, with IV fluids and vasopressors; give atropine for severe bradycardia (suctioning may trigger it).
  • Change position slowly to prevent orthostatic hypotension (abdominal binder, elastic stockings, tilt table).
  • DVT prophylaxis – low-molecular-weight heparin, compression devices and passive leg exercises (very high risk).

4. Neurological monitoring

  • Check motor power and sensory level every 1–2 hours initially and report any upward progression (cord oedema).

5. Bladder and bowel care

  • Indwelling catheter in the acute stage, then clean intermittent catheterisation every 4–6 hours; adequate fluids; watch for UTI.
  • Nasogastric tube for paralytic ileus; later a bowel programme – high-fibre diet, fluids, stool softeners and a suppository or digital stimulation at the same time every day.

6. Skin care

  • The patient cannot feel pressure – 2-hourly turning, pressure-relieving mattress, daily skin inspection, keeping skin clean and dry, and padding of bony prominences.

7. Temperature and nutrition

  • Control room temperature and avoid hot water bags; provide a high-protein, high-calorie diet with fibre; give stress-ulcer prophylaxis as ordered.

8. Musculoskeletal care

  • Passive range-of-motion exercises, splints to prevent foot drop and contractures, and treatment of spasticity (e.g. baclofen) as prescribed; early physiotherapy.

9. Prevention and management of autonomic dysreflexia (injuries at or above T6)

  • Recognise sudden severe hypertension, pounding headache, flushing and sweating above the injury and bradycardia; sit the patient up, loosen tight clothing, check for and relieve bladder distension (the commonest trigger) or faecal impaction, and give antihypertensives as ordered.

10. Psychological and sexual counselling

  • Expect grief, anger and depression; give honest information, involve the family, provide counselling and peer support; discuss sexuality and fertility options sensitively.

11. Rehabilitation and discharge teaching

  • Training in transfers, wheelchair use and activities of daily living; self-catheterisation, bowel programme and skin checks with a mirror; home modifications; vocational rehabilitation; help in obtaining a disability certificate and UDID card and benefits under the RPwD Act, 2016.

Nursing importance

  • Correct handling at the scene and in hospital prevents an incomplete injury from becoming complete.
  • Respiratory failure, pressure injuries, UTI, DVT and autonomic dysreflexia are leading causes of complications and death in SCI – all largely preventable by meticulous nursing care.

Conclusion Spinal cord injury causes loss of motor, sensory and autonomic function below the level of injury, with spinal and neurogenic shock in the early phase. Careful pre-hospital immobilisation, maintenance of spinal alignment, respiratory and cardiovascular support, bladder, bowel and skin care, prevention of autonomic dysreflexia and long-term rehabilitation help Mr. X achieve the best possible independence.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurological Disorders
question: (a) Define head injury and classify it. (3 marks) (b) Explain the clinical features of raised intracranial pressure and the use of the Glasgow Coma Scale in head injury. (4 marks) (c) Describe the medical and nursing management of a patient with severe head injury. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Types of traumatic intracranial haematoma
labels: extradural haematoma – lens-shaped blood collection between skull and dura from middle meningeal artery tear; subdural haematoma – crescent-shaped collection under the dura from torn bridging veins; intracerebral haematoma within brain tissue

answer_html:
(a) Definition and classification (3 marks) Head injury (traumatic brain injury, TBI) is any injury to the scalp, skull or brain caused by an external force – a blow, fall, acceleration–deceleration or penetrating object – that may result in temporary or permanent impairment of brain function. Road traffic accidents (especially two-wheeler riders without helmets), falls and assaults are the main causes in India, and head injury is the leading cause of trauma deaths.

Classification 1. According to mechanism

  • Closed (blunt) injury – the dura remains intact; includes coup–contrecoup injury, where the brain strikes the skull at the site of impact and on the opposite side.
  • Open (penetrating) injury – the skull and dura are breached (gunshot, sharp objects, compound depressed fractures).

2. According to the structure injured

  • Scalp injuries – lacerations (bleed profusely) and haematomas.
  • Skull fractures – linear, depressed, compound and basal skull fractures; signs of basal fracture include CSF rhinorrhoea or otorrhoea, periorbital bruising ("raccoon eyes"), bruising behind the ear (Battle's sign) and blood behind the eardrum.
  • Primary brain injuries – concussion (temporary loss of function without structural damage), contusion (bruising of brain tissue), laceration and diffuse axonal injury (shearing of nerve fibres; deep coma).
  • Intracranial haematomas – extradural (epidural) haematoma – arterial bleeding (usually the middle meningeal artery) between skull and dura, classically with a lucid interval followed by rapid deterioration; subdural haematoma – venous bleeding beneath the dura, acute or chronic (elderly and alcoholics); intracerebral haematoma; and traumatic subarachnoid haemorrhage.
  • Secondary brain injury – further damage after the initial impact due to hypoxia, hypotension, raised intracranial pressure, cerebral oedema, hypercapnia, seizures, infection, fever and abnormal blood sugar – much of it preventable.

3. According to severity (GCS) – mild (13–15), moderate (9–12) and severe (3–8).

(b) Raised intracranial pressure and the Glasgow Coma Scale (4 marks) 1. Raised intracranial pressure (ICP)

  • Normal ICP in adults is about 5–15 mmHg; above 20 mmHg is raised. According to the Monro–Kellie doctrine, the skull contains brain, blood and CSF in a fixed space, so an increase in one (haematoma, oedema) raises the pressure. Cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP) = mean arterial pressure − ICP, and is ideally kept at about 60–70 mmHg.
  • Early signs – deterioration in level of consciousness (the earliest and most sensitive sign) – restlessness, confusion, drowsiness; headache worse on coughing or straining; vomiting (often projectile); visual blurring and papilloedema; sluggish or unequal pupils; weakness of the opposite side of the body.
  • Late signs – Cushing's triad (rising systolic BP with widening pulse pressure, bradycardia and irregular breathing), fixed dilated pupil(s), decorticate or decerebrate posturing, loss of brainstem reflexes and deep coma – signs of brain herniation.
  • In infants – bulging fontanelle, enlarging head and high-pitched cry.

2. Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)

  • Assesses the best response in three areas: eye opening (1–4), verbal response (1–5) and motor response (1–6); the total ranges from 3 (deep coma) to 15 (fully alert).
  • Record each component separately (e.g. E2 V3 M5 = 10); write "T" for verbal response in intubated patients.
  • GCS of 8 or less indicates coma and the need for airway protection (intubation); a fall of 2 or more points is significant deterioration and must be reported immediately.
  • GCS is recorded on a neuro-observation chart together with pupil size and reaction, limb power and vital signs.

(c) Medical and nursing management of severe head injury (8 marks) A. Medical management

  1. Primary survey (ABCDE) with cervical-spine protection – all head-injured patients are assumed to have a neck injury until it is excluded.
  2. Airway and breathing – intubate if GCS is 8 or less, avoid hypoxia (keep SpO₂ above 94%) and keep PaCO₂ normal (35–40 mmHg); brief hyperventilation only for signs of herniation as a temporary measure.
  3. Circulation – avoid hypotension (systolic BP at least about 100–110 mmHg) with isotonic fluids (normal saline); hypotonic fluids such as 5% dextrose are avoided because they worsen cerebral oedema.
  4. Urgent CT brain; surgery – craniotomy or burr holes to evacuate extradural or subdural haematoma, elevation of depressed fractures, decompressive craniectomy for uncontrolled ICP, and insertion of an ICP monitor or external ventricular drain (EVD).
  5. Control of raised ICP – head elevation 30° with the neck straight, mannitol 20% (0.25–1 g/kg IV) or hypertonic saline, sedation and analgesia, normothermia, CSF drainage and seizure control; steroids are not recommended in head injury.
  6. Antiepileptic drugs (levetiracetam or phenytoin) to prevent early post-traumatic seizures; tranexamic acid within 3 hours in selected patients; tetanus prophylaxis for open wounds; DVT and stress-ulcer prophylaxis; early enteral nutrition.

B. Nursing management

  1. Neurological observation – record GCS, pupils, limb movements and vital signs every 15 minutes initially, then hourly as the condition stabilises; report immediately a fall in GCS, a new unequal or non-reacting pupil, new weakness, seizures or Cushing's triad.
  2. Airway care – lateral or semi-prone position in the unintubated patient; suction gently for no more than 10–15 seconds after pre-oxygenation (excessive suctioning raises ICP); ventilator and endotracheal tube care; ABG monitoring.
  3. Positioning to reduce ICP – head of bed at 30°, head in the midline, avoid neck flexion or rotation and tight tube ties or collars, avoid hip flexion above 90° and the prone position; prevent coughing, straining and Valsalva manoeuvres (stool softeners); space out nursing activities and keep the environment quiet.
  4. Fluid and electrolyte balance – strict intake–output, daily weight and serum sodium; watch for diabetes insipidus (large volumes of dilute urine, high sodium) and SIADH or cerebral salt wasting (low sodium).
  5. CSF leak – look for clear fluid from the nose or ear that forms a "halo" or ring sign on gauze; do not pack, suction or pass a nasogastric tube through the nose in basal skull fracture (use the mouth); tell the patient not to blow the nose; observe for meningitis.
  6. Temperature control – treat fever promptly with antipyretics and cooling, because fever increases brain metabolism and ICP.
  7. Seizure precautions – padded side rails, suction and oxygen ready, antiepileptics on time.
  8. EVD care – keep the drip chamber at the prescribed level relative to the ear (tragus), maintain a closed sterile system, record CSF volume and colour, clamp only on order and never flush.
  9. Care of the unconscious patient – eye care, mouth care, pressure-area care, bladder and bowel care, nasogastric feeding, passive exercises and DVT prevention.
  10. Family support and rehabilitation – explain the condition honestly, involve the family in care, and prepare for cognitive, behavioural and physical rehabilitation; teach warning signs after discharge (increasing headache, vomiting, drowsiness, seizures).
  11. Prevention education – helmets for two-wheeler riders and pillion riders, seat belts, no drink-driving or using mobile phones while driving, child safety and fall prevention in the elderly.

Nursing importance

  • Most deaths after head injury that reach hospital are due to secondary brain injury; careful neuro-observation, airway care, positioning and prevention of hypoxia, hypotension and fever by the nurse directly improve survival.

Conclusion Head injury ranges from scalp wounds and skull fractures to contusions, diffuse axonal injury and intracranial haematomas. Raised ICP and falling GCS signal danger. Early airway control, CT, surgery where needed, control of ICP and vigilant nursing observation and care prevent secondary brain damage and promote recovery.

question: (a) Define seizure and epilepsy and classify seizures. (3 marks) (b) Explain the causes, clinical features and diagnosis of epilepsy. (4 marks) (c) Describe the management of status epilepticus and the nursing care of a patient with epilepsy. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Phases of a generalised tonic-clonic seizure
labels: post-ictal phase with confusion and sleep

answer_html:
(a) Definitions and classification (3 marks)

  • A seizure is a transient occurrence of signs and symptoms due to abnormal, excessive or synchronous electrical activity of neurons in the brain. It may be provoked (by fever, low blood sugar, alcohol withdrawal, eclampsia) or unprovoked.
  • Epilepsy is a chronic brain disorder characterised by an enduring tendency to have recurrent, unprovoked seizures. Practically, it is diagnosed when a person has two or more unprovoked seizures more than 24 hours apart, one unprovoked seizure with a high risk of recurrence, or an epilepsy syndrome. India has about 10–12 million people with epilepsy, and many remain untreated because of stigma and myths.
  • Status epilepticus is a seizure lasting 5 minutes or more, or repeated seizures without regaining consciousness in between – a medical emergency.

Classification (ILAE 2017) 1. Focal-onset seizures (begin in one part of one hemisphere)

  • Focal aware (earlier "simple partial") – consciousness preserved; motor jerking of one limb that may spread (Jacksonian march), sensory, autonomic or psychic symptoms (déjà vu, fear).
  • Focal impaired-awareness (earlier "complex partial") – altered awareness with staring and automatisms (lip smacking, chewing, fumbling), often from the temporal lobe.
  • Focal to bilateral tonic–clonic (earlier "secondary generalised").

2. Generalised-onset seizures (involve both hemispheres from the start)

  • Motor – tonic–clonic (grand mal), tonic, clonic, myoclonic and atonic (drop attacks).
  • Non-motor – absence seizures (petit mal), mainly in children.

3. Unknown-onset seizures – when the beginning was not observed.

(b) Causes, clinical features and diagnosis (4 marks) 1. Causes

  • Structural – stroke (common in the elderly), head injury, brain tumour, birth asphyxia and injury, developmental brain malformations and hippocampal sclerosis.
  • Infections – neurocysticercosis (the commonest cause of acquired epilepsy in India), tuberculoma, meningitis, encephalitis, cerebral malaria and HIV-related infections.
  • Metabolic – hypoglycaemia, hyponatraemia, hypocalcaemia, uraemia and liver failure.
  • Genetic epilepsies (e.g. juvenile myoclonic epilepsy), immune (autoimmune encephalitis) and unknown causes.
  • Seizure triggers in known epilepsy – missed medicines (the commonest), sleep deprivation, alcohol, fever, stress, flashing lights and menstruation.

2. Clinical features

  • Generalised tonic–clonic seizure
    • An aura (strange smell, rising feeling in the stomach) may occur if it begins focally.
    • Tonic phase (10–30 seconds) – sudden loss of consciousness, a cry, fall, stiffening of the body, apnoea and cyanosis.
    • Clonic phase (1–2 minutes) – rhythmic jerking of limbs, frothing, tongue bite (on the side) and urinary incontinence.
    • Post-ictal phase – confusion, deep sleep, headache and muscle aches; temporary weakness of a limb (Todd's paralysis) may occur.
  • Absence seizure – brief (5–10 seconds) staring spells with eyelid flickering, many times a day, without falling or post-ictal confusion; often mistaken for inattention in school.
  • Myoclonic – sudden, brief jerks, often in the morning; atonic – sudden loss of muscle tone with falls and head injuries.
  • Focal seizures – features depend on the brain area involved, as described above.

3. Diagnosis

  • Detailed eyewitness history – a mobile-phone video of the event is very helpful; history of triggers, birth, development, head injury, infections and family history.
  • EEG – shows epileptiform discharges (spikes, spike–wave); sleep-deprived and video-EEG increase yield.
  • MRI brain (preferred) or CT – shows tumours, scars and the ring-enhancing lesions or calcifications of neurocysticercosis.
  • Blood tests – glucose, electrolytes, calcium, magnesium, renal and liver function; drug levels in known epilepsy.
  • ECG to exclude cardiac causes of loss of consciousness; differentiate seizures from syncope and psychogenic non-epileptic seizures.

(c) Management of status epilepticus and nursing care (8 marks) A. Long-term medical management (brief)

  • Antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) are usually started after a second unprovoked seizure; monotherapy is preferred – e.g. levetiracetam, valproate, lamotrigine, carbamazepine or phenytoin according to seizure type, age and sex (valproate is avoided in women who may become pregnant because it harms the fetus).
  • Treatment continues for at least 2–3 seizure-free years before gradual withdrawal under medical supervision.
  • Drug-resistant epilepsy – epilepsy surgery (e.g. temporal lobectomy), vagus nerve stimulation and ketogenic diet in children.
  • Neurocysticercosis – albendazole with steroids and AEDs as prescribed.

B. Management of status epilepticus – a time-critical emergency

  1. 0–5 minutes – stabilise: note the time of onset; protect from injury; turn on the side; clear the airway with suction; give high-flow oxygen; monitor SpO₂, pulse and BP; secure IV access; check capillary blood glucose and give IV dextrose (with thiamine in alcoholics or malnourished patients) if low; send blood for electrolytes, calcium and AED levels.
  2. 5–20 minutes – first-line drug: an IV benzodiazepine – lorazepam or diazepam, repeated once if needed; if IV access is not available, IM, buccal or intranasal midazolam or rectal diazepam.
  3. 20–40 minutes – second-line drug if seizures continue: IV levetiracetam, fosphenytoin/phenytoin or valproate; phenytoin is given slowly in normal saline with ECG and BP monitoring.
  4. 40–60 minutes – refractory status: transfer to ICU, intubation and ventilation, anaesthetic infusions (midazolam, propofol, thiopentone) with continuous EEG monitoring.
  5. Treat the cause – hypoglycaemia, electrolyte imbalance, infection, head injury, drug withdrawal, and magnesium sulphate for eclampsia.
  6. Nursing during status – one nurse stays with the patient continuously, records the time, type and duration of each seizure, drugs given and response; watch for respiratory depression and hypotension after benzodiazepines; monitor temperature (hyperthermia), urine output (myoglobinuria) and neurological status; prevent aspiration and injury; keep the family informed.

C. Nursing care during a seizure

  1. Stay with the patient, call for help and note the time.
  2. Protect from injury – lower the patient to the floor or keep in bed with padded side rails; move hard or sharp objects away; place something soft under the head; loosen tight clothing around the neck.
  3. Turn the patient on the side (recovery position) as soon as possible so that saliva and vomit drain out and the tongue does not block the airway.
  4. Do not put anything into the mouth (spoon, fingers, cloth), do not restrain the movements, and do not give water or medicines by mouth during or immediately after the seizure.
  5. Give oxygen and suction as needed.
  6. Observe and record – any warning or aura, how the seizure began, parts of the body involved, type of movements, eye deviation, colour, incontinence, tongue bite, duration and the post-ictal state.

D. Nursing care after a seizure

  • Keep in the recovery position; check airway, vital signs, GCS and pupils; reorient gently; allow rest; check for injuries (tongue, head, fractures); provide privacy and change soiled clothes; inform the doctor and document.

E. Seizure precautions in hospital

  • Bed in the lowest position with padded side rails; oxygen and suction ready at the bedside; IV access in high-risk patients; supervision while bathing and toileting; avoid glass oral thermometers.

F. Medication management

  • Give AEDs on time; monitor drug levels (e.g. phenytoin) and side effects – gum hypertrophy (good oral hygiene), ataxia and nystagmus (phenytoin); hyponatraemia and skin rash (carbamazepine); weight gain, hair loss and liver toxicity (valproate); sleepiness and mood changes (levetiracetam); watch for serious rashes (Stevens–Johnson syndrome).

G. Health education

  1. Never stop AEDs suddenly – this can cause status epilepticus; take them at fixed times; use reminders; keep a seizure diary; attend regular follow-up.
  2. Avoid triggers – sleep deprivation, alcohol, skipping meals, stress and flashing lights.
  3. Safety – no swimming alone, climbing heights, working near fire, wells or moving machinery; take showers rather than tub baths; cook with supervision until seizures are controlled; drive only when permitted by the licensing rules and the doctor.
