  4. Women with epilepsy – plan pregnancy; take folic acid before conception; review the choice of AED; many AEDs reduce the effect of oral contraceptives; breastfeeding is usually possible.
  5. Teach the family seizure first aid and when to call 108 (seizure lasting more than 5 minutes, repeated seizures, injury or breathing difficulty); carry an identity card.
  6. Correct myths and stigma – epilepsy is not madness, possession or contagious; people with epilepsy can study, marry, work and lead normal lives; discourage harmful practices such as making the person smell shoes or onions during a seizure.

H. Psychosocial support

  • Depression and anxiety are common; counsel the patient and family; inform teachers and employers as needed; link to support groups.

Nursing importance

  • Correct first aid prevents injury and aspiration, while timely recognition and treatment of status epilepticus prevents brain damage and death.
  • Nurses play a key role in closing the large treatment gap in India by promoting regular drug intake and fighting stigma.

Conclusion Epilepsy is a chronic tendency to recurrent unprovoked seizures, which are classified as focal or generalised. Accurate diagnosis, regular antiepileptic treatment, rapid time-based management of status epilepticus, safe first aid, seizure precautions and education against stigma enable most people with epilepsy to live normal lives.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurological Disorders
question: (a) Classify brain tumours. (3 marks) (b) Explain the clinical manifestations and diagnosis of brain tumours. (4 marks) (c) Describe the pre-operative and post-operative nursing care of a patient undergoing craniotomy. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Common sites and effects of brain tumours
labels: frontal lobe tumour – personality change and weakness; temporal lobe – seizures and memory problems; occipital – visual field loss; cerebellum – ataxia; pituitary – visual field defect and hormone changes; meningioma arising from the dura

answer_html:
(a) Classification of brain tumours (3 marks) A brain (intracranial) tumour is an abnormal growth of cells within the skull, arising from the brain, its coverings, cranial nerves, pituitary gland or blood vessels, or spreading from elsewhere. Because the skull cannot expand, even a benign tumour can be life-threatening.

1. According to origin

  • Primary tumours – arise from tissues inside the skull.
  • Secondary (metastatic) tumours – spread from cancers of the lung, breast, kidney, colon and skin (melanoma); they are the commonest brain tumours in adults.

2. According to tissue type

  • Gliomas (from glial cells) – astrocytoma, including glioblastoma (the commonest and most malignant primary tumour in adults), oligodendroglioma and ependymoma.
  • Meningioma – from the meninges; usually benign and slow-growing; commoner in women.
  • Pituitary adenoma – may secrete hormones or press on the optic chiasma.
  • Nerve sheath tumours – acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma).
  • Embryonal tumours – medulloblastoma in children.
  • Others – craniopharyngioma, primary CNS lymphoma, haemangioblastoma.

3. According to location – supratentorial (cerebral hemispheres; commoner in adults) and infratentorial (cerebellum and brainstem; commoner in children).

4. According to WHO grade – grade 1 (benign, slow-growing) to grade 4 (highly malignant), based on microscopy and molecular features.

(b) Clinical manifestations and diagnosis (4 marks) 1. General features (due to raised intracranial pressure)

  • Headache – often worse in the early morning and on coughing or bending.
  • Vomiting, often projectile and in the morning.
  • Papilloedema with blurring of vision.
  • Seizures – a new seizure in an adult must be investigated for a tumour.
  • Drowsiness, slowing of thinking and personality change.

2. Focal features (depending on location)

  • Frontal lobe – personality and behaviour change, poor judgement, weakness of the opposite side, and expressive aphasia (dominant side).
  • Parietal lobe – sensory loss, neglect of one side and difficulty with spatial tasks.
  • Temporal lobe – seizures with smell or taste auras, memory problems and receptive aphasia.
  • Occipital lobe – visual field defects.
  • Cerebellum – unsteady gait (ataxia), incoordination, nystagmus and intention tremor.
  • Brainstem – cranial nerve palsies, difficulty in swallowing and limb weakness.
  • Pituitary tumours – bitemporal hemianopia (loss of outer visual fields) and hormonal effects (acromegaly, Cushing's syndrome, amenorrhoea and galactorrhoea from prolactinoma).
  • Acoustic neuroma – one-sided deafness, tinnitus and imbalance.

3. Diagnosis

  • MRI brain with contrast – the investigation of choice; CT in emergencies; MR spectroscopy and perfusion studies.
  • Stereotactic or open biopsy – confirms the type and grade.
  • Hormone assays and visual field charting for pituitary tumours; search for a primary cancer (CT chest and abdomen) in suspected metastases.

4. Treatment (brief) – surgical removal by craniotomy or transsphenoidal surgery (pituitary); radiotherapy, including stereotactic radiosurgery; chemotherapy (temozolomide) for gliomas; dexamethasone to reduce brain oedema; AEDs for seizures; ventriculoperitoneal shunt for hydrocephalus; and palliative care for advanced tumours.

(c) Nursing care of a patient undergoing craniotomy (8 marks) A. Pre-operative care

  1. Baseline assessment – record GCS, pupils, limb power, speech, vision, cranial nerve function and vital signs, so that post-operative changes can be compared.
  2. Psychological preparation – patients fear death, disability and change in personality or appearance; explain the procedure, ICU stay, tubes and head dressing; involve the family; obtain informed consent.
  3. Medicines – give dexamethasone as ordered (with food, monitor blood sugar) to reduce oedema, AEDs and gastric protection; stop anticoagulants and antiplatelets as advised.
  4. Investigations – blood counts, coagulation profile, electrolytes, blood grouping and cross-matching, ECG and chest X-ray.
  5. Skin preparation – antiseptic hair wash; hair is clipped only as advised by the surgeon (minimal hair removal is now preferred); be sensitive to the emotional and cultural importance of hair, especially for women.
  6. Keep NPO, apply anti-embolism stockings, and teach deep breathing (but avoid vigorous coughing after surgery).
  7. For transsphenoidal surgery, explain that the nose will be packed, breathing will be through the mouth, and sneezing, nose-blowing and bending must be avoided.

B. Post-operative care

  1. Neurological observation – GCS, pupils, limb power and speech every 15 minutes initially, then hourly; compare with the baseline and report any deterioration immediately (haematoma, oedema or raised ICP).
  2. Airway and breathing – maintain a clear airway; give oxygen; prevent hypoxia and high CO₂, which raise ICP; ventilator care if needed.
  3. Positioning
    • Supratentorial surgery – head of bed at 30° with the head in the midline; avoid neck flexion; do not lie the patient on the operated side if a large tumour or a bone flap has been removed.
    • Infratentorial surgery – keep the bed flat or slightly raised as ordered, nurse on the side and avoid neck flexion; support the head and neck while turning.
  4. Vital signs and BP control – avoid both hypertension (bleeding) and hypotension (poor brain perfusion); monitor temperature – fever may indicate infection or meningitis.
  5. Wound and drain care – observe the head dressing for bleeding or clear fluid (CSF leak); maintain subgaleal or ventricular drains as ordered (never apply suction or alter the drain level without an order) and record drainage; periorbital swelling and bruising are common – apply cold compresses and lubricate the eyes.
  6. Fluid and electrolyte balance – strict intake–output and serum sodium; watch for diabetes insipidus (sudden large volumes of dilute urine, especially after pituitary surgery – report urine output above about 200–250 mL/hour), SIADH and cerebral salt wasting; avoid hypotonic IV fluids.
  7. Seizure prevention – continue AEDs; seizure precautions at the bedside.
  8. Pain, nausea and vomiting – give paracetamol and mild analgesics (avoid heavy sedation that masks neurological signs) and antiemetics (vomiting raises ICP).
  9. Steroids – give dexamethasone and taper as ordered; monitor blood sugar and gastric symptoms.
  10. Prevention of complications – DVT prophylaxis, chest physiotherapy, pressure-area care, eye and mouth care, and early mobilisation when permitted.
  11. After transsphenoidal surgery – watch for clear nasal discharge (CSF leak) and diabetes insipidus; avoid sneezing, coughing, straining, nose-blowing and drinking through straws; provide mouth care; give hormone replacement (cortisol) as prescribed.
  12. Rehabilitation and psychological support – physiotherapy, speech and occupational therapy for deficits; support for changes in personality, memory and body image; counselling about radiotherapy, chemotherapy and prognosis; palliative care for malignant tumours.

C. Discharge teaching

  • Keep the wound clean and dry; protect the head from injury; wear a soft cap or scarf; continue AEDs and steroid taper exactly as prescribed; report fever, wound discharge, increasing headache, vomiting, drowsiness, seizures or new weakness; attend follow-up for radiotherapy, chemotherapy and MRI scans.

Nursing importance

  • Early detection of post-operative bleeding, oedema and sodium disturbances through careful neurological observation and fluid monitoring saves lives after craniotomy; correct positioning and prevention of rises in ICP are core nursing responsibilities.

Conclusion Brain tumours may be primary or metastatic, benign or malignant, and cause both raised ICP and focal deficits according to their location. MRI and biopsy guide treatment by surgery, radiotherapy and chemotherapy. Meticulous pre-operative preparation and post-craniotomy care – neurological monitoring, correct positioning, wound, fluid and seizure management, and rehabilitation – are essential for a good outcome.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurological Disorders
question: Explain the common diagnostic tests in neurological disorders and the nurse's responsibilities, including lumbar puncture.
answer_html:
Introduction Diagnostic tests help locate and identify neurological disease. The nurse explains each test, prepares the patient safely, assists during the procedure, handles specimens correctly and monitors for complications afterwards.

1. Imaging tests

  • CT scan – quick; shows haemorrhage, fractures, oedema and large lesions; the first test in stroke and head injury. If contrast is used, check allergy, renal function and metformin use; remove metal objects; sedate restless patients as ordered.
  • MRI – shows soft tissue in detail (tumours, MS plaques, early infarcts, spinal cord). Screen for metal – pacemakers, cochlear implants, aneurysm clips, metal fragments in the eye (welders), insulin pumps; remove jewellery, hairpins and medication patches; explain the loud noise (ear plugs) and the need to lie still for a long time; sedation for claustrophobia; check renal function before gadolinium contrast.
  • Cerebral angiography (DSA), CT angiography and MR angiography – show aneurysms, AVMs and blocked vessels. For catheter angiography through the femoral artery: consent, coagulation profile and allergy check; after the procedure, keep the leg straight with bed rest for 4–6 hours, check the puncture site for bleeding and distal pulses, colour and warmth of the leg, and encourage fluids to flush the contrast.

2. Electrophysiological tests

  • EEG (electroencephalography) – records the brain's electrical activity; used for epilepsy, encephalopathy and brain death. Wash hair the night before without oil, avoid caffeine, continue AEDs unless told otherwise, keep the patient awake the night before for a sleep-deprived EEG, and reassure that there is no electric shock.
  • EMG and nerve conduction studies – assess nerves and muscles in neuropathy, Guillain–Barré syndrome, myasthenia gravis and motor neuron disease; explain mild discomfort from needles and electric stimuli; no creams on the skin.
  • Evoked potentials (visual, auditory, somatosensory) – useful in multiple sclerosis.

3. Lumbar puncture (LP)

  • Definition – insertion of a needle into the subarachnoid space at the L3–L4 or L4–L5 level (below the end of the spinal cord) to obtain CSF or give drugs.
  • Indications – diagnosis of meningitis and encephalitis, subarachnoid haemorrhage (when CT is normal), Guillain–Barré syndrome (raised protein with normal cells), multiple sclerosis; measurement of CSF pressure; intrathecal drugs and spinal anaesthesia; removal of CSF in raised pressure states.
  • Contraindications – raised ICP due to a mass lesion (risk of brain herniation – a CT scan is done first when ICP is suspected), infection at the puncture site, bleeding disorders or anticoagulant therapy, and spinal deformity.
  • Before – explain, obtain consent, check coagulation and CT report, ask the patient to empty the bladder.
  • During – position on the side with knees drawn to the chest and chin flexed (fetal position) at the edge of the bed, or sitting and leaning forward over a table; strict asepsis; support and reassure the patient; help measure the opening pressure (normally about 60–180 mm H₂O in the lying position); collect CSF in labelled sterile tubes for cell count, protein, glucose (with a simultaneous blood glucose) and microbiology, and send immediately.
  • Normal CSF – clear and colourless; protein about 15–45 mg/dL; glucose about two-thirds of blood glucose; cells fewer than 5 lymphocytes/mm³.
  • After – apply a sterile dressing; position as per hospital policy; encourage fluids; monitor vital signs, neurological status, leg movement and sensation; observe the site for CSF leak or bleeding; watch for post-dural puncture headache (worse on sitting, relieved by lying), infection and signs of herniation.

4. General nursing responsibilities

  • Explain tests in simple language, ensure consent and preparation (fasting, medication adjustments), maintain safety during transport, monitor after invasive procedures, label and send specimens promptly and document findings.

Conclusion CT, MRI, angiography, EEG, EMG and lumbar puncture are the main diagnostic tests in neurology. Thorough preparation, safety screening (especially for MRI and contrast), aseptic assistance during LP and careful post-procedure monitoring are essential nursing responsibilities.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurological Disorders
question: Explain subarachnoid haemorrhage due to a ruptured cerebral aneurysm and its nursing management.
answer_html:
Definition Subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) is bleeding into the subarachnoid space between the arachnoid and pia mater. Apart from head injury, most spontaneous SAH (about 85%) is due to rupture of a saccular ("berry") aneurysm – a weak, balloon-like outpouching at a branching point of the arteries of the circle of Willis; other causes are AVMs and bleeding disorders.

Risk factors – hypertension, smoking, alcohol, family history of aneurysm, polycystic kidney disease, connective tissue disorders and cocaine use; slightly more common in women.

Clinical features

  • Sudden, severe "thunderclap" headache – often described as the worst headache of life, reaching peak intensity within a minute.
  • Vomiting, neck stiffness and photophobia (meningeal irritation), brief loss of consciousness, confusion or coma, seizures.
  • Focal signs – e.g. third nerve palsy (drooping eyelid, dilated pupil) with a posterior communicating artery aneurysm; weakness of limbs.
  • A smaller "sentinel" headache may precede major bleeding by days or weeks.
  • Severity is graded by the Hunt and Hess or WFNS scales, which predict outcome.

Diagnosis

  • Non-contrast CT brain – very sensitive in the first hours.
  • Lumbar puncture (after about 12 hours) if CT is normal but suspicion is high – blood-stained CSF that does not clear and xanthochromia (yellow CSF).
  • CT angiography or digital subtraction angiography to locate the aneurysm.

Complications

  • Rebleeding – highest risk in the first 24 hours; very high mortality.
  • Vasospasm and delayed cerebral ischaemia – narrowing of arteries, usually between days 3 and 14, causing new confusion or weakness.
  • Hydrocephalus, hyponatraemia (cerebral salt wasting or SIADH), seizures, cardiac arrhythmias and neurogenic pulmonary oedema.

Medical and surgical management

  • Secure the aneurysm early – endovascular coiling (platinum coils inserted through a catheter from the groin) or surgical clipping by craniotomy.
  • Nimodipine orally or by nasogastric tube (commonly 60 mg every 4 hours for 21 days) to reduce delayed ischaemia.
  • BP control before the aneurysm is secured; analgesia; antiemetics; laxatives; maintenance of normal blood volume (euvolaemia); external ventricular drain for hydrocephalus; antiepileptics when indicated.

Nursing management

  1. Aneurysm precautions – nurse in a quiet, dimly lit room; bed rest with the head of the bed at about 30°; limit visitors and stimulation; cluster nursing activities.
  2. Prevent rises in pressure – stool softeners; avoid straining, vigorous coughing, sneezing and the Valsalva manoeuvre; provide assistance with all activities.
  3. Pain relief – paracetamol and opioids as ordered; avoid aspirin and NSAIDs (bleeding risk).
  4. Neurological observation – GCS, pupils, limb power and speech hourly; vital signs; report new confusion, drowsiness or weakness (rebleeding, vasospasm or hydrocephalus) at once.
  5. Nimodipine administration – give on time; monitor BP, as it can cause hypotension.
  6. Fluid and electrolyte balance – strict intake–output, daily sodium; avoid dehydration, which worsens vasospasm; fluid restriction is not used for hyponatraemia in SAH unless ordered.
  7. Seizure precautions, EVD care if present, and DVT prevention with compression devices.
  8. Post-procedure care – after coiling, care of the groin puncture site, keeping the leg straight and checking distal pulses; after clipping, routine craniotomy care.
  9. Psychological support and education – explain the condition and plan to the family; after recovery, control BP, stop smoking and avoid excessive alcohol; first-degree relatives may need screening when two or more family members are affected; arrange rehabilitation for cognitive and physical deficits.

Conclusion Aneurysmal SAH presents with a sudden thunderclap headache and carries high risks of rebleeding and vasospasm. Early securing of the aneurysm, nimodipine, BP and fluid control, strict aneurysm precautions and close neurological observation by the nurse improve survival and recovery.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurological Disorders
question: Explain the surgical management of a herniated intervertebral disc and the nursing care of a patient after laminectomy.
answer_html:
Introduction A herniated (prolapsed) intervertebral disc is protrusion of the nucleus pulposus through a tear in the annulus fibrosus, compressing a nerve root or the spinal cord – most often at L4–L5 and L5–S1 in the lumbar region and C5–C6 and C6–C7 in the neck. Most patients recover with conservative treatment, but some need surgery.

1. Indications for surgery

  • Cauda equina syndrome – saddle anaesthesia, retention or incontinence of urine or stool and bilateral leg weakness – a surgical emergency.
  • Progressive motor weakness (e.g. foot drop) or cord compression in the neck.
  • Severe radicular pain not relieved by 6–12 weeks of conservative treatment, or frequent recurrences that affect work and life.

2. Surgical procedures

  • Laminectomy – removal of the lamina (posterior arch of a vertebra) to decompress the spinal cord or nerve roots; hemilaminectomy or laminotomy removes part of the lamina.
  • Discectomy / microdiscectomy – removal of the herniated disc fragment through a small incision using an operating microscope; the commonest operation for lumbar disc prolapse.
  • Endoscopic discectomy – minimally invasive removal through a tube, with quicker recovery.
  • Spinal fusion – joining two vertebrae with bone graft, screws and rods when the spine is unstable.
  • Anterior cervical discectomy and fusion (ACDF) – for cervical disc disease, done through the front of the neck.

3. Pre-operative nursing care

  • Record baseline power, sensation and reflexes of the limbs and bladder and bowel function.
  • Explain the operation, obtain consent, and teach log-rolling, deep breathing, leg exercises and use of a bedpan or urinal in bed; routine skin preparation and NPO.

4. Post-operative nursing care

  1. Neurological and neurovascular checks – movement, sensation, colour, warmth and pulses of the legs (arms after cervical surgery) every 1–2 hours initially; compare with the baseline; report new weakness, numbness or severe increasing pain immediately, as this may indicate an epidural haematoma needing urgent surgery.
  2. Positioning – keep the spine straight; log-roll the patient as one unit with a draw sheet; place a pillow between the knees when lying on the side; avoid twisting and flexion; after cervical surgery, maintain the collar and avoid neck movement.
  3. Wound care – observe the dressing and drain for bleeding and clear fluid (CSF leak from a dural tear); a CSF leak with headache on sitting needs flat positioning and reporting; watch for signs of infection.
  4. Pain relief – analgesics or patient-controlled analgesia and muscle relaxants for spasm, given on time before mobilisation.
  5. Bladder function – urinary retention is common; check that the patient voids within 6–8 hours; palpate for bladder distension; allow men to stand to void if permitted; catheterise if needed; new loss of bladder or bowel control must be reported (cauda equina compression).
  6. Bowel function – listen for bowel sounds (paralytic ileus may occur); start diet gradually; give stool softeners to avoid straining.
  7. Respiratory care and DVT prevention – deep breathing, leg exercises and stockings; after ACDF, watch for neck swelling, breathlessness, difficulty in swallowing and hoarseness (haematoma or recurrent laryngeal nerve injury).
  8. Early ambulation – usually the same or next day after microdiscectomy; teach the patient to roll to the side and push up with the arms while swinging the legs down to get out of bed; walking is encouraged, but prolonged sitting is limited in the first weeks; a brace may be advised after fusion.

5. Discharge teaching

  • Avoid bending, lifting heavy objects and twisting for about 6 weeks; no driving for 2–4 weeks as advised; sit for short periods in a chair with back support.
  • Increase walking gradually; start back- and core-strengthening exercises with the physiotherapist after about 4–6 weeks.
  • Use correct body mechanics, reduce weight and stop smoking (especially after fusion).
  • Report fever, wound discharge, new weakness or numbness, severe headache, or bladder and bowel problems.

Conclusion Surgery for a herniated disc – laminectomy, microdiscectomy or fusion – is reserved for emergencies, progressive weakness and intractable pain. Careful neurovascular monitoring, log-rolling, wound and bladder care, early ambulation and discharge teaching about spinal protection ensure a safe recovery and prevent recurrence.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurological Disorders
question: Explain the rehabilitation of a patient with hemiplegia following stroke.
answer_html:
Introduction Hemiplegia is paralysis of one side of the body (arm, leg and often face), and hemiparesis is weakness of one side, caused by a lesion of the opposite cerebral hemisphere – most commonly a stroke. Rehabilitation aims to prevent complications, restore maximum function and independence, and help the patient return to family and community life. It begins as soon as the patient is medically stable, usually within 24–48 hours.

1. Rehabilitation team – doctor, nurse, physiotherapist, occupational therapist, speech therapist, dietitian, psychologist, social worker, and above all the patient and family.

2. Positioning and prevention of deformities

  • Lying on the back – support the affected shoulder and arm on a pillow with the shoulder brought forward, elbow straight and hand open; place a trochanter roll at the hip to prevent external rotation; keep the foot at 90° with a splint to prevent foot drop.
  • Lying on the affected side is encouraged with the shoulder brought forward, as it increases sensory input; lying on the unaffected side with the weak arm supported in front on a pillow.
  • Never pull the patient by the affected arm – this causes shoulder subluxation and painful shoulder; support the arm on a table or trough when sitting.
  • Use a resting hand splint to prevent flexion contracture; positioning against the typical spastic pattern (flexed arm, extended leg).

3. Exercises and mobility

  • Passive range-of-motion exercises of the affected limbs 3–4 times a day and active exercises of the unaffected limbs.
  • Progress through rolling, bridging, sitting balance, standing and walking with the physiotherapist; parallel bars, walker or quadripod cane held in the unaffected hand.
  • Transfers from bed to chair towards the unaffected side; stairs – "up with the good leg, down with the affected leg".
  • Task-oriented training, constraint-induced movement therapy (restraining the good arm to encourage use of the weak arm) and mirror therapy.

4. Activities of daily living (occupational therapy)

  • Dressing – dress the affected limb first and undress it last; loose clothing, Velcro fasteners and elastic laces.
  • Feeding – adapted utensils with large handles, plate guards, non-slip mats.
  • Grooming, bathing (shower chair, grab bars) and toileting (raised seat, commode) with gradual independence.

5. Communication and swallowing

  • Speech therapy for aphasia and dysarthria – simple sentences, yes/no questions, picture boards and patience.
  • Swallowing therapy for dysphagia – upright posture, modified textures and swallowing exercises.

6. Bladder and bowel training – timed voiding every 2–3 hours, adequate fluids, high-fibre diet and a regular toilet routine.

7. Cognitive and perceptual problems

  • Unilateral neglect (common in right-hemisphere strokes) – teach the patient to turn the head and scan towards the neglected side, arrange the environment to encourage attention to that side, and ensure safety; memory aids, calendars and routines for cognitive deficits.

8. Psychological support

  • Post-stroke depression, anxiety and emotional lability are common; encourage expression of feelings, praise progress, counsel, involve the family and treat depression.

9. Home and community reintegration

  • Home modifications – ramps, grab bars, raised toilet seats, non-slip floors, good lighting and removal of loose rugs.
  • Caregiver training in transfers, exercises, positioning and feeding.
  • Vocational rehabilitation, sexual counselling, disability certificate under the RPwD Act, 2016, and community-based rehabilitation services.
  • Continue secondary prevention – BP and sugar control, drugs and lifestyle change.

Conclusion Rehabilitation of a hemiplegic patient is a long, team-based process that starts early with correct positioning and exercises and progresses to mobility, self-care, communication, cognitive retraining, emotional support and home reintegration. Consistent nursing care and family involvement help the patient regain maximum independence.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurological Disorders
question: Explain trigeminal neuralgia and its nursing management.
answer_html:
Definition Trigeminal neuralgia (tic douloureux) is a disorder of the fifth cranial (trigeminal) nerve characterised by sudden, severe, brief (seconds to 2 minutes), stabbing or electric-shock-like pain in the area supplied by one or more of its branches, usually the maxillary and mandibular divisions, on one side of the face. It is commoner in women and in people above 50 years.

Causes

  • Compression of the nerve root by a blood vessel (often the superior cerebellar artery) near the brainstem – the commonest cause.
  • Multiple sclerosis (suspect in young patients and when both sides are affected), tumours such as meningioma or acoustic neuroma, and idiopathic cases.

Clinical features

  • Paroxysms of excruciating pain over the cheek, lips, gums, jaw or forehead, often many times a day, with pain-free intervals.
  • Attacks are triggered by touching "trigger zones" around the nose, lips and cheek, or by chewing, talking, brushing teeth, shaving, washing the face, cold wind or hot and cold drinks.
  • Facial grimacing or wincing during attacks ("tic"); sensation between attacks is normal.
  • Patients avoid eating, washing and oral hygiene – leading to weight loss, poor oral hygiene, dehydration, depression and social withdrawal.

Diagnosis – mainly clinical; MRI brain to look for vascular compression, MS or tumour.

Medical management

  • Carbamazepine – the drug of choice; started at a low dose and increased gradually; monitor blood counts, liver function and sodium; screening for HLA-B*1502 is advised in people of Asian descent because of the risk of severe skin reactions.
  • Oxcarbazepine; others – baclofen, lamotrigine, gabapentin, pregabalin and phenytoin. Ordinary painkillers are usually ineffective.

Surgical management (when drugs fail or cause intolerable side effects)

  • Microvascular decompression – through a small craniotomy behind the ear, a Teflon pad is placed between the vessel and the nerve; gives long-lasting relief and preserves facial sensation.
  • Percutaneous procedures – radiofrequency thermal rhizotomy, glycerol injection or balloon compression of the Gasserian ganglion; quicker but may leave facial numbness.
  • Stereotactic radiosurgery (Gamma Knife); peripheral nerve blocks.

Nursing management

  1. Pain assessment – frequency, intensity, triggers and effect on eating and sleep; encourage a pain diary.
  2. Avoid triggers – maintain an even room temperature; avoid fans or cold draughts blowing on the face; do not touch the patient's face unnecessarily or startle the patient.
  3. Nutrition – soft, lukewarm, high-calorie, high-protein foods in small, frequent meals; chewing on the unaffected side; fluids through a straw; nutritional supplements; monitor weight and hydration.
  4. Oral and personal hygiene – plan care when the patient is pain-free or soon after medication; lukewarm mouthwash instead of brushing during severe phases, soft toothbrush; cotton pads and lukewarm water for washing the face; electric razor for men.
  5. Medication care – give carbamazepine regularly with food; watch for drowsiness, dizziness, unsteadiness, rash, sore throat (bone-marrow suppression) and low sodium; arrange regular blood tests; do not stop the drug suddenly.
  6. Care after rhizotomy or ganglion procedures – if the corneal reflex is lost, protect the eye: avoid rubbing, use artificial tears and protective glasses or a shield, inspect the eye daily for redness; chew on the unaffected side, avoid very hot food (to prevent burns of the numb mouth), and have regular dental check-ups because pain may not warn of dental problems.
  7. Care after microvascular decompression – routine craniotomy care; watch for CSF leak, facial weakness and hearing loss.
  8. Psychological support – fear of attacks causes anxiety and depression; reassure, teach relaxation, involve the family and refer to counselling or support groups.

Conclusion Trigeminal neuralgia produces brief, excruciating, triggered attacks of facial pain. Carbamazepine controls most cases, while microvascular decompression or percutaneous procedures help resistant cases. Nursing care focuses on avoiding triggers, maintaining nutrition and hygiene, protecting the eye after procedures and providing emotional support.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurological Disorders
question: Explain Bell's palsy and its nursing management.
answer_html:
Definition Bell's palsy is an acute, usually idiopathic, one-sided lower motor neuron paralysis of the facial (seventh cranial) nerve, caused by inflammation and swelling of the nerve within the narrow bony facial canal. Reactivation of herpes simplex virus is thought to be a common cause. It can occur at any age; risk is higher in pregnancy, diabetes and after viral infections.

Clinical features

  • Sudden onset over hours, reaching a peak within about 72 hours; often noticed on waking.
  • Weakness of the whole of one side of the face – inability to wrinkle the forehead, raise the eyebrow or close the eye (lagophthalmos); on attempting closure, the eyeball rolls upwards (Bell's phenomenon).
  • Drooping of the corner of the mouth, flattened nasolabial fold, drooling, difficulty whistling or puffing the cheeks, food collecting between the cheek and gums.
  • Loss of taste over the front two-thirds of the tongue, hyperacusis (sounds seem too loud), pain behind the ear, watering or dryness of the eye.
  • Difference from stroke – in a stroke (upper motor neuron lesion) the forehead is spared, whereas in Bell's palsy the forehead is also paralysed.

Diagnosis – mainly clinical; exclude stroke, Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster of the ear with vesicles and severe pain), ear infections, tumours, diabetes and Guillain–Barré syndrome; severity graded by the House–Brackmann scale; nerve conduction studies for prognosis in severe cases.

Medical management

  • Oral prednisolone started within 72 hours for about 10 days improves recovery; antivirals (acyclovir or valacyclovir) may be added in severe cases.
  • Eye protection, physiotherapy and, rarely, surgery (eyelid gold weight implant, facial reanimation) for persistent paralysis.
  • Prognosis – most patients recover fully within 3–6 months.

Nursing management

  1. Eye care – the most important nursing measure to prevent exposure keratitis and corneal ulcer:
    • Artificial tears every 1–2 hours by day and lubricating ointment at night.
    • Tape the eyelid closed or use an eye shield at night (make sure the lid is closed under any pad).
    • Wear wraparound glasses or goggles outdoors to protect from dust and wind; avoid rubbing the eye.
    • Report eye pain, redness, discharge or blurred vision.
  2. Nutrition and oral care – soft diet; chew on the unaffected side; check and clear food from the cheek; mouth care after every meal to prevent dental caries; fluids through a straw if needed.
  3. Facial exercises – once recovery begins: wrinkling the forehead, closing the eyes, smiling, whistling, puffing the cheeks, in front of a mirror several times a day; gentle upward massage of the face with warm, moist heat to improve circulation and comfort.
  4. Pain relief – analgesics and warm compresses behind the ear.
  5. Medication care – give steroids with food; monitor blood sugar (especially in diabetics) and BP; complete the course and taper as advised.
  6. Psychological support – facial disfigurement causes embarrassment and anxiety; reassure that most patients recover completely; encourage social interaction.
  7. Education and follow-up – continue eye protection until the eye closes fully; report incomplete recovery; explain possible late effects such as synkinesis (involuntary movement of one part of the face with another) and "crocodile tears" (tearing while eating).

Conclusion Bell's palsy is a sudden, one-sided facial nerve paralysis that usually recovers within months. Early steroids, meticulous eye care to protect the cornea, nutritional and oral care, facial exercises and reassurance are the key elements of nursing management.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurological Disorders
question: Explain the clinical features, management and nursing care of a patient with Parkinson's disease.
answer_html:
Definition Parkinson's disease (PD) is a chronic, progressive neurodegenerative disorder caused by loss of dopamine-producing neurons in the substantia nigra of the basal ganglia, leading to an imbalance between dopamine and acetylcholine and disturbed control of movement. Abnormal protein deposits called Lewy bodies are found in the affected neurons. It usually begins after 60 years and is slightly commoner in men.

Causes and risk factors

  • Idiopathic in most cases; genetic forms in some young patients.
  • Secondary parkinsonism – drugs (haloperidol and other antipsychotics, metoclopramide), toxins (pesticides, manganese), repeated head injuries, encephalitis and multiple small strokes.

Clinical features 1. Cardinal motor features ("TRAP")

  • Tremor – resting "pill-rolling" tremor of the hand, which reduces on movement and disappears in sleep; often begins on one side.
  • Rigidity – stiffness of muscles; lead-pipe or cogwheel rigidity on passive movement.
  • Akinesia/bradykinesia – slowness and poverty of movement, difficulty in starting movements, mask-like face with reduced blinking, small handwriting (micrographia), soft monotonous speech and freezing.
  • Postural instability – stooped posture, shuffling, festinant gait with short quick steps, reduced arm swing, difficulty turning and frequent falls.

2. Non-motor features

  • Depression, anxiety, apathy, sleep disturbances, loss of smell (early), constipation, urinary urgency, orthostatic hypotension, drooling, dysphagia, oily skin and sweating, pain, and dementia and hallucinations in late stages.

Diagnosis – clinical, supported by a good response to levodopa; MRI to exclude other causes.

Management

  • Levodopa with carbidopa – the most effective drug; long-term use leads to "wearing-off", "on–off" fluctuations and dyskinesias (involuntary writhing movements).
  • Dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole), MAO-B inhibitors (selegiline, rasagiline), COMT inhibitors (entacapone), amantadine and anticholinergics (trihexyphenidyl – mainly for tremor in younger patients; avoided in the elderly).
  • Deep brain stimulation (electrodes in the subthalamic nucleus) for selected patients with motor fluctuations.
  • Physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy.

Nursing care

  1. Mobility and fall prevention
    • Daily exercises – walking, stretching, range-of-motion and posture exercises ("stand tall, look ahead").
    • Gait training – take big steps, lift the feet, heel-to-toe walking, walk to a rhythm, music or counting; to overcome freezing, rock gently from side to side or step over a line on the floor; turn in a wide arc.
    • Home safety – remove loose rugs and clutter, provide grab bars, night lights, raised toilet seats and firm chairs with arms; teach to rise slowly to prevent postural hypotension.
  2. Medication management
    • Give antiparkinsonian drugs exactly on time – delays cause "off" periods with severe stiffness and falls; do not omit doses when the patient is NPO for procedures – consult the doctor about giving them through a nasogastric tube.
    • Give levodopa about 30 minutes before meals if advised; spread protein-rich foods through the day, since a heavy protein meal reduces levodopa absorption.
    • Avoid drugs that block dopamine (metoclopramide, haloperidol, prochlorperazine).
    • Watch for dyskinesias, nausea, postural hypotension, hallucinations and compulsive behaviour (dopamine agonists); never stop the drugs suddenly.
  3. Nutrition and swallowing – swallowing assessment; upright posture, small mouthfuls, soft or thickened foods; allow extra time for meals; monitor weight; high-fibre diet and fluids to prevent constipation; remind the patient to swallow saliva frequently to reduce drooling.
  4. Self-care – adaptive devices (Velcro fastenings, elastic laces, large-handled spoons, plate guards, electric razor); allow enough time; encourage independence.
  5. Communication – speech therapy (voice exercises to speak loudly); encourage deep breaths before speaking and short sentences; use writing aids or boards if needed.
  6. Elimination – fibre, fluids and laxatives for constipation; timed voiding for urgency.
  7. Psychosocial support – screen for depression and anxiety; involve the family; support groups; caregiver education and support; advance care planning in advanced disease.

Conclusion Parkinson's disease is a progressive disorder due to dopamine deficiency, presenting with tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia and postural instability, along with many non-motor problems. Timely medication, exercise, gait training, fall prevention, nutritional and swallowing care, communication support and caregiver education help patients maintain function and quality of life.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurological Disorders
question: Explain Alzheimer's disease and the nursing management of a patient with dementia.
answer_html:
Definition Dementia is an acquired, progressive decline in memory and other mental functions (thinking, language, judgement, orientation) severe enough to interfere with daily life. Alzheimer's disease (AD) is the commonest cause of dementia (about 60–70%). It is a neurodegenerative disease in which beta-amyloid plaques and neurofibrillary (tau) tangles accumulate in the brain, causing loss of neurons, brain atrophy and deficiency of acetylcholine.

Risk factors – increasing age (mainly above 65 years), family history, the APOE ε4 gene, Down syndrome, and modifiable factors such as hypertension, diabetes, obesity, smoking, physical and mental inactivity, hearing loss, depression, head injury and low education.

Clinical features (stages)

  • Early (mild) stage – loss of recent memory (forgetting recent events, repeating questions, misplacing things), difficulty managing money and household tasks, word-finding difficulty, disorientation to time, mood changes and poor judgement.
  • Middle (moderate) stage – worsening memory and disorientation to place (getting lost), difficulty with dressing and bathing, aphasia (language disturbance), apraxia (inability to carry out purposeful movements), agnosia (failure to recognise objects or people), behavioural and psychological symptoms – agitation, wandering, aggression, suspicion (e.g. accusing others of theft), hallucinations, sleep disturbance, sundowning (worsening in the evening) and incontinence.
  • Late (severe) stage – loss of speech, failure to recognise family members, total dependence, immobility, dysphagia, incontinence, weight loss, aspiration pneumonia and pressure sores.

Diagnosis

  • History from family members; cognitive screening tests – MMSE, MoCA and Indian adaptations such as the Hindi Mental State Examination.
  • Exclude reversible causes – hypothyroidism, vitamin B12 deficiency, depression (pseudodementia), normal-pressure hydrocephalus, drug side effects, infections (syphilis, HIV) and subdural haematoma.
  • CT or MRI (brain atrophy), PET scans and CSF biomarkers in specialised centres.

Medical management

  • There is no cure; cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) for mild to moderate disease and memantine for moderate to severe disease may slow symptom progression.
  • Treatment of depression, insomnia and behavioural symptoms – non-drug methods first; antipsychotics only with caution (risk of stroke and death in the elderly).
  • Control of vascular risk factors; newer anti-amyloid antibody drugs are available in some countries for early disease.

Nursing management

  1. Safety
    • Supervise the patient; prevent wandering with an identity bracelet (name, address, phone), door alarms and secure locks; inform neighbours.
    • Remove hazards (gas-stove knobs, knives, medicines, chemicals); good lighting and night lights; grab bars; fall prevention; avoid physical restraints.
  2. Communication
    • Approach calmly from the front, maintain eye contact and call the person by name; use short, simple sentences and one instruction at a time; use gestures and pictures; do not argue or correct harshly; use reminiscence (talking about old memories).
  3. Orientation and routine
    • Maintain a consistent daily routine and familiar caregivers; use calendars, clocks, labelled doors and family photographs; avoid noise, crowds and overstimulation; reality orientation in early stages.
  4. Activities of daily living
    • Encourage independence with step-by-step prompting; lay out clothes in order of dressing; offer finger foods and supervise meals; regular toileting every 2–3 hours; ensure adequate fluids and nutrition; monitor weight; dysphagia care in late stages.
  5. Managing behavioural problems
    • Look for triggers – pain, hunger, need to use the toilet, constipation, noise or infection; use distraction, music, light exercise and meaningful activities; daytime activity and limited naps improve night sleep; bright light in the evening for sundowning.
  6. Medication care – supervise intake using pill organisers; watch for side effects of cholinesterase inhibitors (nausea, diarrhoea, slow pulse, vivid dreams).
  7. Caregiver support
    • Educate the family about the disease; recognise caregiver stress and burnout; arrange respite care, counselling and support groups such as the Alzheimer's and Related Disorders Society of India (ARDSI).
    • Encourage legal and financial planning (will, nominee, advance directives) while the patient can still take decisions.
  8. Palliative and end-of-life care in the late stage, with attention to comfort, nutrition, skin care and dignity.
  9. Risk reduction in the community – regular physical exercise, mental and social activity, control of BP and diabetes, correction of hearing loss, and avoidance of smoking and excess alcohol.

Conclusion Alzheimer's disease is the commonest cause of dementia, progressing from memory loss to total dependence. Although there is no cure, cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine may help symptoms. Safe surroundings, patient-centred communication, a structured routine, support with daily activities, management of behavioural symptoms and strong support for caregivers are the cornerstones of nursing care.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurological Disorders
question: Explain myasthenia gravis, its management and the nursing care of a patient in myasthenic crisis.
answer_html:
Definition Myasthenia gravis (MG) is a chronic autoimmune disorder of the neuromuscular junction in which antibodies against acetylcholine receptors (or related proteins such as MuSK) reduce the number of functioning receptors. The result is fluctuating weakness of voluntary muscles that increases with activity and improves with rest. It commonly affects women aged 20–40 years and men aged 60–80 years, and is associated with thymic hyperplasia or thymoma.

Clinical features

  • Ocular – ptosis (drooping eyelids) and diplopia – often the first symptoms.
  • Bulbar – difficulty chewing and swallowing, nasal voice, slurred speech, weak facial expression ("snarling" smile), choking.
  • Limb and neck weakness – mainly proximal muscles; difficulty climbing stairs, combing hair or holding up the head.
  • Respiratory muscle weakness – breathlessness and weak cough.
  • Symptoms are worse in the evening and with heat, infection, stress, menstruation, pregnancy, surgery and certain drugs (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, magnesium, beta blockers, muscle relaxants).

Diagnosis – ice-pack test (ptosis improves after cooling the eyelid), acetylcholine receptor and MuSK antibodies, repetitive nerve stimulation (decreasing muscle response) and single-fibre EMG, CT chest for thymoma, and lung function tests.

Management

  • Anticholinesterase drugs – pyridostigmine, which increases acetylcholine at the junction.
  • Immunosuppression – corticosteroids, azathioprine, mycophenolate, rituximab and newer biological drugs.
  • Thymectomy – improves the disease in many patients and is essential when a thymoma is present.
  • Rapid short-term therapies – plasmapheresis (plasma exchange) and IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) for crisis and before surgery.

Crises

  • Myasthenic crisis – severe worsening with respiratory and bulbar failure, usually triggered by infection, under-treatment or drugs; needs ventilation, plasma exchange or IVIG.
  • Cholinergic crisis – due to overdose of anticholinesterase drugs; weakness with excess secretions, sweating, small pupils, abdominal cramps, diarrhoea, slow pulse and muscle twitching; treated by stopping the drug and giving atropine.

Nursing care in crisis and during treatment

  1. Respiratory monitoring – respiratory rate, depth, cough strength, ability to count to 20 in one breath, and serial vital capacity; a vital capacity below about 20 mL/kg or rapidly falling values indicate the need for intubation – SpO₂ falls late, so do not rely on it alone; keep suction and ventilator ready; chest physiotherapy.
  2. Swallowing and nutrition – assess swallowing before every meal; schedule meals 45–60 minutes after pyridostigmine, when strength is best; soft food, small mouthfuls, upright posture and rest between bites; nasogastric feeding if swallowing is unsafe; suction at the bedside.
  3. Medication care – give pyridostigmine exactly on time; observe for cholinergic side effects; avoid drugs that worsen MG; monitor blood sugar and BP with steroids.
  4. Energy conservation – plan activities when strength is at its peak, allow rest periods, and avoid heat, fatigue and stress.
  5. Eye care – artificial tears, eyelid support for ptosis, and alternate eye patching for diplopia.
  6. Communication – provide alternative methods (writing, boards) for patients with weak speech or on a ventilator; reassure, as the patient is fully conscious and anxious.
  7. Care during plasma exchange or IVIG – watch for hypotension, tingling from low calcium, bleeding, allergic reactions, headache and fluid overload.
  8. Post-thymectomy care – chest drain, respiratory care and pain relief after sternotomy or thoracoscopy.
  9. Education – regular medicines, recognising signs of crisis, carrying a medical alert card with the list of drugs to avoid, early treatment of infections, vaccinations, and planning pregnancy (the newborn may have temporary weakness).

Conclusion Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disease causing fatigable weakness of eye, bulbar, limb and respiratory muscles. Anticholinesterases, immunosuppressants, thymectomy and rescue therapies control it, while close respiratory monitoring, safe feeding, punctual medication and education help prevent and manage life-threatening crises.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurological Disorders
question: Explain Guillain–Barré syndrome and its nursing management.
answer_html:
Definition Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) is an acute, immune-mediated inflammation of the peripheral nerves and nerve roots (polyradiculoneuropathy). After an infection, antibodies formed against the organism mistakenly attack the myelin sheath or axons of peripheral nerves. Types include acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (AIDP) and axonal forms (AMAN), which are relatively common in India; the Miller Fisher variant causes eye-muscle paralysis, ataxia and loss of reflexes.

Causes and triggers – often follows, by 1–4 weeks, an infection such as diarrhoea due to Campylobacter jejuni, respiratory infections, cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, Zika and other viral infections; rarely after surgery or vaccination.

Clinical features

  • Ascending, symmetrical, flaccid weakness, starting in the legs and spreading to the arms, trunk and face over days to 4 weeks.
  • Loss of tendon reflexes (areflexia), tingling and numbness of hands and feet, and back or limb pain.
  • Cranial nerve involvement – bilateral facial weakness, difficulty in swallowing and speaking.
  • Respiratory muscle weakness – about a quarter of patients need ventilation.
  • Autonomic dysfunction – fluctuating BP, arrhythmias, urinary retention, paralytic ileus and abnormal sweating.
  • Consciousness remains normal.

Diagnosis

  • CSF – raised protein with normal cell count (albuminocytologic dissociation), usually after the first week.
  • Nerve conduction studies – slowed conduction or reduced responses.
  • In children below 15 years, any acute flaccid paralysis must be reported under AFP surveillance for polio eradication.

Management

  • IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days or plasma exchange, preferably within the first two weeks; steroids are not effective.
  • Supportive care, often in ICU – ventilation, cardiac monitoring, DVT prophylaxis, pain relief (gabapentin, pregabalin) and early rehabilitation.
  • Most patients recover over weeks to months, though some have residual weakness.

Nursing management

  1. Respiratory care – monitor vital capacity every 4–6 hours, respiratory rate, cough, swallowing and SpO₂; a vital capacity below about 20 mL/kg or a weak cough calls for elective intubation; chest physiotherapy, suction and ventilator care.
  2. Cardiovascular monitoring – continuous ECG and frequent BP checks for autonomic instability; suction can trigger bradycardia; treat hypotension and hypertension as ordered.
  3. Neurological assessment – daily muscle power charting to detect progression or recovery.
  4. Care of the immobile patient – 2-hourly turning, pressure-relieving mattress, passive range-of-motion exercises, splints to prevent foot drop and wrist drop, and DVT prophylaxis with heparin and stockings.
  5. Nutrition – swallowing assessment; nasogastric feeding if needed; adequate calories, protein and fluids.
  6. Elimination – catheterise for retention; monitor bowel sounds and prevent constipation.
  7. Pain relief – neuropathic pain drugs, positioning and gentle handling.
  8. Communication and psychological support – the patient is conscious but may be unable to move or speak; use eye blinks, letter boards and simple yes/no systems; explain every procedure; reassure that recovery is expected; involve the family.
  9. Care during IVIG – correct infusion rate, watch for headache, allergic reactions, fluid overload and renal impairment; during plasma exchange – watch for hypotension, tingling (low calcium), bleeding and central line infection.
  10. Rehabilitation – intensive physiotherapy and occupational therapy, graded activities and management of fatigue; support for return to work.

Conclusion GBS is an acute post-infectious immune attack on peripheral nerves, causing ascending flaccid paralysis that may involve breathing and autonomic functions. IVIG or plasma exchange, close respiratory and cardiac monitoring, prevention of immobility complications and compassionate communication enable most patients to recover.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurological Disorders
question: Explain multiple sclerosis and its nursing management.
answer_html:
Definition Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic, immune-mediated, demyelinating disease of the central nervous system in which patches of inflammation and loss of myelin (plaques) occur in the brain, spinal cord and optic nerves, followed by scarring. It usually begins between 20 and 40 years and is commoner in women. Risk factors include genetic tendency, vitamin D deficiency, Epstein–Barr virus infection and smoking. In India, neuromyelitis optica (NMO), a related condition, must be distinguished from MS because treatment differs.

Types

  • Relapsing–remitting MS (about 85% at onset) – attacks followed by partial or complete recovery.
  • Secondary progressive MS – later steady worsening after a relapsing course.
  • Primary progressive MS – gradual worsening from the start.
  • Clinically isolated syndrome – a first attack suggestive of MS.

Clinical features

  • Visual – optic neuritis (painful blurring or loss of vision in one eye, poor colour vision), double vision and nystagmus.
  • Sensory – numbness, tingling, a band-like feeling, and Lhermitte's sign (electric-shock sensation down the spine on bending the neck).
  • Motor – weakness, spasticity, stiffness and gait difficulty.
  • Cerebellar – ataxia, intention tremor, nystagmus and scanning speech (Charcot's triad).
  • Fatigue – the commonest and most disabling symptom.
  • Bladder, bowel and sexual dysfunction; depression, emotional lability and memory problems; pain and trigeminal neuralgia.
  • Uhthoff's phenomenon – temporary worsening of symptoms with heat (hot weather, fever, hot baths, exercise).

Diagnosis – MRI brain and spinal cord showing lesions spread in time and space (McDonald criteria), CSF oligoclonal bands, visual evoked potentials and blood tests to exclude NMO (anti-aquaporin-4 antibodies) and other diseases.

Management

  • Acute relapse – IV methylprednisolone (about 1 g daily for 3–5 days); plasma exchange for severe relapses.
  • Disease-modifying therapies – interferon-beta, glatiramer acetate, teriflunomide, dimethyl fumarate, fingolimod, natalizumab, ocrelizumab and rituximab – reduce relapses and slow disability.
  • Symptomatic treatment – baclofen or tizanidine for spasticity, oxybutynin for urgency, amantadine for fatigue, gabapentin for pain, antidepressants, physiotherapy and occupational therapy.

Nursing management

  1. Fatigue and energy conservation – plan important activities for the morning, schedule rest periods, use aids; avoid heat – cool showers, fans or air-conditioning, avoid hot baths and midday sun; treat fever promptly.
  2. Mobility and spasticity – daily stretching, range-of-motion and strengthening exercises, physiotherapy, walking aids and fall prevention.
  3. Vision – eye patching for double vision, good lighting, a clutter-free environment.
  4. Bladder and bowel care – timed voiding, clean intermittent catheterisation for retention, adequate fluids (do not restrict fluids to control urgency), prevention of UTI; high-fibre diet and bowel routine.
  5. Skin care and safety – check for injuries in numb areas; avoid hot-water bottles.
  6. Medication care – teach correct self-injection technique and site rotation for injectable drugs; flu-like symptoms after interferon are reduced by taking it at bedtime with paracetamol; watch for infections and liver problems; steroid care during relapses.
  7. Cognitive and psychological support – memory aids, lists and routines; screen for depression; counselling; support groups and family education.
  8. Education – recognise relapses (new symptoms lasting more than 24 hours) and report them; avoid triggers such as infection, stress and overheating; stop smoking; adequate vitamin D; plan pregnancy (relapses are fewer during pregnancy and more common after delivery).

Conclusion Multiple sclerosis is a chronic demyelinating disease with varied neurological symptoms and a relapsing or progressive course. Steroids for relapses, disease-modifying drugs, symptom management and nursing care focused on fatigue, mobility, bladder function, safety and emotional support help patients live as independently as possible.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurological Disorders
question: Explain neurocysticercosis and its nursing management.
tags: commonest cause of acquired epilepsy in India
answer_html:
Definition Neurocysticercosis (NCC) is infection of the central nervous system by the larval stage (cysticercus) of the pork tapeworm Taenia solium. It is the commonest parasitic infection of the CNS and the commonest cause of acquired epilepsy in India.

Mode of transmission

  • A person develops cysticercosis by swallowing Taenia solium eggs through the faeco-oral route – contaminated food or water, unwashed raw vegetables and salads, unwashed hands, or eggs from a household member who carries the adult tapeworm.
  • Eating undercooked pork with cysts causes intestinal tapeworm (taeniasis); the carrier then passes eggs that infect others – so even vegetarians can develop NCC.
  • The eggs hatch in the intestine, larvae enter the bloodstream and form cysts in the brain, muscles, eyes and skin.
  • Cysts pass through stages – viable (vesicular), degenerating (colloidal, when inflammation and symptoms are maximum), nodular and finally calcified.

Clinical features

  • Seizures – the commonest presentation (focal or generalised).
  • Headache, vomiting and signs of raised intracranial pressure, especially with hydrocephalus from cysts in the ventricles or subarachnoid space.
  • Focal neurological deficits, confusion, behavioural changes and cognitive decline.
  • Cysticercal encephalitis (many cysts with severe brain swelling) in children and young women.
  • Cysts in the eye (visual loss), spinal cord and under the skin (nodules).

Diagnosis

  • CT scan – calcifications and ring-enhancing lesions, sometimes with a visible scolex (a "hole with a dot" appearance).
  • MRI – better for viable cysts and scolex.
  • Serology (enzyme-linked immunoelectrotransfer blot).
  • Fundoscopy before treatment – to exclude eye cysts and papilloedema.
  • Stool examination of household members for tapeworm eggs.

Medical and surgical management

  • Antiepileptic drugs – control seizures; continued until imaging improves and the patient is seizure-free for an adequate period.
  • Cysticidal drugs – albendazole (commonly 15 mg/kg/day for 8–14 days), with praziquantel added for multiple cysts; given with corticosteroids (dexamethasone or prednisolone), started before the cysticidal drug, to reduce inflammation caused by dying cysts; not used for calcified lesions alone or in cysticercal encephalitis.
  • Raised ICP – steroids and mannitol; ventriculoperitoneal shunt or endoscopic removal for hydrocephalus and intraventricular cysts.

Nursing management

  1. Seizure care and precautions – as for epilepsy; padded side rails, suction and oxygen ready; observe and record seizures.
  2. Monitoring during cysticidal therapy – headache, vomiting and seizures may increase for a few days because of inflammation around dying cysts; monitor GCS, pupils and vital signs and report signs of raised ICP.
  3. Medication care – give steroids before and during albendazole; give albendazole with a fatty meal to improve absorption; monitor blood counts and liver function; ensure regular AED intake and explain the expected duration.
  4. Comfort and safety – analgesics for headache, quiet environment, fall prevention.
  5. Patient and family education – drug adherence, seizure first aid, follow-up imaging, and screening and treatment of household members for tapeworm.
  6. Prevention in the community
    • Wash hands with soap after using the toilet and before eating or cooking.
    • Drink safe water; wash raw vegetables and fruits thoroughly (salads, coriander, radish, cabbage).
    • Stop open defecation and use sanitary toilets (Swachh Bharat Mission).
    • Cook pork thoroughly; meat inspection; rear pigs in enclosures away from human faeces.
    • Treat tapeworm carriers (praziquantel or niclosamide) and educate food handlers.

Conclusion Neurocysticercosis, caused by larvae of Taenia solium, is a leading cause of seizures in India. Antiepileptic drugs, cysticidal therapy with steroids, management of raised ICP and careful neurological monitoring treat the disease, while hand hygiene, safe food and water and sanitation prevent it.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurological Disorders
question: Explain encephalitis and brain abscess with their nursing management.
answer_html:
1. Encephalitis Definition – inflammation of the brain tissue, usually caused by viruses. In India, the term acute encephalitis syndrome (AES) is used for acute onset of fever with change in mental status (confusion, disorientation, coma) and/or new-onset seizures in a person of any age.

Causes

  • Japanese encephalitis (JE) – spread by Culex mosquitoes breeding in paddy fields; pigs and water birds act as reservoirs; affects mainly children in endemic districts.
  • Herpes simplex virus – the commonest cause of sporadic viral encephalitis; treatable.
  • Dengue, measles, mumps, rabies, enteroviruses, Chandipura virus (spread by sandflies; first identified in Chandipura village near Nagpur), Nipah virus (Kerala outbreaks) and scrub typhus (a bacterial cause of AES).
  • Autoimmune encephalitis (e.g. anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis).

Clinical features – fever, headache, vomiting, altered sensorium, seizures, behavioural changes, focal weakness, speech problems, coma and signs of raised ICP; herpes encephalitis often causes personality change, aphasia and temporal-lobe seizures.

Diagnosis – CSF (raised lymphocytes and protein with normal glucose), CSF PCR for herpes simplex virus, JE IgM antibodies in CSF or serum, MRI (temporal lobe changes in herpes, thalamic changes in JE), EEG, and tests for dengue, malaria and scrub typhus.

Management – IV acyclovir (10 mg/kg every 8 hours) started early until herpes is excluded and continued for 14–21 days if confirmed; doxycycline or azithromycin for scrub typhus; steroids or IVIG for autoimmune encephalitis; supportive care for airway, seizures, raised ICP, fever, fluids and nutrition.

Prevention – JE vaccination under the Universal Immunization Programme in endemic districts (at 9–12 months and 16–24 months) and adult campaigns where indicated; mosquito control (nets, repellents, fogging, larval control), keeping pigs away from homes; sandfly control for Chandipura; isolation and infection control for Nipah.

2. Brain abscess Definition – a localised collection of pus within the brain tissue.

Causes and sources

  • Spread from nearby infection – chronic suppurative otitis media and mastoiditis (temporal lobe and cerebellar abscess), sinusitis (frontal lobe) and dental infections.
  • Blood-borne spread – lung abscess, bronchiectasis, infective endocarditis and cyanotic congenital heart disease in children.
  • Penetrating head injury and neurosurgery; in immunocompromised patients – toxoplasma, tuberculosis and fungi.

Clinical features – headache (the commonest symptom), fever (not always present), focal neurological deficits, seizures, vomiting, drowsiness and signs of raised ICP.

Diagnosis – contrast CT or MRI showing a ring-enhancing lesion with surrounding oedema; blood cultures and culture of aspirated pus; lumbar puncture is avoided because of the risk of brain herniation.

Management – IV antibiotics for 6–8 weeks (e.g. ceftriaxone with metronidazole, adding vancomycin when needed); burr-hole or stereotactic aspiration or excision of the abscess; treatment of the source (e.g. mastoidectomy); steroids for severe oedema and antiepileptics.

3. Nursing management (both conditions)

  1. Neurological observation – GCS, pupils, limb power and vital signs; report deterioration.
  2. Reduce ICP – head of bed at 30°, head in the midline, prevent straining and coughing, give mannitol as ordered.
  3. Seizure precautions and timely antiepileptic drugs.
  4. Control fever with antipyretics and tepid sponging.
  5. Fluid balance – strict intake–output; avoid over-hydration; watch for SIADH.
  6. Medication care – give acyclovir by slow infusion with good hydration and monitor kidney function; complete the long antibiotic course for abscess; watch for phlebitis.
  7. Care of the unconscious patient – airway, eye and mouth care, positioning, pressure-area care, nasogastric feeding, bladder and bowel care.
  8. Infection control – standard precautions; strict isolation for Nipah; notify cases of AES and JE to health authorities.
  9. Post-operative care after abscess aspiration or craniotomy.
  10. Family support and rehabilitation – many survivors of encephalitis have seizures, memory and behaviour problems or weakness; arrange physiotherapy, speech therapy and follow-up.

Conclusion Encephalitis, commonly viral (JE, herpes simplex and others), and brain abscess, usually spreading from ear, sinus or heart infections, both present with fever, altered sensorium, seizures and raised ICP. Early specific treatment, surgical drainage when needed, intensive neurological nursing and prevention through vaccination, vector control and treatment of ear infections improve outcomes.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurological Disorders
question: Explain the types of headache, with special reference to migraine, and its nursing management.
answer_html:
Introduction Headache is one of the commonest complaints in clinical practice. Most headaches are harmless primary headaches, but some are warning signs of serious disease, so careful assessment is essential.

1. Classification

  • Primary headaches – tension-type headache (the commonest), migraine and cluster headache.
  • Secondary headaches – due to another condition: raised ICP (tumour), meningitis, subarachnoid haemorrhage, sinusitis, refractive errors, glaucoma, severe hypertension, temporal arteritis in the elderly and medication-overuse headache.

2. Red flags (need urgent evaluation)

  • Sudden "thunderclap" headache, headache with fever and neck stiffness, neurological deficits, new headache after 50 years, progressively worsening headache, headache worse on lying down or straining, papilloedema, headache in pregnancy or in immunocompromised patients.

3. Tension-type and cluster headache

  • Tension-type – bilateral, band-like pressing pain, mild to moderate, without vomiting; associated with stress, poor posture, eye strain and lack of sleep; relieved by simple analgesics, relaxation and posture correction.
  • Cluster headache – very severe, one-sided pain around the eye lasting 15–180 minutes, with watering of the eye, nasal blockage and drooping eyelid on the same side, occurring in clusters for weeks; commoner in men; treated with 100% oxygen and sumatriptan injection.

4. Migraine

  • Definition – a recurrent primary headache disorder with attacks of moderate to severe, usually one-sided, throbbing headache lasting 4–72 hours, accompanied by nausea, vomiting, sensitivity to light (photophobia) and sound (phonophobia), and worsened by routine activity. It is about three times commoner in women and often runs in families.
  • Types – migraine without aura (most common) and migraine with aura – visual disturbances (zig-zag lines, flashing lights, blind spots), tingling or speech difficulty for 5–60 minutes before the headache.
  • Phases – prodrome (yawning, food cravings, mood change, neck stiffness), aura, headache and postdrome (tiredness, poor concentration).
  • Mechanism – activation of the trigeminovascular system with release of inflammatory peptides (CGRP) and dilation of meningeal vessels.
  • Common triggers – stress, lack of sleep or oversleeping, skipping meals or fasting, menstruation and oral contraceptives, bright or flickering light, loud noise, strong smells, travel, hot weather, dehydration, and certain foods (aged cheese, chocolate, processed foods with MSG, alcohol, excess caffeine or caffeine withdrawal).

5. Management of migraine

  • Acute attack – rest in a dark, quiet room; paracetamol or NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) with an antiemetic (domperidone), taken early; triptans (sumatriptan) for moderate to severe attacks (avoided in heart disease, uncontrolled hypertension, stroke and pregnancy); avoid opioids.
  • Limit acute medicines to fewer than about 10–15 days a month to prevent medication-overuse headache.
  • Preventive treatment (frequent or disabling attacks) – propranolol, flunarizine, amitriptyline, topiramate, candesartan; newer CGRP-blocking drugs and botulinum toxin for chronic migraine.

6. Nursing management

  1. Assessment – teach the patient to keep a headache diary (date, time, duration, severity, triggers, food, sleep, menstrual cycle, medicines taken); check BP and vision; look for red flags.
  2. During an attack – provide a dark, quiet, cool room; rest; cold compress on the forehead or neck; give medicines early; antiemetics and fluids; relaxation and deep breathing.
  3. Lifestyle education – regular sleep, regular meals and adequate water, regular aerobic exercise, stress management (yoga, meditation, pranayama), limiting screen time, correct posture and regular eye check-ups.
  4. Trigger avoidance – identify personal triggers from the diary and avoid them.
  5. Medication education – correct timing and dose, avoid overuse of painkillers, adherence to preventive drugs, side effects (drowsiness and weight gain with flunarizine, fatigue with propranolol).
  6. Women – combined oestrogen pills are avoided in migraine with aura (stroke risk); plan treatment for menstrual migraine; paracetamol is preferred in pregnancy.
  7. Psychological support – frequent headaches affect work and mood; screen for depression and anxiety and provide counselling.

Conclusion Headaches may be primary (tension-type, migraine, cluster) or secondary to serious disease, and red flags must never be missed. Migraine is a recurrent, disabling throbbing headache with nausea and sensory sensitivity. Early acute treatment, preventive drugs when needed, trigger avoidance, a headache diary and healthy lifestyle teaching by the nurse greatly reduce its burden.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurological Disorders
question: Explain peripheral neuropathy with special reference to diabetic neuropathy, and its nursing management.
answer_html:
Definition Peripheral neuropathy is damage to or dysfunction of peripheral nerves, which may affect sensory, motor and autonomic fibres. It may involve a single nerve (mononeuropathy – e.g. carpal tunnel syndrome, ulnar palsy, foot drop), several separate nerves (mononeuritis multiplex), or many nerves symmetrically (polyneuropathy, typically in a "glove and stocking" distribution).

Causes

  • Diabetes mellitus – the commonest cause.
  • Alcohol and nutritional deficiencies – vitamin B1 (thiamine), B12, B6 and folate.
  • Drugs – isoniazid (prevented by pyridoxine), vincristine, cisplatin, nitrofurantoin, phenytoin and some antiretrovirals.
  • Infections – leprosy (still important in India; thickened nerves and anaesthetic patches), HIV and diphtheria.
  • Toxins – lead, arsenic (contaminated groundwater) and organophosphates (delayed neuropathy).
  • Others – Guillain–Barré syndrome, chronic kidney disease, hypothyroidism, vasculitis, cancer, amyloidosis and hereditary neuropathies.

Clinical features

  • Sensory – tingling, numbness, burning pain worse at night, loss of touch, pain, temperature, vibration and position sense; unsteady gait in the dark; painless injuries, burns and ulcers.
  • Motor – weakness and wasting of small muscles of the hands and feet, foot drop, cramps and reduced tendon reflexes.
  • Autonomic – postural hypotension, resting tachycardia, gastroparesis (early fullness, vomiting), diarrhoea or constipation, bladder dysfunction, erectile dysfunction and abnormal sweating.

Diabetic neuropathy

  • The commonest form is distal symmetrical sensory polyneuropathy, beginning in the toes and feet; it leads to diabetic foot ulcers, infections, Charcot foot and amputations.
  • Annual screening of all diabetics with the 10 g monofilament test, a 128 Hz tuning fork for vibration and ankle reflexes; the feet are inspected at every visit.

Diagnosis – history and examination, nerve conduction studies and EMG, blood sugar and HbA1c, vitamin B12, thyroid, renal and liver tests, HIV testing, skin smear and nerve examination for leprosy, and nerve biopsy in selected cases.

Management

  • Treat the cause – good glycaemic control, stopping alcohol, thiamine and B12 supplementation, changing neurotoxic drugs, multidrug therapy for leprosy.
  • Neuropathic pain – pregabalin or gabapentin, duloxetine, amitriptyline, topical capsaicin; ordinary painkillers are often ineffective.
  • Physiotherapy, splints and ankle-foot orthoses for foot drop; surgery for nerve entrapment (e.g. carpal tunnel release).

Nursing management

  1. Foot care – the most important measure
    • Inspect the feet daily (use a mirror) for cuts, blisters, redness and cracks.
    • Wash feet daily with lukewarm water – test the water with the elbow or a thermometer, not the feet; dry well between the toes; apply moisturiser (not between the toes).
    • Cut nails straight across; never walk barefoot, even at home or in places of worship; wear well-fitting, soft footwear such as microcellular rubber (MCR) footwear; check shoes for stones or nails before wearing.
    • Avoid hot-water bottles, heating pads, corn cutters and home remedies; seek early treatment for any wound.
  2. Safety – fall prevention with good lighting and walking aids; rise slowly to avoid postural hypotension; protect numb hands with pot holders while cooking.
  3. Pain relief – give neuropathic pain drugs (often at bedtime); use a bed cradle to keep sheets off painful feet; warm (not hot) soaks, relaxation and distraction.
  4. Mobility – exercises, physiotherapy and correct use of splints and orthoses.
  5. Autonomic symptoms – small frequent meals for gastroparesis; bowel and bladder programmes; elastic stockings and adequate fluids for postural hypotension.
  6. Education – control of blood sugar, BP and lipids; stop smoking and alcohol; balanced diet; regular foot and nerve screening; for leprosy patients – self-care of anaesthetic hands, feet and eyes and removal of stigma.
  7. Psychological support – chronic pain and disability cause depression; counselling and family involvement.
