Conclusion Peripheral neuropathy, most often due to diabetes, causes sensory loss, pain, weakness and autonomic problems. Treating the cause, relieving neuropathic pain and, above all, meticulous foot care and safety education by the nurse prevent ulcers, injuries and amputations.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurological Disorders
question: What is the Glasgow Coma Scale? Write its components.
answer_html:
The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is a standard tool to assess and record the level of consciousness by scoring the patient's best response in three areas.

Components

  1. Eye opening (E) – spontaneous 4, to sound 3, to pressure/pain 2, none 1.
  2. Verbal response (V) – oriented 5, confused 4, inappropriate words 3, incomprehensible sounds 2, none 1.
  3. Motor response (M) – obeys commands 6, localises pain 5, normal flexion/withdrawal 4, abnormal flexion (decorticate) 3, extension (decerebrate) 2, none 1.

Total score 3–15. In head injury: 13–15 mild, 9–12 moderate, 8 or less severe (coma – airway protection needed). Record each part separately (e.g. E3 V4 M6 = 13), use "T" for intubated patients, and report a fall of 2 or more points immediately. Pupils and limb power are recorded alongside.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurological Disorders
question: Define hemiplegia, paraplegia and quadriplegia, with one cause of each.
answer_html:
• Hemiplegia – paralysis of one side of the body (arm, leg and often face) due to a lesion of the opposite cerebral hemisphere; commonest cause – stroke (also head injury, brain tumour).
  • Paraplegia – paralysis of both lower limbs (and the lower trunk) due to damage of the thoracic or lumbar spinal cord or cauda equina; causes – spinal cord injury below T1, tuberculosis of the spine (Pott's paraplegia), spinal tumours.
  • Quadriplegia (tetraplegia) – paralysis of all four limbs and the trunk due to injury of the cervical spinal cord; cause – cervical spine injury (e.g. diving or falls), and also GBS or motor neuron disease.
  • Related terms – monoplegia (one limb, e.g. poliomyelitis) and diplegia (symmetrical paralysis of corresponding parts, often legs more than arms, as in cerebral palsy). "-paresis" means weakness rather than complete paralysis.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurological Disorders
question: What is autonomic dysreflexia? How is it managed?
answer_html:
Autonomic dysreflexia is a life-threatening emergency in patients with spinal cord injury at or above T6, in which a stimulus below the level of injury triggers an uncontrolled sympathetic reflex, causing a sudden, severe rise in BP.

  • Triggers – distended bladder (commonest), blocked catheter, faecal impaction, pressure sores, tight clothing, ingrown toenails and menstruation.
  • Features – sudden severe hypertension, pounding headache, flushing and sweating above the injury, nasal congestion, blurred vision, bradycardia, and pale, cold skin below the injury; it may cause stroke or seizures.
  • Management – sit the patient upright and lower the legs; loosen tight clothing; check and empty the bladder (unblock or change the catheter); check for faecal impaction (with anaesthetic gel); monitor BP every 2–5 minutes; give fast-acting antihypertensives (nifedipine, nitrates) as ordered if BP stays high; teach patients and families to recognise and prevent it.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurological Disorders
question: What is Cushing's triad? Give its significance.
answer_html:
Cushing's triad is a group of three signs of severely raised intracranial pressure with compression of the brainstem:

  1. Rising systolic blood pressure with widening pulse pressure (hypertension).
  2. Bradycardia (slow, bounding pulse).
  3. Irregular or slow respiration (e.g. Cheyne–Stokes breathing or apnoea).

Mechanism – as ICP rises, cerebral blood flow falls; the brain raises the BP to maintain perfusion (Cushing reflex), and the baroreceptor response slows the heart, while pressure on the medulla disturbs breathing.

Significance – it is a late and ominous sign of impending brain herniation; the nurse must report it immediately, ensure the airway, elevate the head of the bed to 30°, and prepare for emergency measures such as mannitol, hyperventilation and surgery.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Neurological Disorders
question: What is motor neuron disease (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis)?
tags: upper and lower motor neuron signs
answer_html:
Motor neuron disease (MND), the commonest form of which is amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), is a progressive degenerative disease of the motor neurons in the brain, brainstem and spinal cord, usually beginning after 50 years.

  • Features – a mixture of upper and lower motor neuron signs: progressive weakness and wasting of limb muscles, fasciculations (muscle twitching), cramps, spasticity with brisk reflexes, and bulbar involvement (slurred speech, difficulty swallowing, choking); eventually respiratory muscle weakness. Sensation, bladder and bowel control and eye movements are usually spared, and intellect is often preserved.
  • Management – no cure; riluzole (and edaravone in some cases) may slow progression; supportive care – physiotherapy, speech therapy, nutritional support (PEG feeding), non-invasive ventilation, and early palliative care and advance care planning.
  • Nursing – maintain safety, nutrition, communication aids, skin care and emotional support for patient and family.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Immunological Problems
question: Mr. Saw, aged 45 years, is admitted with chronic diarrhoea, weight loss and oral thrush and is diagnosed with AIDS. (a) Define AIDS. (2 marks) (b) Explain the clinical manifestations and WHO clinical staging of HIV infection. (5 marks) (c) Describe the management and nursing care of Mr. Saw. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Natural history of HIV infection
labels: graph of CD4 count falling over years and viral load rising
clinical latency (years) and AIDS stage when CD4 falls below 200 cells/mm³

answer_html:
(a) Definition (2 marks) AIDS (acquired immunodeficiency syndrome) is the advanced stage of infection with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), in which progressive destruction of CD4 T-lymphocytes leads to severe immunodeficiency. It is diagnosed when the CD4 count falls below 200 cells/mm³ or when the patient develops WHO stage 4 (AIDS-defining) conditions such as Pneumocystis pneumonia, oesophageal candidiasis, cryptococcal meningitis or HIV wasting syndrome. HIV is a retrovirus spread mainly through unprotected sexual contact, infected blood and needles, and from mother to child.

(b) Clinical manifestations and WHO clinical staging (5 marks) 1. Course of HIV infection

  • Acute HIV infection (acute retroviral syndrome) – 2–4 weeks after infection; fever, sore throat, rash, swollen lymph nodes, muscle aches and diarrhoea, resembling flu or glandular fever; the viral load is very high and the person is highly infectious, but antibody tests may still be negative (window period).
  • Clinical latency (asymptomatic stage) – usually lasts several years; the person looks well, but the virus keeps multiplying and the CD4 count slowly falls; persistent generalised lymphadenopathy may be present.
  • Symptomatic HIV disease – recurrent infections, weight loss, fever, diarrhoea, skin problems and oral thrush as CD4 falls.
  • AIDS – severe opportunistic infections and cancers when CD4 is below 200 cells/mm³; without treatment, death usually follows within a few years.

2. WHO clinical staging (adults and adolescents)

  • Stage 1 (asymptomatic) – no symptoms or persistent generalised lymphadenopathy.
  • Stage 2 (mild symptoms) – unexplained weight loss less than 10%, recurrent respiratory infections (sinusitis, otitis, pharyngitis), herpes zoster, angular cheilitis, recurrent oral ulcers, papular itchy skin eruptions, seborrhoeic dermatitis and fungal nail infections.
  • Stage 3 (advanced symptoms) – weight loss more than 10%, unexplained chronic diarrhoea for more than 1 month, unexplained persistent fever for more than 1 month, persistent oral candidiasis, oral hairy leukoplakia, pulmonary tuberculosis, severe bacterial infections (pneumonia, meningitis), acute necrotising gingivitis, and unexplained anaemia, neutropenia or low platelets.
  • Stage 4 (severe – AIDS-defining) – HIV wasting syndrome, Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, recurrent severe bacterial pneumonia, chronic herpes simplex ulcers, oesophageal candidiasis, extrapulmonary tuberculosis, Kaposi's sarcoma, cytomegalovirus retinitis, cerebral toxoplasmosis, HIV encephalopathy, cryptococcal meningitis, disseminated mycobacterial infections, chronic cryptosporidiosis, lymphoma and invasive cervical cancer.

3. Mr. Saw's picture – chronic diarrhoea, marked weight loss and oral thrush place him in at least WHO stage 3; his CD4 count, viral load and screening for tuberculosis and other opportunistic infections will complete the assessment.

(c) Management and nursing care of Mr. Saw (8 marks) A. Medical management

  1. Baseline investigations – CD4 count, viral load (later monitoring), CBC, liver and kidney function, blood sugar, lipids, TB screening (symptom screen, sputum CBNAAT, chest X-ray), hepatitis B and C, syphilis serology, stool examination for parasites, and cryptococcal antigen when CD4 is low.
  2. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) – under NACO's "Test and Treat" policy, every person with HIV is started on free lifelong ART at ART centres regardless of CD4 count; the preferred first-line regimen is TLD – tenofovir, lamivudine and dolutegravir as a single daily tablet; ART is started quickly, but is delayed for some weeks in TB meningitis and cryptococcal meningitis to avoid immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS).
  3. Prophylaxis – co-trimoxazole preventive therapy (prevents Pneumocystis pneumonia, toxoplasmosis and bacterial infections) and TB preventive treatment (isoniazid or weekly isoniazid–rifapentine) once active TB is excluded.
  4. Treatment of opportunistic infections – e.g. fluconazole for oral and oesophageal candidiasis; investigation and specific treatment of diarrhoea (cryptosporidium, isospora, giardia); anti-TB treatment if TB is found.
  5. Monitoring – viral load at 6 and 12 months and then yearly (target: undetectable), CD4 as needed, adherence and side effects.

B. Nursing management (by nursing diagnoses) 1. Diarrhoea and risk of deficient fluid volume

  • Record frequency and character of stools, intake–output and weight; give ORS and IV fluids as ordered; check electrolytes; give antidiarrhoeal and specific drugs; perianal skin care with gentle cleansing and barrier cream; send stool samples correctly.

2. Imbalanced nutrition – less than body requirements (weight loss, oral thrush)

  • Oral care – soft brush, saline or prescribed mouthwash after meals, antifungal drugs; avoid spicy and very hot foods while the mouth is sore.
  • High-calorie, high-protein diet in small, frequent meals (milk, curd, eggs, dal, soya, paneer, khichdi, bananas); nutritional supplements; safe food and boiled or filtered water to prevent infections; weekly weight; link to nutrition support schemes where available.

3. Risk for infection related to severe immunodeficiency

  • Hand hygiene, clean environment, avoid contact with people having infections; early recognition of fever, cough, breathlessness, headache or skin lesions; give prophylactic drugs regularly; vaccinations as advised (no live vaccines when CD4 is very low).

4. Risk for non-adherence to ART

  • Adherence counselling – take ART at the same time every day (more than 95% adherence is needed to keep the virus suppressed); use alarms, pill boxes and a treatment supporter; explain that ART is lifelong and must never be stopped on feeling better; explain side effects and when to report; check pill counts and attendance at the ART centre.

5. Fatigue and activity intolerance

  • Plan rest periods, assist with daily activities and encourage gradual activity as strength improves.

6. Anxiety, fear of stigma and ineffective coping

  • Provide privacy and a non-judgemental attitude; maintain strict confidentiality; allow expression of feelings; support disclosure to spouse or family when he is ready; counsel about partner testing; screen for depression; link with positive people's networks and counsellors.

7. Infection control and safety in hospital

  • Follow standard precautions for all patients (gloves for blood and body fluids, safe sharps handling, no recapping of needles); no separate utensils, linen or isolation are needed for HIV itself – isolation is only for transmissible infections such as pulmonary TB.

8. Education for Mr. Saw and his family

  • How HIV spreads and does not spread (not by touching, sharing food, toilets or caring for him); consistent condom use; partner testing; no blood or organ donation; no sharing of razors and needles.
  • Importance of nutrition, hygiene, safe water, regular follow-up and early reporting of new symptoms.
  • His rights under the HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017 – protection against discrimination at work, in health care and in education.

Nursing importance

  • With early ART and good adherence, people with HIV now have a near-normal life expectancy; the nurse's counselling, adherence support, nutrition care and fight against stigma largely determine whether this is achieved.

Conclusion AIDS is the advanced stage of HIV infection marked by low CD4 counts and opportunistic illnesses, graded by WHO clinical stages 1 to 4. Free lifelong ART under the test-and-treat policy, prophylaxis and treatment of opportunistic infections, and compassionate, confidential nursing care focused on nutrition, infection prevention, adherence and psychosocial support help Mr. Saw recover and live a productive life.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Immunological Problems
question: Explain the National AIDS and STD Control Programme (NACP) Phase V.
tags: National AIDS and STD Control Programme
answer_html:
Introduction India's national response to HIV began in 1992 with the first National AIDS Control Programme, implemented by the National AIDS Control Organisation (NACO) under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, through State AIDS Control Societies (SACS) and district units. NACP Phase V ran from 1 April 2021 to 31 March 2026 as a fully government-funded Central Sector Scheme with an outlay of about ₹15,472 crore. India is now moving into NACP Phase VI (2026–31), which aims to end AIDS as a public health threat by 2030 (SDG 3.3).

1. Goals of NACP Phase V

  • Reduce annual new HIV infections and AIDS-related deaths by 80% by 2025–26, compared with 2010.
  • Dual elimination of vertical (parent-to-child) transmission of HIV and syphilis.
  • Elimination of HIV/AIDS-related stigma and discrimination.
  • Universal access to quality STI/RTI services for at-risk and vulnerable populations.
  • 95-95-95 targets – 95% of people with HIV know their status, 95% of them receive ART, and 95% of those on ART have suppressed viral load.

2. Main strategies and components

  • Prevention
    • Targeted interventions for high-risk groups – female sex workers, men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, transgender people – and bridge populations (migrants, truckers) through peer outreach.
    • Opioid substitution therapy and needle–syringe exchange for people who inject drugs.
    • Link Worker Scheme in rural areas; condom promotion; blood safety through licensed blood banks and voluntary donation.
    • IEC and youth programmes – Red Ribbon Clubs in colleges, adolescent education.
  • Testing
    • Integrated Counselling and Testing Centres (ICTC) – stand-alone, facility-integrated and community-based screening; universal HIV and syphilis screening of pregnant women.
  • Treatment, care and support
    • "Test and Treat" – free lifelong ART for every person with HIV regardless of CD4 count, at ART centres and Link ART centres.
    • Universal viral load testing, multi-month dispensing of drugs and community ART refills.
    • Mission Sampark – tracing and bringing back people who have dropped out of treatment.
    • Management of HIV–TB co-infection and opportunistic infections; care and support centres.
  • STI/RTI services – designated STI clinics (Suraksha clinics) with syndromic management.
  • Legal and social protection – the HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017; social protection schemes for people living with HIV.
  • Strategic information – HIV sentinel surveillance and programme monitoring.
  • National AIDS helpline 1097 for information and counselling.

3. Achievements

  • India's adult HIV prevalence is low (about 0.2%), and new infections and AIDS-related deaths have declined substantially since 2010, though not fully to the targets; prevalence remains higher in some north-eastern states.

4. Role of the nurse

  • Counselling and testing at ICTCs and antenatal clinics; support for ART adherence and follow-up; infection prevention with standard precautions; health education in schools, colleges and the community; reduction of stigma; referral and linkage to ART centres; record-keeping and reporting.

Conclusion NACP Phase V (2021–26) focused on cutting new infections and AIDS deaths by 80%, eliminating vertical transmission and stigma, and reaching the 95-95-95 targets through prevention, testing, test-and-treat and legal protection. Nurses are key front-line workers in carrying these goals forward into NACP Phase VI.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Immunological Problems
question: Explain the measures for prevention and control of HIV/AIDS.
answer_html:
Introduction There is no vaccine or cure for HIV, but its spread can be prevented effectively. Prevention depends on interrupting each route of transmission – sexual, blood-borne and mother-to-child – and on treating every infected person so that the virus is suppressed.

1. Prevention of sexual transmission

  • ABC approach – Abstinence (delay of sexual debut among adolescents), Be faithful to one uninfected partner, consistent and correct Condom use.
  • Free condom distribution and social marketing; early diagnosis and treatment of STIs, which increase HIV transmission.
  • Targeted interventions for high-risk groups through peer educators.
  • Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) – daily antiretroviral drugs for HIV-negative people at very high risk, under programme guidelines.
  • Partner testing of people with HIV.

2. Prevention of blood-borne transmission

  • Safe blood – voluntary non-remunerated blood donation and screening of all donated blood for HIV, hepatitis B and C, syphilis and malaria (nucleic acid testing in many blood banks).
  • Harm reduction for people who inject drugs – needle and syringe exchange and opioid substitution therapy (buprenorphine, methadone).
  • Sterile equipment in hospitals, clinics, tattooing, ear piercing and barber shops; never share razors, needles or toothbrushes.
  • Safe organ, tissue and semen donation after screening.

3. Prevention of vertical (parent-to-child) transmission

  • Universal HIV and syphilis screening of pregnant women; lifelong ART for HIV-positive pregnant and breastfeeding women; infant antiretroviral prophylaxis; institutional delivery; safe infant-feeding counselling; early infant diagnosis.

4. Prevention in health-care settings

  • Standard precautions for every patient – hand hygiene, gloves and protective equipment, safe handling and disposal of sharps (no recapping), biomedical waste management.
  • Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) after needle-stick or mucosal exposure – wash the site, report immediately and start ART within 72 hours (ideally within 2 hours) for 28 days.

5. Treatment as prevention

  • "Test and Treat" – early ART for all people with HIV; a person with a sustained undetectable viral load does not transmit HIV sexually ("Undetectable = Untransmittable").
  • Expansion of testing (ICTCs, community-based screening) so that people know their status early.

6. Health education and community measures

  • IEC through mass media, schools, colleges (Red Ribbon Clubs) and workplaces; life-skills and adolescent education; the national AIDS helpline 1097.
  • Reduction of stigma and discrimination, so that people come forward for testing and treatment; implementation of the HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017.

7. Role of the nurse

  • Health education in hospitals and the community; pre- and post-test counselling; antenatal screening; strict standard precautions; PEP management for staff; adherence support; non-judgemental, confidential care.

Conclusion HIV prevention combines safe sexual behaviour, safe blood and injections, elimination of vertical transmission, standard precautions, PEP and PrEP, harm reduction and early treatment of all infected people, supported by education and stigma reduction. Nurses play a key role in each of these measures.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Immunological Problems
question: Explain the common opportunistic infections in people living with HIV and their prevention and nursing management.
answer_html:
Introduction Opportunistic infections (OIs) are infections that occur more often or more severely in people with weakened immunity. In people living with HIV (PLHIV), they appear as the CD4 count falls, and they are the main cause of illness and death in untreated HIV. Early ART and prophylaxis prevent most of them.

1. Common opportunistic infections

  • Tuberculosis – the commonest OI and leading cause of death among PLHIV in India; may occur at any CD4 count; pulmonary or extrapulmonary (lymph node, pleural, meningeal, abdominal); sputum may be negative, so CBNAAT and chest X-ray are used.
  • Oral and oesophageal candidiasis – white plaques in the mouth; pain on swallowing in oesophageal disease; treated with fluconazole.
  • Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) – dry cough, breathlessness and fever, often with low oxygen saturation (CD4 below 200); treated with high-dose co-trimoxazole.
  • Cryptococcal meningitis – headache, fever, vomiting and altered sensorium (CD4 below 100); treated with amphotericin B and flucytosine or fluconazole; repeated lumbar punctures reduce raised pressure.
  • Cerebral toxoplasmosis – headache, seizures and focal weakness with ring-enhancing brain lesions.
  • Cytomegalovirus (CMV) retinitis – blurred vision and floaters, which may lead to blindness.
  • Chronic diarrhoea – cryptosporidium, isospora, microsporidia and giardia, causing wasting.
  • Herpes zoster, chronic herpes simplex ulcers, bacterial pneumonia and sepsis, and Mycobacterium avium complex.

2. Prevention

  • Early ART for all PLHIV – restoring immunity is the best protection.
  • Co-trimoxazole preventive therapy – prevents PCP, toxoplasmosis and many bacterial infections in patients with low CD4 or advanced disease.
  • TB preventive treatment (isoniazid or isoniazid–rifapentine) after excluding active TB; regular TB symptom screening at every visit.
  • Cryptococcal antigen screening and pre-emptive fluconazole in patients with very low CD4.
  • Safe food and water, hand hygiene and vaccination (hepatitis B, pneumococcal, influenza) as advised.

3. Nursing management

  1. Assessment – fever, cough, breathlessness, headache, visual change, mouth lesions, swallowing pain, diarrhoea and weight; SpO₂ and neurological status.
  2. Respiratory care – oxygen, positioning, sputum collection for CBNAAT; airborne infection control (masks, ventilation) for suspected TB.
  3. Oral care – frequent mouth care, antifungal medicines, soft bland diet and fluids.
  4. Diarrhoea care – ORS and fluids, intake–output, perianal skin care and hygiene.
  5. Neurological care – seizure precautions, monitoring for raised intracranial pressure, care during lumbar puncture.
  6. Medication care – give prophylactic and treatment drugs on time; watch for drug interactions (e.g. rifampicin with dolutegravir needs dose adjustment) and side effects; observe for immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (worsening of an infection after ART is started).
  7. Nutrition – high-calorie, high-protein diet; supplements.
  8. Education – take prophylaxis and ART regularly; report new symptoms early; safe food and water.

Conclusion Tuberculosis, candidiasis, PCP, cryptococcal meningitis, toxoplasmosis, CMV retinitis and diarrhoeal infections are the major OIs in HIV. Early ART, co-trimoxazole and TB preventive therapy prevent most of them, while early recognition and skilled nursing care reduce their mortality.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Immunological Problems
question: Explain HIV counselling and testing services (ICTC), with the role of the nurse in pre-test and post-test counselling.
answer_html:
Introduction An Integrated Counselling and Testing Centre (ICTC) is a facility where a person can get HIV counselling and testing, usually free of cost, on their own initiative or on referral by a health worker. ICTCs are the gateway to HIV prevention, care and treatment services under the national programme. They may be stand-alone (in medical colleges and district hospitals), facility-integrated (in PHCs and CHCs) or community-based screening services.

1. Who should be tested

  • Pregnant women (universal screening), patients with TB, STI clinic attendees, people with symptoms suggestive of HIV, partners and children of PLHIV, high-risk groups, and anyone who wishes to know their status.

2. Principles – the WHO "5 Cs"

  1. Consent – testing is voluntary with informed consent.
  2. Confidentiality – results are shared only with the client (or with written consent).
  3. Counselling – before and after the test.
  4. Correct test results – quality-assured testing; in India, HIV is diagnosed by using three different rapid tests.
  5. Connection – linkage to prevention, care and ART services.

3. Pre-test counselling (information and preparation)

  • Build rapport in a private setting; explain what HIV is, how it spreads and how it can be prevented.
  • Assess the client's risk behaviour and explain the window period (a recent infection may not be detected).
  • Explain the benefits of knowing one's status, the testing procedure and the meaning of possible results.
  • Discuss how the client may cope with a positive result and whom they would tell.
  • Obtain informed consent; for minors, consent rules as per guidelines.

4. Post-test counselling

  • Negative result – explain the result and window period; advise repeat testing after 3 months if there was recent risk; reinforce prevention (condoms, avoid sharing needles); encourage staying negative.
  • Positive result
    • Give the result privately, clearly and calmly; allow time for emotional reactions (shock, denial, fear, anger); listen and support.
    • Explain that HIV is a manageable chronic illness – free lifelong ART allows a near-normal life.
    • Immediate linkage to the ART centre for registration, tests and treatment initiation.
    • Discuss disclosure to spouse or partner and partner and family testing; safer sex; prevention of transmission to others.
    • Screen for TB and STIs; refer pregnant women for prevention of vertical transmission.
    • Assess suicide risk and social support; refer to support groups and positive networks.
  • Follow-up counselling – adherence, coping, family and social issues, nutrition and legal rights.

5. Role of the nurse

  • Provide counselling (as trained) or refer to the ICTC counsellor; ensure privacy and confidentiality of records; collect blood samples safely using standard precautions; maintain registers and reports; trace patients lost to follow-up; educate the community about ICTC services and reduce fear and stigma around testing.

Conclusion ICTCs provide voluntary, confidential HIV counselling and testing guided by the 5 Cs. Good pre-test and post-test counselling helps people understand their risk, cope with their results and connect quickly to prevention and treatment, and nurses are key members of this service.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Immunological Problems
question: Explain the elimination of vertical (parent-to-child) transmission of HIV and syphilis, with the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction Vertical (parent-to-child) transmission means passage of HIV or syphilis from an infected mother to her baby during pregnancy, labour and delivery, or breastfeeding. Without intervention, about 15–45% of babies born to HIV-positive mothers become infected; with ART and good care, the risk falls to below 2%. India's programme, earlier called PPTCT, now aims at dual elimination of vertical transmission of HIV and syphilis (EVTHS).

1. Strategies

  • Primary prevention of HIV among women of reproductive age.
  • Prevention of unintended pregnancies among women living with HIV through family-planning counselling.
  • Prevention of transmission to the baby – testing, ART, safe delivery and infant prophylaxis.
  • Care, treatment and support for the mother, baby and family.

2. Key services

  • Universal screening of every pregnant woman for HIV and syphilis, preferably in the first trimester, at the first antenatal visit; repeat testing in high-risk situations.
  • HIV-positive pregnant women – start lifelong ART (TLD regimen) immediately, irrespective of CD4 count or stage; viral load testing to confirm suppression before delivery.
  • Institutional delivery with safe obstetric practices – avoid unnecessary episiotomy, artificial rupture of membranes and instrumental delivery; standard precautions.
  • Infant prophylaxis – syrup nevirapine for the HIV-exposed baby from birth for 6 weeks (extended to 12 weeks, with added zidovudine, for high-risk babies as per guidelines).
  • Co-trimoxazole prophylaxis for the exposed infant from 6 weeks of age until HIV infection is excluded.
  • Early infant diagnosis – HIV DNA PCR at 6 weeks (and repeat tests as per schedule, with antibody testing at 18 months).
  • Infant feeding – exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months while the mother continues ART, then complementary feeds; mixed feeding is avoided.
  • Syphilis – positive pregnant women and their partners are treated with benzathine penicillin; newborns are examined and treated for congenital syphilis if needed.

3. Role of the nurse

  1. Counsel and test every antenatal woman; ensure confidentiality and informed consent.
  2. Link HIV-positive women to the ART centre on the same day; support adherence and disclosure to the partner; arrange partner testing.
  3. Follow standard precautions during labour; ensure institutional delivery; give nevirapine to the newborn within 6–12 hours of birth.
  4. Counsel on exclusive breastfeeding, family planning, nutrition and immunisation (routine vaccines are given to HIV-exposed infants).
  5. Track mother–baby pairs for early infant diagnosis and follow-up up to 18 months; trace those who miss visits.
  6. Treat syphilis and record and report as per programme formats.

Conclusion Universal antenatal screening, lifelong ART for HIV-positive mothers, safe delivery, infant prophylaxis, early infant diagnosis and syphilis treatment can almost eliminate vertical transmission. Nurses in antenatal clinics, labour rooms and the community are central to achieving this goal.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Immunological Problems
question: Explain home-based care and palliative care of a person living with HIV/AIDS.
answer_html:
Introduction Most people living with HIV (PLHIV) live at home with their families. Home-based care is the care given to them in their own homes by family members, supported by health workers, nurses and community organisations. Palliative care focuses on relieving pain and other symptoms and improving quality of life at every stage of illness, including the end of life. With free ART, most PLHIV stay well, but those with advanced disease, drug resistance or other illnesses still need such care.

1. Aims

  • Keep the person comfortable, active and independent; support ART adherence; prevent infections; reduce hospital admissions; support the family; and provide dignified end-of-life care.

2. Components of home-based care

  • Clinical care
    • Regular ART and prophylactic medicines; follow-up at the ART centre; recognition of warning signs (fever, cough, breathlessness, headache, diarrhoea, weight loss, confusion).
    • Symptom management – fever (tepid sponging, paracetamol, fluids), diarrhoea (ORS, perianal care), cough, sore mouth (salt-water gargles, soft food), itching and skin rashes, pain (analgesic ladder), nausea and fatigue.
  • Nutrition – balanced, high-energy, high-protein home food in small frequent meals; safe drinking water; hygienic food preparation; avoid raw eggs and undercooked meat.
  • Nursing care at home – personal hygiene, mouth care, pressure-area care for bedridden patients, positioning, exercises, toileting.
  • Infection control at home
    • HIV is not spread by casual contact, sharing food, utensils, toilets or touching; no isolation is needed.
    • Wear gloves or plastic bags on hands when handling blood, pus, vomit or stool; cover wounds.
    • Soak linen soiled with blood or body fluids in household bleach solution before washing; burn or safely dispose of dressings; do not share razors or toothbrushes.
    • Protect the patient from people with TB, chickenpox or other infections.
  • Psychosocial and spiritual support – counselling for fear, depression, guilt and stigma; encouragement of social and spiritual activities; support with disclosure; connection to positive people's networks and care and support centres.
  • Social and legal support – help in obtaining government welfare schemes, nutrition support, travel concessions and pensions where available; education about rights under the HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017; planning for children's care (succession and guardianship).

3. Palliative and end-of-life care

  • Relief of pain and distressing symptoms (breathlessness, delirium, severe diarrhoea), mouth and skin care, and nutrition according to tolerance.
  • Respect for the patient's wishes about place of care and treatment; advance care planning.
  • Emotional and spiritual support to the patient and family; dignity and privacy at the time of death; bereavement support to the family; support for orphaned children.

4. Role of the nurse

  • Train family caregivers in care skills and infection control; visit regularly; supervise ART adherence; provide supplies (gloves, ORS, dressings); refer early when complications arise; coordinate with ART centres, NGOs and community health workers; reduce stigma in the family and neighbourhood.

Conclusion Home-based and palliative care allow people with HIV to live and, when necessary, die with comfort and dignity among their families. Clinical care, nutrition, simple infection control, symptom relief and psychosocial and social support, organised and supervised by nurses, are its key elements.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Immunological Problems
question: Explain immunodeficiency disorders and the nursing care of an immunocompromised patient.
answer_html:
Definition Immunodeficiency is a state in which the immune system's ability to fight infection is absent or reduced, so that the person suffers frequent, severe, unusual or recurrent infections and some cancers. A patient with such reduced immunity is called immunocompromised.

1. Classification A. Primary (congenital) immunodeficiencies – inherited defects, usually showing in childhood:

  • B-cell (antibody) defects – X-linked agammaglobulinaemia, common variable immunodeficiency, selective IgA deficiency – recurrent bacterial infections of sinuses, ears and lungs.
  • T-cell defects – DiGeorge syndrome (absent thymus, low calcium, heart defects) – viral, fungal and opportunistic infections.
  • Combined defects – severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) – severe infections in early infancy; needs bone-marrow transplantation.
  • Phagocyte and complement defects – chronic granulomatous disease, complement deficiency (recurrent meningococcal infections).

B. Secondary (acquired) immunodeficiencies – far more common:

  • HIV infection, malnutrition (protein–energy malnutrition), uncontrolled diabetes, chronic kidney and liver disease.
  • Drugs – cancer chemotherapy, long-term corticosteroids, immunosuppressants after transplantation, biological therapies.
  • Cancers – leukaemia, lymphoma, multiple myeloma; radiotherapy.
  • Splenectomy (risk of overwhelming pneumococcal infection), extensive burns, ageing, alcoholism and pregnancy (mild).

2. Clinical features

  • Frequent, recurrent or persistent infections; infections with unusual organisms (fungi, Pneumocystis, cytomegalovirus); poor response to standard antibiotics; failure to thrive in children; chronic diarrhoea; skin infections and oral thrush.
  • Fever may be the only sign of serious infection, because the usual inflammatory signs (pus, redness) may be absent in neutropenic patients.

3. Medical management

  • Treat the cause (ART for HIV, nutritional rehabilitation, sugar control, reduction of immunosuppressive drugs where possible).
  • Immunoglobulin replacement (IVIG) for antibody deficiencies; bone-marrow or stem-cell transplantation for SCID; growth factors (G-CSF) for neutropenia; prophylactic antimicrobials; early aggressive treatment of infection.

4. Nursing care of an immunocompromised patient

  1. Protective environment – single room where possible; strict hand hygiene by everyone before contact; restrict visitors with coughs, colds or other infections; no fresh flowers, plants or stagnant water in the room.
  2. Monitoring – temperature every 4 hours; check skin, mouth, perineum, IV and catheter sites daily; report fever of 38 °C or more immediately – febrile neutropenia is an emergency needing antibiotics within one hour.
  3. Avoid invasive procedures where possible – minimise catheters, injections and rectal temperatures or enemas; strict asepsis for lines.
  4. Personal hygiene – daily bath, oral care with soft brush and mouthwash, perineal care, skin moisturising.
  5. Food safety – well-cooked food, safe drinking water, washed fruits; avoid raw or undercooked meat and eggs and unpasteurised milk.
  6. Vaccination – avoid live vaccines (oral polio, MMR, varicella, BCG) in severely immunocompromised patients; give recommended inactivated vaccines (influenza, pneumococcal) and vaccinate household contacts.
  7. IVIG administration – correct infusion rate, watch for headache, fever, chills and allergic reactions.
  8. Nutrition – high-protein, high-calorie diet with vitamins and minerals.
  9. Education – hand washing, avoiding crowds and sick contacts, early reporting of fever, adherence to prophylaxis, and wearing a medical alert card (e.g. after splenectomy).
  10. Psychosocial support – isolation causes loneliness and anxiety; maintain communication and allow family contact safely.

Conclusion Immunodeficiency may be primary (inherited) or, much more often, secondary to HIV, malnutrition, drugs, cancer and other diseases. Treating the cause, replacing missing components and, above all, preventing and promptly treating infections through careful nursing in a protective environment are the keys to care.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Immunological Problems
question: Explain the HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017 and the role of the nurse in reducing stigma and discrimination.
tags: HIV and AIDS Prevention and Control Act 2017
answer_html:
Introduction People living with HIV (PLHIV) have long faced stigma (negative attitudes and labelling) and discrimination (unfair treatment) at home, at work and even in hospitals. India enacted the HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017, which came into force in 2018, to protect their rights and promote access to prevention and treatment.

1. Main provisions of the Act

  • Prohibition of discrimination against PLHIV and those living with them in employment, health care, education, housing, insurance, public facilities, property rights and holding public office; denial or unfair treatment in any of these areas is an offence.
  • Informed consent is required for HIV testing, treatment and research, except in specific situations (e.g. court orders, screening of donated blood, organs or semen).
  • Confidentiality – no person can be forced to disclose HIV status; disclosure of a person's status requires their informed consent, except as permitted (for example, to a partner at significant risk, by a doctor under specified conditions, or by court order).
  • No HIV test as a condition for employment, admission to education or access to health care.
  • Right of residence in a shared household and access to facilities; protection of children affected by HIV.
  • Guardianship – an adolescent aged 12–18 years who is mature enough can act as guardian of younger siblings for matters such as school admission and medical care.
  • Duties of government – to provide ART and management of opportunistic infections "as far as possible", promote prevention and IEC, and ensure access to welfare schemes.
  • Safe working environment – health-care establishments must follow universal precautions and provide post-exposure prophylaxis to staff exposed to HIV.
  • Grievance redressal – each establishment (of a prescribed size) appoints a complaints officer, and each state appoints an Ombudsman to inquire into violations; court cases can be heard with the identity of the person kept confidential.
  • Penalties for discrimination, propagation of hatred against PLHIV and breach of confidentiality.

2. Common forms of stigma and discrimination in health care

  • Refusal or delay of treatment or surgery, separate wards or utensils, labelling of files and beds with "HIV positive", unnecessary use of gloves or masks for touching, disclosure of status to others, judgemental remarks and pressure for testing without consent.

3. Role of the nurse in reducing stigma

  1. Treat every patient with respect, dignity and equality; follow standard precautions for all patients, so that no one is singled out.
  2. Keep HIV status confidential – no labels on beds, charts or doors; discuss results only privately and with consent.
  3. Obtain informed consent and provide counselling for HIV testing.
  4. Correct myths among staff, patients and families about casual spread of HIV.
  5. Educate the community, schools and workplaces; involve PLHIV networks in awareness activities.
  6. Speak up against discriminatory practices and report violations to the complaints officer.
  7. Support PLHIV in knowing and using their legal rights.

Conclusion The HIV and AIDS (Prevention and Control) Act, 2017 protects PLHIV from discrimination and safeguards consent and confidentiality. Nurses, by practising standard precautions for all, maintaining confidentiality and treating patients with dignity, play a leading role in eliminating HIV-related stigma.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Immunological Problems
question: Explain systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and its nursing management.
answer_html:
Definition Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic, multisystem autoimmune disease in which the body produces autoantibodies against its own cell nuclei (antinuclear antibodies), forming immune complexes that deposit in tissues and cause inflammation of the skin, joints, kidneys, blood cells, serous membranes and brain. It mainly affects women of child-bearing age (15–45 years) and runs a course of flares and remissions.

Causes and triggers – genetic tendency, female hormones (oestrogen), sunlight (UV rays), infections, stress, pregnancy and certain drugs (hydralazine, procainamide, isoniazid – drug-induced lupus).

Clinical features

  • General – fever, fatigue, weight loss and swollen lymph nodes.
  • Skin and mucosa – butterfly (malar) rash over the cheeks and nose, photosensitivity, discoid rash, painless oral ulcers and hair loss.
  • Joints – arthralgia and non-erosive arthritis of small joints.
  • Kidneys – lupus nephritis (proteinuria, haematuria, oedema, hypertension, kidney failure) – an important cause of morbidity.
  • Serositis – pleurisy and pericarditis (chest pain).
  • Blood – anaemia, low WBC and low platelets; tendency to thrombosis in antiphospholipid syndrome.
  • Nervous system – seizures, psychosis, headache; Raynaud's phenomenon; recurrent miscarriages.

Diagnosis – ANA (positive in almost all), anti-double-stranded DNA and anti-Smith antibodies (specific), low complement (C3, C4), raised ESR, blood counts, urine for protein and casts, kidney function and kidney biopsy for nephritis.

Medical management

  • Hydroxychloroquine for almost all patients – reduces flares; needs regular eye check-ups.
  • NSAIDs for joint pain; corticosteroids for flares (lowest effective dose).
  • Immunosuppressants – azathioprine, mycophenolate, cyclophosphamide (for nephritis), methotrexate, and biological drugs (belimumab, rituximab).
  • Dialysis or transplantation for end-stage kidney disease; anticoagulants for antiphospholipid syndrome.

Nursing management

  1. Assessment – skin, joints, BP, weight, urine output and urine protein, oedema, temperature, mental status, signs of infection and bleeding.
  2. Skin care and sun protection – avoid direct sunlight between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m.; use broad-spectrum sunscreen, full-sleeve clothes, hats and umbrellas; mild soaps; avoid harsh cosmetics; cover lesions with make-up if desired.
  3. Fatigue and joint pain – balance rest and activity; warm compresses; gentle range-of-motion exercises; analgesics as prescribed.
  4. Prevention of infection – patients on steroids and immunosuppressants are at high risk; hand hygiene, avoid sick contacts, vaccination (no live vaccines while on high immunosuppression), early reporting of fever.
  5. Kidney care – monitor BP, weight, oedema and urine; low-salt diet; protein as advised.
  6. Medication care – adherence; side effects of steroids (high sugar, BP, weight gain, mood changes, osteoporosis – calcium and vitamin D), of cyclophosphamide (bladder irritation – plenty of fluids; low counts; hair loss) and of hydroxychloroquine (yearly eye examination).
  7. Mouth care for oral ulcers – soft brush, mouthwash and soft diet.
  8. Pregnancy planning – conceive only when the disease is quiet for at least 6 months; review drugs (mycophenolate and cyclophosphamide harm the fetus); close obstetric follow-up.
  9. Psychosocial support – chronic illness, body-image changes and fear of flares; counselling and support groups; involve the family.
  10. Education – recognise flares (rash, joint pain, fever, swelling of feet, frothy urine) and report early; avoid triggers (sun, stress, infection); regular follow-up and laboratory tests.

Conclusion SLE is a chronic autoimmune disease affecting skin, joints, kidneys, blood and other organs, mainly in young women. Hydroxychloroquine, steroids and immunosuppressants control the disease, while nursing care focuses on sun protection, prevention of infection, kidney monitoring, medication safety, pregnancy planning and emotional support.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Immunological Problems
question: Write four measures to prevent AIDS.
answer_html:
Measures to prevent HIV infection and AIDS:

  1. Safe sexual practices – abstinence or faithfulness to one uninfected partner, and correct and consistent use of condoms; early treatment of sexually transmitted infections.
  2. Safe blood and injections – transfusion of screened blood only, use of sterile, disposable needles and syringes; no sharing of needles, razors or toothbrushes; needle–syringe exchange and opioid substitution for people who inject drugs.
  3. Prevention of mother-to-child transmission – antenatal HIV testing, lifelong ART for HIV-positive pregnant women, safe institutional delivery and infant nevirapine prophylaxis.
  4. Standard precautions and PEP – safe handling of blood and sharps in health care, and post-exposure prophylaxis within 72 hours after exposure. Other measures include early testing and treatment of all PLHIV ("test and treat"), pre-exposure prophylaxis for high-risk people and health education to reduce stigma.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Immunological Problems
question: What is the window period in HIV infection?
answer_html:
The window period is the interval between infection with HIV and the time when a test can reliably detect the infection (appearance of antibodies, antigen or viral genetic material in blood).

  • During this period the person may test negative but is already infected and highly infectious.
  • Its length depends on the test: about 10–33 days for nucleic acid tests, about 3–6 weeks for combined antigen–antibody (fourth-generation) tests, and up to about 3 months for antibody-only rapid tests.
  • Importance – a person with recent risk exposure and a negative result should be retested after 3 months and should practise safe behaviour meanwhile; it is also why donated blood is screened with sensitive tests and donors are asked about recent risk.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Immunological Problems
question: What is the significance of the CD4 count in HIV infection?
answer_html:
CD4 cells are helper T-lymphocytes that HIV infects and destroys. The CD4 count is the number of these cells per mm³ of blood (normal about 500–1,500 cells/mm³).

  • It shows the degree of immune damage – the lower the count, the higher the risk of opportunistic infections.
  • Below 200 cells/mm³ – defines AIDS (risk of PCP, toxoplasmosis); below 100 – risk of cryptococcal meningitis and CMV disease.
  • Used to identify advanced HIV disease, to decide prophylaxis (co-trimoxazole, cryptococcal antigen screening) and to monitor immune recovery on ART.
  • Since all PLHIV now start ART regardless of CD4 count, treatment success is monitored mainly by viral load.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Immunological Problems
question: What is a Red Ribbon Club?
answer_html:
A Red Ribbon Club (RRC) is a voluntary student club set up in colleges and universities under the National AIDS Control Programme, supported by the State AIDS Control Societies. The red ribbon is the international symbol of HIV awareness and solidarity with people living with HIV. Aims and activities

  • Spread correct information about HIV/AIDS and STIs among young people and build life skills to avoid risky behaviour.
  • Promote voluntary blood donation and blood-donation camps.
  • Reduce stigma and discrimination against people living with HIV.
  • Organise awareness rallies, quizzes, poster competitions and peer education, especially on World AIDS Day (1 December). Nursing students can join RRCs and act as peer educators in their colleges and communities.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Immunological Problems
question: Explain the 95-95-95 targets in HIV control.
answer_html:
The 95-95-95 targets, set by UNAIDS and adopted by India's National AIDS and STD Control Programme, aim to end AIDS as a public health threat by 2030:

  1. 95% of all people living with HIV should know their HIV status (testing).
  2. 95% of those diagnosed should be receiving antiretroviral therapy (treatment).
  3. 95% of those on ART should have a suppressed viral load (treatment success). When these targets are met, about 86% of all people with HIV are virally suppressed and cannot transmit the virus sexually, which greatly reduces new infections and AIDS-related deaths. They replaced the earlier 90-90-90 targets.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Oncological Conditions (including Palliative Care Module)
question: (a) Define cancer and list its warning signs. (3 marks) (b) Explain the levels of prevention of cancer. (5 marks) (c) Describe the cancer screening programmes in India and the role of the nurse. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: CAUTION – the seven warning signs of cancer
labels: change in bowel or bladder habits
a sore that does not heal
thickening or lump in breast or elsewhere
obvious change in a wart or mole

answer_html:
(a) Definition and warning signs (3 marks) Cancer is a group of diseases characterised by uncontrolled, abnormal growth of cells that invade surrounding tissues and may spread to distant parts of the body (metastasis) through lymphatics and blood. It results from accumulated genetic changes caused by factors such as tobacco, infections, radiation, chemicals, diet and inherited mutations. In India, the commonest cancers are oral and lung cancers in men and breast and cervical cancers in women, and most are detected at a late stage.

Warning signs – "CAUTION"

  • C – Change in bowel or bladder habits.
  • A – A sore (ulcer) that does not heal, especially in the mouth.
  • U – Unusual bleeding or discharge (from rectum, vagina, nipple, in urine or sputum; bleeding after menopause or after intercourse).
  • T – Thickening or lump in the breast, testis or elsewhere.
  • I – Indigestion or difficulty in swallowing.
  • O – Obvious change in a wart or mole.
  • N – Nagging cough or hoarseness of voice. Other warning signs: unexplained weight loss, persistent fever, unexplained anaemia, persistent pain and white or red patches in the mouth.

(b) Levels of prevention of cancer (5 marks) 1. Primordial and primary prevention – preventing cancer from developing

  • Tobacco control – the single most important measure; avoid smoking, gutkha, khaini, mishri and betel quid with tobacco; enforcement of COTPA, 2003 (no smoking in public places, no sale to minors or near schools, pictorial health warnings); the national tobacco quitline; counselling and nicotine replacement for quitters.
  • Avoid alcohol and areca nut.
  • Vaccination – hepatitis B vaccine (prevents liver cancer) and HPV vaccine (prevents cervical cancer); India launched a free nationwide HPV vaccination campaign for adolescent girls in 2026.
  • Healthy diet – plenty of fruits, vegetables and fibre; less red and processed meat, salt-preserved and burnt foods; maintain healthy weight; regular physical activity.
  • Infection control – treatment of H. pylori, safe sex (HPV, HIV), safe injections and blood (hepatitis B and C).
  • Occupational and environmental safety – protection from asbestos, benzene, dyes, radiation and pesticides; reduction of indoor smoke and air pollution.
  • Sun protection; breastfeeding (reduces breast cancer risk); avoiding unnecessary radiation and hormone use.

2. Secondary prevention – early detection and prompt treatment

  • Screening of apparently healthy people (oral, breast and cervical cancer) and early diagnosis of people with warning signs – cancer detected early is often curable and cheaper to treat.
  • Self-examination – breast self-examination, testicular self-examination and mouth self-examination.
  • Treatment of pre-cancerous lesions (leukoplakia, oral submucous fibrosis, cervical intraepithelial neoplasia).

3. Tertiary prevention – limiting disability and improving quality of life

  • Complete treatment (surgery, radiotherapy, chemotherapy), rehabilitation (prosthesis, speech therapy after laryngectomy, stoma care, lymphoedema care), palliative care, pain relief and psychosocial support; follow-up to detect recurrence.

(c) Cancer screening programmes in India and the role of the nurse (7 marks) 1. National framework

  • Cancer prevention and control is part of the National Programme for Prevention and Control of Non-Communicable Diseases (NP-NCD) (earlier NPCDCS), implemented under the National Health Mission.
  • Population-based screening for the three common cancers is offered to all adults aged 30 years and above at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (health sub-centres and PHCs), with referral to NCD clinics, district hospitals, medical colleges and tertiary cancer centres; tobacco cessation and health promotion are integrated.
  • Treatment is supported through district day-care chemotherapy centres, tertiary cancer care centres, the National Cancer Grid and health insurance under Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY.

2. Screening methods

  • Oral cancer – oral visual examination (OVE) by trained health workers; look for white or red patches, ulcers, growths and restricted mouth opening; recommended every 5 years for people above 30, and more often for tobacco users.
  • Breast cancer – clinical breast examination (CBE) by trained health workers every 5 years for women above 30; breast awareness and self-examination; mammography for high-risk women and for diagnosis.
  • Cervical cancer – visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) every 5 years for women aged 30–65; positive areas turn white; "screen and treat" with cryotherapy or thermal ablation in the same visit; HPV DNA testing and Pap smear where available.

3. Role of the nurse

  1. Community mobilisation – create awareness of cancer warning signs, risk factors and the availability of free screening through ASHAs, self-help groups, schools and workplaces; address fear and stigma.
  2. Enumeration and risk assessment – help prepare the list of people aged 30+ and use the community-based risk assessment checklist.
  3. Performing screening – trained nurses perform oral visual examination, clinical breast examination and VIA, maintaining privacy and dignity (female staff for women).
  4. Teaching self-examination – breast, testicular and mouth self-examination with demonstrations.
  5. Referral and follow-up – ensure screen-positive people reach the higher centre for confirmation (biopsy, mammography, colposcopy) and treatment; track defaulters.
  6. Tobacco cessation counselling using the 5 A's (Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange follow-up); referral to cessation centres and the quitline.
  7. Vaccination – hepatitis B and HPV vaccination and counselling of parents.
  8. Records and reporting on the NCD portal; health education on diet, exercise and alcohol.
  9. Psychological support to people found positive and to their families; linkage to treatment schemes.

Common cancers in India and their main risk factors (for health education)

  • Oral cavity cancer – the commonest cancer in Indian men; caused mainly by chewing tobacco (gutkha, khaini, mishri), betel quid with tobacco, areca nut, smoking (including bidis) and alcohol; preceded by leukoplakia, erythroplakia and oral submucous fibrosis, which can be detected by a simple mouth examination.
  • Lung cancer – smoking, second-hand smoke, indoor smoke from biomass fuels (chulha), air pollution and occupational exposure such as asbestos.
  • Breast cancer – late first pregnancy, fewer children, short or no breastfeeding, obesity, physical inactivity and family history.
  • Cervical cancer – persistent infection with high-risk HPV (types 16 and 18), early marriage and first intercourse, many pregnancies, multiple sexual partners, smoking and HIV infection; almost entirely preventable by vaccination and screening.
  • Oesophageal, stomach and colorectal cancers – very hot beverages, salted, smoked and pickled foods, alcohol, tobacco, low-fibre diet, obesity and H. pylori infection.
  • Liver cancer – chronic hepatitis B and C infection, alcohol-related cirrhosis and aflatoxin-contaminated food.
  • Gall bladder cancer – common in the Gangetic plains, associated with gallstones.
  • Childhood cancers – leukaemias, brain tumours, retinoblastoma and lymphomas; many are curable when children are referred early.

Cancer registration – the National Cancer Registry Programme of ICMR collects data from population-based and hospital-based cancer registries; nurses help by recording and reporting cancer cases accurately, which guides planning of services.

Nursing importance

  • Most cancers in India are diagnosed late; nurses at the primary level can change this by educating people about warning signs, screening them and making sure positive cases reach treatment.

Conclusion Cancer is uncontrolled cell growth with invasion and spread, often announced by the CAUTION warning signs. Tobacco control, vaccination and healthy lifestyles prevent many cancers, while screening for oral, breast and cervical cancers under NP-NCD detects them early. Nurses are central to awareness, screening, referral and follow-up.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Oncological Conditions (including Palliative Care Module)
question: (a) Define radiotherapy and list its types. (3 marks) (b) Explain the side effects of radiotherapy. (4 marks) (c) Describe the nursing care of a patient receiving external radiotherapy and brachytherapy, including radiation safety. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Radiation protection: time, distance and shielding
labels: nurse spending minimum time near a brachytherapy patient
lead shield between nurse and patient
TLD badge worn on the chest
radiation warning sign on the door

answer_html:
(a) Definition and types (3 marks) Radiotherapy is the use of high-energy ionising radiation (X-rays, gamma rays, electrons, protons) to destroy cancer cells by damaging their DNA, so that they cannot divide. Normal cells are also affected but recover better, which is why radiation is given in small daily doses (fractions). It may be curative (e.g. cancer cervix, head and neck), adjuvant (after surgery), neoadjuvant (before surgery) or palliative (bone pain, bleeding, spinal cord compression, brain metastases). About half of all cancer patients need radiotherapy at some stage.

Types

  1. External beam radiotherapy (teletherapy) – radiation from a machine outside the body – linear accelerator (LINAC) or cobalt-60 unit; modern techniques include 3D conformal radiotherapy, IMRT (intensity-modulated), image-guided radiotherapy, stereotactic radiosurgery (e.g. Gamma Knife) and proton therapy. The patient is not radioactive.
  2. Brachytherapy (internal, sealed-source radiotherapy) – a sealed radioactive source is placed inside or close to the tumour: intracavitary (uterus and vagina for cancer cervix), interstitial (needles or seeds in the breast, prostate, tongue), intraluminal (oesophagus, bronchus) and surface moulds; given as high dose rate (HDR, e.g. iridium-192) for minutes or low dose rate (LDR) over days or permanent seeds.
  3. Unsealed-source (systemic) radiotherapy – radioactive substances given by mouth or IV, e.g. radioactive iodine (I-131) for thyroid cancer and hyperthyroidism, radium-223 and lutetium-177 therapies; body fluids are radioactive for some days.

(b) Side effects of radiotherapy (4 marks) Side effects depend on the area treated, total dose and fraction size, and are mostly limited to the treated area.

1. Acute (early) effects – during and up to a few weeks after treatment

  • Fatigue – the commonest general effect.
  • Skin reactions in the treated area – redness, dryness, itching, darkening, and dry or moist desquamation in skin folds.
  • Hair loss only in the treated area (e.g. scalp in brain radiotherapy).
  • Head and neck – oral mucositis, sore throat, dry mouth (xerostomia), loss of taste, difficulty swallowing, oral thrush.
  • Chest – oesophagitis (painful swallowing), cough, radiation pneumonitis.
  • Abdomen and pelvis – nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, proctitis, cystitis (frequency, burning), vaginal irritation.
  • Bone-marrow suppression when large areas of marrow are treated – low WBC, platelets and Hb.
  • Loss of appetite and weight loss.

2. Late effects – months to years later

  • Fibrosis and skin thickening, telangiectasia; permanent dry mouth and dental caries; osteoradionecrosis of the jaw.
  • Lymphoedema (after axillary radiation), lung fibrosis, heart damage (left-sided breast cancer).
  • Bowel and bladder changes – chronic proctitis, bleeding, strictures; vaginal stenosis.
  • Infertility, early menopause, hypothyroidism (neck radiation), cataract, growth problems in children, and rarely second cancers.

(c) Nursing care (8 marks) A. Before treatment

  • Explain the purpose, schedule (usually 5 days a week for several weeks), simulation (planning CT), skin marks or tattoos, immobilisation masks or moulds, and that the treatment is painless; reassure that external radiotherapy does not make the patient radioactive.
  • Dental check-up and extraction of decayed teeth before head and neck radiotherapy (prevents osteoradionecrosis); nutrition assessment; obtain consent.

B. Nursing care during external radiotherapy

  1. Skin care in the treated area
    • Do not wash off the marking lines; wash gently with lukewarm water and mild soap and pat dry; do not rub or scrub.
    • Avoid perfumes, talcum powder, deodorants, alcohol-based lotions, and creams unless prescribed (do not apply creams just before treatment).
    • Wear loose, soft cotton clothes; avoid tight bras or collars over the area.
    • Avoid sun exposure, heat (hot-water bags) and ice packs; use an electric razor instead of a blade.
    • Report blistering or weeping skin (moist desquamation) – it is dressed with non-adherent dressings as advised.
  2. Mouth care in head and neck radiotherapy – soft toothbrush, saline or soda bicarbonate mouthwashes several times a day, fluoride gel, no tobacco or alcohol, soft moist bland foods, sips of water for dry mouth, treatment of thrush, analgesics before meals.
  3. Nutrition – high-calorie, high-protein diet with plenty of fluids; small frequent meals; feeding tube when swallowing is very painful; weekly weight.
  4. Gastrointestinal and urinary symptoms – antiemetics; low-residue diet and fluids for diarrhoea; perianal care; plenty of fluids for cystitis.
  5. Fatigue – plan rest periods and light exercise.
  6. Blood counts – weekly CBC when marrow is irradiated; infection precautions.
  7. Emotional support and encouragement to complete the full course without gaps.

C. Nursing care during brachytherapy

  • Intracavitary brachytherapy (cancer cervix) – bowel preparation, urinary catheter, applicator insertion under anaesthesia; the patient lies still in bed during treatment to prevent displacement; low-residue diet; after removal of the applicator, watch for bleeding and discharge; teach vaginal dilator use to prevent stenosis.
  • For LDR or high-activity sources kept in the patient for hours or days, the patient is nursed in a single shielded room with a radiation warning sign; visitors are limited (no pregnant women or children), and staff time is limited.
  • If a source is dislodged – never touch it with the hands; pick it up with long-handled forceps and place it in the lead container kept in the room; inform the radiation safety officer.
  • After the source is removed, the patient is no longer radioactive (except permanent seed implants, which have special instructions).

D. Radiation safety for nurses (ALARA – "as low as reasonably achievable")

  • Time – spend the minimum necessary time near a patient with a radioactive source; plan and do care efficiently; rotate staff.
  • Distance – keep as far as practical from the source (radiation falls with the square of the distance); talk to the patient from the doorway when possible.
  • Shielding – use mobile lead shields and lead aprons where appropriate; sources are stored in lead containers.
  • Monitoring – wear a personal dosimeter (TLD badge); follow the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) limits; pregnant staff should not care for patients with radioactive sources.
  • Unsealed sources (radioiodine) – isolation room, disposable utensils, flushing the toilet twice, careful handling of urine, vomit and linen as per protocol.

E. Discharge teaching

  • Continue skin and mouth care; protect the treated skin from sun for at least a year; report fever, bleeding, severe diarrhoea or difficulty swallowing; attend follow-up; vaginal dilator use and resumption of sexual activity after pelvic radiotherapy as advised; contraception during treatment.

Nursing importance

  • Most side effects of radiotherapy can be prevented or reduced by good skin and mouth care, nutrition and encouragement, which help patients complete the full course – essential for cure.
  • Knowledge of time, distance and shielding protects nurses, other patients and visitors.

Conclusion Radiotherapy uses ionising radiation, given externally, as brachytherapy or as unsealed isotopes, to destroy cancer cells. Its acute and late side effects depend on the area treated. Careful preparation, skin, mouth and nutritional care, emotional support and strict radiation safety based on time, distance and shielding are the key nursing responsibilities.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Oncological Conditions (including Palliative Care Module)
question: Mrs. Z, aged 48 years, has a painless hard lump in her left breast. She is diagnosed with carcinoma of the breast and is posted for modified radical mastectomy. (a) Explain the risk factors and clinical manifestations of breast cancer. (4 marks) (b) Explain the medical and surgical management of breast cancer. (4 marks) (c) Describe the pre-operative and post-operative nursing care of Mrs. Z. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: Arm exercises after mastectomy
labels: squeezing a ball and bending the elbow on day 1
arms raised overhead with hands clasped behind the head

answer_html:
(a) Risk factors and clinical manifestations (4 marks) Breast cancer is the commonest cancer among women in India, increasingly seen in women in their 40s and often diagnosed at an advanced stage.

1. Risk factors

  • Increasing age, female sex.
  • Family history of breast or ovarian cancer; BRCA1 and BRCA2 gene mutations.
  • Long exposure to oestrogen – early menarche (before 12 years), late menopause (after 55 years), nulliparity, first full-term pregnancy after 30 years, not breastfeeding, long-term hormone replacement therapy.
  • Obesity after menopause, physical inactivity, alcohol, high-fat diet.
  • Previous breast cancer, some benign breast diseases (atypical hyperplasia), chest radiation in young age.

2. Clinical manifestations

  • Painless, hard, irregular lump, commonly in the upper outer quadrant, fixed to surrounding tissue.
  • Skin changes – dimpling, peau d'orange (orange-peel skin due to lymphatic blockage), redness, ulceration (fungating growth).
  • Nipple changes – retraction, deviation, bloody discharge, eczema-like changes (Paget's disease).
  • Axillary lymph node enlargement; change in size or shape of the breast.
  • Advanced disease – bone pain (bone metastases), breathlessness (lung, pleural effusion), jaundice (liver), headache (brain).

(b) Medical and surgical management (4 marks) 1. Diagnosis – "triple assessment"

  • Clinical breast examination, imaging (mammography; ultrasound in younger women) and tissue diagnosis by core needle biopsy (or FNAC of nodes).
  • Hormone receptors (ER, PR) and HER2 status guide treatment; staging by TNM with chest, abdominal and bone imaging as needed.

2. Surgery

  • Breast-conserving surgery (lumpectomy/wide local excision) followed by radiotherapy – for early, small tumours.
  • Modified radical mastectomy (MRM) – removal of the whole breast with axillary lymph nodes, preserving the pectoral muscles.
  • Sentinel lymph node biopsy to decide whether full axillary clearance is needed.
  • Breast reconstruction (immediate or delayed) with implants or the patient's own tissue.

3. Systemic and other therapy

  • Chemotherapy – neoadjuvant (before surgery, to shrink the tumour) or adjuvant (after surgery), e.g. anthracycline- and taxane-based regimens.
  • Hormone therapy for ER/PR-positive cancers – tamoxifen (pre-menopausal) or aromatase inhibitors (letrozole, anastrozole) (post-menopausal), usually for 5–10 years.
  • Targeted therapy – trastuzumab for HER2-positive cancers.
  • Radiotherapy to the chest wall, breast and lymph nodes after surgery when indicated.
  • Palliative care for advanced disease (bone-strengthening drugs, pain control).

(c) Nursing care of Mrs. Z (7 marks) A. Pre-operative care

  1. Psychological preparation – breast cancer and loss of a breast threaten femininity and body image; listen to her fears, give accurate information, involve her husband and family, and introduce a recovered survivor if possible.
  2. Explain the operation, drains, arm exercises and the availability of breast prostheses and reconstruction; obtain informed consent.
  3. Routine pre-operative preparation – investigations, blood grouping, skin preparation, NPO; mark the arm on the operated side ("no BP, no injections").
  4. Teach deep breathing and the first arm exercises before surgery.

B. Post-operative care

  1. Vital signs and pain relief – regular analgesics so that she can breathe deeply and start exercises.
  2. Wound and drain care
    • Check the dressing for bleeding; ensure the closed suction drain works – keep it below the wound, maintain vacuum, avoid kinks, record the amount and colour of drainage.
    • Drains are usually removed when drainage falls to about 30–50 mL in 24 hours; watch for seroma (fluid collection) after removal, haematoma and wound infection.
  3. Positioning – semi-Fowler's position with the affected arm elevated on a pillow above the level of the heart to reduce swelling.
  4. Arm exercises (graduated, as advised by the surgeon)
    • Day 1 – flexing and extending the fingers, squeezing a soft ball, bending the elbow and wrist, combing the hair, brushing the teeth with the affected hand.
    • After drains are removed (or as advised) – shoulder exercises: pendulum swings, wall climbing with the fingers, rope turning, pulley exercises and clasping the hands behind the head – to regain full shoulder movement and prevent a frozen shoulder.
  5. Prevention of lymphoedema (lifelong, especially after axillary clearance)
    • No BP measurement, injections, IV lines or blood sampling in the affected arm.
    • Avoid cuts, burns, insect bites, tight bangles, watches and sleeves; wear gloves for gardening and kitchen work; use an electric razor for the armpit.
    • Avoid carrying heavy weights with that arm; keep the arm elevated when resting; report swelling, heaviness or redness early.
  6. Body image and emotional care
    • Encourage her to look at the wound when she is ready; allow expression of grief; involve her spouse.
    • Advise a soft, temporary prosthesis or padded bra after the wound heals, and a fitted silicone prosthesis later; discuss reconstruction options.
    • Address sexuality and intimacy concerns; refer to support groups and counselling.
  7. Adjuvant treatment preparation – explain chemotherapy, radiotherapy and hormone therapy and their side effects (hair loss, nausea, hot flushes).

C. Discharge teaching

  • Wound care, continued arm exercises, lymphoedema precautions.
  • Monthly breast self-examination of the other breast and the chest wall, yearly mammography and regular follow-up.
  • Healthy diet, exercise, weight control; regular intake of hormone tablets; report bone pain, breathlessness, cough or new lumps.
  • Genetic counselling for her daughters and sisters if there is a strong family history or BRCA mutation.

D. Nursing diagnoses for Mrs. Z (examples)

  • Acute pain related to surgical incision – regular analgesics, positioning, splinting the chest wall during coughing.
  • Risk for infection and seroma related to the wound and drains – aseptic drain care, observation of the wound and temperature.
  • Impaired physical mobility of the affected arm – graduated arm and shoulder exercises with the physiotherapist.
  • Risk for lymphoedema related to removal of axillary lymph nodes – arm care teaching and early reporting of swelling.
  • Disturbed body image and anxiety related to loss of the breast and the cancer diagnosis – counselling, prosthesis advice, family and peer support.

E. Care during adjuvant therapy

  • Chemotherapy – antiemetics before each cycle, preparation for hair loss (scarf, wig), infection precautions and regular blood counts, mouth care.
  • Radiotherapy – gentle skin care of the chest wall and axilla, loose cotton clothing, avoidance of sun and heat on the treated area.
  • Tamoxifen – hot flushes; report abnormal vaginal bleeding (risk of endometrial changes), leg swelling or chest pain (blood clots).
  • Aromatase inhibitors – joint pains and bone loss; calcium, vitamin D, exercise and bone-density checks.
  • Trastuzumab – heart function (echocardiography) is checked regularly; report breathlessness or ankle swelling.

Nursing importance
