  • Early arm exercises and lifelong lymphoedema precautions decide how well Mrs. Z regains arm function, while sensitive support for body-image changes helps her return to normal family and social life.

Conclusion Breast cancer, linked to age, genetics and prolonged oestrogen exposure, usually presents as a painless hard lump. Triple assessment, surgery (breast-conserving or modified radical mastectomy), chemotherapy, hormone and targeted therapy and radiotherapy form its treatment. Skilled drain and wound care, graduated arm exercises, lymphoedema prevention and compassionate psychological support are the key nursing responsibilities.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Oncological Conditions (including Palliative Care Module)
question: (a) Define palliative care and explain its principles. (3 marks) (b) Explain the management of pain in cancer, including the WHO analgesic ladder. (5 marks) (c) Describe the nursing management of common distressing symptoms and end-of-life care. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: WHO analgesic ladder for cancer pain
labels: NSAID) with or without adjuvant; step 2 – weak opioid (tramadol
codeine) plus non-opioid; step 3 – strong opioid (morphine) plus non-opioid; adjuvants at every step

answer_html:
(a) Definition and principles (3 marks) According to WHO, palliative care is an approach that improves the quality of life of patients (adults and children) and their families facing the problems associated with life-threatening illness, through the prevention and relief of suffering by early identification, assessment and treatment of pain and other problems – physical, psychosocial and spiritual. It is needed in cancer, advanced heart, lung, kidney and liver disease, HIV, neurological diseases and frailty. India's National Programme for Palliative Care, launched in 2012, has been extended to most districts.

Principles

  1. Provides relief from pain and other distressing symptoms.
  2. Affirms life and regards dying as a normal process; neither hastens nor postpones death.
  3. Integrates the psychological and spiritual aspects of care ("total pain" – physical, emotional, social and spiritual).
  4. Offers a support system to help patients live as actively as possible until death.
  5. Supports the family during the illness and in bereavement.
  6. Uses a team approach – doctors, nurses, counsellors, social workers, volunteers and family.
  7. Is applicable early in the course of illness, together with curative treatments such as chemotherapy or radiotherapy.

(b) Management of cancer pain (5 marks) 1. Assessment

  • Ask about site, nature (aching, burning, shooting), severity (0–10 numerical or faces scale), timing, aggravating and relieving factors and effect on sleep, mood and activity; believe the patient's report.
  • Identify the type – nociceptive (bone, soft tissue, visceral) or neuropathic (nerve compression or damage) – and look for causes needing specific treatment (fracture, spinal cord compression, infection).

2. WHO analgesic ladder

  • Step 1 – mild pain: non-opioid – paracetamol or an NSAID (ibuprofen, diclofenac), ± adjuvant.
  • Step 2 – moderate pain: weak opioid – tramadol or codeine – plus a non-opioid ± adjuvant.
  • Step 3 – severe pain: strong opioid – morphine (drug of choice), fentanyl patches or methadone – plus a non-opioid ± adjuvant.
  • Severe pain may be started directly on step 3; the aim is a pain-free patient, not merely reduced pain.

3. WHO guidelines for giving analgesics

  • By mouth (oral route whenever possible), by the clock (regular doses, not "as needed"), by the ladder, for the individual (dose titrated to relief – there is no fixed maximum for morphine), and with attention to detail.
  • Oral immediate-release morphine is usually started at 2.5–5 mg every 4 hours and titrated; a "rescue" (breakthrough) dose of about one-sixth of the total daily dose is given for pain between regular doses.
  • Adjuvant drugs – dexamethasone (nerve compression, liver capsule pain, raised ICP), amitriptyline, gabapentin or pregabalin (neuropathic pain), bisphosphonates (bone pain), antispasmodics (colic).
  • Prevent opioid side effects – regular laxatives for every patient on opioids (constipation does not improve with time), antiemetics for the first few days, and watch for drowsiness, confusion and myoclonus; respiratory depression is rare when doses are titrated correctly.

4. Non-drug measures and other treatments

  • Positioning, warm or cold application, gentle massage, relaxation, music, distraction, prayer and reassurance; palliative radiotherapy for bone pain; nerve blocks.

5. Access to opioids

  • The NDPS (Amendment) Act, 2014 created "Essential Narcotic Drugs" (including morphine, fentanyl and methadone) with simplified rules, so that recognised medical institutions can stock and dispense them for pain relief.

(c) Nursing management of distressing symptoms and end-of-life care (7 marks) A. Common distressing symptoms

  1. Constipation – fluids, fibre and regular laxatives; check for impaction.
  2. Nausea and vomiting – find the cause (opioids, constipation, bowel obstruction, raised ICP, hypercalcaemia); antiemetics (metoclopramide, haloperidol, ondansetron); small, cold, bland meals; fresh air; mouth care.
  3. Breathlessness – sit upright, fan or open window, oxygen if hypoxic, low-dose oral morphine relieves the sensation of breathlessness, treatment of effusion or infection, breathing and relaxation techniques; stay calm with the patient.
  4. Anorexia and weight loss – small, frequent, favourite foods; no forced feeding; low-dose steroids may improve appetite; explain to the family that reduced intake is part of the illness.
  5. Mouth problems – regular mouth care, treat thrush, sips of water or ice for dry mouth, soft diet.
  6. Fatigue and weakness – energy conservation, assistance with activities.
  7. Pressure sores and fungating wounds – pressure-relieving measures, gentle cleansing, non-adherent absorbent dressings, metronidazole (oral or topical) to control odour, charcoal dressings and control of bleeding.
  8. Lymphoedema – elevation, skin care, gentle massage and compression.
  9. Delirium and agitation – identify reversible causes (infection, drugs, dehydration, retention of urine, constipation); calm, safe environment; familiar people; haloperidol as ordered.
  10. Anxiety, depression and spiritual distress – listen, allow expression of feelings, involve the family and spiritual leaders, counselling and antidepressants when needed.

B. End-of-life care (last days and hours)

  1. Recognise signs of approaching death – increasing weakness and sleepiness, reduced intake, difficulty swallowing, cold and mottled extremities, falling BP, reduced urine output, irregular breathing (Cheyne–Stokes, apnoea) and noisy breathing.
  2. Review medicines – stop non-essential drugs; give essential drugs (analgesic, antiemetic, sedative) by subcutaneous route if swallowing is not possible.
  3. Comfort care – mouth and lip care, eye care, positioning, pressure-area care, keeping the patient clean and dry, and a calm, quiet environment.
  4. "Death rattle" (noisy secretions) – reposition on the side, gentle suction only if helpful, and anticholinergic drugs (hyoscine butylbromide, glycopyrrolate) as ordered; reassure the family that it is not distressing to the patient.
  5. Respect wishes and dignity – place of death (home or hospital), religious rites and rituals, presence of family members; avoid unnecessary procedures, according to advance directives and decisions about withholding life-sustaining treatment.
  6. Communication with the family – explain what is happening honestly and gently; encourage them to talk to, touch and stay with the patient (hearing is believed to remain until late).
  7. After death – confirm death, show respect, perform last offices according to religious and cultural customs, allow the family time with the body, help with documents (death certificate), and offer bereavement support; care for children who have lost a parent.
  8. Self-care of nurses – debriefing and support to prevent burnout.

C. Communication and family support

  • Share information honestly and gently, at the patient's pace, using a structured approach (for example, the SPIKES steps); allow silence, emotions and questions; never take away all hope – shift hope towards comfort, time with family and achievable goals.
  • Discuss advance care planning – the patient's wishes about place of care, life-sustaining treatment and spiritual needs – and document them.
  • Involve and train family caregivers in feeding, positioning, mouth care, giving oral morphine and recognising danger signs; arrange home-based palliative care visits and respite.
  • Link families with community palliative care networks and volunteers (such as Kerala's neighbourhood palliative care model), social welfare schemes and support groups.

Nursing importance

  • Nurses spend the most time with patients at the end of life; their skill in assessing and relieving pain and other symptoms and their compassionate presence make the greatest difference to the patient's comfort and the family's experience.

Conclusion Palliative care relieves suffering and improves quality of life for patients with life-threatening illness and their families. Regular, oral, titrated analgesia following the WHO ladder controls most cancer pain, while skilful management of symptoms and compassionate end-of-life and bereavement care ensure a peaceful and dignified death.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Oncological Conditions (including Palliative Care Module)
question: Explain the complementary and alternative therapies used in palliative care and the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Introduction Complementary therapies are therapies used along with conventional medical treatment to improve comfort and well-being; alternative therapies are used in place of conventional treatment. In palliative care, complementary therapies are valued because they relieve symptoms such as pain, anxiety, breathlessness, nausea and insomnia, give patients a sense of control and support the "whole person" – body, mind and spirit. They must never replace effective treatment.

1. Types of complementary therapies

  • Mind–body therapies
    • Yoga (gentle asanas adapted to the patient's strength), pranayama and breathing exercises.
    • Meditation, mindfulness, progressive muscle relaxation and guided imagery – reduce anxiety, pain perception and insomnia.
    • Hypnotherapy and biofeedback.
  • Creative and expressive therapies
    • Music therapy – listening to or making music (bhajans, favourite songs) to reduce anxiety and pain and improve mood.
    • Art therapy, writing, reminiscence and life-review (legacy work, e.g. letters or recordings for children).
  • Touch and body-based therapies
    • Gentle massage – relaxation, improved sleep, reduced pain and anxiety.
    • Aromatherapy – essential oils such as lavender inhaled or diluted for massage.
    • Reflexology (pressure on points of the feet or hands) and acupressure (e.g. the P6 point on the wrist for nausea).
    • Acupuncture – for pain, nausea and hot flushes, by trained practitioners.
  • Energy and spiritual therapies – Reiki and therapeutic touch; prayer, chanting, reading of religious texts and spiritual counselling.
  • AYUSH systems – Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha, Homoeopathy and Naturopathy, used by many Indian families along with modern treatment.
  • Others – pet therapy, laughter therapy, hot and cold applications, and TENS (transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation) for pain.

2. Benefits

  • Reduced pain, anxiety, depression and nausea; better sleep and relaxation; improved coping, dignity and quality of life; involvement of family members in care (e.g. hand massage by relatives).

3. Cautions

  • Must not replace proven treatments such as pain medicines, chemotherapy or radiotherapy.
  • Herbal products can interact with chemotherapy, anticoagulants and other drugs, and some contain heavy metals or steroids; they should be disclosed to the treating team.
  • Massage – avoid pressure over tumour sites, radiotherapy fields, fractures, open wounds, swollen legs with suspected DVT and in patients with very low platelets; use gentle touch only.
  • Essential oils must be diluted and avoided in patients with allergies or asthma.
  • Choose qualified practitioners; avoid costly unproven "cures" that exploit desperate families.

4. Role of the nurse

  1. Ask every patient about complementary and herbal therapies in a non-judgemental way and record them.
  2. Provide accurate, evidence-based information on benefits and risks.
  3. Use simple safe measures in daily care – relaxation and breathing exercises, music, gentle hand or foot massage, positioning and comfort measures.
  4. Respect cultural and religious beliefs; arrange spiritual support when requested.
  5. Coordinate with the palliative care team and qualified practitioners; observe and report effects and side effects.
  6. Teach family members simple comfort therapies so that they can participate in care.

Conclusion Complementary therapies such as yoga, meditation, music, massage, aromatherapy, acupressure and spiritual care can relieve symptoms and improve well-being in palliative care when used alongside conventional treatment. The nurse ensures they are safe, evidence-based, culturally respectful and coordinated with the patient's overall care.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Oncological Conditions (including Palliative Care Module)
question: Explain the common oncological emergencies and their nursing management.
answer_html:
Introduction Oncological emergencies are acute, potentially life-threatening conditions caused by the cancer itself or its treatment. Early recognition and prompt treatment can save life and prevent permanent disability such as paralysis.

1. Metabolic emergencies

  • Tumour lysis syndrome (TLS) – rapid breakdown of cancer cells, usually within 1–3 days of starting chemotherapy for fast-growing cancers (acute leukaemias, high-grade lymphomas), releases cell contents into the blood: high potassium, phosphate and uric acid, low calcium → acute kidney injury, arrhythmias, seizures.
    • Prevention and treatment – IV hydration (urine output above about 100 mL/hour), allopurinol or rasburicase before chemotherapy, monitoring of electrolytes and kidney function every 6–12 hours, treatment of hyperkalaemia and dialysis if needed.
  • Hypercalcaemia of malignancy – in myeloma and cancers of breast, lung and kidney (bone metastases or PTH-related peptide): thirst, polyuria, dehydration, constipation, nausea, confusion, drowsiness and arrhythmias.
    • Treatment – IV normal saline, bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid), calcitonin, denosumab; mobilise the patient.
  • SIADH – mainly small-cell lung cancer: low sodium, confusion and seizures; fluid restriction and treatment of the cancer.

2. Structural (obstructive) emergencies

  • Superior vena cava syndrome – compression of the SVC by lung cancer or lymphoma: swelling of the face, neck and arms, distended neck and chest veins, breathlessness and headache.
    • Management – sit the patient upright, oxygen, steroids, radiotherapy or chemotherapy, and stenting; avoid IV lines and BP measurement in the arms.
  • Malignant spinal cord compression – vertebral metastases (breast, prostate, lung, myeloma): back pain (often the first sign, worse on lying or coughing), then weakness of legs, sensory level and bladder and bowel dysfunction.
    • Management – urgent MRI, high-dose dexamethasone, radiotherapy or surgical decompression within 24 hours; log-rolling and spinal precautions; neurological checks. Function at the time of treatment determines outcome.
  • Malignant pericardial effusion and cardiac tamponade – breathlessness, hypotension, raised JVP and muffled heart sounds; urgent pericardiocentesis.
  • Raised intracranial pressure from brain metastases – headache, vomiting and drowsiness; dexamethasone, mannitol and radiotherapy.

3. Haematological and infective emergencies

  • Febrile neutropenia – fever of 38 °C or more with neutrophil count below 500/mm³ after chemotherapy; may progress rapidly to septic shock.
    • Management – blood cultures and broad-spectrum IV antibiotics within one hour, fluids, protective care and growth factors as ordered.
  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation, hyperviscosity (myeloma, very high WBC) and severe bleeding from tumours or low platelets.

4. Nursing management

  1. Educate patients and families about warning signs – fever, back pain, leg weakness, facial swelling, confusion, reduced urine – and to report immediately, day or night.
  2. Monitor vital signs, temperature, intake–output, electrolytes, calcium and creatinine, and neurological status during high-risk treatments.
  3. Ensure hydration and timely prophylactic drugs (allopurinol, antiemetics); record urine output hourly in TLS.
  4. Give antibiotics, steroids and other drugs on time; prepare for urgent procedures (MRI, radiotherapy, pericardiocentesis).
  5. Provide positioning (upright in SVC syndrome, spinal precautions in cord compression), oxygen and cardiac monitoring.
  6. Give psychological support and communicate clearly with the family; involve the palliative care team in advanced disease.

Conclusion Tumour lysis syndrome, hypercalcaemia, SVC syndrome, spinal cord compression, cardiac tamponade and febrile neutropenia are the main oncological emergencies. Prevention in high-risk patients, early recognition of warning signs and rapid treatment, with vigilant nursing monitoring, prevent death and disability.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Oncological Conditions (including Palliative Care Module)
question: Explain the nursing responsibilities in the administration of chemotherapy, including safe handling of cytotoxic drugs.
answer_html:
Introduction Chemotherapy drugs are cytotoxic – they destroy rapidly dividing cells – and have a narrow margin of safety. Errors in dose or route can be fatal, and staff who handle them can be harmed by exposure. Nurses who give chemotherapy must be specially trained and follow strict protocols.

1. Before administration

  1. Verify the prescription – patient identity, diagnosis, protocol, cycle and day, drug, dose calculated by body surface area (BSA) from current height and weight, route, rate and sequence; dose adjustments for kidney or liver function.
  2. Independent double-check of the prescription and the prepared drug by two trained nurses (or nurse and pharmacist).
  3. Check laboratory results – complete blood count (neutrophils and platelets above the required limits), kidney and liver function; inform the doctor of abnormal values.
  4. Ensure informed consent and patient education about the purpose, schedule and side effects.
  5. Give premedications as ordered – antiemetics (ondansetron, dexamethasone, aprepitant), antihistamines or steroids for drugs causing reactions; ensure hydration (e.g. before cisplatin).

2. During administration

  1. Venous access – choose a good vein (avoid joints, the hand dorsum for vesicants, and limbs with lymphoedema); for prolonged or vesicant therapy use a central venous catheter, PICC line or implanted port; check blood return before and during the infusion.
  2. Correct route – never give drugs meant for IV use by other routes (e.g. vincristine must never be given intrathecally – it is fatal); label lines clearly.
  3. Give drugs in the correct sequence and rate using infusion pumps; flush with compatible fluid between drugs.
  4. Monitor for infusion reactions (flushing, breathlessness, chest pain, low BP) – stop the infusion and give emergency treatment; keep the anaphylaxis kit ready.
  5. Extravasation (leakage of a vesicant such as doxorubicin or vincristine into tissues causes severe necrosis):
    • Watch for pain, burning, swelling or redness at the site, or absent blood return.
    • Stop the infusion immediately, leave the cannula in place and aspirate as much drug as possible, then remove the cannula; do not flush.
    • Elevate the limb; apply cold packs for most drugs (e.g. anthracyclines) but warm packs for vinca alkaloids; give antidotes as per protocol (e.g. dexrazoxane, hyaluronidase); mark and document the area and inform the doctor; follow up for tissue damage.

3. Safe handling of cytotoxic drugs

  1. Preparation in a dedicated area within a biological safety cabinet (class II) by trained personnel, ideally using closed-system transfer devices.
  2. Personal protective equipment – chemotherapy-tested gloves (double gloving), long-sleeved impermeable gown, eye protection and mask when there is splash risk.
  3. Transport in sealed, labelled, leak-proof containers.
  4. Spills – use a cytotoxic spill kit; wear PPE, contain and absorb the spill, clean from the outside inwards and dispose of material as cytotoxic waste; report the incident.
  5. Waste disposal – used syringes, vials, IV sets, gloves and gowns go into cytotoxic waste containers (yellow category, labelled "cytotoxic") as per the Biomedical Waste Management Rules, 2016, for incineration.
  6. Patient excreta – wear gloves and gown when handling urine, stool, vomit and soiled linen for about 48 hours after chemotherapy.
  7. Staff protection – no eating or drinking in preparation areas; hand washing after removing gloves; pregnant and breastfeeding staff should avoid handling cytotoxic drugs; health monitoring of staff.

4. After administration

  • Monitor for and manage side effects – nausea and vomiting, mucositis, myelosuppression, alopecia, fatigue and organ toxicity; maintain intake–output; give post-chemotherapy antiemetics.
  • Educate the patient about infection prevention, mouth care, fluids, contraception, when to report fever, bleeding or diarrhoea, and the date of the next cycle.
  • Document drugs, doses, times, site, reactions and patient education.

Conclusion Safe chemotherapy depends on verified prescriptions and doses, correct routes and sequencing, careful venous access, prompt management of reactions and extravasation, and strict protection of staff and the environment from cytotoxic exposure. Trained oncology nurses are responsible for each of these steps.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Oncological Conditions (including Palliative Care Module)
question: Explain haematopoietic stem cell (bone marrow) transplantation and the nursing care of a patient undergoing it.
answer_html:
Definition Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT), commonly called bone marrow transplantation, is the infusion of healthy blood-forming stem cells into a patient whose marrow has been destroyed by disease or by high-dose chemotherapy and/or radiotherapy, so that the new cells can restore normal blood and immune function.

1. Types

  • Autologous – the patient's own stem cells are collected, stored (frozen) and re-infused after high-dose therapy; used in multiple myeloma and lymphomas; no graft-versus-host disease.
  • Allogeneic – stem cells from a donor: an HLA-matched sibling, a matched unrelated donor (through stem cell registries), a half-matched (haploidentical) family member or umbilical cord blood; used in acute leukaemias, aplastic anaemia, thalassaemia major, sickle cell disease and immunodeficiencies; donor immune cells also attack residual cancer (graft-versus-leukaemia effect).

2. Sources of stem cells

  • Peripheral blood stem cells collected by apheresis after mobilisation with G-CSF (the commonest source); bone marrow aspirated from the iliac crests under anaesthesia; umbilical cord blood.

3. Phases

  1. Pre-transplant evaluation – organ function, infections, dental check-up, central line insertion, counselling and consent, fertility preservation.
  2. Conditioning – high-dose chemotherapy ± total body irradiation to destroy the diseased marrow and suppress immunity.
  3. Transplant (day 0) – stem cells are infused through the central line like a blood transfusion.
  4. Pre-engraftment (aplastic) phase – about 2–4 weeks of severe neutropenia, mucositis and bleeding risk.
  5. Engraftment – new cells start producing blood (neutrophils above 500/mm³ for 3 consecutive days), usually around days 10–28.
  6. Post-engraftment and recovery – months of immune recovery, with risk of infections and GVHD.

4. Complications

  • Infections (bacterial, fungal, viral – CMV), oral mucositis, bleeding, anaemia.
  • Graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) in allogeneic transplants – donor T-cells attack the patient's skin (rash), gut (diarrhoea) and liver (jaundice); acute or chronic.
  • Veno-occlusive disease of the liver (painful liver enlargement, jaundice, weight gain), graft failure, relapse, infertility and late organ effects.

5. Nursing care

  1. Protective isolation – single room with HEPA-filtered air, strict hand hygiene, limited visitors, no plants or flowers, safe food and water.
  2. Central line care – aseptic dressing changes and line handling to prevent bloodstream infection.
  3. Stem cell infusion – check identity and product labels with a second nurse, give premedication, infuse promptly (thawed cells), monitor vital signs; frozen cells contain DMSO, which may cause nausea, flushing, a garlic-like odour of the breath and, rarely, reactions.
  4. Monitoring – temperature 4-hourly, daily weight, intake–output, daily blood counts, electrolytes, kidney and liver function; daily skin, mouth and stool assessment for GVHD signs.
  5. Infection prevention and treatment – prophylactic antimicrobials; report fever of 38 °C or more immediately (febrile neutropenia).
  6. Blood product support – irradiated, leucodepleted red cells and platelets as ordered; bleeding precautions.
  7. Mouth care and nutrition – frequent mouth care for mucositis, pain relief, nutritional support (enteral or parenteral nutrition when needed).
  8. Psychological support – long isolation causes anxiety, loneliness and depression; maintain communication, allow safe family contact and video calls; support the donor and family.
  9. Discharge teaching – infection precautions, medications (immunosuppressants for GVHD), avoidance of crowds, food safety, revaccination schedule after recovery, recognition of GVHD and infection, and regular follow-up.

Conclusion HSCT replaces diseased or destroyed bone marrow with healthy stem cells from the patient or a donor and is curative in many blood cancers and in thalassaemia. Its success depends on meticulous infection prevention, careful infusion and monitoring, early detection of GVHD and other complications, nutritional and psychological support – all central nursing responsibilities.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Oncological Conditions (including Palliative Care Module)
question: Explain the psychosocial care of a patient with cancer and the family.
answer_html:
Introduction A diagnosis of cancer affects not only the body but also the mind, family, finances, work and spiritual life of the patient. Many patients experience significant psychological distress, which reduces quality of life, adherence to treatment and even survival. Psychosocial care is therefore an essential part of oncology nursing.

1. Common emotional reactions

  • Shock, disbelief and denial at diagnosis; fear of pain, death, disfigurement and treatment; anger ("why me?"); guilt and self-blame (e.g. about tobacco use); anxiety, sadness and depression; and gradual acceptance – similar to the stages of grief described by Kübler-Ross (denial, anger, bargaining, depression, acceptance), though not always in this order.
  • Fear of recurrence in survivors; demoralisation and hopelessness in advanced disease.

2. Psychosocial problems

  • Altered body image – hair loss, mastectomy, stoma, facial surgery, weight loss.
  • Sexual dysfunction, infertility and relationship strain.
  • Role changes – loss of job, inability to care for children or elders.
  • Financial burden ("financial toxicity") – treatment costs, travel to distant cancer centres and loss of income.
  • Social stigma and isolation; myths that cancer is contagious or a punishment.
  • Caregiver burden – exhaustion, anxiety and depression among family members.

3. Psychosocial assessment

  • Screen for distress at diagnosis and at key points using simple tools such as the distress thermometer (0–10) and a problem checklist; assess coping style, support systems, beliefs, finances and suicide risk.

4. Nursing interventions

  1. Therapeutic communication – establish trust, listen actively, allow expression of fear and anger, accept silence and tears; give honest, step-by-step information in simple language.
  2. Support hope – realistic hope for cure, control of symptoms or meaningful time with family.
  3. Involve the family in decisions and care; respect the patient's wishes about how much information is shared (collusion is common in Indian families and needs sensitive handling).
  4. Body-image support – preparation for hair loss (scarves, wigs), prosthesis advice, stoma counselling, grooming and make-up help.
  5. Sexuality and fertility – discuss openly and privately; refer for fertility preservation before treatment when possible.
  6. Financial and social support – inform about Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY, state schemes, the Health Minister's Cancer Patient Fund and NGO help for travel, stay and medicines; involve medical social workers.
  7. Support groups and survivors – peer support from cancer survivors and patient groups reduces fear and isolation.
  8. Spiritual care – respect religious practices, arrange prayer or visits from spiritual leaders when requested.
  9. Children of patients – age-appropriate honest explanation and support; inform teachers.
  10. Referral to psycho-oncologists, counsellors or psychiatrists for severe anxiety, depression or suicidal thoughts.
  11. Caregiver support – teach care skills, encourage rest and sharing of tasks, arrange respite and bereavement support.

Conclusion Cancer brings shock, fear, grief, body-image changes, financial strain and family stress. Through regular distress screening, compassionate communication, information, family involvement, social and spiritual support and timely referral, nurses help patients and families cope and maintain quality of life throughout the illness.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Oncological Conditions (including Palliative Care Module)
question: Explain hospice care and the role of the nurse.
answer_html:
Definition Hospice care is specialised, comfort-focused care for people with a terminal illness in the last phase of life – usually when life expectancy is measured in months (often 6 months or less) and curative treatment is no longer beneficial or desired. It aims to help patients live as fully and comfortably as possible and die with dignity, while supporting their families, including in bereavement. Hospice is part of the wider palliative care approach.

1. History and philosophy

  • The modern hospice movement was founded by Dame Cicely Saunders, a nurse and later physician, who opened St Christopher's Hospice, London, in 1967 and introduced the concept of "total pain".
  • In India, Shanti Avedna Sadan (Mumbai, 1986) was the first hospice; Kerala's community-based palliative care network, involving trained volunteers, is a widely praised model for home-based end-of-life care.
  • Philosophy: death is a natural part of life; the focus shifts from cure to comfort; the patient and family are the unit of care; care is holistic and given by an interdisciplinary team.

2. Types of hospice services

  • Inpatient hospice – a homelike residential unit for patients whose symptoms cannot be managed at home or who have no caregivers.
  • Home hospice – visits by nurses, doctors and volunteers to the patient's home, with equipment and medicines provided; most patients prefer to die at home.
  • Day hospice – patients attend for a day of care, therapy and social contact.
  • Hospital-based palliative care teams and respite care for caregivers.

3. Services provided

  • Expert pain and symptom control (including oral morphine), nursing care, nutrition and mouth care.
  • Psychological, social and spiritual support; help with unfinished business, reconciliation and legacy.
  • Equipment (air mattress, commode, oxygen), training of family caregivers, 24-hour telephone advice.
  • Care at the time of death and bereavement support for the family for months afterwards.

4. The hospice team

  • Doctors, nurses (the core members), counsellors, social workers, physiotherapists, spiritual care providers, pharmacists and trained volunteers.

5. Role of the nurse

  1. Assess and manage pain and other symptoms; give medicines, including opioids, safely and on time.
  2. Provide comfort care – hygiene, positioning, pressure-area, mouth and eye care.
  3. Communicate honestly and gently; help patients and families express wishes, fears and goals; support advance care planning.
  4. Educate and support family caregivers; arrange respite.
  5. Recognise signs of approaching death and prepare the family; provide dignified care at death and last offices according to the family's beliefs.
  6. Provide bereavement follow-up and identify complicated grief.
  7. Coordinate with the team and community resources; train volunteers; maintain records.
  8. Take care of personal emotional well-being through debriefing and peer support.

Conclusion Hospice care provides holistic, comfort-oriented care to terminally ill patients and support to their families, at home or in specialised units. Nurses, at the heart of the hospice team, ensure that patients live their last days free of distressing symptoms and die with dignity, and that families are supported through bereavement.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Oncological Conditions (including Palliative Care Module)
question: Explain carcinoma of the prostate and its nursing management.
answer_html:
Introduction Carcinoma of the prostate is a malignant tumour, usually an adenocarcinoma, arising mostly in the peripheral zone of the prostate gland. It is a common cancer in older men and is increasing in India with longer life expectancy and better detection. Many prostate cancers grow slowly, but some are aggressive and spread to bones.

Risk factors – increasing age (mostly above 60 years), family history, inherited mutations (BRCA2), African ancestry, obesity and a diet high in animal fat.

Clinical features

  • Early disease is often silent and found through PSA testing or rectal examination.
  • Lower urinary tract symptoms – hesitancy, poor stream, frequency, nocturia, retention (similar to BPH); haematuria.
  • Advanced disease – bone pain, especially in the back and pelvis; pathological fractures; spinal cord compression (back pain, leg weakness, bladder dysfunction); weight loss, anaemia and swelling of legs.

Diagnosis

  • Serum PSA; digital rectal examination (hard, nodular, irregular gland with loss of the median groove).
  • Multiparametric MRI of the prostate, biopsy (transrectal or transperineal) with Gleason score/grade group, and staging by bone scan, CT or PSMA PET scan.

Management

  • Localised, low-risk cancer – active surveillance (regular PSA, MRI and biopsy) or watchful waiting in the elderly.
  • Curative treatment – radical prostatectomy (open, laparoscopic or robotic) or radiotherapy (external beam or brachytherapy), often with hormone therapy.
  • Advanced or metastatic cancer – androgen deprivation therapy (ADT): bilateral orchidectomy or LHRH agonists/antagonists (leuprolide, goserelin, degarelix), plus newer hormonal drugs (abiraterone, enzalutamide) and chemotherapy (docetaxel); bone-protecting drugs (zoledronic acid, denosumab); palliative radiotherapy for painful bones; radionuclide therapy.

Nursing management

  1. Screening and education – inform men above 50 (or earlier with family history) about the benefits and limits of PSA testing; report urinary symptoms and bone pain early.
  2. Care after radical prostatectomy
    • Care of the urinary catheter (usually kept 1–2 weeks), drains and wound; fluids; prevention of constipation and straining.
    • Urinary incontinence is common after catheter removal – teach pelvic floor (Kegel) exercises, use of pads and reassurance that it usually improves over months.
    • Erectile dysfunction – counsel sensitively; explain treatment options (PDE-5 inhibitors, devices).
  3. Care during radiotherapy – skin care, management of diarrhoea, frequency and burning of urine; adequate fluids.
  4. Care during hormone therapy (ADT) – explain and manage side effects: hot flushes, loss of libido, erectile dysfunction, fatigue, weight gain, breast enlargement, loss of muscle and bone (osteoporosis), high sugar and lipids; advise exercise, calcium and vitamin D, and regular monitoring of bone density, sugar and lipids; give injections on schedule.
  5. Advanced disease – pain control (WHO ladder, palliative radiotherapy), fall and fracture prevention, watch for signs of spinal cord compression (new back pain, leg weakness, retention) and report as an emergency; catheter care for retention; palliative care.
  6. Psychological support – address fears about masculinity, sexuality and incontinence; involve the partner; support groups.

Conclusion Prostate cancer is common in older men, often silent early and prone to spread to bones. PSA, rectal examination, MRI and biopsy establish the diagnosis; active surveillance, surgery, radiotherapy and hormone therapy are the main treatments. Nursing care focuses on post-operative continence and catheter care, managing hormone-therapy side effects, recognising spinal cord compression and providing psychological and palliative support.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Oncological Conditions (including Palliative Care Module)
question: Explain immunotherapy and targeted therapy in cancer, with their nursing implications.
answer_html:
Introduction Unlike conventional chemotherapy, which kills all rapidly dividing cells, targeted therapy acts on specific molecules needed for the growth and spread of cancer cells, and immunotherapy stimulates or restores the body's own immune system to recognise and destroy cancer cells. These treatments have improved survival in many cancers but have their own unique side effects.

1. Targeted therapy

  • Monoclonal antibodies (names end in "-mab") – laboratory-made antibodies against a target on cancer cells or their blood supply:
    • Trastuzumab – HER2-positive breast and stomach cancer.
    • Rituximab – CD20-positive lymphomas and leukaemias.
    • Bevacizumab – blocks VEGF (new blood vessel formation) in colorectal, lung and ovarian cancers.
    • Cetuximab – EGFR in colorectal and head and neck cancers.
  • Small-molecule inhibitors (names end in "-nib"), usually oral tablets:
    • Imatinib – chronic myeloid leukaemia and GIST (transformed the outlook of CML).
    • Gefitinib, erlotinib, osimertinib – EGFR-mutated lung cancer.
    • Others – sunitinib, lenvatinib, palbociclib, PARP inhibitors (olaparib) in BRCA-related cancers.
  • Requires biomarker or mutation testing of the tumour to select patients.

2. Immunotherapy

  • Immune checkpoint inhibitors – pembrolizumab, nivolumab (PD-1), atezolizumab (PD-L1), ipilimumab (CTLA-4) – release the "brakes" on T-cells; used in melanoma, lung, kidney, bladder, head and neck cancers and others.
  • CAR-T cell therapy – the patient's T-cells are genetically modified to attack cancer cells and re-infused; used in some leukaemias and lymphomas; India approved its own indigenous CAR-T therapy in 2023, making it far more affordable.
  • Other immunotherapies – intravesical BCG for bladder cancer, interferons and interleukins, cancer vaccines (and preventive vaccines such as HPV and hepatitis B).

3. Side effects

  • Infusion reactions with monoclonal antibodies – fever, chills, rash, breathlessness, low BP (especially the first dose of rituximab).
  • Specific toxicities – cardiotoxicity with trastuzumab; hypertension, bleeding, poor wound healing and proteinuria with bevacizumab; acne-like rash, diarrhoea and nail changes with EGFR inhibitors; fluid retention with imatinib.
  • Immune-related adverse events with checkpoint inhibitors – the immune system attacks normal organs: colitis (diarrhoea), pneumonitis (cough, breathlessness), hepatitis, thyroiditis, hypophysitis, skin rash and type 1 diabetes, which may appear weeks or months later.
  • CAR-T – cytokine release syndrome (high fever, low BP, low oxygen) and neurotoxicity (confusion, seizures).

4. Nursing implications

  1. Before treatment – baseline assessment (vital signs, weight, ECG/echocardiography for trastuzumab, BP and urine protein for bevacizumab, thyroid and liver function, blood sugar for checkpoint inhibitors); premedication as ordered.
  2. During infusion – correct rate (slower for first doses), vital signs, observation for reactions; emergency drugs ready; stop the infusion and inform the doctor if a reaction occurs.
  3. Oral targeted drugs – teach correct timing (with or without food), adherence, safe handling at home, drug and food interactions (e.g. grapefruit, some antibiotics and antacids) and what to do if a dose is missed.
  4. Monitoring and education – teach patients to report diarrhoea, cough, breathlessness, rash, yellow eyes, extreme tiredness, headache or vision change promptly, as early steroid treatment of immune-related effects prevents serious harm; skin care for rashes; BP monitoring at home.
  5. CAR-T care – close monitoring of temperature, BP, oxygen and neurological status; readiness to treat cytokine release syndrome.
  6. Psychosocial and financial support – these drugs are costly; help patients access insurance, government schemes and patient-assistance programmes.

Conclusion Targeted therapies (monoclonal antibodies and small-molecule inhibitors) and immunotherapies (checkpoint inhibitors, CAR-T cells) offer precise and often more effective cancer treatment, but bring unique toxicities such as infusion reactions, cardiotoxicity and immune-related inflammation. Careful baseline assessment, monitoring, patient education and early reporting of symptoms are the key nursing responsibilities.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Oncological Conditions (including Palliative Care Module)
question: What is stem cell therapy?
answer_html:
Stem cells are undifferentiated cells that can renew themselves and develop into specialised cells (blood, nerve, muscle). Stem cell therapy is the use of stem cells to replace or repair diseased or damaged cells and tissues.

  • Types of stem cells – embryonic, adult (e.g. haematopoietic stem cells from bone marrow and blood), umbilical cord blood stem cells, and induced pluripotent stem cells made in the laboratory.
  • Established use – haematopoietic stem cell (bone marrow) transplantation for leukaemias, lymphomas, myeloma, aplastic anaemia, thalassaemia major, sickle cell disease and immunodeficiencies.
  • Other uses (heart, spinal cord, diabetes, eye) are still experimental and should be done only in approved clinical trials; ICMR guidelines regulate stem cell research in India and caution against unproven commercial "stem cell cures".

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Oncological Conditions (including Palliative Care Module)
question: Give reason: Patients receiving chemotherapy commonly lose their hair.
answer_html:
• Most chemotherapy drugs act on rapidly dividing cells. Besides cancer cells, the matrix cells of hair follicles are among the fastest-dividing cells in the body.
  • The drugs damage these cells, so the hair shaft becomes thin and weak and falls out – alopecia – usually starting 2–3 weeks after the first dose; drugs such as doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide, paclitaxel and docetaxel commonly cause it. Body, eyebrow and eyelash hair may also be lost.
  • It is usually temporary; hair regrows 3–6 months after treatment ends, sometimes with a different texture or colour.
  • Nursing care – prepare the patient in advance, suggest cutting hair short, scarves, caps or wigs, use of a mild shampoo and soft brush, protection of the scalp from sun and cold, scalp cooling where available, and emotional support for the change in body image.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Oncological Conditions (including Palliative Care Module)
question: What is oral mucositis? Write its nursing care.
answer_html:
Oral mucositis is painful inflammation and ulceration of the mucous membrane of the mouth caused by chemotherapy (e.g. 5-fluorouracil, methotrexate, high-dose therapy before transplant) or head and neck radiotherapy, usually beginning 5–10 days after treatment. It is graded by WHO from 0 (none) to 4 (ulcers preventing eating).

Nursing care

  • Assess the mouth daily; maintain oral hygiene with a soft toothbrush after meals and at bedtime.
  • Bland mouthwashes – normal saline or sodium bicarbonate solution 4–6 times a day; avoid alcohol-containing mouthwashes.
  • Soft, moist, lukewarm, non-spicy food; plenty of fluids; avoid tobacco, alcohol and hot or acidic foods.
  • Pain relief – topical anaesthetics (lignocaine gel), analgesics before meals; benzydamine mouthwash in radiotherapy; sucking ice chips during 5-FU bolus (oral cryotherapy) reduces mucositis.
  • Treat infections (candida, herpes) and monitor nutrition and weight.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Oncological Conditions (including Palliative Care Module)
question: What is brachytherapy?
answer_html:
Brachytherapy (internal or sealed-source radiotherapy) is a form of radiotherapy in which a sealed radioactive source is placed inside or very close to the tumour, so that a high dose reaches the tumour while nearby normal tissues are spared.

  • Types – intracavitary (applicators in the uterus and vagina for cancer cervix), interstitial (needles or seeds in the breast, prostate, tongue), intraluminal (oesophagus, bronchus) and surface moulds.
  • Dose rate – high dose rate (HDR, e.g. iridium-192) given in minutes over a few sessions, or low dose rate (LDR) over days, or permanent seed implants.
  • Nursing care – explain the procedure; keep the patient still to avoid displacement of applicators; follow radiation safety (time, distance, shielding, limited visitors, no pregnant women or children); keep long-handled forceps and a lead container for a dislodged source; after removal of the source the patient is not radioactive.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients with Oncological Conditions (including Palliative Care Module)
question: Write the neutropenic precautions.
answer_html:
Neutropenia is an absolute neutrophil count below 1,500/mm³ (severe when below 500/mm³), common after chemotherapy. Neutropenic precautions protect such patients from infection:

  1. Strict hand hygiene by staff and visitors; a single room where possible; masks if advised.
  2. Restrict visitors with colds, coughs or infections; no fresh flowers, plants or stagnant water in the room.
  3. Safe food – well-cooked, freshly prepared food and boiled or filtered water; avoid raw salads, undercooked eggs and meat, and unpasteurised milk.
  4. Avoid invasive procedures where possible – no rectal temperatures, enemas, suppositories or IM injections; aseptic care of IV lines and catheters.
  5. Daily hygiene – bath, oral care with a soft brush, perineal care; inspect skin, mouth and line sites.
  6. Check temperature every 4 hours and report fever of 38 °C or more immediately – febrile neutropenia needs IV antibiotics within one hour.
  7. Give G-CSF and prophylactic drugs as prescribed.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients in Emergency and Disaster Situations
question: (a) Define disaster and classify disasters. (3 marks) (b) Explain the disaster management cycle. (5 marks) (c) Describe hospital disaster preparedness and mass casualty triage, with the role of the nurse. (7 marks)
answer_html:
(a) Definition and classification (3 marks) A disaster is a serious disruption of the functioning of a community or society, caused by a natural or man-made event, which results in widespread human, material, economic or environmental losses that exceed the ability of the affected community to cope using its own resources. India's Disaster Management Act, 2005 describes it as a catastrophe, mishap, calamity or grave occurrence causing substantial loss of life, suffering or damage beyond the coping capacity of the community. A mass casualty incident is an event in which the number of casualties exceeds the immediate capacity of the local health services.

Classification 1. Natural disasters

  • Hydro-meteorological – floods, cyclones, cloudbursts, droughts, heat waves (a major hazard in Vidarbha, with temperatures above 45 °C), cold waves, lightning and hailstorms.
  • Geological – earthquakes (Latur 1993, Bhuj 2001), landslides, tsunamis (2004) and volcanic eruptions.
  • Biological – epidemics and pandemics (cholera, plague, COVID-19), pest attacks.

2. Man-made (human-induced) disasters

  • Industrial and chemical – gas leaks and explosions (Bhopal gas tragedy, 1984 – methyl isocyanate), factory fires.
  • Nuclear and radiological accidents.
  • Fires in hospitals, markets and buildings; building collapses.
  • Transport accidents – rail, road, air and boat accidents.
  • Stampedes at religious gatherings and festivals, terrorist attacks and bomb blasts, wars and refugee crises.

3. By speed of onset – sudden-onset (earthquake, explosion) and slow-onset (drought, famine, epidemics).

(b) Disaster management cycle (5 marks) Disaster management is a continuous cycle of activities before, during and after a disaster, aimed at reducing risk and loss.

1. Pre-disaster phase

  • Mitigation and prevention – long-term measures that reduce the impact of hazards: earthquake-resistant buildings, flood embankments and drainage, land-use planning, early-warning systems, heat-action plans (cool roofs, drinking-water points), fire safety and industrial safety regulations, vaccination against epidemics.
  • Preparedness – planning and readiness to respond: hazard and vulnerability mapping, disaster plans at national, state, district, city and hospital levels, stockpiling of medicines and equipment, training of staff and volunteers, mock drills, community awareness, communication networks and evacuation plans.

2. Disaster impact – the event itself; damage depends on the hazard and on the vulnerability and preparedness of the community.

3. Post-disaster phase

  • Response (emergency phase) – immediate actions to save lives and meet basic needs: search and rescue, triage, first aid and medical care, evacuation, shelter, safe water, food, sanitation, disease surveillance and prevention of epidemics, mass-casualty management, dead-body management and psychosocial first aid. The first 72 hours are critical.
  • Recovery – rehabilitation (restoring basic services, health care, livelihoods, schools and mental health support) and reconstruction (rebuilding houses, hospitals and infrastructure, preferably "build back better").

4. Development – integrating lessons learned and risk reduction into long-term development, which leads back into mitigation and preparedness.

(c) Hospital disaster preparedness and mass casualty triage, with the role of the nurse (7 marks) A. Hospital disaster management plan Every hospital should have a written, regularly tested plan for external disasters (mass casualties arriving) and internal disasters (fire, flooding, power failure, gas leak).

  1. Hospital disaster committee and an incident command system – a clear chain of command with an incident commander and heads of operations, logistics, planning and communication.
  2. Activation and alert system – a disaster code announced on the public-address system; staff call-in lists and telephone trees.
  3. Surge capacity – rapid discharge or transfer of stable patients, cancellation of elective surgery, opening of extra beds and wards, extra operation theatres and ICU beds.
  4. Designated areas – triage area at the entrance, separate red, yellow and green treatment areas, decontamination area for chemical incidents, isolation area for infectious disasters, family information centre, media area and mortuary.
  5. Resources – stocks of emergency drugs, IV fluids, blood, dressings, splints, oxygen and ventilators; disaster kits; backup power, water and communication.
  6. Staff roles – action cards for each category of staff; trained rapid response teams.
  7. Documentation – disaster tags and registers to track every patient; police and medico-legal formalities.
  8. Coordination with district disaster management authorities, ambulance services (108/112), blood banks, police and other hospitals.
  9. Training and mock drills at regular intervals; review and updating of the plan after every drill or event.

B. Mass casualty triage Triage (from the French word for "sorting") is the rapid classification of casualties according to the urgency of their need for treatment and their chance of survival, so that the greatest good is done for the greatest number with limited resources.

Colour-coded categories

  • Red – immediate (priority 1) – life-threatening but salvageable injuries needing treatment within minutes: airway obstruction, breathing difficulty, shock, severe bleeding.
  • Yellow – delayed (priority 2) – serious injuries that can wait a few hours: fractures without shock, burns without airway involvement.
  • Green – minor (priority 3) – "walking wounded" with minor injuries.
  • Black – dead or expectant – dead, or injuries so severe that survival is unlikely with available resources.

START (Simple Triage and Rapid Treatment) method – each casualty is assessed in less than a minute:

  1. Can the person walk? → Green.
  2. Is the person breathing? If not, open the airway; if still not breathing → Black; if breathing starts → Red.
  3. Respiratory rate above 30/min → Red.
  4. Perfusion – radial pulse absent or capillary refill more than 2 seconds → Red (control bleeding).
  5. Mental status – cannot follow simple commands → Red; otherwise → Yellow. Triage is repeated (re-triage) at intervals because a patient's condition can change. Simplified versions such as JumpSTART are used for children.

C. Role of the nurse

  1. Preparedness – know the hospital disaster plan and one's own role; participate in training and mock drills; maintain disaster kits and stocks; teach community first aid and preparedness.
  2. Triage – trained nurses act as triage officers, tag patients and direct them to the right area.
  3. Emergency care – airway management, oxygen, bleeding control, IV access, fluid resuscitation, splinting, wound care, pain relief and monitoring in red and yellow areas.
  4. Coordination and documentation – tracking of patients, beds, supplies and staff; communication with the control room.
  5. Infection control and public health – safe water, sanitation, vaccination and surveillance in relief camps; prevention of epidemics after floods and earthquakes.
  6. Special groups – care of children, pregnant women, the elderly and people with disabilities.
  7. Psychosocial support – psychological first aid to victims and families; information to relatives; respectful care of the dead.
  8. Self-care – staff rest, rotation and debriefing to prevent burnout.

Nursing importance

  • Nurses are the largest health workforce at every level; their preparedness, triage skills and calm leadership determine how many lives are saved in the chaotic first hours of a disaster.

Conclusion Disasters may be natural or man-made, sudden or slow, and are managed through a continuous cycle of mitigation, preparedness, response and recovery. A tested hospital disaster plan, surge capacity and rapid colour-coded triage such as START allow hospitals to cope with mass casualties, with nurses playing a central role in every phase.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients in Emergency and Disaster Situations
question: (a) Define polytrauma and explain the "golden hour". (3 marks) (b) Explain the primary survey and resuscitation of a patient with multiple injuries. (5 marks) (c) Describe the secondary survey and nursing management of a patient with polytrauma. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: Primary survey of a trauma patient (ABCDE)

answer_html:
(a) Definition and the golden hour (3 marks) Polytrauma means significant injuries to two or more body regions or organ systems (for example head, chest, abdomen, pelvis and limbs), at least one of which, or their combination, is life-threatening. It commonly results from road traffic accidents, falls from height, assaults, building collapses and blasts. Road injuries are a leading cause of death in young adults in India.

Golden hour – the first hour after major injury, during which prompt resuscitation and definitive care offer the best chance of survival and of preventing complications. India's Motor Vehicles Act defines it as the first hour after a traumatic injury, and the Cashless Treatment of Road Accident Victims Scheme, 2025 provides cashless treatment up to ₹1.5 lakh per victim for up to 7 days at designated hospitals so that care is not delayed for want of money.

Trimodal distribution of trauma deaths – (1) immediate deaths within minutes (brain, heart or major vessel injury – reduced mainly by prevention); (2) early deaths within minutes to a few hours (airway obstruction, tension pneumothorax, bleeding, intracranial haematoma – preventable by golden-hour care); (3) late deaths after days or weeks (sepsis, multi-organ failure).

(b) Primary survey and resuscitation (5 marks) The Advanced Trauma Life Support (ATLS) approach identifies and treats life-threatening problems in order of priority – "treat first what kills first" – with simultaneous resuscitation by a trauma team.

Catastrophic external haemorrhage – direct pressure, haemostatic dressings and a tourniquet for uncontrollable limb bleeding.

A – Airway with cervical-spine protection

  • Check for obstruction (blood, vomit, teeth, tongue fall, facial fractures); suction; jaw thrust (no head tilt); oral or nasal airway; definitive airway (intubation) if GCS is 8 or less or the airway is threatened; manual in-line stabilisation and cervical collar.

B – Breathing and ventilation

  • Look, listen and feel; give high-flow oxygen; detect and treat immediately life-threatening chest injuries: tension pneumothorax (needle decompression then chest tube), open pneumothorax (three-sided occlusive dressing), massive haemothorax (chest tube, blood), flail chest and cardiac tamponade.

C – Circulation with haemorrhage control

  • Recognise haemorrhagic shock – rapid pulse, low BP, cold clammy skin, delayed capillary refill, anxiety or confusion.
  • Stop bleeding – pressure, splints, pelvic binder for unstable pelvic fractures, surgery or angio-embolisation.
  • Two large-bore IV cannulas (or intraosseous access); bloods for cross-matching.
  • Limited warm crystalloid (about 1 litre) and early blood transfusion – O-negative or group-specific blood; massive transfusion protocol with red cells, plasma and platelets in balanced ratios.
  • Tranexamic acid within 3 hours of injury.
  • FAST ultrasound to detect blood in the abdomen, chest or pericardium.

D – Disability (neurological status)

  • GCS, pupil size and reaction, movement of limbs; check blood sugar.

E – Exposure and environment

  • Remove clothing fully to look for hidden injuries (log-roll to examine the back); then cover with warm blankets and use warmed fluids to prevent hypothermia.

Adjuncts to the primary survey – ECG and pulse-oximetry monitoring, ABG, urinary catheter (not if there is blood at the urethral meatus or a suspected urethral injury), gastric tube (orogastric if a basal skull fracture is suspected), chest and pelvic X-rays and FAST.

  • Avoid the "lethal triad" of hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy, which rapidly worsens bleeding; unstable patients may need damage-control surgery.

(c) Secondary survey and nursing management (7 marks) A. Secondary survey – begins only after the primary survey is complete and resuscitation is under way.

  1. AMPLE history – Allergies, Medications, Past illness and pregnancy, Last meal, Events and environment (mechanism of injury: speed, seat belt or helmet use, height of fall).
  2. Head-to-toe examination – head and face (scalp wounds, skull fractures, eyes), neck, chest, abdomen, pelvis, perineum, spine (log-roll), limbs (deformity, wounds, pulses and nerve function), skin.
  3. Investigations – CT scans (head, cervical spine, chest, abdomen, pelvis), X-rays of injured limbs, blood tests.
  4. Tertiary survey – a repeat full examination within 24 hours to detect injuries missed earlier.

B. Nursing management

  1. Continuous monitoring – vital signs, SpO₂, GCS and pupils, urine output (target about 0.5 mL/kg/hour), temperature and fluid balance; report deterioration immediately.
  2. Airway and breathing – suction, oxygen, ventilator care; chest drain care (underwater seal below chest level, record drainage, observe for air leak and bleeding).
  3. Circulation – maintain IV lines; give blood and products with correct checks; watch for transfusion reactions, hypothermia and low calcium during massive transfusion; observe dressings and drains for bleeding.
  4. Spinal precautions – keep the spine aligned and log-roll until spinal injury is excluded.
  5. Fracture care – splints, traction, elevation, neurovascular checks and early recognition of compartment syndrome and fat embolism.
  6. Pain relief – IV opioids titrated to effect, and non-drug measures; reassessment.
  7. Wound care and infection prevention – cleaning and dressing of wounds, tetanus prophylaxis, antibiotics for open fractures.
  8. Prevention of complications – DVT prophylaxis, pressure-area care, chest physiotherapy, early nutrition and stress-ulcer prophylaxis.
  9. Psychological support – explain procedures, reassure the conscious patient; inform and support the family; allow presence where appropriate.
  10. Medico-legal duties – register the case as an MLC, inform the police, preserve clothing and foreign bodies, and document injuries, times and treatment accurately.
  11. Safe transfer to theatre, ICU or a higher centre with monitoring, equipment and records.
  12. Rehabilitation and prevention education – physiotherapy and follow-up; helmets, seat belts, no drink-driving and safe speed.

C. Trauma team and the nurse's role in the resuscitation bay

  • Preparation before arrival – warm the room, check airway equipment and suction, oxygen, monitors, defibrillator, chest-drain and cut-down sets, pelvic binder, splints, a blood warmer and rapid infuser, and keep the massive-transfusion request ready; wear protective equipment.
  • Team roles – a team leader directs the resuscitation; an airway doctor manages the airway and cervical spine; one nurse attaches monitors, records vital signs and assists procedures; another nurse secures IV access, sends blood samples and manages fluids and blood with warming; a scribe nurse documents times, findings, drugs and fluids.
  • Closed-loop communication – orders are repeated back and confirmed when done, which prevents errors in a noisy, crowded resuscitation room.
  • Family liaison – a designated nurse meets the relatives, gives honest updates and collects history and identity details.
  • Reassessment – after every intervention, the primary survey is repeated ("ABCDE again"), especially before and after transfer.

Nursing importance

  • Trauma care is team work; the nurse ensures that each step of the primary survey is done quickly and in the right order, monitors continuously and coordinates resuscitation, which directly reduces preventable deaths in the golden hour.

Conclusion Polytrauma involves serious injuries to more than one body region. Rapid golden-hour care following the ATLS primary survey – control of catastrophic bleeding, airway with spinal protection, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure – followed by a detailed secondary survey and meticulous nursing management, saves lives and limits disability.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients in Emergency and Disaster Situations
question: Mr. K, a 35-year-old cotton farmer from Yavatmal district, is brought to the emergency department with organophosphate poisoning. (a) Explain the clinical features of organophosphate poisoning. (4 marks) (b) Describe the emergency management of Mr. K. (5 marks) (c) Write the nursing care of Mr. K. (6 marks)

diagram.caption: Targets of atropinisation in organophosphate poisoning
labels: clear chest on auscultation with no bronchorrhoea

answer_html:
(a) Clinical features (4 marks) Organophosphates (chlorpyrifos, profenofos, dimethoate, quinalphos, monocrotophos and others) are widely used insecticides in cotton and other crops. They irreversibly inhibit the enzyme acetylcholinesterase, so acetylcholine accumulates at muscarinic, nicotinic and central nervous system receptors. Poisoning occurs by ingestion (often intentional self-harm), inhalation and absorption through the skin during spraying – as seen in the cluster of poisonings among cotton farmers spraying pesticides in Yavatmal district in 2017. Carbamates cause a similar, but shorter, picture.

1. Muscarinic features ("SLUDGE" + "killer Bs")

  • Salivation, Lacrimation, Urination, Diarrhoea, Gastrointestinal cramps, Emesis.
  • Bronchorrhoea (copious secretions), bronchospasm and bradycardia – the main causes of early death.
  • Miosis (pinpoint pupils), sweating, blurred vision and hypotension.

2. Nicotinic features

  • Muscle fasciculations and twitching, cramps, weakness and paralysis (including respiratory muscles); tachycardia and hypertension may occur.

3. Central nervous system features

  • Anxiety, restlessness, confusion, seizures, drowsiness, coma and depression of the respiratory centre.

4. Other features

  • Characteristic odour (garlic or kerosene-like from solvents), hypothermia or fever, high blood sugar, pancreatitis and arrhythmias.

5. Later complications

  • Intermediate syndrome – 24–96 hours after poisoning: weakness of neck flexors, proximal limb muscles, cranial nerves and respiratory muscles, leading to respiratory failure despite atropine.
  • Organophosphate-induced delayed polyneuropathy – 1–3 weeks later: weakness and tingling of legs and arms.

Diagnosis – history (container, product name), clinical toxidrome and a low serum (pseudo)cholinesterase or RBC acetylcholinesterase level.

(b) Emergency management (5 marks)

  1. Protect staff – wear gloves and gown; avoid contact with vomitus and contaminated clothes.
  2. Airway, breathing and circulation
    • Suction secretions; position on the left side, head down if not intubated; high-flow oxygen.
    • Intubate and ventilate if the patient has respiratory failure, a GCS of 8 or less or uncontrollable secretions (avoid succinylcholine).
    • Two IV lines; IV fluids; ECG monitoring.
  3. Atropine – the life-saving antidote
    • Give 1.8–3 mg IV bolus, and double the dose every 5 minutes until atropinisation is achieved: clear chest (no crepitations), heart rate above 80/min, systolic BP above 80 mmHg, dry axillae and pupils no longer pinpoint.
    • Then continue an atropine infusion (about 10–20% of the total loading dose per hour), adjusted to maintain these targets.
    • Avoid atropine toxicity – agitation, confusion, fever, absent bowel sounds, urinary retention and very fast pulse – by reducing the infusion.
  4. Pralidoxime (oxime) – may be given as ordered (e.g. a loading dose followed by an infusion) to reactivate the enzyme, ideally early.
  5. Decontamination – remove all clothing and wash the skin and hair thoroughly with soap and water (especially after spraying exposure); gastric lavage is considered only in selected patients presenting very early with a protected airway; activated charcoal as advised.
  6. Control seizures and agitation with diazepam or midazolam.
  7. ICU care – monitoring for intermediate syndrome and respiratory failure; correction of electrolytes, glucose and acid–base balance.
  8. Psychiatric assessment after stabilisation if the poisoning was intentional.

(c) Nursing care of Mr. K (6 marks) 1. Ineffective airway clearance related to bronchorrhoea and weakness

  • Frequent oral and tracheal suction; positioning on the side; oxygen; ventilator care and VAP prevention if intubated; assess breath sounds every 15–30 minutes during atropinisation.

2. Risk for respiratory failure (intermediate syndrome)

  • Monitor respiratory rate, SpO₂, ABG, single-breath count, cough strength and neck-flexion strength at regular intervals for 4–5 days; report weakness early so that ventilation can be started.

3. Atropine therapy monitoring

  • Maintain an atropine chart – time, dose, heart rate, BP, pupil size, chest sounds, axillary sweating, temperature, bowel sounds, urine output and sensorium – and adjust as ordered; avoid both under- and over-atropinisation; catheterise for retention.

4. Fluid, electrolyte and nutritional balance

  • Strict intake–output; IV fluids; monitor potassium, sodium, sugar and renal function; start feeds when safe.

5. Safety

  • Padded side rails, seizure precautions, protection of the delirious patient from injury; avoid restraints where possible.

6. Risk of self-harm (if intentional)

  • Suicide precautions – constant observation, removal of harmful objects, non-judgemental approach; psychiatric referral; counselling for stress, debt and crop loss common among farmers; inform the family about the national tele-mental health helpline Tele-MANAS (14416); involve social support and farmer-welfare schemes.

7. Medico-legal responsibilities

  • Register as a medico-legal case, inform the police, preserve gastric aspirate, vomitus, blood and the container in sealed, labelled containers, and document carefully.

8. Family support and discharge teaching

  • Explain the condition and treatment in simple language; allow the family to stay with Mr. K and involve them in care.
  • Teach the warning signs of delayed neuropathy (tingling, weakness or difficulty in walking 1–3 weeks later) and of recurrent weakness, and advise immediate return if they appear.
  • Arrange follow-up with the physician and, where needed, the psychiatrist and counsellor; link the family with social support and farmer-welfare schemes.

9. Prevention education for farmers and the community

  • Wear protective clothing while spraying – gloves, mask, goggles, long-sleeved clothes and boots; do not spray against the wind; do not eat, drink, smoke or chew tobacco while spraying; bathe and change clothes after spraying.
  • Store pesticides locked away, out of reach of children and away from food; never reuse pesticide containers; read labels; use less toxic products.
  • Seek treatment immediately for headache, giddiness, vomiting, sweating or blurred vision after spraying.

10. Care during recovery and tapering of atropine

  • Atropine is tapered gradually over 24–48 hours once the patient has been stable; observe closely for return of cholinergic signs (secretions, bradycardia, small pupils, sweating), because some fat-soluble organophosphates are released slowly from fat stores; restart or increase atropine as ordered if signs recur.
  • Continue to watch for intermediate syndrome for several days even when the patient looks well; do not shift the patient out of a monitored bed too early.
  • Weaning from the ventilator with breathing exercises and chest physiotherapy; mouth care, eye care and pressure-area care during sedation and paralysis.
  • Bowel and bladder care – atropine causes constipation and retention; monitor bowel sounds and urine output; remove the catheter as early as possible.
  • Gradual mobilisation with physiotherapy for muscle weakness; nutritional support.
  • Evaluation criteria – clear airway and chest, stable heart rate and BP without atropine, normal sensorium, adequate breathing without support, no recurrence of cholinergic signs, and a safe plan for discharge with mental-health follow-up where needed.

Nursing importance

  • Organophosphate poisoning is one of the commonest poisonings in rural India and Vidarbha; deaths are largely preventable by rapid atropinisation, airway care and vigilant monitoring for intermediate syndrome – all nurse-led – and by prevention and mental-health support in the community.

Conclusion Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase, producing muscarinic, nicotinic and CNS features, with later intermediate syndrome and delayed neuropathy. Rapid decontamination, airway support, titrated atropine and oximes, intensive monitoring, suicide prevention, medico-legal care and education about safe pesticide use form the complete management of Mr. K.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients in Emergency and Disaster Situations
question: Explain the general principles of management of a patient with poisoning and the nursing responsibilities.
answer_html:
Introduction Poisoning is the harmful effect produced when a substance enters the body by ingestion, inhalation, injection, skin or eye contact, in an amount that damages tissues. In India, common poisons include pesticides (organophosphates, aluminium phosphide or "celphos", paraquat), rodenticides, kerosene, corrosives (acids, toilet cleaners), drugs (paracetamol, sleeping pills), alcohol and methanol, plants (yellow oleander, datura) and envenomation by snakes and scorpions. Poisoning may be accidental (children, farmers), suicidal or homicidal.

1. Resuscitation first – ABCDE

  • Clear and protect the airway (suction, recovery position, intubation if GCS is 8 or less), oxygen, IV access, treatment of shock, arrhythmias and seizures; check blood sugar.

2. History and assessment

  • What substance (bring the container or label), how much, when, route and whether intentional; symptoms since exposure; previous illness.
  • Recognise toxidromes – cholinergic (pinpoint pupils, secretions), anticholinergic (dry hot skin, dilated pupils, delirium), opioid (pinpoint pupils, slow breathing), sympathomimetic (agitation, tachycardia, sweating) and sedative patterns.
  • Investigations – blood sugar, electrolytes, ABG, renal and liver function, ECG, specific drug levels (e.g. paracetamol), cholinesterase levels.

3. Decontamination

  • Skin and eyes – remove clothing; wash skin with soap and water; irrigate eyes for at least 15–20 minutes.
  • Gastric lavage – considered only for a potentially life-threatening ingestion within about one hour, with a protected airway; contraindicated in corrosive and hydrocarbon (kerosene) poisoning, an unprotected airway, convulsions and bleeding tendency.
  • Activated charcoal (about 1 g/kg) within one hour for poisons it can bind; not useful for alcohols, iron, lithium, corrosives and hydrocarbons.
  • Whole bowel irrigation for selected poisons (iron, packets of drugs).

4. Enhanced elimination – urinary alkalinisation (salicylates), haemodialysis (methanol, lithium, salicylates), repeated doses of charcoal.

5. Specific antidotes (examples) – atropine and pralidoxime (organophosphates), naloxone (opioids), flumazenil (benzodiazepines, with caution), N-acetylcysteine (paracetamol), fomepizole or ethanol (methanol), vitamin K (warfarin and superwarfarin rodenticides), anti-snake venom, desferrioxamine (iron), digoxin-specific antibody (digoxin).

6. Supportive care – ventilation, fluids, electrolytes, control of temperature and seizures, nutrition and organ support; most poisoned patients recover with good supportive care.

7. Psychiatric evaluation – every intentional poisoning needs suicide risk assessment and mental-health follow-up.

Nursing responsibilities

  1. Rapid triage and ABC care; continuous monitoring of vital signs, GCS, pupils, SpO₂, ECG and urine output.
  2. Gastric lavage (when ordered) – explain the procedure; place the patient in the left lateral, slightly head-down position; pass a large-bore orogastric tube and confirm its position; instil small volumes (about 200–300 mL in adults, 10 mL/kg in children) of lukewarm water or saline and drain by gravity until the return is clear; save the first aspirate for analysis; watch for aspiration, laryngospasm, hypothermia and fluid imbalance.
  3. Give activated charcoal and antidotes as ordered and observe their effects.
  4. Safety – seizure precautions, padded side rails, observation of restless patients; remove potential means of self-harm.
  5. Medico-legal duties – register as a medico-legal case, inform the police, preserve gastric aspirate, vomitus, blood, urine and the container in sealed, labelled containers, maintain the chain of custody and document carefully.
  6. Psychological support – non-judgemental attitude, counselling, involvement of the family and referral to psychiatry; inform about Tele-MANAS (14416).
  7. Health education and prevention – safe storage of pesticides, medicines and household chemicals out of reach of children; never store kerosene or chemicals in drink bottles; safe pesticide spraying; consult the National Poisons Information Centre when unsure.
