Conclusion Management of poisoning follows the principles of resuscitation, assessment, decontamination, enhanced elimination, antidotes and supportive care, with psychiatric and medico-legal attention. Nurses play a vital role in monitoring, safe gastric lavage, preservation of evidence, emotional support and prevention.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients in Emergency and Disaster Situations
question: Explain triage in the emergency department and the role of the triage nurse.
answer_html:
Definition Triage is the process of rapidly assessing patients on arrival at the emergency department (ED) and prioritising them according to the urgency of their condition, so that the sickest patients are treated first and resources are used efficiently. It differs from mass-casualty triage in a disaster, where the aim is to do the greatest good for the greatest number.

1. Objectives

  • Identify patients with life-threatening conditions immediately.
  • Allocate each patient to the right area and level of care, and decide how long it is safe to wait.
  • Reduce overcrowding and delays, start early interventions, and reassess waiting patients.

2. Triage systems

  • Colour-coded three-level triage (widely used in Indian EDs, as recommended in national emergency-care guidelines):
    • Red – immediate – e.g. cardiac arrest, airway obstruction, severe breathlessness, shock, major trauma, active seizures, unconsciousness; treated at once in the resuscitation area.
    • Yellow – urgent – e.g. chest pain with stable vital signs, moderate breathlessness, fractures, high fever with stable vitals; seen within a short time.
    • Green – non-urgent – minor injuries and illnesses; can wait or be directed to OPD.
  • Five-level systems – the Emergency Severity Index (ESI 1–5), based on acuity and expected resource needs; the Manchester Triage System (red – immediate, orange – very urgent within 10 minutes, yellow – urgent within 60 minutes, green – standard within 2 hours, blue – non-urgent within 4 hours); Canadian and Australasian scales.
  • Paediatric triage – WHO Emergency Triage Assessment and Treatment (ETAT) – emergency signs (obstructed breathing, shock, coma, convulsions, severe dehydration) and priority signs.

3. Process of triage

  1. Quick look ("across the room") – airway, breathing, circulation, colour, consciousness.
  2. Brief history – chief complaint, onset, relevant past illness and medicines.
  3. Vital signs – pulse, BP, respiratory rate, SpO₂, temperature, blood sugar where indicated; pain score; GCS.
  4. Assign the triage category and send the patient to the appropriate area; start protocol-based early measures (oxygen, ECG within 10 minutes for chest pain, splinting, antipyretics).
  5. Re-triage waiting patients at regular intervals or when their condition changes.
  6. Document time of arrival, category, findings and actions.

4. Special considerations

  • Children, pregnant women and the elderly may hide serious illness; infectious patients (TB, COVID-19) need isolation; aggressive or psychiatric patients need a safe area; medico-legal and brought-dead cases need specific procedures.

5. Role and qualities of the triage nurse

  • An experienced nurse trained in triage, with sound clinical judgement, quick decision-making and good communication skills.
  • Performs rapid assessment, allocates priority, initiates first-line care as per protocol, monitors and re-triages waiting patients, communicates with the medical team, manages crowd flow, keeps relatives informed and documents accurately.
  • Maintains infection control and personal safety; remains calm under pressure.

Conclusion ED triage rapidly sorts patients by urgency using colour-coded or five-level systems, so that life-threatening conditions are treated first and waiting is safe. The triage nurse's skilled assessment, early interventions and repeated reassessment are central to a safe and efficient emergency department.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients in Emergency and Disaster Situations
question: Explain the emergency management of heat stroke, hypothermia and near-drowning.
tags: not dead until warm and dead
answer_html:
Introduction Environmental emergencies are caused by exposure to extreme heat, cold or water. Heat stroke is a growing threat during heat waves in central India, including Vidarbha; hypothermia affects the elderly, newborns and the homeless during cold waves and is also seen after drowning and trauma; drowning is a leading cause of accidental death in children and young people.

1. Heat stroke

  • Definition – a life-threatening rise of core body temperature above about 40 °C with central nervous system dysfunction (confusion, delirium, seizures, coma) due to failure of heat regulation.
  • Types – classic (elderly, chronically ill, infants during heat waves; skin often hot and dry) and exertional (labourers, farmers, athletes, soldiers working in heat; may sweat).
  • Complications – rhabdomyolysis, acute kidney injury, liver injury, DIC, cardiac arrhythmias and death.
  • Emergency management
    • Move to a cool, shaded place; ABC; oxygen; measure core (rectal) temperature.
    • Rapid cooling – cold-water immersion (best for exertional heat stroke), or evaporative cooling (spray lukewarm water on the bare skin and fan continuously), ice packs to the neck, axillae and groin, cool IV fluids; stop active cooling at about 38.5–39 °C to avoid overshoot.
    • IV fluids carefully; treat seizures with benzodiazepines; monitor urine output, electrolytes, CK, renal and liver function and clotting.
    • Antipyretics (paracetamol) do not help in heat stroke.
  • Prevention – drink water and ORS regularly, avoid outdoor work in the hottest hours (about noon to 3 p.m.), wear light cotton clothes and head cover, never leave children in parked vehicles; heat action plans with early warnings and cooling centres.

2. Hypothermia

  • Definition – core temperature below 35 °C; mild (32–35 °C: shivering, confusion), moderate (28–32 °C: shivering stops, drowsiness, slow pulse), severe (below 28 °C: coma, very low BP, risk of ventricular fibrillation).
  • Management
    • Handle the patient gently and keep horizontal (rough movement can trigger VF); remove wet clothes.
    • Passive external rewarming (blankets, warm room) for mild cases; active external rewarming (warm blankets, forced-air warmers, warm packs on the trunk) for moderate cases; active internal rewarming (warmed IV fluids at about 38–42 °C, warm humidified oxygen, body-cavity lavage, ECMO) for severe cases.
    • Continuous ECG monitoring; prolonged CPR may be needed – a hypothermic patient is "not dead until warm and dead".
    • Monitor for rewarming shock, arrhythmias and electrolyte changes.

3. Near-drowning (submersion injury)

  • Pathophysiology – the main injury is hypoxia; aspiration of water damages surfactant, causing pulmonary oedema and ARDS; hypothermia and cervical-spine injury (diving) may coexist.
  • Management
    • Rescue safely; start rescue breaths and CPR early (ventilation is the priority); do not try to drain water from the lungs.
    • In hospital – 100% oxygen, CPAP or intubation with PEEP, monitoring of ABG and chest X-ray; rewarming; cervical-spine protection if diving injury is suspected; treat hypoglycaemia and seizures.
    • Observe even apparently well patients for at least 6–8 hours, because breathlessness and pulmonary oedema can develop later.
  • Prevention – constant supervision of children near water, covering wells and water tanks, fencing ponds, swimming lessons, life jackets during boat travel and avoidance of alcohol near water.

Nursing responsibilities (all three)

  • Continuous monitoring of core temperature, vital signs, SpO₂, ECG, GCS and urine output; airway management and oxygen; correct use of cooling or warming devices with skin protection; fluid and electrolyte balance; seizure precautions; emotional support to the family; and community education on prevention.

Conclusion Heat stroke needs immediate rapid cooling, hypothermia needs careful graded rewarming with gentle handling, and near-drowning needs early ventilation and close observation for delayed lung injury. Prompt emergency care and community prevention measures greatly reduce deaths from these environmental emergencies.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients in Emergency and Disaster Situations
question: Explain the emergency management of dog bite, snake bite and scorpion sting.
answer_html:
Introduction Bites and stings are common emergencies in rural India, especially among farmers, labourers and children. Correct first aid and hospital care prevent deaths from rabies, snake envenoming and scorpion stings.

1. Dog bite (and other mammal bites) – prevention of rabies

  • Immediate wound care – wash the wound thoroughly with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes and apply an antiseptic (povidone-iodine); do not apply chilli, oil or herbs; avoid suturing immediately (if essential, after infiltrating rabies immunoglobulin).
  • Categories of exposure (WHO)
    • Category I – touching, feeding, licks on intact skin: no post-exposure prophylaxis.
    • Category II – nibbling of uncovered skin, minor scratches without bleeding: anti-rabies vaccine.
    • Category III – single or multiple transdermal bites or scratches, licks on broken skin or mucous membranes, any bat exposure: anti-rabies vaccine plus rabies immunoglobulin infiltrated into and around the wounds.
  • Vaccine by IM or intradermal schedule as per national guidelines; tetanus prophylaxis; antibiotics for deep or infected wounds; record and follow up for completion of the schedule.
  • India aims at elimination of dog-mediated rabies by 2030 under the National Action Plan for dog-mediated Rabies Elimination (NAPRE).

2. Snake bite

  • Venomous snakes ("big four") – cobra and common krait (neurotoxic: ptosis, double vision, difficulty swallowing and breathing, paralysis; krait bites often painless, at night while sleeping on the floor), Russell's viper and saw-scaled viper (haemotoxic: local swelling, bleeding from gums and bite site, blood in urine, acute kidney injury).
  • First aid – "Do it R.I.G.H.T." – Reassure, Immobilise the limb like a fracture, Go to hospital quickly, Tell the doctor about symptoms; no tourniquet, cutting, sucking, ice or herbal remedies.
  • Hospital management
    • Assess ABC and signs of envenoming; 20-minute whole blood clotting test (20WBCT) – blood that does not clot in 20 minutes indicates haemotoxic envenoming.
    • Polyvalent anti-snake venom (ASV) for signs of systemic envenoming, with adrenaline ready for reactions.
    • Neostigmine with atropine for neurotoxic (cobra) envenoming; intubation and ventilation for respiratory paralysis (especially krait); dialysis for kidney injury; tetanus prophylaxis.
  • India's National Action Plan for Prevention and Control of Snakebite Envenoming (2024) aims to halve snakebite deaths by 2030.

3. Scorpion sting

  • The Indian red scorpion causes severe envenoming, especially in children; the venom produces an "autonomic storm" – initially vomiting, sweating, salivation and priapism, then high BP, fast pulse, cold extremities, followed by myocarditis, heart failure, pulmonary oedema and shock.
  • Management
    • Local pain: ice packs and local lignocaine infiltration; reassurance.
    • Prazosin (an alpha-1 blocker; oral, repeated every few hours according to response) – the key drug that has greatly reduced deaths, a treatment developed through research in Maharashtra; scorpion antivenom together with prazosin speeds recovery.
    • Treat pulmonary oedema and heart failure (oxygen, dobutamine, ventilation as needed); avoid atropine.
    • Keep the patient lying down after the first dose of prazosin (risk of postural hypotension).

Nursing responsibilities

  • First aid and rapid transfer; monitoring of vital signs, oxygen saturation, urine output, neurological signs, bleeding and the bitten limb (swelling, compartment syndrome); safe administration of vaccines, ASV and other drugs with emergency equipment ready; tetanus prophylaxis; reassurance; documentation and follow-up for vaccine schedules; community education – wearing footwear and using a torch at night, sleeping on cots under mosquito nets, keeping surroundings clear of rubbish and rodents, shaking out shoes and clothes, and vaccination of pet dogs.

Conclusion Thorough wound washing with timely vaccine and immunoglobulin prevents rabies; immobilisation, rapid transfer and ASV save snake-bite victims; and prazosin with antivenom has transformed the outcome of scorpion stings. Nurses provide life-saving first aid, monitoring and community education.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients in Emergency and Disaster Situations
question: Explain the principles of emergency nursing and the organisation of an emergency department.
answer_html:
Introduction Emergency nursing is the care of patients of all ages with sudden, acute or life-threatening illness or injury, often before a diagnosis is known. The emergency department (ED) is the "front door" of the hospital, and its organisation strongly affects patient outcomes.

1. Principles of emergency nursing

  1. Rapid assessment and prioritisation (triage) – treat the most critical first.
  2. ABCDE approach – airway, breathing, circulation, disability and exposure; treat life threats as they are found ("treat first, diagnose later").
  3. Team approach – clearly defined roles, a team leader and closed-loop communication.
  4. Continuous monitoring and reassessment of every patient, including those waiting.
  5. Evidence-based protocols – for chest pain, stroke, trauma, sepsis, poisoning and obstetric emergencies.
  6. Safety – standard precautions, isolation of infectious patients, safe medication practices, prevention of falls and violence.
  7. Communication and family-centred care – timely, honest information to patients and relatives.
  8. Legal and ethical duties – emergency care cannot be refused; stabilisation before transfer; consent, medico-legal documentation and confidentiality.
  9. Accurate documentation – times, findings, treatment and handover.
  10. Continuity of care – safe handover and transfer to ward, ICU, OT or another hospital.

2. Organisation of the emergency department A. Location

  • Ground floor with easy ambulance access and a covered drop-off, clear signage, a separate entrance from OPD; close to radiology, laboratory, blood bank, operation theatres and ICU.

B. Zones

  • Triage and registration area at the entrance.
  • Resuscitation (red) area – fully equipped beds for critically ill patients.
  • Acute (yellow) area – monitored beds for urgent patients.
  • Minor (green) area – minor injuries and illnesses; minor procedure room or minor OT, plaster room.
  • Observation unit for short stays.
  • Isolation room (infections) and decontamination area (chemical exposure).
  • Special areas – paediatric corner, obstetric emergency room, safe room for psychiatric patients, medico-legal room, mortuary access.
  • Support areas – nursing station with a clear view of beds, drug store, clean and dirty utility rooms, staff room, relatives' waiting area.

C. Equipment

  • Crash cart with emergency drugs, defibrillator, monitors, oxygen and suction at every bed, airway trolley (laryngoscopes, endotracheal tubes, supraglottic devices), ventilators, infusion pumps, ECG machine, point-of-care testing (glucometer, ABG), splints, spine boards, cervical collars, warming devices, ultrasound and portable X-ray.

D. Staffing and training

  • Round-the-clock trained doctors and nurses; nurse–patient ratio according to acuity (1:1 for resuscitation beds); BLS, ACLS, ATLS and paediatric life-support training; support staff and security.

E. Systems and quality

  • Links with 108/112 ambulance services, inter-hospital referral protocols, disaster plan, policies for medico-legal cases, infection control and biomedical waste, audit of time-sensitive indicators (door-to-ECG, door-to-needle times) and accreditation standards.

3. Role of the emergency nurse

  • Triage, resuscitation and stabilisation, monitoring, medication administration, procedures (IV access, catheterisation, splinting, wound care), patient and family communication, documentation, coordination with other departments and maintenance of equipment and supplies.

Conclusion Emergency nursing rests on rapid prioritisation, the ABCDE approach, teamwork, protocols, safety and continuous reassessment. A well-located ED with clear zones, complete equipment, trained staff and good systems allows nurses to deliver timely, life-saving care.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients in Emergency and Disaster Situations
question: Explain the medico-legal aspects of emergency care and the nurse's responsibilities.
answer_html:
Introduction Many patients reaching the emergency department have injuries or illnesses with legal implications. Correct handling protects the patient's rights, helps the justice system and protects health professionals from legal problems.

1. Medico-legal case (MLC)

  • A case of injury or illness where investigation by law-enforcement agencies is needed to fix responsibility.
  • Examples – road traffic accidents, assaults, burns, poisoning, gunshot and stab wounds, suspected homicide or suicide attempts, sexual assault, dowry-related injuries, injuries in custody, unknown unconscious patients, brought-dead cases and suspicious deaths, and criminal abortion.

2. Duties of health professionals

  1. Treatment comes first – emergency care must never be delayed or refused for police formalities; the Supreme Court in Parmanand Katara v. Union of India (1989) held that every doctor must give immediate medical aid to injured persons.
  2. Inform the police promptly and register the case in the MLC register; give a copy of the MLC report to the police on request.
  3. Consent – in an emergency, life-saving treatment can be given under implied consent when the patient cannot consent and relatives are not available; consent for examination in assault cases is taken from the victim (or guardian for minors).
  4. Documentation – date and time of arrival, who brought the patient, history in the patient's own words, level of consciousness, detailed description of every injury (type, size, site, shape), treatment given and condition; entries must be legible, signed and never altered.
  5. Preservation of evidence – clothing, bullets, weapons, gastric aspirate, blood and urine samples are preserved in sealed, labelled containers and handed over with a record (chain of custody).
  6. Dying declaration – arrange recording by a magistrate when the patient's life is in danger (admissible under Section 26 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023); the doctor certifies fitness to make the statement.
  7. Brought dead – do not issue a death certificate in suspicious cases; inform the police for inquest and post-mortem.

3. Protective laws and schemes

  • Good Samaritan protection – Section 134A of the Motor Vehicles Act (added in 2019) protects people who help road accident victims in good faith: they cannot be detained, forced to disclose identity or held liable, and hospitals cannot demand payment from them.
  • Cashless Treatment of Road Accident Victims Scheme, 2025 – cashless treatment up to ₹1.5 lakh per victim for up to 7 days at designated hospitals.
  • Free immediate treatment of victims of acid attacks and sexual offences by all hospitals, public or private (Section 397, BNSS), with intimation to the police.
  • POCSO Act – mandatory reporting of sexual offences against children.
  • Mental Healthcare Act, 2017 – a person who attempts suicide is presumed to be under severe stress and is to be cared for and rehabilitated rather than punished.

4. Other legal issues

  • Leaving against medical advice (LAMA) – explain the risks and obtain a signed refusal; document carefully.
  • Confidentiality – share information only with authorised persons; protect the identity of sexual-assault victims.
  • Restraints – only when necessary, as per policy, with documentation.
  • Negligence – following standard protocols, documenting care and communicating clearly protect against allegations.

5. Nurse's responsibilities

  • Recognise MLCs and inform the doctor in charge; give treatment without delay; maintain the MLC register; document injuries and nursing care accurately; preserve and hand over evidence; maintain confidentiality; act as a witness when required; support victims and families; and know the relevant laws and hospital policies.

Conclusion Emergency care often has medico-legal implications. Prompt treatment, proper intimation to the police, accurate documentation, preservation of evidence and knowledge of protective laws such as the Good Samaritan provisions safeguard patients, the justice process and health professionals.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients in Emergency and Disaster Situations
question: Explain the disaster management framework in India.
answer_html:
Introduction India is one of the most disaster-prone countries – vulnerable to floods, cyclones, droughts, heat waves, earthquakes, landslides and industrial accidents. After the 2004 tsunami, India shifted from a relief-centred approach to a holistic, proactive disaster risk-reduction approach with a legal and institutional framework.

1. Legal and policy framework

  • Disaster Management Act, 2005 – created a three-tier structure of authorities, response forces, funds and plans.
  • Disaster Management (Amendment) Act, 2025 – in force from April 2025; it allows states to set up Urban Disaster Management Authorities for state capitals and cities with municipal corporations (urban flooding, heat waves, building collapses), provides for national and state disaster databases, empowers NDMA and SDMAs to prepare disaster plans directly, gives statutory status to crisis-management committees and enables states to form State Disaster Response Forces.
  • National Policy on Disaster Management (2009) and the National Disaster Management Plan (2016, revised 2019), aligned with the Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction (2015–2030).

2. Institutional structure

  • National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) – chaired by the Prime Minister; lays down policies, plans and guidelines.
  • State Disaster Management Authority (SDMA) – chaired by the Chief Minister.
  • District Disaster Management Authority (DDMA) – chaired by the District Collector, with the elected head of the local body as co-chairperson; the key level for planning and response.
  • Urban Disaster Management Authorities – headed by the Municipal Commissioner (under the 2025 amendment).
  • National Crisis Management Committee (Cabinet Secretary) for major crises.
  • Ministry of Home Affairs – nodal ministry; other ministries have specific roles (e.g. health for epidemics and biological disasters).

3. Response forces and institutions

  • National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) – specialised battalions for search and rescue, flood, collapsed-structure and CBRN response.
  • State Disaster Response Forces, civil defence, home guards, fire services and the armed forces.
  • National Institute of Disaster Management (NIDM) – training, research and capacity building.
  • Aapda Mitra – training of community volunteers as first responders.
  • Emergency numbers – 112 (integrated emergency response), 108 (ambulance), 1070 (state control room) and 1077 (district control room).

4. Funds

  • National and State Disaster Response Funds for immediate relief and Mitigation Funds for risk reduction.

5. Sendai Framework priorities

  1. Understanding disaster risk.
  2. Strengthening disaster risk governance.
  3. Investing in disaster risk reduction for resilience.
  4. Enhancing preparedness for effective response and to "build back better" in recovery.

6. Health sector preparedness

  • NDMA guidelines on hospital safety and medical preparedness and mass casualty management; hospital disaster plans and mock drills; surveillance and outbreak response through the Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme; stockpiles of drugs and equipment; heat-action plans; psychosocial support services.

7. Role of the nurse

  • Participate in hospital and community disaster planning, drills and training; serve as first responders and triage officers; provide public health and psychosocial care in relief camps; educate communities about preparedness.

Conclusion India's disaster management framework, built on the Disaster Management Act, 2005 and strengthened by the 2025 amendment, works through NDMA, SDMAs, DDMAs and urban authorities, specialised response forces, funds and plans aligned with the Sendai Framework. Nurses contribute at every level, from preparedness to recovery.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients in Emergency and Disaster Situations
question: Explain the psychosocial care of disaster survivors, including psychological first aid.
answer_html:
Introduction Disasters cause not only physical injuries but also severe emotional and social distress – loss of family members, homes, livelihoods and a sense of safety. Most survivors recover with basic support, but some develop lasting mental-health problems. Psychosocial care addresses both psychological and social needs and is an essential part of disaster response.

1. Psychological reactions

  • Normal reactions (common in the first days and weeks) – shock, numbness, fear, anxiety, sadness, anger, guilt (especially survivor guilt), sleep disturbance, nightmares, poor concentration, physical complaints (headache, palpitations).
  • Disorders in some survivors – acute stress reaction, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) (re-experiencing through flashbacks and nightmares, avoidance of reminders, hyper-arousal), depression, anxiety disorders, complicated grief and alcohol or substance misuse; increased risk of suicide.
  • Children – clinging, regression (bed-wetting, thumb-sucking), fear of separation, nightmares, behavioural and school problems.
  • Vulnerable groups – children, women, the elderly, people with disabilities or prior mental illness, those who lost family members, and rescue workers.

2. Psychological first aid (PFA) PFA is humane, supportive, practical help to people in distress, which can be given by trained non-specialists, including nurses. WHO describes its action principles as Look, Listen and Link:

  • Look – check for safety, people with urgent basic needs and those with serious distress reactions.
  • Listen – approach respectfully, ask about needs and concerns, listen without pressuring people to talk, help them feel calm.
  • Link – help people meet basic needs and access services, cope with problems, obtain accurate information and connect with loved ones and social support. PFA follows the principles of promoting safety, calm, connectedness, self-efficacy and hope; forcing people to describe their traumatic experiences in detail ("debriefing") is avoided.

3. Psychosocial interventions

  • Meet basic needs – food, water, shelter, medical care; reunite families; trace missing persons.
  • Provide accurate, regular information to reduce rumours and anxiety.
  • Encourage community and family support, restoration of routines, and cultural and religious rituals for the dead.
  • Child-friendly spaces, early reopening of schools and play activities.
  • Livelihood support and help with compensation procedures.
  • Screen and refer people with severe or persistent distress, suicidal thoughts, psychosis or substance misuse to mental-health professionals; continue follow-up for months, as PTSD may appear later.
  • Use helplines such as Tele-MANAS (14416) for continued support.

4. Care of responders

  • Health workers and rescuers are exposed to traumatic scenes and long hours – ensure rest, rotation, peer support, debriefing opportunities and access to counselling.

5. Role of the nurse

  • Provide PFA, identify high-risk individuals, give emotional support and health education, involve families and communities, refer appropriately, care for special groups and practise self-care.

Conclusion Disasters produce normal distress reactions in most survivors and serious mental-health problems in some. Psychological first aid based on Look, Listen and Link, attention to basic needs and social support, and timely referral – all within the scope of nursing – help survivors recover and rebuild their lives.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients in Emergency and Disaster Situations
question: What is a hospital disaster protocol? List its key components.
answer_html:
A hospital disaster protocol (plan) is a written, pre-planned set of procedures that tells every department and staff member what to do when a disaster occurs – either an external disaster bringing mass casualties or an internal disaster such as fire, flood or power failure – so that the hospital can continue to function and care for many patients.

Key components

  1. Disaster committee and incident command system with clear roles (action cards).
  2. Alert and activation – disaster code, staff call-in lists, communication system.
  3. Triage area and designated red, yellow and green treatment areas; decontamination and isolation areas.
  4. Surge capacity – discharge of stable patients, cancellation of elective surgery, extra beds, staff and supplies.
  5. Logistics – drugs, blood, oxygen, equipment, power and water backup.
  6. Patient tracking, documentation, information centre for relatives and media.
  7. Coordination with external agencies (ambulance, police, district authority).
  8. Training and regular mock drills, evaluation and updating of the plan.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients in Emergency and Disaster Situations
question: List the phases of disaster management.
answer_html:
Disaster management is a continuous cycle with the following phases:

  1. Mitigation (prevention) – long-term measures to reduce the impact of hazards, e.g. earthquake-resistant buildings, embankments, land-use planning, early-warning systems.
  2. Preparedness – plans, training, mock drills, stockpiling of supplies, public awareness and evacuation plans.
  3. Response – immediate actions during and after the disaster: search and rescue, triage, medical care, shelter, water, food, sanitation and prevention of epidemics.
  4. Recovery – rehabilitation (restoring services and livelihoods, psychosocial support) and reconstruction (rebuilding infrastructure, "build back better"). Some descriptions add the disaster impact phase and development, which integrates lessons learned into future planning. Phases 1 and 2 are pre-disaster, and 3 and 4 are post-disaster activities.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients in Emergency and Disaster Situations
question: List four emergency drugs with their actions.
answer_html:
Drug Main action and use
Adrenaline (epinephrine) Stimulates alpha and beta receptors – raises BP and heart rate, bronchodilates; used in cardiac arrest and anaphylaxis
Atropine Anticholinergic – increases heart rate; used in symptomatic bradycardia and organophosphate poisoning
Amiodarone Antiarrhythmic – used in shock-refractory VF/pulseless VT and other tachyarrhythmias
Sodium bicarbonate Alkalinising agent – corrects severe metabolic acidosis, hyperkalaemia and tricyclic overdose
Calcium gluconate Stabilises the heart muscle in hyperkalaemia; treats low calcium and magnesium toxicity
50% dextrose Raises blood sugar in hypoglycaemia
Naloxone Opioid antagonist – reverses opioid overdose
Midazolam / diazepam Anticonvulsant and sedative – stops seizures
Other emergency drugs include hydrocortisone, furosemide, adenosine, nitroglycerin and magnesium sulphate. The nurse keeps these drugs checked and ready on the crash cart and knows their doses and side effects.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients in Emergency and Disaster Situations
question: What is the "golden hour" in trauma care?
answer_html:
The golden hour is the first 60 minutes after a serious injury, during which rapid resuscitation and definitive treatment (control of bleeding, airway and breathing support, transfer to a trauma centre, surgery) give the patient the best chance of survival and reduce disability. Many trauma deaths in this period – from airway obstruction, tension pneumothorax, haemorrhage or intracranial bleeding – are preventable.

  • The first 10 minutes at the scene are sometimes called the "platinum ten minutes" – on-scene care should be quick and focused on life-saving steps.
  • India's Motor Vehicles Act defines the golden hour, and the cashless treatment scheme for road accident victims and Good Samaritan protection encourage bystanders to bring victims to hospital quickly.
  • Nursing role – rapid triage, ABCDE care, preparation of the resuscitation area and quick coordination with the trauma team.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients in Emergency and Disaster Situations
question: What is decompression sickness?
answer_html:
Decompression sickness (caisson disease, "the bends") is a condition caused by formation of nitrogen gas bubbles in the blood and tissues when a person moves too quickly from high pressure to lower pressure – for example, divers ascending rapidly, tunnel and caisson workers, or pilots and astronauts at high altitude. Dissolved nitrogen comes out of solution as bubbles that block vessels and damage tissues.

  • Features – joint and muscle pain ("bends"), itching and skin mottling, fatigue (type I); neurological symptoms (numbness, weakness, paralysis, confusion), breathlessness and chest pain ("chokes") and shock (type II).
  • Management – lie flat, 100% oxygen, IV fluids and urgent recompression in a hyperbaric oxygen chamber.
  • Prevention – slow ascent with decompression stops, adherence to diving tables, avoiding flying for about 24 hours after diving.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Care of the Elderly
question: (a) Define ageing and explain the theories of ageing. (5 marks) (b) Explain the "geriatric giants" and describe the nursing management of an elderly patient. (10 marks)

diagram.caption: The geriatric giants (the "I's" of geriatrics)
labels: isolation and inanition (malnutrition) as additional problems

answer_html:
(a) Definition and theories of ageing (5 marks) Ageing is the natural, progressive and irreversible process of change in the structure and function of the body and mind that occurs with the passage of time, leading to reduced reserve capacity, reduced ability to adapt to stress and increased vulnerability to disease. In India, a person aged 60 years and above is called a senior citizen; about one in ten Indians is now elderly, and this proportion is expected to roughly double by 2050. Gerontology is the study of ageing, and geriatrics is the branch of medicine concerned with the health care of older people.

Theories of ageing A. Biological theories

  1. Genetic (programmed) theory – ageing is controlled by a "biological clock" in the genes; cells can divide only a limited number of times (Hayflick limit), partly because telomeres (protective ends of chromosomes) shorten with each division.
  2. Wear-and-tear theory – cells and organs wear out with repeated use and accumulated damage, like a machine.
  3. Free-radical theory – unstable oxygen molecules (free radicals) produced during metabolism damage cell membranes, proteins and DNA; antioxidants may slow this damage.
  4. Cross-linkage theory – proteins such as collagen develop cross-links and become stiff, causing wrinkled skin, stiff joints and blood vessels.
  5. Immunological theory – the immune system declines (immunosenescence), increasing infections, cancers and autoimmune diseases.
  6. Neuroendocrine theory – changes in hormones (growth hormone, sex hormones, cortisol) and their regulation lead to ageing changes.

B. Psychosocial theories

  1. Disengagement theory (Cumming and Henry) – older people and society gradually withdraw from each other, which is considered natural and mutually beneficial (now widely criticised).
  2. Activity theory (Havighurst) – remaining active and socially involved promotes satisfaction and successful ageing; lost roles should be replaced by new ones.
  3. Continuity theory – people tend to keep their personality, habits and preferences; successful ageing involves continuing familiar patterns adapted to new limitations.
  4. Developmental theory (Erikson) – the last stage of life involves integrity versus despair; looking back on life with satisfaction gives wisdom and acceptance, whereas regret leads to despair.

C. Sociological theory

  • Age-stratification theory – society groups people by age, and each cohort experiences ageing differently according to social and historical circumstances.

(b) Geriatric giants and nursing management (10 marks) A. The geriatric giants The term (described by Bernard Isaacs) refers to the common, disabling problems of old age that usually have multiple causes, cause loss of independence and are often wrongly accepted as "normal ageing":

  1. Immobility – due to arthritis, stroke, Parkinson's disease, fractures, weakness, pain or fear of falling; leads to pressure sores, contractures, constipation, pneumonia, DVT and depression.
  2. Instability and falls – due to poor balance, weak muscles, poor vision, postural hypotension, sedative drugs and home hazards; falls cause fractures (especially hip fractures), head injury and fear of falling.
  3. Incontinence – urinary (urge, stress, overflow, functional) and faecal; causes skin breakdown, embarrassment and isolation.
  4. Intellectual impairment – dementia (chronic, progressive) and delirium (acute confusion due to infection, drugs, dehydration, retention of urine or constipation – a medical emergency).
  5. Iatrogenesis – harm from medical care, especially polypharmacy (many medicines, drug interactions and side effects), hospital-acquired infections and complications of bed rest. Additional problems often included: impaired vision and hearing, isolation and loneliness, insomnia and inanition (malnutrition).

B. Comprehensive geriatric assessment A multidimensional assessment by the team:

  • Physical health – history, examination, list of diseases and all medicines (including over-the-counter and herbal); vision, hearing, teeth, nutrition (weight, BMI, Mini Nutritional Assessment), continence, sleep, pain.
  • Functional status – Activities of Daily Living (Katz index – bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, continence, feeding) and Instrumental ADL (Lawton – cooking, shopping, money, medicines, telephone).
  • Mobility and fall risk – gait, balance, Timed Up and Go test.
  • Cognition and mood – Mini-Mental State Examination or Mini-Cog; Geriatric Depression Scale.
  • Social and environmental – family support, caregiver stress, finances, living conditions and home safety, risk of abuse.

C. Nursing management of an elderly patient

  1. Promoting mobility and preventing falls
    • Early mobilisation, range-of-motion and strengthening exercises, balance training (walking, yoga); walking aids.
    • Safe environment – low beds, side rails as appropriate, good lighting and night lights, non-slip floors, grab bars, call bell within reach, proper footwear; rise slowly (postural hypotension); review sedatives.
  2. Continence care – regular toileting schedule, easy access to toilet or commode, pelvic-floor exercises, treatment of infection and constipation, skin care with barrier creams; avoid unnecessary catheters.
  3. Cognitive care – screen for delirium daily in hospital; identify and treat causes; reorientation (clock, calendar, familiar objects, family presence), glasses and hearing aids in place, good sleep, avoid restraints and unnecessary sedatives.
  4. Medication safety – review all medicines and stop unnecessary ones (deprescribing); simple regimens, pill organisers, large-print labels; watch for side effects (dizziness, confusion, bleeding, low sugar).
  5. Nutrition and hydration – balanced diet adequate in protein, calcium, vitamin D and fibre; soft foods for poor dentition; regular fluids (thirst sensation is reduced); weight monitoring; help with feeding.
  6. Skin care – pressure-area care, 2-hourly turning in bed-bound patients, moisturisers for dry skin, prevention of injuries.
  7. Elimination – fibre, fluids, activity and regular toileting habits to prevent constipation.
  8. Sensory support – spectacles, cataract surgery referral, hearing aids, speaking slowly and clearly while facing the person.
  9. Sleep – regular routine, daytime activity, limited daytime naps, avoidance of tea and coffee in the evening, quiet environment.
  10. Psychosocial care – respect, dignity and privacy; encourage independence and decision-making; listen to life stories (reminiscence); prevent loneliness through family and community involvement; screen for depression and abuse.
  11. Health promotion – vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal), screening for BP, diabetes, cancers and vision; exercise; safe living environment.
  12. Caregiver support and discharge planning – teach family caregivers, arrange home care and community services, link to government schemes for senior citizens.

D. Atypical presentation of illness in the elderly (points for nursing assessment)

  • Pneumonia and urinary infection may present with confusion, falls or loss of appetite rather than fever or cough.
  • Myocardial infarction may cause only breathlessness, fatigue or confusion without chest pain ("silent MI"), especially in diabetics.
  • Acute abdomen (appendicitis, perforation) may show little pain or tenderness.
  • Thyroid disease and depression may appear as tiredness, weight loss or memory problems.
  • Drug side effects often appear as dizziness, falls, confusion, constipation or urinary retention. Therefore, any sudden change in function or behaviour in an older person must be treated as a sign of possible illness and reported, not dismissed as "old age".

Nursing importance

  • Older people often present atypically (e.g. confusion or a fall instead of fever in pneumonia), so nurses who know the geriatric giants and use comprehensive assessment detect problems early and preserve independence.

Conclusion Ageing is a natural, progressive process explained by biological, psychosocial and sociological theories. The geriatric giants – immobility, instability, incontinence, intellectual impairment and iatrogenesis – threaten independence in old age. Comprehensive geriatric assessment and holistic, respectful nursing care that promotes mobility, safety, continence, cognition, nutrition and social participation help elderly people live with dignity and the best possible function.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Care of the Elderly
question: Explain the age-related changes in the body systems of the elderly and their nursing implications.
answer_html:
Introduction With ageing, every body system shows gradual structural and functional changes that reduce reserve capacity. These changes are normal, but they increase the risk of disease, alter how illness presents and affect nursing care.

1. Integumentary system – thin, dry, less elastic skin with wrinkles; reduced subcutaneous fat and sweat glands; slow wound healing; grey hair and thin nails.

  • Implications – risk of pressure injuries, skin tears and heat or cold injury; gentle handling, moisturisers, protection from extreme temperatures.

2. Cardiovascular system – stiffer arteries, raised systolic BP, reduced cardiac output on exertion, slower heart-rate response, reduced baroreceptor sensitivity.

  • Implications – postural hypotension (rise slowly), reduced exercise tolerance, careful IV fluid administration.

3. Respiratory system – reduced lung elasticity and chest-wall movement, weaker respiratory muscles and cough, reduced vital capacity.

  • Implications – higher risk of pneumonia and atelectasis; deep-breathing exercises, early mobilisation, vaccination.

4. Renal and urinary system – fewer nephrons, reduced GFR and concentrating ability; smaller bladder capacity, weaker detrusor muscle; enlarged prostate in men.

  • Implications – drug doses adjusted to kidney function, risk of dehydration and electrolyte imbalance, nocturia, urgency and incontinence.

5. Gastrointestinal system – tooth loss, dry mouth, reduced taste and smell, slower gastric emptying and gut motility, reduced absorption of some nutrients.

  • Implications – constipation, malnutrition, choking risk; soft balanced diet, fibre, fluids, oral care and dentures.

6. Musculoskeletal system – loss of muscle mass and strength (sarcopenia), bone loss (osteoporosis), joint cartilage wear (osteoarthritis), reduced height and posture changes.

  • Implications – falls and fractures, reduced mobility; exercise, calcium and vitamin D, fall prevention.

7. Nervous system – loss of neurons, slower reaction time and processing, mild memory changes, altered sleep pattern (lighter, more fragmented sleep), reduced temperature and pain perception.

  • Implications – allow more time for learning, safety measures, risk of delirium when ill.

8. Special senses – presbyopia, cataract, reduced night vision and colour discrimination; presbycusis (high-frequency hearing loss); reduced taste, smell and touch.

  • Implications – good lighting, large print, spectacles and hearing aids; speak slowly and clearly while facing the person; check food temperature.

9. Endocrine and reproductive systems – reduced insulin sensitivity (risk of diabetes), menopause and decline in sex hormones, thyroid changes.

  • Implications – screening for diabetes and thyroid disease; counselling on sexuality.

10. Immune system – immunosenescence – reduced response to infection and vaccines; atypical presentation without fever.

  • Implications – vaccination, infection prevention, high index of suspicion (confusion may be the only sign of infection).

Conclusion Ageing brings gradual changes in all systems – thinner skin, stiffer vessels, weaker lungs and muscles, reduced kidney function, sensory decline and weaker immunity. Understanding these changes helps nurses adapt care, prevent complications such as falls, pressure injuries and drug toxicity, and recognise illness early in older people.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Care of the Elderly
question: Explain the role of the nurse in the care of the elderly.
tags: role of nurse in geriatric care
answer_html:
Introduction Nurses care for older people in hospitals, homes, communities, day-care centres and old-age homes. Because elderly people often have several chronic illnesses, disabilities and social needs, the nurse takes on many roles to help them stay healthy, independent and dignified.

1. Care provider

  • Holistic nursing care – hygiene, nutrition, mobility, elimination, sleep, pain relief, wound and skin care, medication administration and monitoring for side effects.
  • Management of acute illness, chronic diseases (diabetes, hypertension, COPD, arthritis) and the geriatric giants.

2. Assessor

  • Comprehensive geriatric assessment – physical, functional (ADL and IADL), cognitive, emotional, nutritional, social and environmental; risk assessment for falls, pressure injuries, malnutrition, delirium and abuse.

3. Health promoter and educator

  • Education on healthy diet, exercise, vaccination, regular screening (BP, sugar, vision, cancers), medication adherence, foot care, home safety and prevention of falls.
  • Teaching family caregivers about care skills, warning signs and caregiver self-care.

4. Counsellor and psychological supporter

  • Support during loss of spouse, retirement, chronic illness and loneliness; screening for depression and suicidal thoughts; encouragement of social participation and spiritual well-being.

5. Advocate

  • Protect the rights, dignity, privacy and autonomy of older people; involve them in decisions; recognise and report elder abuse; fight ageism in health care.

6. Care coordinator and manager

  • Coordinate with doctors, physiotherapists, dietitians, social workers and community services; discharge planning; continuity of care between hospital and home; management of geriatric wards and day-care centres.

7. Rehabilitator

  • Help regain function after stroke, fractures or surgery; encourage self-care with assistive devices; arrange physiotherapy and occupational therapy.

8. Community and home-care nurse

  • Home visits, care of bed-bound elderly, palliative care at home, organisation of elderly health camps; link elderly people with schemes such as geriatric clinics under the National Programme for Health Care of the Elderly, pensions, Ayushman Vay Vandana health cover and the Elderline (14567) helpline.

9. End-of-life care provider

  • Palliative care, advance care planning, comfort at the end of life and bereavement support.

10. Researcher and policy contributor

  • Participate in studies on ageing and evidence-based geriatric care; contribute to policies and elder-friendly services.

Conclusion The nurse in elderly care is a caregiver, assessor, educator, counsellor, advocate, coordinator, rehabilitator and community link. By combining clinical skill with respect and compassion, the nurse helps older people live healthy, independent and dignified lives.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Care of the Elderly
question: What is elder abuse? Explain its types, with special reference to psychological and sexual abuse, and the role of the nurse.
tags: Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007
answer_html:
Definition WHO defines elder abuse as a single or repeated act, or lack of appropriate action, occurring within any relationship where there is an expectation of trust, which causes harm or distress to an older person. In India it occurs mostly within families, often by sons, daughters-in-law and other relatives, and is greatly under-reported because of shame, dependence and fear.

1. Types of elder abuse

  • Physical abuse – hitting, pushing, burning, improper restraint or over-medication.
  • Psychological (emotional) abuse – verbal insults, humiliation, threats, shouting, ignoring, isolating the person from friends and family, threatening to send them to an old-age home or to abandon them, infantilisation (treating them like a child).
  • Sexual abuse – any non-consensual sexual contact or behaviour, including touching, exposure, forced viewing of sexual material or rape; it may affect older people with dementia or disability who cannot consent or report.
  • Financial (material) abuse – misuse of pension, property or savings; forcing transfer of property or signing of documents.
  • Neglect – failure to provide food, clothing, medicines, hygiene or care; self-neglect in isolated elderly.
  • Abandonment – deserting the older person, e.g. at hospitals, railway stations or religious places.

2. Psychological abuse – signs

  • Fearfulness, anxiety, withdrawal, depression, unusual silence or agitation in the presence of the caregiver, low self-esteem, sleep disturbance, loss of appetite, helplessness, suicidal ideas.

3. Sexual abuse – signs

  • Unexplained bruises around the breasts, genitals or inner thighs; genital bleeding, pain or infections (STIs); torn or stained underclothing; difficulty in walking or sitting; sudden fear of a particular person; behaviour changes in persons with dementia.

4. Risk factors

  • Dependence due to dementia, disability or chronic illness; living with the abuser; caregiver stress, alcoholism or mental illness; financial dependence of the abuser on the elder; social isolation; family conflicts over property.

5. Legal protection

  • Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007 – children and relatives are legally bound to maintain parents and senior citizens; maintenance tribunals; transfer of property can be cancelled if the elder is neglected; abandonment is a punishable offence.
  • Criminal laws on assault, cruelty, sexual offences and cheating apply equally; police and senior-citizen help desks; Elderline – 14567 (national helpline for senior citizens).

6. Role of the nurse

  1. Recognise abuse – look for unexplained injuries, delays in seeking care, inconsistent history, poor hygiene, malnutrition, fearful behaviour; interview the older person privately.
  2. Document findings objectively (injuries, statements in the person's own words, photographs with consent).
  3. Ensure immediate safety – treatment of injuries, admission or shelter if needed; medico-legal procedures in serious cases.
  4. Report and refer – inform the doctor in charge, social worker, police or maintenance tribunal as appropriate; provide information about Elderline and legal aid.
  5. Support – counselling for the elder; respect their wishes and autonomy; address shame and fear.
  6. Prevention – educate families about the needs of the elderly, support stressed caregivers (respite care, day care, counselling), promote community awareness on World Elder Abuse Awareness Day (15 June) and social inclusion.

Conclusion Elder abuse may be physical, psychological, sexual, financial, neglect or abandonment, and is often hidden within families. Psychological and sexual abuse have subtle signs that nurses must recognise. Through careful assessment, documentation, reporting, support, legal awareness and caregiver education, nurses protect the safety and dignity of older people.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Care of the Elderly
question: Explain the national policies, programmes and welfare measures for the elderly in India.
tags: National Programme for Health Care of the Elderly
Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act 2007
Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme
answer_html:
Introduction India's elderly population is growing rapidly, with increasing chronic illness, disability and social insecurity. The government has introduced policies, laws, health programmes and welfare schemes to protect the health, income and dignity of senior citizens (aged 60 years and above).

1. Policies and laws

  • National Policy on Older Persons (1999) – financial and food security, health care, shelter, education, welfare and protection of life and property of the elderly.
  • Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007 – legal obligation of children and relatives to maintain parents and senior citizens, maintenance tribunals, protection of life and property, revocation of property transfer in case of neglect, punishment for abandonment and provision for old-age homes and geriatric care.

2. Health programmes

  • National Programme for Health Care of the Elderly (NPHCE, 2010) – dedicated, comprehensive and affordable health care at all levels:
    • Health promotion, screening and home-based care by health workers at Ayushman Arogya Mandirs (sub-centres and PHCs).
    • Geriatric clinics and rehabilitation services at CHCs.
    • Geriatric OPDs and 10-bed geriatric wards at district hospitals.
    • Regional Geriatric Centres in medical colleges (geriatric departments, training, research).
    • National Centres for Ageing at AIIMS New Delhi and Madras Medical College, Chennai.
  • Ayushman Bharat PM-JAY – since October 2024, all citizens aged 70 years and above, irrespective of income, are covered for hospital care through the Ayushman Vay Vandana card (₹5 lakh per year).
  • National programmes for NCDs, blindness and visual impairment (free cataract surgery), mental health and palliative care also serve the elderly.

3. Social security and welfare schemes

  • Indira Gandhi National Old Age Pension Scheme (IGNOAPS) under the National Social Assistance Programme – monthly pension for elderly people from below-poverty-line families, with state top-ups.
  • Atal Vayo Abhyuday Yojana (AVYAY) – umbrella scheme of the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, including:
    • Integrated Programme for Senior Citizens – grants for old-age homes, day-care centres, mobile medicare units and physiotherapy clinics.
    • Rashtriya Vayoshri Yojana – free assistive devices (walking sticks, hearing aids, spectacles, wheelchairs, dentures) for eligible senior citizens.
    • Elderline (14567) – national toll-free helpline for information, guidance, emotional support and help in abuse cases.
    • Support for start-ups providing elder-care products and services.
  • Other benefits – higher interest rates on senior-citizen savings schemes, income-tax relief, priority counters and reserved seats, and state-specific schemes.

4. Observances – International Day of Older Persons (1 October) and World Elder Abuse Awareness Day (15 June).

5. Role of the nurse

  • Inform elderly people and families about these schemes and help with enrolment (pensions, Ayushman Vay Vandana card, assistive devices); provide services in geriatric clinics and home care under NPHCE; refer to Elderline and legal aid in cases of neglect or abuse; organise elderly health camps and awareness programmes.

Conclusion India protects its senior citizens through the National Policy on Older Persons, the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, NPHCE, PM-JAY coverage for those above 70, pensions and welfare schemes under AVYAY, and the Elderline helpline. Nurses help elderly people access these benefits and services.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Care of the Elderly
question: Explain the common health problems of the elderly and their nursing management.
answer_html:
Introduction Most older people live with several chronic conditions at the same time (multimorbidity), which reduce function and quality of life. Problems are often under-reported because they are wrongly accepted as "part of old age". Early recognition and simple nursing measures can greatly improve independence.

1. Musculoskeletal problems

  • Osteoarthritis of knees, hips and spine, osteoporosis with fractures, back pain and frailty (weakness, slowness, weight loss, low activity).
  • Nursing – pain relief, warm compresses, weight reduction, quadriceps and range-of-motion exercises, walking aids, calcium and vitamin D, fall prevention, referral for joint replacement when needed.

2. Sensory impairment

  • Cataract, presbyopia, glaucoma, diabetic retinopathy; age-related hearing loss (presbycusis) and ear-wax impaction.
  • Nursing – regular eye and hearing checks, referral for free cataract surgery, spectacles and hearing aids, good lighting, speaking slowly and clearly while facing the person.

3. Cardiovascular and metabolic diseases

  • Hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, heart failure, stroke, diabetes, high cholesterol.
  • Nursing – regular BP and sugar checks, adherence to medicines, low-salt and balanced diet, exercise, foot care, recognition of warning signs.

4. Respiratory problems – COPD, asthma, pneumonia and tuberculosis.

  • Nursing – breathing exercises, inhaler technique, smoke-free home, influenza and pneumococcal vaccination.

5. Gastrointestinal and oral problems

  • Dental loss, ill-fitting dentures, dry mouth, poor appetite, constipation, indigestion.
  • Nursing – oral hygiene and denture care, soft nutritious diet, fibre, fluids, regular toilet habits, review of constipating drugs.

6. Genitourinary problems

  • Urinary incontinence, frequency and nocturia, BPH in men, urinary infections, post-menopausal problems in women.
  • Nursing – timed toileting, pelvic-floor exercises, adequate fluids by day, skin care, early treatment of infections.

7. Neurological and mental health problems

  • Dementia, delirium, Parkinson's disease, stroke, depression, anxiety and sleep problems (insomnia, early waking).
  • Nursing – cognitive screening, safe environment, sleep hygiene (regular schedule, daytime activity, limited naps, no evening tea or coffee), social engagement, screening for depression.

8. Skin problems – dry itchy skin, pressure injuries, fungal infections, herpes zoster and skin cancers.

  • Nursing – moisturisers, mild soaps, pressure-area care, vaccination against herpes zoster where available.

9. Chronic pain and polypharmacy – pain from arthritis and neuropathy; side effects and interactions of multiple drugs.

  • Nursing – regular pain assessment (including in people with dementia), safe analgesia, medication review and simplification.

General nursing principles

  • Comprehensive geriatric assessment; prioritising function and quality of life; involving the older person and family in decisions; preventive care (vaccination, screening); encouraging physical, mental and social activity; and linking with geriatric clinics and community services.

Conclusion Older people commonly suffer from arthritis, sensory loss, cardiovascular and metabolic diseases, respiratory, digestive and urinary problems, cognitive and mood disorders, skin problems and chronic pain. Holistic assessment, prevention, symptom management and support for independence are the key nursing responsibilities.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Care of the Elderly
question: Explain depression and stress in the elderly and the nursing management.
answer_html:
Introduction Old age brings many losses – of spouse, friends, health, income, work role, independence and sometimes home. These stresses make older people vulnerable to depression, which is common but often missed because it is mistaken for normal ageing or for physical illness. Untreated depression worsens physical diseases, causes disability and increases the risk of suicide.

1. Causes of stress in old age

  • Bereavement – death of spouse, friends and relatives.
  • Retirement – loss of income, status and daily routine; financial insecurity.
  • Chronic illness, pain and disability; fear of dependence and death.
  • Changes in family structure – migration of children ("empty nest"), loss of respect or role in the joint family, conflicts, neglect or abuse.
  • Loneliness and social isolation, especially in widows and the homebound.
  • Relocation to old-age homes or children's homes in new cities.

2. Features of depression in the elderly

  • Persistent sadness, loss of interest and pleasure, hopelessness and feelings of being a burden.
  • More physical (somatic) complaints – pains, tiredness, poor appetite, weight loss, sleep disturbance, constipation – rather than reported sadness.
  • Cognitive complaints – poor memory and concentration that may look like dementia ("pseudodementia").
  • Withdrawal, irritability, neglect of self-care, refusal to eat or take medicines.
  • Suicidal thoughts – older men living alone with chronic illness are at high risk.

3. Assessment

  • Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS-15); screening for suicidal ideas; assessment of physical illness, medicines (e.g. beta blockers, steroids) and thyroid function; distinguishing from dementia and delirium.

4. Management

  • Psychotherapy – supportive counselling, cognitive behaviour therapy, problem-solving therapy, reminiscence and life-review therapy, grief counselling.
  • Antidepressants (e.g. SSRIs such as sertraline or escitalopram, started at low doses and increased slowly – "start low, go slow"); monitoring for side effects such as low sodium, falls and bleeding.
  • Treatment of physical illness and pain; ECT for severe or life-threatening depression.

5. Nursing management

  1. Build a trusting relationship; listen patiently and allow the person to express grief and fears.
  2. Ensure safety – assess suicide risk regularly, remove means of self-harm, observe closely when risk is high.
  3. Meet physical needs – nutrition, fluids, sleep, hygiene and elimination; encourage gradual self-care.
  4. Encourage activity and social contact – daily routine, light exercise, walks, hobbies, religious and community activities, senior citizens' clubs and day-care centres.
  5. Reminiscence – encourage sharing of life stories and achievements to restore self-worth.
  6. Medication care – adherence, monitoring of side effects, explaining that improvement takes 2–4 weeks.
  7. Family involvement – educate the family about depression, encourage regular contact and inclusion in family decisions; prevent neglect and abuse.
  8. Stress management – relaxation, breathing exercises, yoga, meditation, spiritual practices.
  9. Referral and follow-up – psychiatrist, counsellor, Tele-MANAS (14416) and Elderline (14567).

Conclusion Losses and life changes make older people vulnerable to stress and depression, which often presents with physical and memory complaints and carries a high suicide risk. Early screening, psychotherapy, careful drug treatment and compassionate nursing care focused on safety, activity, social connection and family support help elderly people recover.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Care of the Elderly
question: Explain home care and institutional care of the elderly.
answer_html:
Introduction Most older people in India live with their families and prefer to stay at home. However, migration of children, smaller families, chronic illness and dementia increase the need for organised home care and institutional care. A continuum of care allows the elderly to receive the right level of support at the right place.

1. Home care

  • Meaning – health and social care provided to the older person in their own home by family members, supported by nurses, health workers and community services.
  • Services – nursing care (wound care, injections, catheter care, monitoring of chronic diseases), physiotherapy, help with bathing, feeding and toileting, medication supervision, nutrition advice, palliative care, equipment (walkers, commodes, air mattresses) and telemedicine follow-up.
  • Advantages – familiar surroundings, family bonding, dignity and independence, lower cost, less risk of hospital infections and delirium.
  • Problems – caregiver stress and burnout, lack of trained help, unsafe homes, loneliness when family members work.
  • Nursing role – home visits, assessment and care planning, training family caregivers, home-safety modifications (grab bars, ramps, lighting), linking with community health workers and schemes, and respite arrangements for carers.

2. Community-based services

  • Day-care centres – the elderly spend the day in a safe, social environment with meals, recreation and health checks, returning home at night.
  • Senior citizens' clubs, mobile medical units and geriatric clinics at health centres under the National Programme for Health Care of the Elderly.

3. Institutional care

  • Types
    • Old-age homes – free (government or charitable) or paid homes for elderly people without family support or by choice.
    • Assisted-living facilities – housing with help in daily activities and meals.
    • Long-term care (nursing) homes – for frail, bed-bound or dementia patients needing 24-hour nursing care.
    • Geriatric wards in hospitals, rehabilitation units and hospices for end-of-life care.
  • Advantages – round-the-clock care and supervision, companionship, safety, access to health care.
  • Disadvantages – loss of family contact and home environment, loss of privacy and independence, risk of neglect and abuse in poorly run homes, cost.

4. Standards for good institutional care

  • Safe, clean, accessible buildings; adequate trained staff; individual care plans; respect for privacy, dignity, choice and cultural and religious practices; nutritious food; recreation and social activities; regular medical check-ups; family visits; registration and inspection by authorities; zero tolerance of abuse.

5. Role of the nurse in institutions

  • Comprehensive assessment and care planning; nursing care and medication management; prevention of falls, pressure injuries, infections and malnutrition; dementia care; restraint-free care; organisation of activities and exercise; communication with families; palliative and end-of-life care; supervision and training of care assistants.

Conclusion Home care keeps older people in familiar surroundings with family support, while day-care centres, old-age homes, assisted-living and long-term care facilities serve those who need more help. Nurses ensure safe, high-quality, dignified care in both settings and support family caregivers.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Care of the Elderly
question: Discuss the legal and ethical issues in the care of the elderly.
tags: Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act
answer_html:
Introduction Care of the elderly raises special legal and ethical questions because of frailty, cognitive impairment, dependence on others, end-of-life decisions and limited resources. Nurses must apply ethical principles – autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice – and know the relevant laws.

1. Autonomy and decision-making capacity

  • Older adults have the right to make their own decisions about treatment, place of living and finances; age alone does not mean loss of capacity.
  • Capacity is assessed for each decision (understanding, remembering, weighing information and communicating a choice); when capacity is lacking (e.g. advanced dementia), decisions are made in the person's best interests with their previously expressed wishes and family involvement.

2. Informed consent

  • Information must be given in simple language, with hearing aids, glasses and enough time; consent must be voluntary, without pressure from family members.

3. Advance directives and end-of-life decisions

  • The Supreme Court (Common Cause v. Union of India, 2018, with simplified procedures in 2023) recognised the right to die with dignity, permitting advance directives (living wills) and withholding or withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment in terminally ill patients through a defined medical-board process.
  • Ethical issues – futile treatment, artificial feeding in advanced dementia, resuscitation (DNR) decisions, palliative care and respecting cultural and family values.

4. Use of physical and chemical restraints

  • Restraints cause injuries, pressure sores, agitation and loss of dignity; they should be used only as a last resort, for the shortest time, with documentation, consent and regular review; sedatives must not be used merely for staff convenience.

5. Elder abuse and neglect

  • Ethical and legal duty to recognise, document and report abuse; the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007 obliges children and relatives to maintain parents, provides maintenance tribunals, allows cancellation of property transfers in case of neglect and punishes abandonment.

6. Financial and property matters

  • Protection against financial exploitation; encourage making a will, nominations and a power of attorney while the person has capacity; guardianship arrangements when capacity is lost.

7. Confidentiality and privacy

  • Health information is shared only with the person's consent or as legally required; privacy during personal care.

8. Justice and ageism

  • Ageism (discrimination based on age) may lead to under-treatment or exclusion; care decisions should be based on need, benefit and the person's wishes, not age alone; fair allocation of scarce resources such as ICU beds.

9. Rights of the elderly

  • Rights to dignity, health care, social security, safe housing, participation and protection; access to government schemes and legal aid.

10. Role of the nurse

  • Act as an advocate, respect autonomy and dignity, ensure informed consent, minimise restraints, recognise and report abuse, support advance care planning, maintain confidentiality, document carefully and provide fair, non-discriminatory care.

Conclusion Legal and ethical issues in elderly care centre on autonomy and capacity, informed consent, end-of-life decisions and advance directives, restraints, abuse, financial protection, confidentiality and ageism. Nurses protect the rights and dignity of older people by applying ethical principles and relevant laws in everyday care.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Care of the Elderly
question: Define gerontological nursing.
answer_html:
Gerontological nursing is the specialty of nursing concerned with the assessment of the health and functional status of older adults, planning and implementing nursing care and services to meet their needs, and evaluating the effectiveness of that care. It aims to promote healthy ageing, maximise independence and function, prevent and manage illness and disability, and ensure comfort and dignity until the end of life.

  • It is broader than geriatric nursing (care of sick elderly people), because it also includes health promotion and the social, psychological and spiritual aspects of ageing.
  • Gerontology is the scientific study of ageing; geriatrics is the branch of medicine dealing with the diseases of old age.
  • Gerontological nurses work in hospitals, homes, communities, day-care centres and long-term care facilities.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Care of the Elderly
question: What is ageism?
answer_html:
Ageism is stereotyping, prejudice and discrimination against people on the basis of their age, most often directed towards older people (the term was introduced by Robert Butler in 1969).

  • Examples – assuming that all elderly people are forgetful, useless, sick or burdensome; talking to them like children; ignoring their opinions in decisions; dismissing treatable symptoms as "just old age"; denying jobs, loans or treatment because of age.
  • Effects – poor health care, depression, isolation, reduced self-esteem and shorter life; it is also internalised by older people themselves.
  • Prevention – respectful, person-centred care, education of health workers and families, intergenerational activities, elder-friendly policies and laws against discrimination; nurses should base care on the person's needs and wishes, not on age.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Care of the Elderly
question: What is comprehensive geriatric assessment?
answer_html:
Comprehensive geriatric assessment (CGA) is a multidimensional, multidisciplinary process to identify the medical, functional, psychological and social problems and capabilities of a frail older person, so that a coordinated plan of treatment and long-term follow-up can be made. Components

  1. Medical – diseases, all medicines, nutrition, vision, hearing, continence, pain.
  2. Functional – activities of daily living (Katz ADL) and instrumental activities (Lawton IADL); gait, balance and fall risk (Timed Up and Go test).
  3. Psychological – cognition (MMSE, Mini-Cog) and mood (Geriatric Depression Scale).
  4. Social and environmental – family support, caregiver stress, finances, home safety, risk of abuse. CGA improves function, reduces hospital admissions and helps plan care at home or in institutions.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Care of the Elderly
question: List the common myths about ageing.
answer_html:
Common myths about ageing (and the facts):

  1. "All old people become senile (demented)" – most older people keep good cognitive function; dementia is a disease, not normal ageing.
  2. "Old people are always sick and disabled" – many remain healthy and active; disability is often preventable.
  3. "Older people cannot learn new things" – learning continues throughout life, only more slowly.
  4. "Old people are not interested in sex" – many remain sexually interested and active.
  5. "Depression and loneliness are normal in old age" – depression is a treatable illness, not a part of ageing.
  6. "Older people are unproductive and a burden" – they contribute through work, caregiving, wisdom and volunteering.
  7. "It is too late to change lifestyle" – exercise, stopping smoking and good nutrition benefit people at any age. Correcting these myths reduces ageism and encourages healthy, active ageing.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients in Critical Care Units
question: (a) Describe the physical set-up and organisation of a critical care unit, including its policies and staffing norms. (7 marks) (b) Explain the critical care team and the responsibilities of the critical care nurse. (8 marks)

diagram.caption: Layout of an intensive care unit
labels: central nursing station with view of all beds
bed spaces with bed-head service panel (oxygen
entry with hand-wash and changing area

answer_html:
