Introduction A critical care unit (CCU), also called an intensive care unit (ICU), is a separate, specially designed, staffed and equipped area of the hospital for the continuous observation, monitoring and treatment of patients with life-threatening illness or injury, who need support of failing organs (such as mechanical ventilation, vasopressors or dialysis) or very close monitoring. The ICU supports the patient's vital functions while the underlying disease is treated, and aims to prevent complications and restore the patient to the best possible health.

Levels of critical care

  • Level 1 (high-dependency or step-down unit) – patients who need closer observation than a general ward can provide, e.g. after major surgery or when stepping down from the ICU.
  • Level 2 – patients needing detailed monitoring or support of a single failing organ, e.g. non-invasive ventilation.
  • Level 3 – patients needing invasive ventilation alone, or support of two or more organ systems. Types of ICU – medical, surgical, coronary care (ICCU), cardiothoracic, neuro, trauma, burns, respiratory, paediatric (PICU) and neonatal (NICU) units.

(a) Physical set-up and organisation (7 marks) 1. Location

  • Close to the emergency department, operation theatres, radiology, laboratory and blood bank, with a dedicated lift, so that critically ill patients can be moved quickly and safely.
  • A self-contained area with restricted entry; it should not be used as a passage to other departments.

2. Size and bed space

  • ICU beds usually form about 5–10% of total hospital beds (more in tertiary and trauma centres); a unit of about 8–12 beds is efficient to staff and manage.
  • Adequate floor space around each bed (roughly 18–20 m², more in isolation rooms) with about 2 m or more between beds, so that equipment, staff and emergency procedures such as CPR or intubation can be accommodated.
  • Isolation rooms – at least one or two single rooms; negative-pressure rooms for airborne infections (e.g. pulmonary tuberculosis) and positive-pressure rooms for immunocompromised patients.

3. Layout

  • Open ward, cubicles or single rooms arranged around a central nursing station that gives a direct view of every patient; a central monitoring station repeats the bedside monitor displays and alarms.
  • Separate routes for clean and dirty traffic; hand-wash basins and alcohol hand-rub at the entrance and at every bed.

4. Facilities at each bed space

  • Bed-head service panel with piped oxygen (two outlets), medical air, vacuum suction (two outlets) and many electrical sockets connected to emergency power and UPS backup.
  • Adjustable ICU bed with a pressure-relieving mattress, multi-parameter monitor (ECG, SpO2, NIBP, invasive pressures, temperature, capnography), ventilator, infusion and syringe pumps, bag-valve-mask device, suction apparatus, examination and procedure lights, and storage for bedside supplies.

5. Environment

  • Central air-conditioning with filtered air and frequent air changes, comfortable temperature and humidity.
  • Natural daylight, windows, a visible clock and calendar to help orientation and reduce delirium; noise control (alarm volumes, quiet hours) and dimmed lights at night to promote sleep.
  • Smooth, washable floors and walls, without carpets or fabric that collect dust and microbes.

6. Support areas

  • Clean utility (sterile supplies), dirty utility/sluice room (disposal, cleaning of bedpans), equipment store, drug room, near-patient laboratory (ABG analyser, glucometer), crash cart and difficult-airway trolley, staff change rooms, doctors' duty room, seminar room, pantry, and a relatives' waiting room and counselling room.

7. Policies and protocols

  • Admission and discharge criteria and triage of beds based on priority and the expected benefit of intensive care.
  • Infection-control policies – hand hygiene, PPE, isolation, care bundles to prevent ventilator-associated pneumonia, central-line bloodstream infection and catheter-associated urinary infection; cleaning and disinfection; antibiotic stewardship.
  • Clinical protocols – sedation and analgesia, ventilator weaning, glucose control, DVT and stress-ulcer prophylaxis, pressure-injury prevention, restraint use, blood transfusion, intra-hospital transport of critically ill patients, and code blue response.
  • Administrative policies – flexible, family-centred visiting, dress code, consent, do-not-resuscitate and end-of-life care, medico-legal cases, documentation and structured handover (SBAR), equipment maintenance, fire and disaster plans, incident reporting.
  • Quality indicators reviewed regularly – ICU mortality, re-admission within 48 hours, rates of ventilator-associated pneumonia and bloodstream infection, pressure injuries, unplanned extubation and medication errors (as required for NABH accreditation).

8. Staffing norms

  • Nurse–patient ratio of 1:1 for ventilated or unstable (level 3) patients and 1:2 for less acute (level 2) patients, in every shift, plus a charge nurse and a leave reserve.
  • An intensivist (critical care specialist) leads the unit in a "closed ICU" model, with resident doctors available round the clock.
  • Nurses should be trained in critical care (post-basic diploma or specialty courses), certified in BLS and ACLS, oriented before independent duty and kept up to date through continuing education and competency checks.
  • Adequate support staff – respiratory therapists, physiotherapists, technicians, housekeeping staff and attendants.

(b) Critical care team and responsibilities of the critical care nurse (8 marks) A. The critical care team

  1. Intensivist and resident doctors – overall medical management, procedures and decisions on goals of treatment.
  2. Critical care nurses – charge nurse (unit management), bedside nurses (direct care), nurse educator and infection-control nurse.
  3. Consultants from other specialties – surgeons, cardiologists, neurologists, nephrologists and others as needed.
  4. Respiratory therapist – ventilator set-up, airway management, oxygen therapy and weaning.
  5. Physiotherapist – chest physiotherapy, positioning, early mobilisation and rehabilitation.
  6. Clinical pharmacist – drug doses (adjusted for kidney and liver function), infusion compatibility, interactions and antibiotic stewardship.
  7. Dietitian – nutritional assessment and plans for enteral or parenteral feeding.
  8. Microbiologist and infection-control team – culture reports, outbreak control and antibiotic policy.
  9. Medical social worker, counsellor or psychologist and spiritual care provider – emotional, social and spiritual support for patients and families.
  10. Biomedical engineer and technicians – maintenance and safety of equipment.
  11. Laboratory, radiology, housekeeping and attendant staff.
  12. The patient and family – partners in decisions and care. The team works through daily multidisciplinary rounds, goal sheets and checklists, clear communication and structured handovers.

B. Responsibilities of the critical care nurse

  1. Continuous assessment and monitoring – vital signs, ECG, SpO2, haemodynamic values, neurological status (GCS, pupils), respiratory status and ventilator settings, fluid balance, blood sugar and laboratory results; early recognition of deterioration and prompt reporting.
  2. Life-saving interventions – airway management, suctioning, oxygen and ventilator care, CPR and defibrillation, and emergency drugs as per protocol.
  3. Medication management – titrating vasopressor, sedative, insulin and other infusions with pumps; double-checking high-alert drugs; monitoring effects and side effects.
  4. Prevention of complications – care bundles for ventilator-associated pneumonia and line and catheter infections, pressure-injury prevention, DVT and stress-ulcer prophylaxis, early mobilisation, and prevention of falls and accidental removal of tubes and lines.
  5. Meeting basic needs and comfort – hygiene, eye and mouth care, nutrition (enteral feeds), elimination, positioning, sleep, and assessment and relief of pain.
  6. Psychological care – reorientation, prevention and early detection of delirium, reassurance, and alternative ways of communicating with intubated patients (picture boards, writing, yes/no questions).
  7. Family-centred care – regular information, involvement in care and decisions, emotional support and flexible visiting.
  8. Equipment management – checking monitors, ventilators, pumps, defibrillator and crash cart; setting appropriate alarm limits and responding to alarms promptly.
  9. Documentation and legal duties – accurate, timely records of observations, interventions and drugs; consent; medico-legal procedures; incident reporting.
  10. Advocacy and ethics – protecting the dignity, privacy and wishes of the patient and taking part in end-of-life discussions.
  11. Coordination and communication – SBAR handover; coordinating investigations, procedures and transfers; informing the doctor promptly of changes.
  12. Education, management and research – teaching patients, families, students and junior staff; charge-nurse duties (staff allocation, supplies, audits); evidence-based practice and quality improvement.

Qualities of a critical care nurse – sound knowledge of pathophysiology and pharmacology, technical skill, critical thinking and quick decision-making, calmness under pressure, teamwork, compassion and ethical sensitivity.

Nursing importance

  • A well-planned ICU with clear policies, adequate nurse staffing and a competent team reduces mortality and complications; because the bedside nurse is with the patient round the clock, the nurse is usually the first to detect deterioration and start life-saving action.

Conclusion A critical care unit is a specially located, designed and equipped area with central monitoring, isolation facilities, piped gases and backup power, run according to clear admission, infection-control, clinical and administrative policies with a 1:1 or 1:2 nurse–patient ratio. A multidisciplinary team led by an intensivist cares for the patient, and the critical care nurse, through continuous monitoring, skilled interventions, prevention of complications, comfort, family support and advocacy, is central to good outcomes.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients in Critical Care Units
question: (a) Define mechanical ventilation and list its indications. (3 marks) (b) Explain the types and modes of mechanical ventilation and the important ventilator settings. (5 marks) (c) Describe the nursing management of a patient on mechanical ventilation, including prevention of complications and weaning. (7 marks)

diagram.caption: Patient on a mechanical ventilator
labels: ventilator with control panel and alarms
endotracheal tube with inflated cuff and pilot balloon

answer_html:
(a) Definition and indications (3 marks) Mechanical ventilation is the use of a machine (ventilator) to move air or oxygen into and out of the lungs, fully or partly taking over the work of breathing, in a patient who cannot maintain adequate ventilation (removal of CO2) or oxygenation. It is a supportive, not curative, treatment that keeps the patient alive while the underlying cause is treated.

Indications

  1. Acute respiratory failure
    • Type I (hypoxaemic) – PaO2 below about 60 mmHg (SpO2 below 90%) despite high-flow oxygen, e.g. severe pneumonia, ARDS, pulmonary oedema.
    • Type II (hypercapnic) – PaCO2 above 50 mmHg with acidosis (pH below about 7.25), e.g. COPD exacerbation not responding to NIV, severe asthma.
  2. Clinical signs of respiratory distress and fatigue – respiratory rate above 35/min, use of accessory muscles, paradoxical breathing, exhaustion, apnoea.
  3. Inability to protect the airway – coma (GCS 8 or less), head injury, stroke, drug overdose or poisoning.
  4. Neuromuscular weakness – Guillain–Barré syndrome, myasthenic crisis, high cervical spinal cord injury, tetanus, neurotoxic snake bite, organophosphate poisoning.
  5. Circulatory failure – cardiac arrest and post-resuscitation care, severe shock.
  6. Post-operative ventilation after major surgery (cardiac, neurosurgery, major abdominal) or prolonged anaesthesia.
  7. Therapeutic – controlled ventilation in raised intracranial pressure, and to reduce the work of breathing in severe sepsis.

(b) Types, modes and settings (5 marks) A. Types of ventilation

  • Negative-pressure ventilation – creates negative pressure around the chest (iron lung, cuirass); now rarely used.
  • Positive-pressure ventilation – pushes gas into the lungs:
    • Invasive – through an endotracheal tube or tracheostomy.
    • Non-invasive ventilation (NIV) – through a tight-fitting face or nasal mask: CPAP (one continuous pressure) and BiPAP (higher inspiratory pressure, IPAP, and lower expiratory pressure, EPAP); used in COPD exacerbations, cardiogenic pulmonary oedema and obstructive sleep apnoea.
  • By the variable controlled – volume-controlled ventilation delivers a set tidal volume (pressure varies with lung stiffness); pressure-controlled ventilation delivers a set pressure (tidal volume varies).

B. Common modes

  1. Controlled mandatory ventilation (CMV) – the machine delivers all breaths at a set rate and volume; the patient cannot breathe on his own; used in deeply sedated or paralysed patients.
  2. Assist-control (A/C) ventilation – set rate and tidal volume; the patient can trigger extra breaths, and every breath receives the full set volume; risk of over-breathing (respiratory alkalosis) and air trapping in an anxious, fast-breathing patient.
  3. Synchronised intermittent mandatory ventilation (SIMV) – a set number of mandatory breaths, synchronised with the patient's own effort; between them the patient breathes spontaneously, usually with pressure support; also used for weaning.
  4. Pressure support ventilation (PSV) – every breath is started by the patient and supported by a set pressure; the patient controls rate and depth; needs an intact respiratory drive; widely used in weaning.
  5. Pressure-controlled ventilation (PCV) – set inspiratory pressure and time; limits airway pressure, useful in ARDS.
  6. CPAP – continuous positive pressure throughout the breathing cycle in a spontaneously breathing patient; keeps alveoli open and improves oxygenation.
  7. PEEP (positive end-expiratory pressure) – an adjunct to all modes that keeps pressure in the airways at the end of expiration to prevent alveolar collapse.
  8. Newer modes – pressure-regulated volume control (PRVC), airway pressure release ventilation (APRV), adaptive support ventilation, and high-frequency oscillatory ventilation (mainly in neonates).

C. Important ventilator settings

  • FiO2 – start high (up to 1.0) in an emergency, then reduce to the lowest value that keeps SpO2 about 92–96% (88–92% in COPD with CO2 retention); prolonged FiO2 above 0.6 risks oxygen toxicity.
  • Tidal volume – 6–8 mL/kg of predicted (ideal) body weight; 6 mL/kg in ARDS (lung-protective ventilation) with plateau pressure kept at or below 30 cm H2O.
  • Respiratory rate – usually 12–20 breaths/min, adjusted to the PaCO2 and pH.
  • PEEP – usually 5 cm H2O; higher in ARDS according to oxygen needs.
  • I:E ratio – normally 1:2; a longer expiratory time (1:3 or 1:4) in asthma and COPD to prevent air trapping.
  • Trigger sensitivity, inspiratory flow and pressure-support level set for patient comfort and synchrony.
  • Alarm limits – high and low airway pressure, low exhaled tidal or minute volume, apnoea, high respiratory rate, oxygen supply and power failure.

(c) Nursing management (7 marks) 1. Assessment and monitoring

  • Vital signs, SpO2 and end-tidal CO2 (capnography), chest expansion and bilateral breath sounds, colour, level of consciousness.
  • Hourly check of ventilator settings and readings – mode, FiO2, tidal and minute volume, rate, PEEP, peak and plateau pressures; record them.
  • ABG about 20–30 minutes after any change in settings and as ordered; chest X-ray to confirm tube position.
  • Observe patient–ventilator synchrony; "fighting the ventilator", coughing or agitation needs assessment, not just sedation.

2. Care of the artificial airway

  • Note and record the tube length at the teeth or lips, secure the tube, and recheck its position every shift and after turning; listen for air entry on both sides.
  • Keep cuff pressure about 20–30 cm H2O, checked with a cuff manometer every 8 hours – too low causes leak and aspiration; too high damages the tracheal wall.
  • Suction only when needed (secretions, coarse sounds, rising pressure, falling SpO2): pre-oxygenate, use sterile technique or a closed in-line catheter, limit each pass to 10–15 seconds, and use moderate suction pressure (about 100–150 mmHg).
  • Humidify inspired gas (heated humidifier or heat-moisture exchanger); drain condensate away from the patient; prevent kinking and disconnection.
  • Keep a bag-valve-mask device with oxygen, suction and reintubation equipment at the bedside.
  • Prevent accidental self-extubation – explanation, adequate analgesia and sedation, and soft restraints only as per policy.

3. Prevention of ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP)

  • Head of bed raised 30–45° unless contraindicated.
  • Daily sedation interruption ("sedation vacation") and daily assessment of readiness to breathe spontaneously.
  • Regular oral care with tooth brushing and an antiseptic as per policy; subglottic secretion drainage tubes where available.
  • Maintain cuff pressure; strict hand hygiene; closed suction; change circuits only when soiled or faulty.
  • Stress-ulcer and DVT prophylaxis as prescribed.

4. Recognising and preventing other complications

  • Sudden deterioration – remember "DOPE": Displacement of the tube, Obstruction (secretions, kinking, biting), Pneumothorax, Equipment failure. Disconnect and ventilate with a bag and 100% oxygen while the cause is found.
  • Barotrauma and volutrauma (pneumothorax, surgical emphysema) – watch for rising airway pressures, sudden fall in SpO2, absent breath sounds or tracheal shift; use low tidal volumes.
  • Hypotension and reduced cardiac output due to raised intrathoracic pressure (especially with high PEEP) – monitor BP, urine output and fluid balance.
  • Oxygen toxicity, respiratory alkalosis or acidosis – avoid by monitoring ABG and using the lowest effective FiO2.
  • Gastrointestinal – stress ulcer bleeding, abdominal distension, constipation; fluid retention.
  • Tracheal injury – stenosis, tracheomalacia, tracheo-oesophageal fistula; laryngeal oedema after extubation.
  • Immobility problems – pressure injuries, DVT, muscle wasting and ICU-acquired weakness; delirium.
  • Never silence an alarm without checking the patient first.

5. Comfort, sedation and basic needs

  • Assess pain and sedation with valid scales; aim for a light level of sedation in which the patient is calm but rousable; analgesia first.
  • Early enteral feeding through a nasogastric or orogastric tube with head elevation; blood sugar control.
  • Eye care (lubricants, keeping lids closed) to prevent corneal exposure; mouth care every 2–4 hours; skin care and 2-hourly turning; passive and active exercises and early mobilisation; bladder and bowel care.

6. Communication and psychological support

  • The intubated patient cannot speak: explain every procedure, use communication boards, writing or yes/no questions, keep the call bell within reach, reassure, and promote sleep and orientation.
  • Keep the family informed and involve them in care.

7. Weaning from the ventilator Weaning is the gradual withdrawal of ventilatory support until the patient breathes on his own.

  • Readiness criteria – underlying cause improving; haemodynamically stable with little or no vasopressor support; adequate oxygenation on FiO2 of 0.4–0.5 or less and PEEP of 5–8 cm H2O or less; acceptable pH; awake and able to follow commands; good cough and gag reflexes; spontaneous breathing efforts; rapid shallow breathing index (respiratory rate ÷ tidal volume in litres) below 105; normal electrolytes, no high fever.
  • Methods – a spontaneous breathing trial (SBT) of 30–120 minutes on a T-piece, CPAP or low pressure support; or gradual reduction of pressure support.
  • Nursing during weaning – explain the procedure; choose a time when the patient is rested (usually morning); position upright; minimise sedation; suction before the trial; stay with the patient and monitor closely.
  • Stop the trial and return to the previous settings if there are signs of intolerance – respiratory rate above 35/min, SpO2 below 90%, heart rate above 140/min or a 20% rise, very high or low BP, sweating, agitation, paradoxical breathing.
  • Extubation – suction the tube and mouth, deflate the cuff, remove the tube at the end of a deep breath, give humidified oxygen, and encourage deep breathing and coughing. Watch for stridor (laryngeal oedema), respiratory distress and aspiration; check ABG; assess swallowing before oral feeds; high-risk patients may receive NIV or high-flow nasal oxygen after extubation.

8. Documentation and safety – record settings, observations, suctioning, cuff pressures, sedation scores and weaning trials; ensure the ventilator is checked before use and serviced regularly.

Conclusion Mechanical ventilation supports patients with respiratory failure, airway compromise, neuromuscular weakness and shock. Modes range from controlled ventilation to patient-triggered pressure support, and settings such as FiO2, tidal volume, rate and PEEP are adjusted to keep oxygenation and CO2 within safe limits while protecting the lungs. Careful nursing – monitoring, airway care, VAP prevention, quick response to sudden deterioration, comfort and communication, and systematic weaning – reduces complications and helps the patient return to spontaneous breathing.

question: (a) Define advanced cardiac life support (ACLS) and list its components. (3 marks) (b) Explain the ACLS management of adult cardiac arrest with shockable and non-shockable rhythms, including drugs and reversible causes. (8 marks) (c) Explain the ACLS approach to symptomatic bradycardia and to tachycardia with a pulse. (4 marks)

diagram.caption: Adult cardiac arrest algorithm (ACLS)
labels: CPR 2 min with adrenaline every 3–5 min and advanced airway
CPR 2 min with amiodarone or lidocaine; non-shockable (asystole/PEA) – CPR 2 min
treat reversible causes (H's and T's); check for ROSC and begin post-cardiac arrest care

answer_html:
(a) Definition and components (3 marks) Advanced cardiac (cardiovascular) life support (ACLS) is the set of clinical interventions, performed by trained health-care teams, for the urgent treatment of cardiac arrest, stroke and other life-threatening cardiovascular emergencies. It builds on basic life support (high-quality CPR and early defibrillation) by adding advanced airway management, ECG rhythm interpretation, electrical therapy, intravenous drugs, treatment of reversible causes and post-resuscitation care, following algorithms of the American Heart Association (AHA), last updated in its 2025 Guidelines.

Components of ACLS

  1. High-quality CPR and early defibrillation (the BLS foundation).
  2. Airway management and ventilation – bag-mask ventilation, advanced airways (endotracheal tube or supraglottic airway) and oxygen.
  3. Rhythm recognition on the monitor – VF, pulseless VT, asystole, PEA, bradycardias and tachycardias.
  4. Electrical therapy – defibrillation, synchronised cardioversion and transcutaneous pacing.
  5. Vascular access and drugs – IV (preferred) or intraosseous (IO) access; adrenaline, amiodarone, lidocaine, atropine, adenosine and others.
  6. Identification and treatment of reversible causes (H's and T's).
  7. Management of peri-arrest conditions – acute coronary syndromes, stroke, unstable arrhythmias.
  8. Post-cardiac arrest care, and effective team dynamics with debriefing after each event.

(b) ACLS management of adult cardiac arrest (8 marks) 1. Initial steps

  • Confirm unresponsiveness and absence of normal breathing and pulse; call for help and activate the code team; start high-quality CPR at once.
  • Give oxygen with a bag-mask device; attach the monitor/defibrillator as soon as it arrives and check the rhythm.

2. Standards of high-quality CPR (throughout)

  • Compressions on the lower half of the sternum at 100–120/min, depth 5–6 cm, allowing full chest recoil; minimise interruptions (pauses under 10 seconds).
  • 30:2 compression–ventilation ratio until an advanced airway is placed; then continuous compressions with 1 breath every 6 seconds (10/min); avoid excessive ventilation.
  • Change the compressor every 2 minutes to prevent fatigue.
  • Waveform capnography – a low end-tidal CO2 (below about 10 mmHg) suggests poor-quality CPR; a sudden sustained rise (often to 40 mmHg or more) suggests return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC).

3. Shockable rhythms – ventricular fibrillation (VF) and pulseless ventricular tachycardia (pVT)

  1. Give one shock – biphasic defibrillator at the manufacturer's recommended energy (usually 120–200 J; use the maximum if unknown) or monophasic 360 J; resume CPR immediately for 2 minutes without a pulse check.
  2. Obtain IV access (IO if IV is not possible) during CPR.
  3. Rhythm check after 2 minutes – if still shockable, second shock, then CPR for 2 minutes.
  4. Adrenaline (epinephrine) 1 mg IV/IO after the initial shocks have failed, repeated every 3–5 minutes; consider an advanced airway with capnography.
  5. Rhythm check – if still shockable, shock, CPR for 2 minutes, and give an antiarrhythmic: amiodarone 300 mg IV/IO bolus (second dose 150 mg) or lidocaine 1–1.5 mg/kg (then 0.5–0.75 mg/kg).
  6. Continue cycles of shock → CPR 2 minutes → drug, while searching for and treating reversible causes. Double sequential defibrillation and changing pad position are not established as routine practice.

4. Non-shockable rhythms – asystole and pulseless electrical activity (PEA)

  1. Continue CPR for 2-minute cycles – do not shock.
  2. Give adrenaline 1 mg IV/IO as soon as possible, then every 3–5 minutes.
  3. Consider an advanced airway and capnography.
  4. Search for and treat reversible causes – PEA in particular often has a treatable cause.
  5. If the rhythm becomes shockable at a rhythm check, follow the shockable pathway. In asystole, confirm that leads are connected and the gain is adequate ("flat-line protocol").

5. Reversible causes – the H's and T's

  • Hypovolaemia – fluids, blood.
  • Hypoxia – oxygenation, airway management.
  • Hydrogen ion (acidosis) – adequate ventilation; treat the cause.
  • Hypo-/hyperkalaemia (and other electrolyte disorders) – e.g. calcium, insulin–glucose for hyperkalaemia.
  • Hypothermia – rewarming.
  • Tension pneumothorax – needle decompression.
  • Tamponade (cardiac) – pericardiocentesis.
  • Toxins – antidotes (e.g. naloxone for opioids).
  • Thrombosis, pulmonary – consider thrombolysis.
  • Thrombosis, coronary – reperfusion (PCI) after ROSC.

6. Return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) and post-cardiac arrest care (brief)

  • Signs: palpable pulse and measurable BP, sudden rise in end-tidal CO2, spontaneous arterial pressure waves.
  • Optimise ventilation and oxygenation (SpO2 about 92–98%, normal PaCO2), maintain mean arterial pressure of at least 65 mmHg, obtain a 12-lead ECG (urgent PCI for STEMI), and in adults who do not follow commands start temperature control at a chosen value between 32 °C and 37.5 °C for at least 36 hours, with prevention of fever, glucose control, seizure management and later neuroprognostication.

7. Team dynamics and the nurse's role

  • Clear roles – team leader, compressors, airway manager, monitor/defibrillator operator, IV/IO and medication nurse, and timer/recorder.
  • Closed-loop communication (the order is repeated back and confirmed when done), clear messages, mutual respect, and knowing one's limits.
  • The nurse brings the crash cart, attaches pads, rotates compressions, prepares and gives drugs with a flush, records times of shocks and drugs, supports the family, and takes part in debriefing; the crash cart is restocked after the event.

(c) Symptomatic bradycardia and tachycardia with a pulse (4 marks) A. Bradycardia (heart rate usually below 50/min) with poor perfusion

  • Signs of poor perfusion – hypotension, altered mental status, signs of shock, ischaemic chest pain, acute heart failure.
  • Maintain the airway, give oxygen if hypoxic, attach monitor, obtain IV access and a 12-lead ECG; look for causes (e.g. drugs, hyperkalaemia, myocardial infarction).
  • Atropine 1 mg IV bolus, repeated every 3–5 minutes up to a maximum of 3 mg.
  • If atropine is ineffective: transcutaneous pacing, and/or dopamine infusion (5–20 mcg/kg/min) or adrenaline infusion (2–10 mcg/min); arrange expert consultation and transvenous pacing.

B. Tachycardia (heart rate usually 150/min or more) with a pulse

  • Unstable (hypotension, altered mental status, shock, chest pain, acute heart failure) → immediate synchronised cardioversion after sedation if possible. Typical initial energies: narrow regular rhythms 50–100 J; atrial fibrillation and flutter – at least 200 J biphasic (2025 recommendation); wide regular rhythms about 100 J. A wide, irregular (polymorphic) tachycardia is treated with defibrillation (unsynchronised) doses.
  • Stable, narrow QRS (below 0.12 s), regular – vagal manoeuvres; then adenosine 6 mg rapid IV push followed by a 20 mL saline flush, and 12 mg if needed; then beta-blockers or calcium-channel blockers.
  • Stable, wide QRS (0.12 s or more) – adenosine only if regular and monomorphic; antiarrhythmic infusion such as amiodarone 150 mg over 10 minutes; expert consultation.
  • Nursing role – continuous ECG monitoring, defibrillator with pads attached, IV access in a large vein (antecubital) for adenosine, warning the patient about the brief chest discomfort and flushing adenosine causes, and recording the rhythm strips.

Nursing importance

  • Nurses are often the first responders to cardiac arrest in hospital; regular ACLS training, mock codes, a checked crash cart and clear team roles improve survival.

Conclusion ACLS adds airway management, rhythm recognition, electrical therapy, drugs, treatment of reversible causes and post-arrest care to high-quality CPR. Shockable rhythms are treated with early defibrillation, adrenaline after the initial shocks and amiodarone or lidocaine for persisting VF/pVT, while non-shockable rhythms need CPR, early adrenaline and a search for the H's and T's. Atropine and pacing for symptomatic bradycardia, and cardioversion, vagal manoeuvres or adenosine for tachycardia complete the approach, delivered by a well-coordinated team in which the nurse plays a vital role.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients in Critical Care Units
question: Explain the principles of critical care nursing.
answer_html:
Introduction Critical care nursing is the specialty of nursing that deals with human responses to life-threatening problems. Critically ill patients are unstable, dependent and vulnerable to complications, so their care is guided by certain principles that keep them safe and help them recover.

Principles of critical care nursing

  1. Holistic, patient- and family-centred care
    • The patient is a person, not a set of monitors and machines; physical, psychological, social and spiritual needs are met, and the family is treated as part of the care unit.
  2. Continuous, vigilant monitoring and early recognition of deterioration
    • Close observation of vital signs, ECG, oxygenation, haemodynamics, neurological status, fluid balance and laboratory values; trends are interpreted, not just recorded; changes are reported and acted upon immediately.
  3. Prioritisation and prompt intervention
    • Problems are dealt with in order of threat to life – Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability (neurological status), Exposure – according to protocols and standing orders.
  4. Maintenance of physiological stability
    • Adequate oxygenation and ventilation, tissue perfusion, fluid–electrolyte and acid–base balance, nutrition, glucose control and temperature.
  5. Prevention of complications and patient safety
    • Care bundles against ventilator-associated pneumonia, line and catheter infections; prevention of pressure injuries, DVT, stress ulcers, delirium and ICU-acquired weakness; safe medication practices (double-checking high-alert drugs); prevention of falls and accidental removal of tubes and lines.
  6. Infection prevention
    • Strict hand hygiene, aseptic technique, isolation when needed, environmental cleaning and antibiotic stewardship.
  7. Evidence-based, protocol-driven practice
    • Standardised protocols for sedation, weaning, glucose control, transfusion and resuscitation reduce errors and variation.
  8. Teamwork and effective communication
    • Daily multidisciplinary rounds, clear goals, structured handover (SBAR) and closed-loop communication during emergencies.
  9. Comfort and dignity (humanised care)
    • Regular assessment and relief of pain, appropriate light sedation, sleep promotion, privacy, respect and gentle handling even of unconscious patients.
  10. Psychological support and communication
    • Explanation of procedures, reorientation, alternative communication for intubated patients, reassurance of patient and family.
  11. Ethical and legal practice
    • Informed consent, respect for autonomy and advance wishes, confidentiality, accurate documentation and appropriate end-of-life decisions.
  12. Early rehabilitation and continuity of care
    • Mobilisation and physiotherapy from the earliest safe time; planned transfer and follow-up to prevent problems after ICU discharge.
  13. Competence with technology
    • Safe use of ventilators, monitors, pumps and defibrillators, with appropriate alarm settings and regular checks.
  14. Continuous learning, quality improvement and staff well-being
    • Updating knowledge and skills (BLS, ACLS), audit of outcomes, and attention to stress, burnout and moral distress among staff.

Conclusion The principles of critical care nursing are holistic and family-centred care, vigilant monitoring, prioritised and prompt intervention, physiological stability, prevention of complications, infection control, evidence-based protocols, teamwork, comfort and dignity, psychological support, ethical practice, early rehabilitation and continuing competence. Following them improves survival and the quality of recovery of critically ill patients.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients in Critical Care Units
question: Explain the nursing management of a critically ill patient.
tags: nursing management of critically ill patient
answer_html:
Introduction A critically ill patient is one whose life is threatened by failure of one or more vital organ systems and who needs continuous monitoring and organ support. Nursing care is systematic, anticipatory and holistic, so that problems are prevented or detected early.

1. Initial and ongoing assessment (ABCDE approach)

  • Airway – patency, artificial airway position and security.
  • Breathing – rate, pattern, SpO2, breath sounds, ventilator settings, ABG.
  • Circulation – heart rate and rhythm, BP and mean arterial pressure, capillary refill, peripheral pulses, CVP, urine output, lactate.
  • Disability – level of consciousness (GCS), pupils, blood sugar, pain and sedation scores, delirium screening.
  • Exposure – skin, wounds, drains, lines, temperature, signs of bleeding or infection. This is repeated at least hourly and whenever the condition changes.

2. Nursing diagnoses commonly identified

  • Impaired gas exchange; ineffective airway clearance; decreased cardiac output; ineffective tissue perfusion; risk for infection; risk for impaired skin integrity; imbalanced nutrition; acute pain; anxiety; impaired verbal communication; risk for injury; interrupted family processes.

3. Daily care checklist – "FAST HUGS BID"

  • F – Feeding: early enteral nutrition within 24–48 hours if the gut works; parenteral nutrition only when enteral feeding is not possible.
  • A – Analgesia: regular pain assessment and adequate pain relief.
  • S – Sedation: lightest effective sedation; daily sedation interruption where appropriate.
  • T – Thromboprophylaxis: heparin and/or mechanical devices to prevent DVT.
  • H – Head of bed elevation to 30–45° to prevent aspiration and VAP.
  • U – Ulcer (stress-ulcer) prophylaxis in high-risk patients.
  • G – Glucose control, usually 140–180 mg/dL.
  • S – Spontaneous breathing trial – daily assessment of readiness for weaning.
  • B – Bowel care – prevent constipation and diarrhoea.
  • I – Indwelling catheters – remove unnecessary urinary catheters and central lines early.
  • D – De-escalation of antibiotics according to culture reports.

4. System-wise nursing interventions

  • Respiratory – oxygen or ventilator care, suctioning, chest physiotherapy, positioning (prone position in severe ARDS as ordered).
  • Cardiovascular – titration of fluids, vasopressors and inotropes as ordered, monitoring of arterial and central pressures, ECG.
  • Renal – hourly urine output, fluid balance, electrolytes, care during dialysis.
  • Neurological – GCS and pupils, seizure precautions, prevention of raised intracranial pressure.
  • Skin – 2-hourly repositioning, pressure-relieving mattress, care of wounds and line sites.
  • Hygiene and comfort – bed bath, eye care (lubricants, lid closure), oral care, hair and perineal care.
  • Mobility – passive and active exercises, early mobilisation with physiotherapy.
  • Infection control – hand hygiene, aseptic care of lines and catheters, care bundles.

5. Psychological and family care

  • Explain procedures; reorient frequently; promote day–night routine and sleep; prevent and detect delirium.
  • Use communication boards or writing for intubated patients.
  • Keep the family informed; allow flexible visiting and involvement in simple care; provide emotional support.

6. Safety, documentation and coordination

  • Correct alarm settings, safe medication administration, secure lines and tubes, fall prevention.
  • Accurate records of observations, drugs and intake–output; structured handover; coordination with the team for investigations and procedures.

Conclusion Nursing management of the critically ill patient involves frequent ABCDE and system assessment, a daily FAST HUGS BID checklist, organ-specific interventions, prevention of complications, comfort and psychological care, family support, safety and accurate documentation – all aimed at survival and a good-quality recovery.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients in Critical Care Units
question: Discuss the ethical and legal aspects of nursing in the critical care unit.
tags: withholding and withdrawal of life support
answer_html:
Introduction In the ICU, decisions about life and death are made every day for patients who often cannot speak for themselves. Expensive technology, uncertain outcomes and limited beds create ethical dilemmas, and every action has legal consequences. Nurses must apply ethical principles and know the relevant laws.

A. Ethical principles applied in the ICU

  • Autonomy – respecting the patient's own wishes, including those expressed earlier or in an advance directive.
  • Beneficence and non-maleficence – giving treatment that benefits the patient and avoiding treatment that only prolongs suffering.
  • Justice – fair use of ICU beds, ventilators and costly drugs, based on need and likely benefit, not on status or ability to pay.
  • Veracity and fidelity – honest information to patient and family, and keeping commitments.

B. Common ethical and legal issues

  1. Informed consent
    • Many ICU patients lack capacity, so consent is taken from the legal guardian or next of kin (surrogate), who should decide according to the patient's known wishes and best interests.
    • In emergencies, life-saving treatment may be given without consent; this must be documented.
  2. Do-not-resuscitate (DNR) orders and limitation of treatment
    • Decisions are taken by the senior doctor with the family, written clearly in the record and communicated to the team; DNR does not mean "do not care" – comfort, nursing care and dignity continue.
  3. Withholding and withdrawal of life-sustaining treatment
    • The Supreme Court of India (Common Cause v. Union of India, 2018, with procedures simplified in 2023) recognised the right to die with dignity, allowing advance directives (living wills) and passive withdrawal of life support in terminally ill patients, after review by a primary medical board in the hospital and confirmation by a secondary medical board, with intimation to the magistrate. Active euthanasia remains illegal.
    • Medical futility – treatment that cannot achieve a meaningful goal raises questions of continuing it.
  4. Brain death and organ donation
    • Under the Transplantation of Human Organs and Tissues Act (THOTA, 1994, amended 2011), brain-stem death is certified by a board of four doctors, with tests repeated after an interval; ICU staff must ask the family about organ donation (required request) and inform the transplant coordinator; commercial dealing in organs is a punishable offence.
  5. Physical and chemical restraints – used only when essential, with a doctor's order, the least restrictive method, frequent checks and documentation.
  6. Confidentiality and privacy – information shared only with those entitled; screens and covering during procedures; careful use of phones and photographs.
  7. Medico-legal cases – trauma, poisoning, burns and assaults: police intimation, preservation of evidence (clothes, samples, gastric lavage fluid), dying declaration procedures, and careful records.
  8. Negligence and accountability
    • Errors such as wrong drug or dose, unattended alarms, accidental extubation, falls or pressure injuries may lead to complaints under consumer protection law or criminal charges; every nurse is accountable for her actions.
  9. Documentation – accurate, timely, legible records are the best legal protection; never alter entries.
  10. Allocation of scarce resources – transparent triage policies for admission and discharge.
  11. Conflicts between family and team, or within the team – resolved through family meetings and, if needed, the hospital clinical ethics committee.
  12. Moral distress of nurses – when nurses feel unable to do what they think is right; addressed by open discussion and support.

C. Role of the nurse

  • Act as the patient's advocate, ensuring that wishes, dignity and comfort are respected.
  • Participate in family meetings; ensure consent and DNR or withdrawal decisions are properly documented and understood.
  • Follow hospital policy and law in restraints, MLC, brain death and organ donation.
  • Maintain confidentiality and accurate records, and report errors honestly.

Conclusion Ethical and legal issues in the ICU include consent and surrogate decisions, DNR, withdrawal of life support under the Common Cause guidelines, brain death and organ donation under THOTA, restraints, confidentiality, medico-legal cases, negligence and fair resource allocation. By applying ethical principles, knowing the law and documenting carefully, nurses protect both their patients and themselves.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients in Critical Care Units
question: Explain how to break bad news to patients and families in the critical care unit, using the SPIKES protocol.
answer_html:
Introduction Bad news is any information that seriously and adversely changes a person's view of their future – for example, a poor prognosis, a new diagnosis of cancer, failure of treatment or the likely death of a loved one. In the ICU, bad news is frequent and families are often frightened and exhausted. How the news is given affects their understanding, trust, decisions and grief.

The SPIKES protocol (Baile and Buckman, 2000) gives six steps:

  1. S – Setting up the interview
    • Prepare: know the facts, read the records, agree with the team on the message.
    • Use a private, quiet room; sit down; invite the key family members (and the patient if able); switch phones to silent; allow enough time; have tissues available.
  2. P – Perception
    • Ask what they already know or understand: "What have the doctors told you so far about his condition?" This shows misunderstandings and the gap between hope and reality.
  3. I – Invitation
    • Ask how much information they want and how they want it: "Would you like me to explain everything in detail?" Respect cultural preferences, but the patient who has capacity has the right to know.
  4. K – Knowledge (giving the information)
    • Give a warning shot ("I'm afraid I have some serious news"); use simple language, no jargon; give information in small pieces; check understanding; avoid false reassurance and also avoid harsh bluntness.
  5. E – Emotions (respond with empathy)
    • Observe and name the emotion (shock, crying, anger, silence); allow silence; respond empathically: "I can see this is very hard for you." Do not argue with anger or denial.
  6. S – Strategy and Summary
    • Summarise; discuss the plan of care and choices (including goals of care and comfort measures); answer questions; arrange the next meeting; tell them who to contact.

Communicating with families in the ICU

  • Early family meeting after admission and regular updates by a consistent team, so that messages do not conflict.
  • VALUE approach in family meetings – Value what the family says, Acknowledge their emotions, Listen, Understand the patient as a person (ask about his values and wishes), Elicit questions.
  • Use interpreters when needed; give written information; allow flexible visiting and participation in simple care.
  • Collusion – when relatives ask that the patient should not be told, explore their fears, explain the patient's right to information, and find out gently how much the patient wishes to know.

Role of the nurse

  • Be present during the discussion with the doctor; support the family afterwards, clarify information in simple words and repeat as needed.
  • Notice when the family needs more information or a meeting, and arrange it.
  • Provide emotional and spiritual support, privacy, and help with contacting relatives.
  • Document what was said and who was present; ensure the team gives consistent messages.
  • Care for self – breaking bad news is stressful; debriefing and peer support help.

Conclusion Breaking bad news well is a clinical skill. The SPIKES protocol – Setting, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Emotions and Strategy/Summary – together with regular, empathic family meetings helps patients and families understand the situation, cope with their emotions and take part in decisions. Nurses support families before, during and after these conversations.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients in Critical Care Units
question: Explain end-of-life care in the critical care unit.
answer_html:
Introduction Many patients die in the ICU despite full treatment. When recovery is no longer possible, the goal of care changes from cure and life-prolongation to comfort, dignity and support for the family. Good end-of-life care is an essential part of critical care, not a failure of it.

1. Recognising the need and deciding on goals of care

  • Recognise when treatment is no longer beneficial (multi-organ failure not responding, irreversible brain injury).
  • Family meeting with the senior doctor, nurse and, if possible, the patient: discuss prognosis honestly, explore the patient's values and wishes (including any advance directive), and agree on a plan.
  • Document decisions (DNR, limitation or withdrawal of treatment) clearly, according to law and hospital policy, and inform the whole team.

2. Withdrawing or withholding non-beneficial treatment

  • Stop treatments that do not add comfort – vasopressors, dialysis, frequent blood tests, routine vital-sign monitoring, unnecessary antibiotics.
  • Ventilator support may be reduced or withdrawn (terminal weaning or compassionate extubation) with adequate medication for comfort beforehand.
  • Switch off bedside alarms and monitors (central monitoring may continue); remove unnecessary tubes and restraints.

3. Symptom control

  • Pain and breathlessness – opioids such as morphine, given regularly and titrated to comfort.
  • Anxiety and agitation – benzodiazepines such as midazolam as ordered.
  • Noisy breathing ("death rattle") – repositioning, gentle oral suction, anticholinergic drugs such as glycopyrrolate.
  • Dry mouth and eyes – frequent mouth care, lip balm, eye lubricants.
  • Fever, nausea, delirium and seizures – treated for comfort.
  • Gentle skin care and positioning; no unnecessary procedures.

4. Care of the family

  • Unrestricted visiting, privacy (single room or screens), chairs to sit close, permission to touch and hold the patient.
  • Explain what to expect – changes in breathing pattern, colour, mottling of skin, unresponsiveness – and that the patient is kept comfortable.
  • Respect cultural and religious practices (prayers, holy water, sacred thread, presence of a priest) as far as possible; involve the spiritual care provider.
  • Encourage life review, saying goodbye, and the presence of children if the family wishes.

5. Organ and tissue donation

  • Where suitable (brain-stem death, or eye and tissue donation after death), the family is approached sensitively by the team or transplant coordinator, as required by law.

6. Care after death

  • Confirm and record the time of death; inform the family with empathy; allow time with the body.
  • Last offices with respect, according to religious customs; handling of belongings; death certificate; medico-legal procedures if applicable.

7. Bereavement support

  • Information about practical matters, emotional support, and referral to counselling if grief is complicated.

8. Support for staff

  • Debriefing, recognition of moral distress and grief among staff, and peer support.

Conclusion End-of-life care in the ICU involves honest discussion of goals, documented decisions to withhold or withdraw non-beneficial treatment, meticulous symptom control, respect for cultural and spiritual needs, family presence and support, sensitive discussion of organ donation, dignified care after death and support for staff. Nurses, who are at the bedside throughout, make a peaceful and dignified death possible.
