question: Explain haemodynamic monitoring in the critically ill patient and the nurse's responsibilities.

diagram.caption: Invasive pressure monitoring set-up
labels: pressure bag at 300 mmHg with heparinised or normal saline flush
transducer levelled at the phlebostatic axis (4th intercostal space
cable to monitor showing waveform and values

answer_html:
Introduction Haemodynamic monitoring is the measurement of pressure, flow and oxygenation within the cardiovascular system to assess heart function, circulating volume and tissue perfusion. In shock, sepsis, heart failure, major surgery and trauma, it guides fluid therapy and the use of vasopressors and inotropes.

1. Non-invasive (clinical) monitoring

  • Heart rate and rhythm (ECG), non-invasive BP and mean arterial pressure (MAP) – normal about 70–100 mmHg; target at least 65 mmHg in shock.
  • SpO2, respiratory rate, temperature, capillary refill time (normally under 2–3 seconds), skin colour and warmth, level of consciousness.
  • Urine output – at least 0.5 mL/kg/hour indicates adequate kidney perfusion.
  • Serum lactate – raised (above 2 mmol/L) in poor tissue perfusion.
  • Bedside echocardiography and the passive leg-raise test to judge fluid responsiveness.

2. Invasive monitoring A. Arterial line (intra-arterial BP)

  • A cannula, usually in the radial artery, connected to a transducer gives continuous beat-to-beat BP and allows frequent ABG sampling.
  • Collateral circulation is checked before radial cannulation (modified Allen test).
  • Complications – bleeding, haematoma, thrombosis and distal ischaemia, infection, accidental injection of drugs into the artery (never use the line for drugs).

B. Central venous pressure (CVP)

  • Measured through a central venous catheter in the internal jugular or subclavian vein, with its tip near the right atrium; reflects right-heart filling pressure (normal about 2–8 mmHg).
  • Trends are more useful than single readings; it is not a reliable guide to fluid responsiveness by itself.
  • Complications – pneumothorax at insertion, arterial puncture, air embolism, catheter-related bloodstream infection, thrombosis.

C. Pulmonary artery (Swan–Ganz) catheter

  • A balloon-tipped catheter passed through the right heart into the pulmonary artery; measures pulmonary artery pressure (about 15–30/8–15 mmHg), pulmonary artery wedge pressure (about 6–12 mmHg; reflects left-heart filling), cardiac output (about 4–8 L/min), cardiac index (about 2.5–4 L/min/m²) and mixed venous oxygen saturation (about 60–80%).
  • Used now mainly in complex cardiac and shock cases; complications include arrhythmias, pulmonary infarction, pulmonary artery rupture and infection.

D. Less invasive cardiac output monitors – pulse-contour devices attached to an arterial line, and central venous oxygen saturation (ScvO2, target above 70%).

3. Nurse's responsibilities

  1. Preparation – explain the procedure, obtain consent, assist with aseptic insertion, prepare the pressure bag (inflated to 300 mmHg) with flush solution, tubing and transducer free of air bubbles.
  2. Levelling and zeroing – place the transducer at the phlebostatic axis (4th intercostal space, mid-axillary line); zero to atmosphere at the start of each shift, after changes in position and whenever readings are doubtful.
  3. Accurate readings – take readings at end-expiration with the patient in the same position; check the waveform quality (damped or exaggerated traces give false values) and correlate with the clinical picture.
  4. Alarm limits set appropriately for every pressure; respond promptly.
  5. Prevention of complications – check limb colour, warmth and pulses distal to the arterial line; keep all connections tight and visible to prevent bleeding and air entry; secure lines; aseptic site care and dressing changes; daily review of the need for each line.
  6. Documentation – readings, trends, site condition, and the response to fluids and drugs; report abnormal values early.

Conclusion Haemodynamic monitoring ranges from clinical signs, urine output and lactate to arterial lines, CVP and pulmonary artery catheters. Correct levelling, zeroing, waveform interpretation, prevention of complications and prompt reporting by the nurse make the numbers reliable and useful for guiding life-saving treatment.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients in Critical Care Units
question: Explain the safe use and care of biomedical equipment in the critical care unit.
answer_html:
Introduction Critically ill patients depend on equipment that monitors and supports their vital functions. Faulty, wrongly set or poorly maintained equipment can cause serious harm, so nurses must know how to use, check, clean and troubleshoot each device.

1. Cardiac (multi-parameter) monitor

  • Displays ECG, heart rate, SpO2, NIBP, invasive pressures, temperature and end-tidal CO2.
  • Correct electrode placement on clean, dry skin; change electrodes daily; choose the lead with the clearest P waves and QRS.
  • Set individualised alarm limits; never switch alarms off; check the patient first, then the equipment, when an alarm sounds.

2. Pulse oximeter

  • Correct probe site (finger, ear lobe); poor perfusion, cold extremities, nail polish, movement and bright light give false readings; change the site regularly to prevent pressure injury.

3. Infusion and syringe pumps

  • Volumetric infusion pumps for larger volumes; syringe pumps for small volumes of concentrated, high-alert drugs (vasopressors, insulin, sedatives, heparin).
  • Smart pumps with drug libraries and dose limits reduce dosing errors.
  • Check the drug, concentration, rate, line and patient at the start of each shift and at every change; label lines; use anti-siphon and anti-free-flow sets; respond to occlusion and air-in-line alarms; avoid interruption of vasopressor infusions (prepare the next syringe in advance).

4. Defibrillator

  • Daily check – battery charged, test discharge as per manufacturer, pads and gel available, paper and leads present; record in the check book.
  • During use – correct pad placement, "all clear" before shock, oxygen moved away, synchronised mode for cardioversion.

5. Ventilator

  • Pre-use check (leak test, calibration), clean circuit with humidifier or filter, alarms set; a bag-valve-mask device and oxygen always at the bedside in case of failure.

6. Resuscitation equipment (crash cart)

  • Contains airway equipment (laryngoscope, tubes, bag-valve mask), emergency drugs, IV supplies and suction; checked every shift or day and restocked immediately after each use; sealed and dated.

7. Other equipment – suction apparatus (working, with catheters of correct size), oxygen flow meters and cylinders, ECG machine, ABG analyser, glucometer, warming and cooling devices, air mattresses, sequential compression devices.

General safety measures

  1. Training and competency of all staff before they use any device; manufacturer's instructions available.
  2. Electrical safety – properly earthed sockets, UPS and generator backup, no damaged cables, avoid overloaded extension boards; keep fluids away from electrical equipment.
  3. Preventive maintenance and calibration by the biomedical engineering department; equipment history records; faulty equipment tagged and removed from use.
  4. Infection control – clean and disinfect equipment surfaces between patients and daily; use disposable items once; clean circuits and probes as per policy.
  5. Alarm management – prevent alarm fatigue by setting meaningful limits, responding promptly and never silencing without assessment.
  6. Reporting – equipment-related incidents and adverse events reported within the hospital and to the Materiovigilance Programme of India (medical device adverse event reporting).
  7. Documentation – daily check lists, maintenance logs and incident records.

Conclusion Monitors, pulse oximeters, infusion and syringe pumps, defibrillators, ventilators and the crash cart are life-supporting in the ICU. Proper use, daily checks, correct alarm settings, cleaning, preventive maintenance, electrical safety and reporting of faults by trained nurses protect patients from equipment-related harm.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients in Critical Care Units
question: What is transitional care? Explain the care of a patient during transfer from the ICU to the ward, including post-intensive care syndrome.
answer_html:
Introduction Transitional care is the set of actions that ensure coordination and continuity of care when a patient moves between different levels or settings of care – for example, from the ICU to a step-down unit or ward, and later from hospital to home. The period after ICU discharge is risky: patients may deteriorate on the ward, information may be lost during handover, and both patients and families may feel anxious about leaving close monitoring.

1. Problems after ICU discharge

  • Readmission to the ICU or unexpected death, often from unrecognised deterioration, infection or respiratory problems.
  • Loss of information about drugs, allergies, lines and plans.
  • Transfer (relocation) anxiety – fear of having fewer staff and less monitoring.
  • Weakness, poor nutrition, swallowing problems, sleep disturbance and delirium.

2. Care during transfer from ICU to ward

  1. Assess readiness – stable vital signs and oxygenation without organ support, improving trend, needs that the ward can meet; consider a step-down (high-dependency) unit for those still needing close observation.
  2. Timing – avoid transfers at night or during shift changes when possible.
  3. Prepare the patient and family – explain the reason for transfer as a sign of progress, what to expect on the ward, and whom to contact; reduce anxiety.
  4. Structured handover – verbal and written, using ISBAR (Identify, Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation): diagnosis, ICU course, current problems, drugs and allergies, lines and drains (with insertion dates), diet, mobility, pending results and the plan; note any limitation-of-treatment decisions.
  5. Medication reconciliation – stop ICU-only drugs (e.g. stress-ulcer prophylaxis if no longer needed), continue essential ones, restart regular home medicines as appropriate.
  6. Remove unnecessary lines and catheters before transfer.
  7. Safe transport with appropriate monitoring, oxygen and staff.
  8. Follow-up on the ward – early warning scores (e.g. NEWS2) to detect deterioration; visits by a critical care outreach or rapid response team / ICU liaison nurse; clear criteria for calling for help.
  9. Rehabilitation and nutrition plans – physiotherapy, swallowing assessment, nutritional support continued.

3. Post-intensive care syndrome (PICS) PICS is new or worsening impairment in physical, cognitive or mental health that arises after critical illness and persists beyond hospital discharge.

  • Physical – muscle weakness (ICU-acquired weakness), fatigue, breathlessness, joint stiffness, poor exercise tolerance.
  • Cognitive – poor memory, attention and problem-solving.
  • Mental health – anxiety, depression, sleep problems, post-traumatic stress (nightmares, flashbacks of ICU experiences).
  • PICS-Family (PICS-F) – anxiety, depression and stress in family members.

Prevention and management

  • In the ICU – light sedation, delirium prevention, early mobilisation, family involvement (the ABCDEF approach), sleep promotion, ICU diaries written by staff and family to help the patient understand gaps in memory.
  • After discharge – rehabilitation programmes, ICU follow-up clinics, screening for anxiety, depression and PTSD, support groups, counselling for families, and clear discharge information for the primary care team.

Role of the nurse

  • Prepares the patient and family, gives a complete handover, reconciles medicines, ensures safe transfer, monitors early warning signs on the ward, encourages mobility and self-care, and identifies and refers patients and families with PICS.

Conclusion Transitional care bridges the gap between intensive and ward care. Careful assessment of readiness, preparation, structured handover, medication reconciliation, outreach follow-up, rehabilitation and attention to post-intensive care syndrome reduce readmissions and help survivors and their families recover.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients in Critical Care Units
question: Explain the assessment and management of pain, agitation and delirium in ICU patients.
answer_html:
Introduction Critically ill patients commonly suffer pain (from surgery, procedures, tubes and lying still), agitation (from pain, fear, hypoxia, withdrawal or delirium) and delirium (acute brain dysfunction). These are linked – poorly treated pain causes agitation, and too much sedation causes delirium. Delirium is associated with longer ventilation, longer ICU stay, higher mortality and long-term cognitive problems, so regular assessment and prevention are essential.

1. Pain assessment

  • Patient's self-report is the gold standard – numerical rating scale (0–10) if the patient can communicate, even by nodding or pointing.
  • For patients who cannot communicate (intubated, sedated):
    • Behavioural Pain Scale (BPS) – facial expression, upper limb movements and compliance with ventilation (score 3–12; above 5 suggests pain).
    • Critical-Care Pain Observation Tool (CPOT) – facial expression, body movements, muscle tension, and compliance with the ventilator or vocalisation (score 0–8; above 2 suggests pain).
  • Vital signs alone are not reliable indicators of pain.

2. Sedation and agitation assessment

  • Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS) – from +4 (combative) through 0 (alert and calm) to −5 (unrousable); the usual target is light sedation, RASS 0 to −2 (calm, opens eyes to voice).
  • Look for and treat causes of agitation – pain, hypoxia, full bladder, low sugar, drug or alcohol withdrawal, delirium.

3. Delirium assessment

  • Confusion Assessment Method for the ICU (CAM-ICU) – delirium is present when there is (1) an acute change or fluctuating course of mental status and (2) inattention, plus either (3) an altered level of consciousness or (4) disorganised thinking.
  • Types – hyperactive (restless, pulling at tubes), hypoactive (quiet, withdrawn – most common and easily missed) and mixed.
  • Risk factors – old age, dementia, severe illness, sepsis, benzodiazepines, deep sedation, sleep deprivation, immobility, restraints, hypoxia, metabolic disturbances.
  • Screen at least once every shift.

4. Management – the ABCDEF bundle

  • A – Assess, prevent and manage pain ("analgesia first").
  • B – Both spontaneous awakening trials and spontaneous breathing trials daily.
  • C – Choice of analgesia and sedation – lightest effective sedation; prefer short-acting agents such as propofol or dexmedetomidine; avoid benzodiazepines where possible.
  • D – Delirium: assess, prevent and manage.
  • E – Early mobility and exercise.
  • F – Family engagement and empowerment.

5. Non-pharmacological measures

  • Frequent reorientation; clock, calendar and familiar objects; spectacles and hearing aids in place.
  • Sleep promotion – lights dimmed and noise reduced at night, clustering of care, eye masks and earplugs, day-time activity.
  • Early mobilisation; adequate hydration and nutrition; correction of hypoxia, electrolytes and sugar; bladder and bowel care.
  • Avoid physical restraints as far as possible; remove unnecessary tubes and lines.
  • Family presence and involvement; calm, simple communication.

6. Drug treatment

  • Treat pain with opioids (e.g. fentanyl, morphine) and non-opioids (paracetamol), using multimodal analgesia.
  • Antipsychotics are not used routinely to prevent or treat delirium; short-term use may be considered for distressing agitation or hallucinations as ordered; dexmedetomidine may help agitated ventilated patients.

Role of the nurse

  • Assesses pain, sedation and delirium regularly with valid tools and records the scores; titrates analgesia and sedation to targets as ordered; carries out daily awakening trials with the team; implements non-drug measures and early mobility; ensures safety; educates and involves the family.

Conclusion Regular use of pain scales (self-report, BPS, CPOT), RASS for sedation and CAM-ICU for delirium, together with the ABCDEF bundle, light sedation, sleep promotion, early mobilisation and family involvement, reduces suffering, shortens ventilation and ICU stay, and improves long-term recovery.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients in Critical Care Units
question: List the complications of mechanical ventilation.
answer_html:
Complications of mechanical ventilation

  1. Airway problems – tube displacement (oesophageal or right main bronchus intubation), accidental extubation, tube blockage by secretions, cuff leak, laryngeal oedema, tracheal stenosis or tracheomalacia, tracheo-oesophageal fistula.
  2. Lung injury – barotrauma (pneumothorax, surgical emphysema) and volutrauma from high pressures or volumes; oxygen toxicity; atelectasis.
  3. Infection – ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP), sinusitis.
  4. Cardiovascular – hypotension and reduced cardiac output due to raised intrathoracic pressure (especially with high PEEP).
  5. Acid–base disturbance – respiratory alkalosis (over-ventilation) or acidosis (under-ventilation).
  6. Gastrointestinal – stress ulcer and bleeding, abdominal distension, ileus; fluid retention.
  7. Others – patient–ventilator asynchrony, ICU-acquired weakness, pressure injuries, DVT, delirium, ventilator dependence and psychological distress.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients in Critical Care Units
question: Differentiate between hyperventilation and hypoventilation.
answer_html:
Hyperventilation

  • Meaning – breathing faster and/or deeper than the body needs, so that excess CO2 is removed.
  • Blood gases – PaCO2 below 35 mmHg, leading to respiratory alkalosis.
  • Causes – anxiety and panic, pain, fever, hypoxia (high altitude, pneumonia, pulmonary embolism), early asthma, salicylate poisoning, brain lesions, excessive mechanical ventilation.
  • Features – rapid breathing, dizziness, tingling of fingers and around the mouth, carpopedal spasm, palpitations, chest tightness.
  • Management – treat the cause; reassure and coach slow breathing; adjust ventilator settings.

Hypoventilation

  • Meaning – breathing too slowly or too shallowly, so that CO2 accumulates (and oxygen falls).
  • Blood gases – PaCO2 above 45 mmHg, leading to respiratory acidosis with hypoxaemia.
  • Causes – depression of the respiratory centre (opioids, sedatives, head injury), neuromuscular weakness (Guillain–Barré syndrome, myasthenia gravis), chest wall deformity, severe obesity, COPD, airway obstruction.
  • Features – drowsiness, headache, confusion, warm flushed skin, bounding pulse, cyanosis, and CO2 narcosis (coma) in severe cases.
  • Management – treat the cause (e.g. naloxone for opioid overdose), controlled oxygen, non-invasive or mechanical ventilation.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients in Critical Care Units
question: What is positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP)?
answer_html:
Positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) is the positive pressure maintained in the airways and alveoli at the end of expiration during mechanical ventilation, so that airway pressure does not fall to zero (atmospheric) at the end of each breath.

  • Usual level – about 5 cm H2O (physiological PEEP); higher levels (often 8–15 cm H2O or more) in ARDS and severe hypoxaemia.
  • Benefits – prevents alveolar collapse, recruits collapsed alveoli, increases functional residual capacity, improves oxygenation and allows a lower FiO2.
  • Hazards – raised intrathoracic pressure reducing venous return, hypotension and fall in cardiac output, barotrauma, and possible rise in intracranial pressure.
  • Auto-PEEP (intrinsic PEEP) is unintended trapping of air when expiration is incomplete, as in asthma and COPD.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Patients in Critical Care Units
question: What is temperature control (targeted temperature management) after cardiac arrest?
answer_html:
Temperature control (formerly called targeted temperature management or therapeutic hypothermia) is the deliberate control of body temperature after return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) in adults who remain unresponsive to verbal commands, to protect the brain from hypoxic–ischaemic injury.

  • According to current AHA guidance, one temperature between 32 °C and 37.5 °C is chosen and maintained for at least 36 hours, and fever is actively prevented.
  • Methods – surface cooling pads or blankets, cold IV fluids, intravascular cooling catheters, with continuous core temperature monitoring (bladder, oesophageal or rectal probe).
  • Nursing care – prevent and treat shivering (sedation, warming of hands and face), monitor ECG (bradycardia), electrolytes (low potassium), blood sugar and bleeding; skin checks under cooling pads; slow, controlled rewarming.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Adults including Elderly with Occupational and Industrial Disorders
question: (a) Define pneumoconiosis and classify the pneumoconioses. (3 marks) (b) Describe the causes, pathophysiology, clinical features, diagnosis and complications of silicosis and asbestosis. (7 marks) (c) Explain the prevention and the medical and nursing management of pneumoconioses. (5 marks)

diagram.caption: Pathogenesis of silicosis
labels: inhaled respirable silica particles reach alveoli
alveolar macrophages ingest silica and are damaged
release of inflammatory and fibrogenic mediators
whorled silicotic nodules in upper lobes
impaired macrophage defence leading to tuberculosis

answer_html:
(a) Definition and classification (3 marks) Pneumoconiosis is defined (ILO) as the accumulation of dust in the lungs and the tissue reactions to its presence. It is caused by prolonged inhalation of dust at work, is usually irreversible and progressive, and has no specific cure – so prevention is the only real solution. Dust particles of about 0.5–5 micrometres (respirable dust) reach the alveoli and are the most harmful.

Classification according to the type of dust A. Inorganic (mineral) dusts

  1. Silicosis – free crystalline silica (quartz): mining, stone quarrying and crushing, sandstone carving, sand-blasting, foundries, glass, pottery and ceramics, slate-pencil and agate-grinding industries, construction and engineered-stone cutting.
  2. Asbestosis – asbestos fibres: asbestos-cement sheets and pipes, brake linings and clutch pads, insulation, ship-breaking and demolition.
  3. Coal workers' pneumoconiosis (anthracosis, "black lung") – coal dust in coal miners.
  4. Others – siderosis (iron oxide – welders, iron-ore miners), stannosis (tin), baritosis (barium), berylliosis (beryllium), talcosis (talc), kaolinosis (china clay).

B. Organic dusts (many act as allergic or hypersensitivity lung diseases)

  1. Byssinosis – cotton, flax and hemp dust in textile mills.
  2. Bagassosis – mouldy sugarcane bagasse (paper and board industry).
  3. Farmer's lung – mouldy hay and grain (thermophilic actinomycetes).
  4. Others – bird fancier's lung, mushroom worker's lung, tobacco and grain dust diseases.

(b) Silicosis and asbestosis (7 marks) A. Silicosis Cause – inhalation of free crystalline silica (silicon dioxide) dust, usually over many years; it is the commonest and most serious pneumoconiosis in India.

Pathophysiology

  • Inhaled silica particles reach the alveoli and are engulfed by alveolar macrophages.
  • Silica is toxic to macrophages – they are damaged and release inflammatory and fibrogenic mediators that stimulate fibroblasts to lay down collagen.
  • This forms silicotic nodules (whorled collagen), mainly in the upper lobes and hilar lymph nodes.
  • Nodules enlarge and join to form progressive massive fibrosis (PMF), causing a stiff, restrictive lung with reduced gas exchange.
  • Damaged macrophages also lose their ability to kill mycobacteria, so tuberculosis risk rises sharply (silicotuberculosis).
  • The disease continues to progress even after exposure stops.

Types

  • Chronic (simple) silicosis – after 10 years or more of exposure; commonest.
  • Accelerated silicosis – after 5–10 years of heavier exposure.
  • Acute silicosis (silicoproteinosis) – within weeks to a few years of very heavy exposure (e.g. sand-blasting); rapidly fatal.

Clinical features

  • Early stages may have no symptoms; later progressive breathlessness on exertion, dry cough (later productive), chest tightness, fatigue and weight loss.
  • Crackles on auscultation; cyanosis and signs of right heart failure (cor pulmonale) in advanced disease.
  • Fever, night sweats, haemoptysis and weight loss suggest tuberculosis.

Diagnosis

  • Detailed occupational history – type of work, duration and intensity of exposure, protective measures.
  • Chest X-ray – multiple small rounded opacities in the upper zones, "eggshell" calcification of hilar lymph nodes, and large opacities in PMF; films are graded by the ILO classification of radiographs of pneumoconioses.
  • HRCT chest – detects early nodules.
  • Pulmonary function tests – restrictive (or mixed) pattern with reduced diffusing capacity.
  • Sputum for AFB and CBNAAT to detect tuberculosis.

Complications – pulmonary tuberculosis, progressive massive fibrosis, respiratory failure, cor pulmonale, spontaneous pneumothorax, lung cancer (crystalline silica is a known human carcinogen), autoimmune diseases (rheumatoid arthritis, scleroderma) and kidney disease.

B. Asbestosis Cause – inhalation of asbestos fibres (chrysotile or white asbestos, and the more dangerous amphiboles – crocidolite or blue, amosite or brown) in asbestos mining and milling, manufacture of cement sheets and pipes, brake linings, insulation, ship-breaking and demolition; families may be exposed to dust carried home on work clothes.

Pathophysiology

  • Long, thin fibres reach the lower airways and alveoli and cannot be cleared; macrophages fail to engulf them completely and release inflammatory mediators.
  • This causes diffuse interstitial fibrosis, mainly in the lower lobes and under the pleura, and pleural plaques and thickening.
  • Fibres coated with iron–protein form "asbestos (ferruginous) bodies", seen in sputum or lung tissue.
  • Latency is long – usually 15–20 years or more for asbestosis and 20–40 years for mesothelioma.

Clinical features

  • Progressive exertional breathlessness, dry cough, fine end-inspiratory crackles at both lung bases, finger clubbing (common), later cyanosis and cor pulmonale.

Diagnosis

  • Occupational history; chest X-ray – lower-zone linear (reticular) shadows, "shaggy" heart border, pleural plaques (often calcified, on the diaphragm); HRCT; restrictive pulmonary function with reduced diffusing capacity; asbestos bodies in sputum or lavage fluid.

Complications

  • Bronchogenic carcinoma – risk greatly multiplied in workers who also smoke.
  • Malignant mesothelioma of the pleura or peritoneum – strongly linked to asbestos, even after low exposure.
  • Pleural effusion, respiratory failure, cor pulmonale; cancers of the larynx and ovary.

Coal workers' pneumoconiosis (brief) – simple form with small nodules, and complicated form (PMF); Caplan syndrome is the combination of rheumatoid arthritis with large lung nodules in dust-exposed workers.

(c) Prevention and management (5 marks) A. Prevention (hierarchy of control)

  1. Elimination or substitution – replacing silica sand with safer abrasives in blasting; safer substitutes for asbestos products.
  2. Engineering controls – wet drilling, cutting and grinding (water sprays), enclosure and automation of dusty processes, local exhaust ventilation, dust suppression; regular monitoring of dust levels at the workplace against permissible limits.
  3. Administrative measures – limiting exposure time and job rotation, wet cleaning or vacuuming instead of dry sweeping, training of workers, prohibition of smoking.
  4. Personal protective equipment – properly fitted respirators (N95/P2 or better, powered respirators for heavy exposure) as the last line of defence, with fit testing.
  5. Medical surveillance – pre-placement examination with baseline chest X-ray and spirometry; periodic examinations to detect early disease and remove the worker from exposure; regular TB screening of silica-exposed workers.
  6. Legal measures – silicosis, asbestosis, coal workers' pneumoconiosis and byssinosis are notifiable and compensable occupational diseases under the labour laws (now the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 and the Code on Social Security, 2020); some states such as Rajasthan have special policies for financial assistance and rehabilitation of silicosis patients.

B. Medical management (there is no cure; damage is permanent)

  • Remove from further exposure; stop smoking.
  • Bronchodilators if airflow obstruction is present; prompt treatment of chest infections.
  • Vaccination – influenza and pneumococcal.
  • Treatment of tuberculosis with standard anti-TB drugs under the National TB Elimination Programme; screening for TB infection.
  • Long-term oxygen therapy for chronic hypoxaemia; treatment of cor pulmonale (diuretics, oxygen).
  • Pulmonary rehabilitation.
  • Whole-lung lavage for acute silicosis; lung transplantation in selected advanced cases; treatment of cancers (surgery, chemotherapy, palliative care) as needed.

C. Nursing management Nursing diagnoses – impaired gas exchange; ineffective breathing pattern; activity intolerance; risk for infection; imbalanced nutrition; anxiety; deficient knowledge about the disease and occupational risk.

  1. Respiratory care – monitor respiratory rate, SpO2, breath sounds and sputum; position upright (high Fowler's); teach pursed-lip and diaphragmatic breathing and controlled coughing; chest physiotherapy if secretions are present.
  2. Oxygen therapy as prescribed, with safety precautions and guidance on home oxygen.
  3. Activity and energy conservation – plan rest periods, graded exercise, pulmonary rehabilitation exercises.
  4. Nutrition – high-calorie, high-protein, small frequent meals; adequate fluids to loosen secretions; monitor weight.
  5. Infection prevention – early reporting of fever, increased sputum or haemoptysis; sputum testing for TB; adherence to anti-TB treatment; vaccination.
  6. Health education – smoking cessation, avoidance of further dust exposure, correct use of respirators, recognition of warning signs.
  7. Psychosocial support – the disease is chronic and disabling and often causes loss of livelihood; counsel the worker and family, support a change of job, and help with compensation claims and social security benefits (ESIC, state schemes).
  8. Palliative and end-of-life care in advanced disease or cancer.

Nursing importance

  • Because pneumoconioses cannot be reversed, the nurse's greatest contribution is prevention and early detection – through workplace education, surveillance examinations and prompt referral – along with supportive care that improves quality of life.

Conclusion Pneumoconiosis is the deposition of dust in the lungs with a fibrotic tissue reaction, caused by inorganic dusts such as silica, asbestos and coal, or organic dusts such as cotton and bagasse. Silicosis causes upper-lobe nodular fibrosis with a high risk of tuberculosis, while asbestosis causes lower-lobe fibrosis, pleural plaques, lung cancer and mesothelioma. As there is no cure, dust control, protective equipment, medical surveillance, legal protection and supportive medical and nursing care are the cornerstones of management.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Adults including Elderly with Occupational and Industrial Disorders
question: Explain the role of the nurse in the prevention and control of occupational diseases.
tags: role of nurse in occupational health
answer_html:
Introduction Occupational diseases are diseases caused mainly by exposure to hazards at the place of work – dusts, chemicals, noise, heat, radiation, infections, poor ergonomics and stress. Most of them are preventable. The occupational health nurse works in factories, mines, plantations, hospitals and community settings to protect and promote the health and safety of workers.

1. Primary prevention (preventing the disease)

  • Workplace walk-through surveys with the safety officer to identify hazards (dust, fumes, noise, unsafe machines, poor lighting, heat, faulty posture).
  • Health education of workers on the nature of hazards, correct use of personal protective equipment (respirators, ear plugs and muffs, gloves, goggles, aprons, safety shoes), safe handling and storage of chemicals, personal hygiene (washing before eating, changing clothes before going home), and safe lifting and posture.
  • Promotion of healthy lifestyles – avoidance of smoking, tobacco and alcohol; nutrition; exercise; stress management.
  • Immunisation – tetanus for all workers; hepatitis B for health-care workers; other vaccines as needed.
  • Pre-placement examination – to place workers in suitable jobs and record baseline health (chest X-ray, spirometry, audiometry, vision, blood tests).
  • Advice on environmental sanitation – safe drinking water, toilets, canteen hygiene, ventilation and lighting.

2. Secondary prevention (early detection and treatment)

  • Periodic medical examinations and special tests for exposed workers (spirometry and chest X-ray for dust, audiometry for noise, blood lead levels, serum cholinesterase for pesticide handlers).
  • Screening for TB, hypertension, diabetes and anaemia; early recognition of symptoms and prompt referral.
  • First aid and emergency care for injuries, burns, chemical splashes, poisoning and heat stroke; maintaining first-aid boxes and ambulance rooms.
  • Treatment of minor illnesses and follow-up of chronic diseases at the workplace clinic.

3. Tertiary prevention (limiting disability)

  • Rehabilitation after injury or illness; help with return to work, modified or alternative duties.
  • Support for workers with permanent disability; guidance on compensation and social security benefits (ESIC, Employees' Compensation).

4. Administrative and legal role

  • Maintaining health records of every worker, registers of accidents and occupational diseases.
  • Helping the employer meet legal requirements – medical examinations, notification of occupational diseases and accidents, welfare facilities – under the labour laws (now the OSH Code, 2020 and the Code on Social Security, 2020).
  • Participation in safety committees, emergency and disaster planning.

5. Counselling and special groups

  • Counselling for work stress, alcohol and substance use, family problems.
  • Care of women workers (antenatal care, crèche, protection from hazards during pregnancy) and elderly workers (age-related changes, safer job placement).

6. Research and quality improvement

  • Collecting data on absenteeism, injuries and diseases; evaluating preventive programmes.

Conclusion The occupational health nurse prevents occupational diseases through hazard identification, health education, PPE promotion, immunisation and pre-placement examinations; detects them early through periodic examinations and screening; limits disability through first aid, treatment and rehabilitation; and maintains records, ensures legal compliance and counsels workers.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Adults including Elderly with Occupational and Industrial Disorders
question: Explain the occupational history, physical examination and diagnostic tests in the assessment of a patient with an occupational disorder.
answer_html:
Introduction Occupational disorders often look like ordinary diseases (asthma, dermatitis, anaemia, hearing loss, cancer). The diagnosis depends on suspecting a work connection and taking a careful occupational history, supported by examination and specific tests. Making this link is important for treatment, prevention in co-workers and compensation.

1. Occupational history

  • Present job – name of the job and industry, what the worker actually does, materials and machines used, hours and shifts.
  • Past jobs – a chronological list of all jobs, including part-time and seasonal work (e.g. farming, construction).
  • Exposures – dusts, chemicals, fumes, solvents, metals, pesticides, noise, vibration, heat, radiation, infections, heavy lifting or repetitive work; duration and intensity of exposure.
  • Protective measures – ventilation, wet methods, PPE used and its condition.
  • Relation of symptoms to work – symptoms that improve on weekends or holidays and worsen on return to work (e.g. occupational asthma, byssinosis – "Monday chest tightness").
  • Similar illness in co-workers.
  • Non-occupational exposures – hobbies, home environment, family members' jobs (take-home dust), smoking and alcohol.
  • A simple screening aid is "WHACS" – What do you do? How do you do it? Are you concerned about any exposures? Co-workers with similar problems? Satisfied with your job?

2. General history – presenting complaints, past illnesses, medicines, family history, socio-economic status.

3. Physical examination

  • General – pallor (lead, benzene), cyanosis, clubbing (asbestosis), weight loss, a blue "lead line" on the gums, tremors (mercury).
  • Respiratory – respiratory rate, chest expansion, crackles (fibrosis), wheeze (occupational asthma).
  • Skin – dermatitis, burns, ulcers, pigment changes, warts or cancers (tar, arsenic).
  • ENT and eyes – hearing (whisper and tuning-fork tests), nasal septum perforation (chromium), conjunctivitis, cataract (heat, radiation).
  • Neurological – peripheral neuropathy, wrist or foot drop (lead), tremor, memory changes (solvents, mercury).
  • Musculoskeletal – back pain, carpal tunnel syndrome, tenderness from repetitive strain.
  • Cardiovascular – blood pressure (noise, lead), signs of right heart failure.

4. Diagnostic tests

  • Chest X-ray graded by the ILO classification, HRCT – pneumoconioses.
  • Spirometry and diffusing capacity; serial peak expiratory flow at work and away from work – occupational asthma.
  • Audiometry – noise-induced hearing loss shows a typical notch at about 4000 Hz.
  • Blood lead level, zinc protoporphyrin, urinary aminolevulinic acid – lead poisoning; blood and urine mercury and arsenic levels.
  • Serum or red-cell cholinesterase – organophosphate pesticide exposure.
  • Complete blood count – benzene (aplastic anaemia, leukaemia), lead (anaemia, basophilic stippling).
  • Patch test and skin-prick tests – allergic contact dermatitis and occupational allergies.
  • Sputum – AFB and CBNAAT (TB in silicosis), asbestos bodies, cytology.
  • Nerve conduction studies, liver and kidney function tests (solvents, metals), urine cytology (bladder cancer in dye workers), biopsy where needed.
  • Workplace (environmental) monitoring of dust, noise or chemical levels and biological monitoring of workers support the diagnosis and guide prevention.

5. Role of the nurse

  • Takes a thorough occupational history, assists in examination, collects specimens correctly, prepares workers for tests (e.g. avoiding noise before audiometry), maintains records and informs the doctor and employer as required for notification.

Conclusion A detailed occupational history – job, exposures, protective measures and the relation of symptoms to work – combined with focused physical examination and specific tests such as chest X-ray, spirometry, audiometry, blood lead levels and cholinesterase confirms occupational disorders and guides treatment, prevention and compensation.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Adults including Elderly with Occupational and Industrial Disorders
question: Explain occupational dermatoses and occupational cancers, with their prevention.
answer_html:
Introduction The skin is the organ most often affected by work, and some workplace substances can cause cancer after many years. Both occupational dermatoses and occupational cancers are largely preventable by controlling exposure.

A. Occupational dermatoses

  1. Contact dermatitis – the commonest occupational skin disease.
    • Irritant contact dermatitis (most cases) – from wet work, detergents, soaps, solvents, cement, acids and alkalis; affects health workers, cleaners, construction workers and cooks.
    • Allergic contact dermatitis – a delayed hypersensitivity reaction to chromium in cement, nickel, rubber chemicals and latex, epoxy resins, dyes and hair dyes.
  2. Occupational acne – oil acne (folliculitis from mineral and cutting oils) and chloracne (from chlorinated hydrocarbons such as dioxins).
  3. Pigmentary changes – occupational leucoderma (depigmentation) from phenolic compounds in rubber industries; hyperpigmentation from tar and pitch.
  4. Photodermatitis – tar, pitch and some plants with sunlight.
  5. Chemical burns and ulcers – acids, alkalis, wet cement burns; chrome ulcers.
  6. Mechanical injuries – calluses, blisters, cuts.
  7. Infections – fungal infections in wet work, cutaneous anthrax in wool and hide workers, erysipeloid in fish and meat handlers.
  8. Skin cancers – from tar, soot, mineral oils, arsenic and long exposure to sunlight (outdoor workers).

B. Occupational cancers | Cancer | Agents and occupations | |---|---| | Lung | Asbestos, crystalline silica, chromium, nickel, arsenic, radon (uranium mining), coal-tar fumes, diesel exhaust | | Mesothelioma | Asbestos | | Bladder | Aromatic amines (benzidine, beta-naphthylamine) – dye and rubber industries | | Leukaemia | Benzene, ionising radiation | | Liver (angiosarcoma) | Vinyl chloride (PVC manufacture) | | Nasal sinuses | Wood dust (furniture making), nickel | | Skin | Soot, tar, mineral oils, arsenic, ultraviolet light | - The first occupational cancer described was cancer of the scrotum in chimney sweeps caused by soot (Percivall Pott, 1775). - Features – a long latent period (often 10–40 years) between exposure and cancer; they look the same as other cancers, so occupational history is essential; smoking multiplies the risk (e.g. asbestos and lung cancer).

C. Prevention

  1. Elimination or substitution of harmful substances (e.g. banning benzidine dyes, safer solvents, low-chromium cement).
  2. Engineering controls – closed processes, automation, local exhaust ventilation, wet methods.
  3. Personal protection – suitable gloves, aprons, sleeves, face shields and respirators; barrier creams have only a limited role.
  4. Personal hygiene – washing exposed skin promptly, mild cleansers and moisturisers, no eating or smoking at the workplace, changing work clothes before going home.
  5. Pre-placement examination – avoid placing workers with skin disease or known allergy in high-risk jobs.
  6. Medical surveillance – periodic skin checks; urine cytology in dye workers; chest examinations in asbestos workers; blood counts in benzene workers.
  7. Health education – early reporting of skin lesions, use of PPE, smoking cessation.
  8. Legal measures – exposure limits, notification and compensation of occupational diseases.

D. Management and role of the nurse

  • Treatment of dermatitis (removal of the cause, emollients, topical steroids), care of burns and ulcers, patch testing to identify allergens, change of job for sensitised workers.
  • Early referral of suspicious lesions; support during cancer treatment; help with compensation.

Conclusion Occupational dermatoses – mainly irritant and allergic contact dermatitis, acne, pigment changes, burns and infections – and occupational cancers of the lung, pleura, bladder, blood, liver, nose and skin result from preventable workplace exposures. Substitution, engineering controls, protective equipment, hygiene, surveillance and education are the key to prevention.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Adults including Elderly with Occupational and Industrial Disorders
question: Explain noise-induced hearing loss and lead poisoning as occupational disorders, with their prevention and management.
answer_html:
Introduction Noise and toxic metals are among the commonest industrial hazards in India. Noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL) and lead poisoning are permanent or serious if neglected, but both are entirely preventable.

A. Noise-induced hearing loss Causes and exposure

  • Prolonged exposure to noise above about 85 dB(A) averaged over an 8-hour day – textile mills, metal and engineering works, stone crushing, mining, printing presses, construction, generator rooms and airports. A single very loud blast causes acoustic trauma. Pathophysiology

  • Noise damages the outer hair cells of the organ of Corti in the cochlea. Early exposure causes a temporary threshold shift (dullness of hearing after a shift that recovers); repeated exposure produces a permanent threshold shift. Clinical features

  • Bilateral, symmetrical sensorineural hearing loss, first for high frequencies; difficulty following speech in noisy places; tinnitus; later difficulty with normal conversation.

  • Non-auditory effects – stress, irritability, sleep disturbance, raised BP, poor concentration and accidents. Diagnosis – history of noise exposure; tuning-fork tests; pure-tone audiometry showing a characteristic dip ("notch") at about 4000 Hz. Prevention – hearing conservation programme
  1. Noise survey and mapping of noisy areas.
  2. Engineering control – quieter machines, enclosures, silencers, vibration dampers, regular maintenance, isolating noisy processes.
  3. Administrative control – reduced exposure time, job rotation, rest in quiet areas.
  4. Hearing protection – ear plugs and ear muffs, correctly fitted and worn throughout exposure.
  5. Audiometry at pre-placement and periodically, to detect early loss and move affected workers.
  6. Education of workers and supervisors. Management – hearing loss is permanent; remove from further exposure, provide hearing aids, communication strategies, and compensation (NIHL is a compensable occupational disease).

B. Lead poisoning (plumbism) Sources – lead smelting, battery manufacture and recycling (especially informal units), lead paints and painting, ceramic glazing, glass, plumbing and soldering, printing and ammunition. Lead enters mainly by inhalation of dust and fumes and by ingestion from contaminated hands. Effects

  • Lead inhibits enzymes of haem synthesis (delta-aminolevulinic acid dehydratase and ferrochelatase) → anaemia with basophilic stippling of red cells; and it damages nerves, kidneys and reproductive organs. Clinical features

  • Gastrointestinal – loss of appetite, metallic taste, constipation, abdominal colic ("lead colic").

  • Blue-black "Burton line" on the gums; pallor and fatigue.
  • Neurological – motor peripheral neuropathy (wrist drop, foot drop), headache, irritability, memory loss; encephalopathy (convulsions, coma) in severe cases, especially in children.

  • Hypertension, chronic kidney damage, gout, infertility and miscarriage. Diagnosis – blood lead level (the key test), zinc protoporphyrin, urinary aminolevulinic acid and coproporphyrin, blood count and peripheral smear. Management

  • Remove from exposure immediately.

  • Chelation therapy as prescribed – calcium disodium EDTA, dimercaprol (BAL) (with EDTA in encephalopathy), or oral succimer (DMSA) or D-penicillamine; monitor kidney function and urine output during chelation.

  • Correct anaemia and nutritional deficiencies (iron, calcium). Prevention

  • Substitution of lead where possible, closed processes, local exhaust ventilation, wet methods; respirators.

  • Personal hygiene – no eating, drinking or smoking in work areas, washing hands and face, changing clothes and bathing before going home (to protect children from "take-home" lead).
  • Periodic blood lead monitoring of workers; education.

Other toxic metals (brief) – mercury (thermometer, chlor-alkali and gold work: tremors, gingivitis, irritability, kidney damage), arsenic (pesticides, smelting, groundwater: skin pigmentation, hyperkeratosis, neuropathy, cancers), chromium (electroplating, tanning: nasal septum perforation, chrome ulcers, lung cancer), cadmium (batteries: kidney damage, bone pain).

Role of the nurse – noise and lead surveys with the safety team, education on PPE and hygiene, audiometry and blood sampling, early detection and referral, care during chelation, and counselling for job change and compensation.

Conclusion NIHL is a permanent, bilateral high-frequency hearing loss with a 4 kHz notch caused by prolonged noise above 85 dB(A); lead poisoning causes colic, anaemia, neuropathy and kidney damage. Both are prevented by engineering controls, protective equipment, hygiene and periodic monitoring, and managed by removal from exposure, hearing aids or chelation, and rehabilitation.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Adults including Elderly with Occupational and Industrial Disorders
question: Explain occupational health services and the legislation for the protection of workers' health in India.
tags: Occupational Safety Health and Working Conditions Code 2020
answer_html:
Introduction Occupational health aims at the promotion and maintenance of the highest degree of physical, mental and social well-being of workers in all occupations, the prevention of ill-health caused by working conditions, and the adaptation of work to the worker and of each worker to his job (ILO/WHO). This is achieved through occupational health services and protective labour laws.

A. Occupational health services

  1. Medical examinations – pre-placement (to place the worker in a suitable job and record baseline health), periodic (for early detection of occupational and general diseases), special examinations after illness, injury or exposure, and on leaving the job.
  2. Treatment and first aid – first-aid boxes, ambulance rooms, dispensary and referral services.
  3. Health education and promotion – safe work practices, PPE, nutrition, family welfare, avoidance of tobacco and alcohol.
  4. Environmental monitoring – measurement and control of dust, fumes, noise, heat and lighting.
  5. Immunisation, nutrition services (canteens), and mental health support.
  6. Records and notification of accidents and occupational diseases.
  7. Rehabilitation and placement of disabled workers.
  8. Care of women and adolescent workers, including maternity benefits and crèches.

B. Legislation India's labour laws were consolidated into four Labour Codes, in force from 21 November 2025, replacing 29 older central laws. 1. Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020 (OSH Code)

  • Replaces 13 laws, including the Factories Act 1948, Mines Act 1952, Dock Workers Act, Building and Other Construction Workers Act, Plantations Labour Act, Contract Labour Act and Inter-State Migrant Workmen Act.
  • Duties of employers to provide a safe and healthy workplace; national safety and health standards for different sectors.
  • Free annual health check-up by employers for workers above 40 years of age; pre-employment, periodic and post-exposure medical examinations in hazardous processes.
  • Notification of accidents and occupational diseases; safety committees; safety officers in hazardous establishments.
  • Welfare facilities – drinking water, toilets, washing facilities, first aid, canteens, crèches, rest rooms, ventilation, lighting and protection from excessive heat and noise.

  • Working hours limited to 48 hours a week, with double wages for overtime; women may work at night with their consent and adequate safety arrangements. 2. Code on Social Security, 2020

  • Replaces 9 laws, including the Employees' State Insurance Act 1948, Employees' Compensation Act 1923, Employees' Provident Funds Act, Maternity Benefit Act 1961 and Payment of Gratuity Act.

  • ESIC benefits – medical care, sickness benefit, maternity benefit, disablement benefit (temporary and permanent) for employment injury and occupational disease, dependants' benefit and funeral expenses; ESIC coverage is now pan-India, voluntary for establishments with fewer than 10 employees and mandatory for any establishment with even one worker in a hazardous process.
  • Compensation for employment injury and listed occupational diseases (e.g. silicosis, asbestosis, byssinosis, lead poisoning, noise-induced hearing loss).

  • Social security extended to unorganised, gig and platform workers (registration on the e-Shram portal). 3. Other related laws

  • Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986 (amended 2016) – no employment of children below 14 (except helping in a family enterprise outside school hours); adolescents (14–18) barred from hazardous occupations and processes.

  • Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 – internal committees in workplaces.
  • Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 and rules on hazardous chemicals and waste.

C. Institutions

  • National Institute of Occupational Health (NIOH), Ahmedabad (ICMR) – research on occupational diseases.
  • Directorate General Factory Advice Service and Labour Institutes (DGFASLI) and the Central Labour Institute, Mumbai.
  • State factory and labour departments; ESIC hospitals and dispensaries.

Role of the nurse – conducts medical examinations and screening, maintains records and registers, educates workers about their rights and benefits, helps them claim ESIC and compensation benefits, and assists employers in meeting legal health requirements.

Conclusion Occupational health services provide medical examinations, first aid, health education, environmental monitoring, records and rehabilitation. Since 21 November 2025, the OSH Code and the Code on Social Security have replaced older laws such as the Factories Act, ESI Act and Employees' Compensation Act, strengthening safety standards, free annual health check-ups, medical examinations, ESIC coverage and compensation for occupational diseases.

subject: Adult Health Nursing II with integrated pathophysiology including Geriatric Nursing (and Palliative Care module)
unit_title: Nursing Management of Adults including Elderly with Occupational and Industrial Disorders
question: Explain the occupational health hazards of agricultural workers and their prevention.
answer_html:
Introduction Agriculture employs the largest share of India's workforce. Farmers and farm labourers – many of them women, children and elderly people – work long hours in the open, handle chemicals and machines, and have limited access to health care. Their hazards are often ignored because farm work is unorganised.

A. Occupational hazards

  1. Chemical hazards – pesticides
    • Organophosphates, carbamates, pyrethroids, paraquat and others cause acute poisoning during mixing and spraying (absorption through skin, inhalation, accidental ingestion) and chronic effects (neurological, skin, respiratory, cancer risk).
    • In 2017, accidental pesticide poisoning during spraying of cotton crops in Yavatmal district of Vidarbha caused several deaths and many hospital admissions, showing the danger of unsafe spraying without protection.
  2. Physical hazards
    • Heat stress and heat stroke, sunburn and skin cancer from sun exposure; lightning; noise and vibration from tractors and threshers.
  3. Mechanical injuries
    • Thresher, chaff-cutter and sugarcane-crusher injuries (hand and arm amputations), tractor overturning, falls from trees and haystacks, cuts from sickles, injuries from animals.
  4. Biological hazards
    • Snake bites and scorpion stings, insect bites; zoonoses – leptospirosis (paddy fields and floods), brucellosis, anthrax, rabies; tetanus; vector-borne diseases (malaria, Japanese encephalitis); worm infestations; fungal infections.
  5. Respiratory hazards from organic dust
    • Farmer's lung (mouldy hay and grain), grain-dust asthma, bagassosis, cotton dust.
  6. Ergonomic hazards – bending, squatting, lifting and carrying loads (paddy transplantation, harvesting) leading to back pain and other musculoskeletal disorders.
  7. Psychosocial hazards – income insecurity, debt, crop failure and stress.

B. Prevention

  1. Safe use of pesticides
    • Use only approved pesticides; follow label instructions; adopt integrated pest management to reduce chemical use.
    • Wear PPE – gloves, mask, goggles, long-sleeved clothing, boots; use non-leaking sprayers.
    • Spray in the direction of the wind, in cooler hours, never against the wind; do not eat, drink or smoke while spraying.
    • Bathe and change clothes after spraying; wash clothes separately.
    • Store pesticides locked, away from food and children; never re-use containers; dispose of them safely.
    • Recognise early symptoms (sweating, salivation, vomiting, blurred vision, weakness) and seek care immediately.
  2. Machine safety – guards on threshers and chaff cutters, training, no loose clothing, rest to prevent fatigue, tractor rollover protection.
  3. Heat protection – work during cooler hours, frequent water and rest in shade, head covering, recognition of heat illness.
  4. Snake bite prevention – boots, torches at night, clearing grass around homes, sleeping off the ground under a net; immediate transport to a health facility for anti-snake venom (no tight tourniquets or cutting).
  5. Infection control – tetanus immunisation, footwear in wet fields, rodent control, chemoprophylaxis for leptospirosis in high-risk periods as advised, animal vaccination.
  6. Dust control – dry storage of hay and grain, masks during threshing.
  7. Ergonomic measures – correct lifting, improved tools, sharing of loads, rest breaks.
  8. Health services – first-aid training of farmers and ASHAs, availability of atropine and anti-snake venom at PHCs, health camps, social security and insurance schemes for farmers and agricultural workers.

C. Role of the nurse

  • Health education in villages on safe spraying, PPE and first aid; early recognition and referral of poisoning, heat illness and snake bite; immunisation; screening for musculoskeletal problems and anaemia; and linking farmers with health and social security schemes.

Conclusion Agricultural workers face chemical (pesticides), physical (heat, noise), mechanical (machines), biological (snake bite, zoonoses), respiratory (organic dust), ergonomic and psychosocial hazards. Safe pesticide practices, PPE, machine guarding, heat and snake-bite precautions, immunisation, education and accessible emergency care can prevent most of this suffering.

question: What is byssinosis?
answer_html:
Byssinosis is an occupational lung disease caused by inhalation of cotton, flax or hemp dust, mainly in textile mill workers (cleaning, carding and spinning rooms).

  • Characteristic feature – chest tightness, cough and breathlessness on the first day back at work after a break ("Monday fever" or Monday chest tightness), improving later in the week; with years of exposure symptoms become permanent, leading to chronic obstructive lung disease.
  • Diagnosis – occupational history and a fall in FEV1 during the work shift on spirometry.
  • Prevention – dust control (exhaust ventilation, wet processes, enclosure), respirators, pre-placement and periodic spirometry, no smoking; it is a notifiable and compensable occupational disease.

question: What are pre-placement and periodic medical examinations?
answer_html:
Pre-placement (pre-employment) examination is the medical examination of a worker before he is given a job, to:

  • assess fitness and place him in a job suited to his physical and mental capacity, so that neither he nor others are endangered;
  • record baseline health data (history, examination, vision, hearing/audiometry, chest X-ray, spirometry, blood tests) for future comparison;
  • detect existing disease (e.g. TB, skin disease, allergies). Periodic medical examination is the examination of workers at regular intervals during employment – especially those exposed to hazards – to detect occupational and other diseases at an early, curable stage (e.g. spirometry for dust, audiometry for noise, blood lead for lead workers) and to remove affected workers from exposure. Under current law, workers above 40 years must receive a free annual health check-up.

question: What is ergonomics?
tags: fitting the job to the worker
answer_html:
Ergonomics is the science of fitting the job, tools and workplace to the worker (rather than forcing the worker to fit the job), so as to improve health, safety, comfort and efficiency (from the Greek ergon – work, nomos – laws).

  • It considers body size, posture, strength, repetitive movements, lifting, lighting, noise, temperature, work hours and mental workload.
  • Poor ergonomics causes back pain, neck and shoulder pain, carpal tunnel syndrome and repetitive strain injuries, fatigue and accidents.
  • Examples of ergonomic measures – adjustable chairs and desks, correct height of work surfaces and computer screens, mechanical lifting aids, rotation of repetitive tasks, rest breaks, and training in correct posture and lifting (important for nurses too, e.g. safe patient handling).
